en: The Sutra of the Descent into Laṅkā on the True Dharma.
Oṃ, homage to the Three Jewels!
Oṃ, homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas!
START Parivarta 1: The First Chapter, "The Request of Rāvaṇa.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Blessed One was dwelling on Mount Malaya in the city of Laṅkā, on a peak adorned with flowers of various jewel-species,
together with a great community of monks and a vast assembly of bodhisattvas— great beings who had gathered from various buddha-fields,
who sported with the mastery of many concentrations, powers, and superknowledges, and who were headed by the bodhisattva Mahāmati and had been consecrated by the hand-sprinkling of all the Buddhas.

They were skilled in the purpose of thoroughly understanding the range of objects perceived by one's own mind; they maintained various methods for disciplining the mental conduct and forms of diverse sentient beings;
and they had reached the realization of the non-duality of the five dharmas, the intrinsic nature, consciousness, and selflessness.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One had emerged from the palace of Sāgara, the king of the nāgas, after seven days.
Being greeted by many tens of millions of Śakras, Brahmās, and nāga maidens, he gazed upon Laṅkā and Mount Malaya and smiled, [saying]:
"On this peak of Mount Malaya in the city of Laṅkā, former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones [also taught]..."

The Dharma has been taught as that which is cultivated within the domain of noble personal realization, beyond the reach of speculative reasoning, and inaccessible to outsiders, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or noble ones.
What if I were also to teach this very same Dharma here, concerning Rāvaṇa, the lord of the yakṣas, and elucidate it for him?

Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas, heard through the supernatural power of the Tathāgata: "The Blessed One, having emerged from the palace of Sāgara, the king of the nāgas, surrounded and honored by many millions of Śakras, Brahmās, and nāga maidens, beheld the waves of the ocean. Observing the minds that have gathered from those [waves]—which are impelled within the domain of the wind of the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) upon the ocean of the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*)—he remained right there and uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*)."
"I should go and, having entreated the Blessed One, cause him to enter Laṅkā;
that would be for the long-term welfare, benefit, and happiness of both gods and humans."

Then Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas, together with his retinue, mounted the Pauṣpaka celestial chariot and approached the place where the Blessed One was. Having arrived, he descended from the chariot and, together with his retinue, circumambulated the Blessed One three times. While musical instruments and cymbals were being played, [he offered] a staff made of sapphire and musāragalva beryl...

Having hung his lute— studded with jewels and draped in a priceless cloth pale as the *priyaṅgu* flower— over his side, and having skillfully tuned it according to the scales (*grāma*), modulations (*mūrcchanā*), and melodic intervals (*svara*) such as *ṣaḍja*, *ṛṣabha*, *gāndhāra*, *dhaivata*, *niṣāda*, *madhyama*, and *kaśika*,

he entered into the lute with grace and sang along with these verses: "The nature of the mind, the method of its cultivation, and the law of phenomena are indeed selfless, free from [wrong] views, and stainless."
O Leader, teach here this method of the Dharma which indicates the state of realization to be personally experienced within.

O Sage, today is the time to go to Laṅkā— you whose body is accumulated from pure dharmas, who manifest through the display of emanations, and who delight in the dharma of the state realized within oneself.
O Lord, teach the supreme Dharma here in this Laṅkā, which was inhabited by former Victors and their sons who assumed many forms; the Yakṣas, assuming many forms, shall hear it.
Then Rāvaṇa, the lord of Laṅkā, having sung in praise using the Toṭaka meter, sang once more with verses in the Gāthā style:
"In seven nights, the Blessed One, having emerged from the ocean, the abode of sea-monsters, from the palace of the Lord of the Sea, stood upon the shore. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 1.4)
As soon as the Buddha was established, Rāvaṇa arrived together with apsarases,
various kinds of yakṣas, and the learned Śuka and Sāraṇa.
Having traveled that path by means of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) to where the Leader resides,
and having descended from his flower-adorned vehicle, he paid homage and worshiped the Tathāgata;
empowered by the Lord of Jinas, he proclaimed his own name to him.
"I am Rāvaṇa, the ten-necked lord of the rākṣasas, who has come here;
please favor my Laṅkā and those who dwell in this city."
For even by the previous perfectly awakened ones, the domain of personal realization was revealed upon a peak studded with jewels in the midst of a city.
May the Blessed One also teach the stainless Dharma right there on that jewel-adorned peak, surrounded by the sons of the Jinas;
for today we, as well as those who dwell in Laṅkā, desire to hear it.
The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, which is free from the methods of verbal teaching and is the domain of personal realization,
was indeed described by former Buddhas.
I remember that this sūtra was spoken by the Buddhas of the past who were preceded by the sons of the Jinas; may the Blessed One also speak it.
In the future time, those Buddhas and sons of the Buddha who shall appear will teach this very same divine method on the jewel-adorned peak out of compassion for the yakṣas, O Leaders.
The delightful city of Laṅkā is adorned with various jewels,
featuring cooling and beautiful overhanging eaves and canopies of jeweled nets.
O Blessed One, there are yakṣas here who are free from passion and hatred, who contemplate the state of personal realization, who have accomplished their purpose through former Buddhas,
who possess faith in the Mahāyāna system, and who are intent on joining with one another.
The yakṣiṇīs and yakṣa sons, desiring to understand the Mahāyāna, [pray]:
"May the Blessed One, the Teacher, come to Laṅkā on Mount Malaya. (Lank_1.15)
And the city-dwelling Rākṣasas, led by Kumbhakarṇa,
shall hear the realization of their own individual nature, being devoted to the Mahāyāna.
Having performed their service for the Buddhas, they shall indeed do so now as well;
out of compassion for me, go to Laṅkā together with your sons.
Accept this house, the hosts of apsarases, various necklaces,
and the delightful Aśoka grove, O Great Sage.
I am an obedient follower of the Buddhas and those who are their sons;
there is nothing that I would not give—have compassion on me, O Great Sage! (Lank_1.19)
Having heard those words of his, the Lord of the Three Worlds said:
"O Lord of Yakṣas, even by the leaders of the past on the Jewel Mountain..."
The dharma of personal realization has been taught, and you yourself have been shown compassion;
those yet to come shall also speak it on the mountain adorned with jewels.
For this is indeed the abode of yogins who dwell in the realization of the present dharma;
O Lord of Yakṣas, you are worthy of compassion from the Sugatas and from me as well.
Having consented by remaining silent with a mind of peace, the Blessed One ascended the Puṣpaka vehicle offered by Rāvaṇa.
Right there, Rāvaṇa and other fearless sons of the Victorious One,
being honored by celestial nymphs with laughter, dance, and so forth, entered the city.
Having gone there to that beautiful city, he again received worship;
he was honored by the hosts of yakṣas led by Rāvaṇa, as well as by the yakṣiṇīs;
he was honored by the sons of the yakṣas and the yakṣa maidens with nets of jewels.
Rāvaṇa also placed necklaces adorned with jewels upon the heads of the Buddha, the Jina,
and the sons of the Jina.
Having accepted the worship from the sons of the Victorious One and the wise,
the Blessed One elucidated the Dharma that is the domain of personal realization.
Rāvaṇa and the hosts of yakṣas, having honored the best of speakers,
worshiped the one of great intelligence and entreated him again and again:
"You are the questioner of all Buddhas regarding the domain of the personally realized state."
For I am the listener, as are the yakṣas and the sons of the Jina who are gathered here;
I, along with the yakṣas and the wise sons of the Jina, entreat you. (Lank_1.29)
Among debaters you are the great debater; among yogis you are the leader of yoga.
O fearless one, I entreat you with devotion: ask about the method.
It is completely free from the faults of the non-Buddhists and from those of the Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas;
it is pure through the personally realized nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and brings forth the stage of Buddhahood.
There the Blessed One manifested peaks adorned with jewels,
as well as other divine objects embellished by millions of gems.
Manifesting his own body upon each of those excellent mountains,
the Yakṣa Rāvaṇa was stationed right there on each one.
In this regard, all those assemblies are indeed seen within each single one;
likewise, all the buddha-fields and the leaders (vināyakas) who reside therein are seen right there.
The lord of the rākṣasas and those who dwell in Laṅkā were right there; however,
another Laṅkā, rivaling that one, was manifested by the Jina,
as well as other Aśoka groves and whatever forest beauties existed there.
On each mountain, the Lord, urged by Mahāmati,
taught the Dharma to the Yakṣa that indicates the state of personal realization;
on a mountain, he taught the entire Sūtra consisting of one hundred thousand [verses].
Then the Teacher and the sons of the Conqueror vanished right there;
thereafter, the Yakṣa Rāvaṇa saw his own body remaining within his house.
He reflects: "What is this? Who is this? By whom was it taught, or by whom was it heard?
What was seen, and by whom was it seen? Where is that city of the Sugata?"
Where are those fields, those Buddhas, and that splendor of jewels? Where are the Sugatas? Is this a dream, or a magical illusion, or a city of the Gandharvas?
What I have seen here is like an optical illusion, a mirage, a dream, the offspring of a barren woman, a whirling firebrand, or smoke. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 1.40)
Alternatively, this is indeed the true nature (dharmatā) of phenomena within the range of the mind;
yet the foolish do not awaken to it, being deluded by manifold conceptual constructions.
There is no seer, nor anything to be seen; there is no speaker, nor even a speaker.
Indeed, apart from this conceptual construction, there is the abiding nature of the Buddha-dharmas.
Those who see according to what is [merely] perceived do not see the Guide.

When one does not perceive a Buddha through the non-occurrence of conceptual construction, and if one perceives the Buddha as awakened within the state of non-occurrence, then one is a perfectly awakened Buddha. (Lankavatara 1.43)

Immediately upon awakening, when the basis had been transformed and he had realized that what is seen is merely the manifestation of his own mind, the Lord of Laṅkā— abiding in the non-conceptual movement [of mind], impelled by his former roots of merit, possessing an intellect refined by all the treatises, seeing according to reality, not led by others, skilled in the investigation of his own intelligence, and having a vision free from speculative views— was no longer led by another.

The Mahāyoga-yogin, who assumes the great universal form (*mahāviśvarūpa*), who has mastered the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), who is adept at attaining the specific characteristics of each successive stage (*bhūmi*), who delights in the discernment of the intrinsic nature of mind, speech, and mental consciousness, who perceives the cessation of the three continuums (*trisaṃtati*), whose intellect is free from all causalist heretics,

who has entered into internal meditative absorption upon the *tathāgatagarbha* and the stage of Buddhahood, and whose Buddha-intellect is firmly established, heard a sound perceived internally from the sky.
"Excellent, excellent, Lord of Laṅkā! Indeed, it is excellent of you, Lord of Laṅkā, that you train in this manner;
a practitioner should train just as you do."
And thus should the Tathāgatas and the dharmas be viewed,
just as they have been seen by you; for if they were viewed otherwise, one would fall into nihilism.
Free from mind, mentation, and mental consciousness, you should discern all phenomena;

moving within [the internal], you should not be attached to views regarding external objects. Furthermore, you must not possess a meditative absorption that falls within the sphere of views or the objective domain of the attainments of Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or non-Buddhist teachers.
One should not be devoted to tales or histories;
one should not hold views regarding intrinsic nature; and one should not fall into the intoxication of royal power.

O Lord of Laṅkā, this is the realization of the great yogins who practice the six dhyānas and so forth— those who crush the doctrines of others, who shatter unwholesome views, who are skilled in turning back the view of self, and who are skilled in the subtle revolution of consciousness;
it belongs to the sons of the Conqueror who follow the Mahāyāna path.
"You must apply yourself to the practice for the sake of attaining entry into the stage of the Tathāgata’s own self-realization.
When this is done, O Lord of Laṅkā, this path which you have embraced will become increasingly purified through the attainment of skill in meditative concentration.
It is not the sphere of the blissful experience of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or non-Buddhist outsiders, as it is for those foolish practitioners of the yoga of the outsiders."

It is conceptualized by those who are attached to the characteristics of the object of the view of self-grasping, who follow after the elements, qualities, and substances, who are attached to views conditioned by ignorance,
who are distracted by emptiness and arising, who are attached to conceptual construction, and whose intentions have fallen into the duality of the characterized and the characteristic.
O Lord of Laṅkā, this realization of the Mahāyāna brings about the attainment of the state of universal form and awakens one to the realization of one’s own inner self-nature.
And it proceeds toward the attainment of birth in a distinguished state of existence;

O Lord of Laṅkā, this entry into the yoga of the Mahāyāna turns back the various waves of consciousness that are like the layers of a sheath, and does not result in falling into the reliance on the yogas of the non-Buddhists.
For the yoga of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), Lord of Laṅkā, proceeds from their dogmatic attachment to a self;
because they perceive and are attached to the duality of the nature of consciousness and external objects, the yoga of the teachers of other schools is not auspicious.
Therefore, Lord of Laṅkā, it is well that you should reflect further upon this very matter.
Just as he had contemplated it through the vision of the Tathāgata,
so too is this very vision of the Tathāgata.

Then, in that interval, this thought occurred to Rāvaṇa: "What if I were once again to approach the Blessed One— who has mastery over all yogas, who turns back the yoga of the heretics, who reveals the domain of personal realization, and who is free from the constructed and the emanated— so that my intellect may attain that realization which occurs for yogins at the time of the clear comprehension of yoga, when they have reached its completion at the entrance of meditative concentration?"

And because of that realization, the word "yoga" is applied to yogins by virtue of their attainment (*adhigamana*). Therefore, by means of that very supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), [I behold] him—the compassionate one, who brings about the destruction of the fuel of afflictions and of conceptual construction; who is surrounded by the sons of the Jina; who has entered into the intentions and inclinations of the minds of all sentient beings; who is omnipresent and omniscient; and who is free from the characteristics of activity.

May I behold them; by beholding them, may I attain what has not yet been attained, and may my practice of non-conceptuality—which brings about the attainment of the dwelling in the blissful samādhi and leads to the stage of the Tathāgata’s destination—reach full increase.

Then, at that time, the Blessed One, perceiving that the Lord of Laṅkā had attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), out of compassion for the Ten-necked one, once again revealed himself upon the peak, which was adorned with such splendor, studded with many jewels, and covered with a lattice of gems.

Daśagrīva, the lord of Laṅkā, again beheld upon each mountain peak the splendor he had previously seen and experienced: the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, his body adorned with the thirty-two marks of excellence;

and himself, before each of those Tathāgatas, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas, engaged in discourse with Mahāmati concerning the realm of the Tathāgata’s personal realization, surrounded by Yakṣas, delivering that very discourse on the recitation of the teachings.
And those fields, together with their leaders.

Then, at that very moment, the Blessed One, having surveyed the assembly with his Buddha-eye and not with his physical eye, yawned like a lion-king and broke into a great laugh. Emitting a ray of light from the circle of hair between his brows, and blazing like the fire at the end of an eon from his sides, thighs, hips, the *śrīvatsa* mark, and all his pores,
he shone intensely with a halo of light resembling Indra’s bow and the rising sun, while Śakra, Brahmā, and the world-protectors were in the expanse of the sky.
Gazing upon [the assembly] while seated on a peak rivaling the summit of Mount Sumeru, he let out a great, loud laugh.

Then, this thought occurred to that assembly of bodhisattvas and to those such as Śakra and Brahmā: "What indeed is the cause, what is the condition, for the Blessed One—who has mastery over all phenomena—to laugh with a smile preceded by a great, loud laugh?"
And he emitted rays from his own body;

having emitted them, he became silent, his intention fixed upon the entrance into the samādhi that is the domain of noble, personally realized gnosis. Without being astonished, he looked toward the directions with the gaze of a lion, reflecting upon the course of Rāvaṇa’s practice of yoga.
Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati—who had already been requested previously—out of compassion for Rāvaṇa, [addressed him].

Having understood the mental inclinations and deliberations of that assembly of bodhisattvas, and having surveyed future generations, [the Blessed One thought]: "There will be a confusion of mind among those beings who delight in the recitation of teachings—those who are attached to the literal meaning, who are fixed in the power of the yoga of all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and non-Buddhists;
even the Blessed Tathāgatas, whose sphere of consciousness has ceased, laugh a great laugh."
In order to dispel their curiosity, he questioned the Blessed One: "What indeed is the cause, what is the condition for this manifestation of a smile?
The Blessed One said: "Excellent, excellent, Mahāmati!"

Excellent indeed, Mahāmati, that you, having observed the nature of the world, have begun to question me for the sake of awakening the minds of people fallen into wrong views regarding the three periods of time.
Thus should the wise be inclined to inquire for the benefit of themselves, others, and both.
Mahāmati, this Rāvaṇa, lord of Laṅkā, has questioned former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas regarding two questions;

now he desires to question me as well concerning the characteristics of the analytical understanding of the distinctions between these two questions—something that has not been tasted by any of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or practitioners of the paths of the non-Buddhists.
This Ten-Necked One, desiring to ask these questions, will also question future Jinas.
Knowing [his intent], the Blessed One said this to the Lord of Laṅkā: "Ask, O Lord of Laṅkā!
The Tathāgata has granted you the opportunity;
do not delay, O you whose crown is trembling!"
Whatever you may desire, I shall satisfy your mind by answering each and every question.

Just as you, having turned away from the basis of conceptual construction and investigating with a discerning intellect through skill in the antidotes to the stages, will attain the dwelling in the bliss of meditative concentration characterized by the personal realization of the nature of reality, along with the Buddhas of meditative concentration...

Sustained [by this], established in the bliss of *śamatha*, and having not transcended the meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, you will be established in the Immovable, Good Intelligence, and Cloud of Dharma stages; being skilled in the suchness of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), you shall obtain the consecration of the Victors (*jinābhiṣeka*) within a palace of great jewel-lotuses through meditative absorption.
With those lotuses corresponding to that [state], which are empowered by the various empowerments of your own body, you will see yourself seated upon those lotuses,
and you will gaze face-to-face with one another.
Such is that inconceivable sphere, brought forth by a single skill in accomplishment while abiding on the stage of conduct.
Through the accomplishment brought about by the mastery of skillful means, you will attain that inconceivable domain and the stage of a Tathāgata, which possesses manifold forms and transformations—
something never before seen by Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, non-Buddhist teachers, Brahmā, Indra, Upendra, and others. You shall attain it.
Then, having been granted leave by the Blessed One, the Lord of Laṅkā rose from that jewel-peak which resembled a jewel-lotus of stainless radiant light;

surrounded by a host of apsarases, he was accompanied by various and manifold kinds of flowers, garlands, perfumes, incense, ointments, umbrellas, banners, flags, necklaces, half-necklaces, crowns, diadems, and other distinguished ornaments never before seen or heard of— along with excellent musical instruments, cymbals, and rhythmic performances that transcended those of gods, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, kinnaras, mahoragas, and humans.

Having miraculously produced all kinds of musical instruments belonging to the desire realm, and having produced those various types of musical instruments seen in other buddha-fields, they covered the Blessed One and the bodhisattvas with a net of jewels, raised various cloth banners and flags,
rose into the sky to the height of seven palm trees, and rained down great clouds of offerings while playing various musical instruments and cymbals.
Then, descending from that resounding sky, he sat down upon a jeweled peak adorned with a great jewel-lotus, which possessed the brilliance of the sun and lightning and was his second [seat].

Having sat down, and having been granted the opportunity by the Blessed One with a welcoming smile, he asked the Blessed One two questions: "I have previously questioned former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones, and they too have answered me."

I now ask the Blessed One as well: this must surely have been described by you, O Buddha, in the recitation of the teachings. Blessed One, these two dharmas were spoken by an emanation of an emanation.
It was not spoken by the Tathāgatas who are in silence;
for, Blessed One, the Tathāgatas are silent, and they manifest only the domain of the bliss of meditative concentration,
yet they do not conceptualize that domain.
They requested:
"It would be well, O Blessed One, if the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One—who himself wields mastery over the Dharma—would personally teach these two dharmas.
These sons of the Conqueror and I shall listen."
The Blessed One said: "Speak, Lord of Laṅkā, concerning the two dharmas.

The Lord of Rākṣasas replied: "O you who are adorned with the splendor of ornaments bound with vajra-threads—diadems, armlets, and necklaces—even dharmas themselves must be abandoned, let alone non-dharmas."
In that case, Blessed One, how does the abandonment of the two-fold dharma occur?
And what are non-dharmas and dharmas?

How can there be a duality among those dharmas to be abandoned which have fallen into the characteristics of conceptualization, whose nature is the absence of conceptualization, which are both non-material and material, and which, due to the lack of thorough knowledge of the *ālayavijñāna*, possess undifferentiated characteristics?
[They are] those who abide in the nature of a hair-net and whose objects are the knowledge of impure destruction.
How, then, can there be the abandonment of such things?
The Blessed One said: "Is it not so, Lord of Laṅkā?"

The distinct differentiation of things such as jars— which are characterized by difference and subject to destruction— is observed through the conceptual constructions of the ignorant. Why, then, is it not accepted here as well that there is a distinct differentiation of dharma and adharma based upon the conceptual constructions of the ignorant?
But it is not by means of vision that one attains noble knowledge.
O Lord of Laṅkā, let alone such things as jars and other objects which fall under various characteristics for the foolish—they do not exist for the noble ones.
For those things that possess a single intrinsic nature are ignited by the arising of a single flame.

The distinction between lamps established in houses, mansions, gardens, and palaces is observed, as are the differences in the length and brevity of their light, and its smallness or greatness, depending on the fuel.
Why, then, is this not accepted here as well?
There is indeed a distinction between merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*).
Lord of Laṅkā, it is not only the differentiation of flames seen within a single continuum of a fire’s blaze that occurs;
even among those continua produced from a single seed, there are specific distinctions such as the stalk, sprout, bulb, joint, leaf, petal, flower, fruit, branch, and so forth.

In the same way, for all phenomena—whether external or internal—which have the nature of growing forth, which issue from ignorance, which pertain to the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, which are born within the triple world, and which consist of perceived pleasure and form, there are specific modes of expression regarding their progression.

O Lord of Laṅkā, it is observed that among the various consciousnesses— which possess a single characteristic and are engaged in the apprehension of objects— there are distinctions of inferior, superior, and intermediate, as well as distinctions based on purification and non-purification, and on being wholesome and unwholesome.

Not only is there this specific differentiation among these phenomena, O Lord of Laṅkā, but even among yogins practicing yoga, a specific distinction in the characteristics of their individual internal realization is observed on the path of yoga.
How much more so, then, would there not be a distinction between merit and demerit when they proceed through conceptual discrimination?
Indeed, there is.
There is, Lord of Laṅkā, a distinction between dharma and adharma because they are characterized by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
In this regard, Lord of Laṅkā, what are dharmas? They are as follows: those imagined through the conceptual constructions of outsiders, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and fools.
Dharmas are taught as being preceded by causes, qualities, and substances;
these are to be abandoned and should not be conceptualized according to their characteristics.
Due to the attachment to the nature of phenomena as being the manifestation of one's own mind, phenomena such as jars—which are imagined by the ignorant and lack any substantial body—do not exist.
For one who observes in this way through analytical insight, they are abandoned.
In that regard, what are non-phenomena (*adharmas*)?

Those phenomena which have not attained self-nature (*alabdhātmaka*), whose conceptualization of characteristics does not function, and which are without cause—their non-arising is seen through both the real and the unreal;
thus, there occurs the abandonment of phenomena.
Furthermore, what are those phenomena that have not attained self-nature?
They are, namely, phenomena such as the horns of a hare, a donkey, a camel, or a horse, and the son of a barren woman.
Because they have not attained self-nature, they cannot be conceptualized by way of characteristics.
These are designated for the sake of conventional usage elsewhere, not out of ontological commitment as in the case of jars and the like;
just as they are to be abandoned by consciousness through non-apprehension.
Likewise, even the states of conceptual construction are to be abandoned;
thus, there comes to be the abandonment of both dharma and adharma.
Regarding what you asked, O Lord of Laṅkā, "How are dharma and adharma to be abandoned?"—[this is the answer].
This has been stated as follows:
Furthermore, O Lord of Laṅkā, as for what you said— "Former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones were questioned by me, and they previously gave their responses"—
O Lord of Laṅkā, this is a designation for conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
The past is likewise conceptualized as "past," and similarly the future and the present are so designated by way of their intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*). Yet,
the Tathāgatas are free from conceptualization, having transcended all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
It is not conceptualized as having the intrinsic nature of form; rather,
it is cultivated for the sake of happiness by those who practice the signless through wisdom, except for the attainment of non-knowledge.
Therefore, the Tathāgatas consist of gnosis and have gnosis as their body;
they do not conceptualize, nor are they conceptualized.
By what means are they not conceptualized?
How is it that they do not conceptualize [the self] as mind, as a living being, or as a person?
It is by means of the mental consciousness, which has the objects of the senses as its cause, and according to the characteristics, configurations, and forms of material phenomena (*rūpa*).
Therefore, one should remain free from both conceptualization and non-conceptualization.
Moreover, O Lord of Laṅkā, the movement of sentient beings is like figures carved upon a wall;
O Lord of Laṅkā, the world-structure is motionless, devoid of karmic activity, because all phenomena are non-existent.
And herein, no one hears nor is anything heard;
for, O Lord of Laṅkā, the arrangement of the world is like a magical creation.
Yet the heterodox, the foolish, and those engaged in yoga do not discern this.
O Lord of Laṅkā, he who sees in this way sees correctly;
those who see otherwise wander in conceptual construction.
One's own conceptual constructions grasp in two ways:
namely, like one's own form and its reflection within a mirror, or the shadow of one's own limbs in water, or the shadow of the limbs in a house illuminated by moonlight or lamps, or echoes.
Then, having grasped these through one's own conceptual constructions, they further discriminate between dharma and adharma.
Nor do they practice by means of the abandonment of merit and demerit;
they conceptualize, nourish [such notions],
and do not attain tranquility.
This is a designation for one-pointedness: that supreme samādhi which arises is the entry into the Tathāgatagarbha, the domain of the noble wisdom of personal realization.
The first chapter, titled "Rāvaṇa’s Entreaty."
START Parivarta 2 (Vaidya 10).
The second chapter, titled "The Compendium of All Dharmas in Thirty-Six Thousand Verses."
Then indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati, accompanied by the Bodhisattva Mahāmati and wandering through all Buddha-fields,
rose from his seat through the power of the Buddhas; having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder and placed his right knee upon the ground,
he bowed with palms joined toward the Blessed One and praised the Blessed One with verses:
The world is devoid of arising and ceasing, resembling a flower in the sky;
through your wisdom and compassion, it is perceived by you as neither existent nor non-existent.
All phenomena are like illusions, devoid of mind and consciousness;
through both wisdom and compassion, you do not perceive them as either existent or non-existent.
The world is always like a dream, free from eternalism and nihilism;
through your wisdom and compassion, neither existence nor non-existence is perceived by you.
What praise can there be for the Dharmakāya, whose nature is like an illusion or a dream?
The non-arising of phenomena that lack intrinsic nature—that is their true arising.
O Sage, how could praise or blame be spoken of one whose vision is invisible and disconnected from the objects of the senses? (Lankavatara Sutra 2.5)
The selflessness of phenomena and persons, as well as the afflictive and cognitive obscurations,
are always purified for you by means of signless wisdom and compassion.

You do not attain nirvāṇa through nirvāṇa; rather, nirvāṇa is established within you—devoid of both the Buddha and that which is to be awakened by him, and free from the positions of existence and non-existence.
Those who see the Sage as thus peaceful and devoid of origination become free from grasping, stainless both in this world and the next.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati, having praised the Blessed One with these appropriate verses, announced his own name and lineage to the Blessed One:
"I am Mahāmati, O Blessed One, who has attained the course of the Mahāyāna;
I ask one hundred and eight questions, O Best of Speakers."

Having heard those words of his, the Buddha, the best among those who know the world, surveyed the entire assembly and spoke to the son of the Sugata: laṅkāvatārasūtra II The Blessed One said this: “Son of the Sugata, listen well and attend closely; I shall explain to you the various kinds of self-nature (svabhāva). The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati said, “So be it, Blessed One,” and listened with an attentive mind. The Blessed One then spoke thus: “Mahāmati, there are three kinds of self-nature: the imagined (parikalpita), the dependent (paratantra), and the perfected (pariniṣpanna). Among these, Mahāmati, the imagined self-nature arises from the attachment to names and characteristics. The dependent self-nature arises from the manifestation of unreal mental constructions (abhūtaparikalpa). And the perfected self-nature, Mahāmati, is the state of being eternally free from the former two. “Furthermore, Mahāmati, the imagined self-nature is like a barren woman’s son, a sky-flower, or a hare’s horn—these are all non-existent yet imagined by the ignorant. The dependent self-nature, Mahāmati, is like a dream, a mirage, a city of Gandharvas, or the reflection of the moon in water; it appears as something external but is devoid of intrinsic reality. The perfected self-nature, Mahāmati, is the realization that the dependent nature is forever free from the imagined nature, and it is the realm of the Tathāgatas, which is beyond words and conceptualization. “Moreover, Mahāmati, there are five kinds of knowledge (jñāna): the knowledge of the worldly, the knowledge of the Śrāvakas, the knowledge of the Pratyekabuddhas, the knowledge of the Bodhisattvas, and the Tathāgata-knowledge. The knowledge of the worldly is characterized by attachment to the duality of subject and object. The knowledge of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas consists in the realization of the non-self of persons and the cessation of the outflows (āsrava). The knowledge of the Bodhisattvas is the realization of the non-self of both persons and phenomena, and the mastery over the various stages (bhūmi). The Tathāgata-knowledge, Mahāmati, is the realization of the equality of all things, the perfection of the powers (bala) and fearlessnesses (vaiśāradya), and the attainment of the great compassion (mahākaruṇā) and the inconceivable liberation. “Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of analytical knowledge (pratisaṃvid): the analytical knowledge of meaning (artha), the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharma), the analytical knowledge of eloquence (nirukti), and the analytical knowledge of confidence (pratibhāna). These are attained by the Bodhisattvas through the purification of their mental continuums and the mastery of the Dharma. “Also, Mahāmati, there are eight kinds of transformation (parāvṛtti) of the basis (āśraya): the transformation of the body, the transformation of the voice, the transformation of the mind, the transformation of the conduct, the transformation of the field, the transformation of the retinue, the transformation of the teaching, and the transformation of the power of mastery. By means of these transformations, the Bodhisattvas manifest in various forms to guide sentient beings according to their dispositions. “Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are three kinds of Nirvana: the Nirvana of the extinction of the aggregates (skandha), the Nirvana of the non-existence of self-nature, and the Nirvana of the ultimate reality (dharmatā). The Nirvana of the extinction of the aggregates belongs to the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas who have not realized the non-arising of phenomena. The Nirvana of the non-existence of self-nature belongs to those who have realized the emptiness of all things. The Nirvana of the ultimate reality, Mahāmati, is the realization of the Tathāgatagarbha, which is eternal, blissful, self, and pure—the true refuge of all beings. “Thus, Mahāmati, you should understand that all dharmas are devoid of self-nature, unborn, and unceasing. You should abandon the views of existence and non-existence, and cultivate the path of the Tathāgatas. By doing so, you will quickly attain the supreme enlightenment and liberate all sentient beings from the ocean of suffering. When the Blessed One had spoken these verses, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati and the entire assembly, having heard the Buddha’s profound teaching, were filled with joy and praised his words. Thus ends the second chapter on the "Analysis of Self-Nature" in the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra.
"Let the sons of the Conqueror question me, and you too ask, O Mahāmati;
I shall teach you the sphere of the realm of personal realization."
Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati, having been granted leave by the Blessed One, prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and questioned the Blessed One:
"How is reasoning purified, and from what does reasoning arise?"
How indeed is delusion perceived, and from what does delusion arise?
Why are the fields, emanations, characteristics, and those who are non-Buddhist heretics? By what means is the stage of non-appearance attained, and from where do the sons of the Victors arise?
Where does the liberated one go? Who is bound, and by whom is one liberated?
What is that object of those who meditate, and how does the triple vehicle come to be?
What is that which is perceived as arising? What is the effect, and what is the cause?
By whom and how does the discourse on both extremes proceed?
How could there be the formless attainments and cessation?
How is there the cessation of perception, and why is one liberated from it?
By what does activity proceed? How is there movement for those who possess bodies? How is the visible world manifested, and how does it function within the stages?
Who is it that pierces through the three realms of existence? What is his station, and what is his body?
Where does the Son of the Victor abide and engage in activity, and how does he come to be?
By what means does one obtain the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), the masteries (*vaśitā*), and the meditative absorptions (*samādhi*)?
O Bull among Conquerors (*jinapuṃgava*), tell me how the mind is brought to concentration (*samādhyate*). (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 2.19)
And how, and for what reason, is there the ālaya? And how does the mental consciousness itself arise?
How does the visible world proceed, and how is one liberated from the visible world?
How and by what means do lineage and non-lineage exist? How can there be "mind-only"? How is the establishment of characteristics and selflessness brought about? (Lankavatara 2.21)
How is it that no sentient being exists? How is there teaching by way of conventional truth?
How is it that the views of eternalism and nihilism do not arise? (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 2.22)
For how is it that you and the non-Buddhist outsiders do not contradict each other regarding characteristics?
Tell me, how will the Naiyāyikas exist in the future?
And how and by what means is emptiness? How is your doctrine of momentary destruction? How does the embryo develop, and how is the world devoid of agency?
By what means and in what manner is the world like an illusion or a dream, resembling a city of Gandharvas, or appearing like a mirage or the moon reflected in water? Tell me this.
How and by what means do the factors of enlightenment arise? From where do the wings of awakening come? How do Māras, the disturbances of the land, and the view of existence come to be?
How can that which is unborn and unceasing be like a flower in the sky?
How do you perceive the world, and how do you speak of it as being beyond syllables?
By what means would it be non-conceptual, and how is it like the sky?
How many kinds of suchness are there, how many minds, and how many perfections? (Lankavatara 2.28)
By what means would there be the sequence of stages, and what is the state of non-appearance?
By what is the twofold selflessness [established], and how is that which is to be known purified? (Lankavatara 2.29)
O Lord, how many kinds of knowledge are there, as well as ethical discipline and the sources of sentient beings?
By what are the lineages produced that give rise to gold, jewels, and pearls?
By what cause does verbal expression arise, and from what do the diverse natures of sentient beings originate?
How and by whom were the fields of knowledge and the arts revealed?
How many kinds of verses (gāthā) are there? How do prose (gadya) and verse (padya) come to be?
What is reasoning (yukti), how many kinds are there, and what is the nature of exposition (vyākhyāna)?
How do diverse foods and drinks and sexual intercourse arise?
And how does one become a universal monarch (cakravartin), a wheel-turning king, or a regional ruler (maṇḍalī)?
How is the kingdom to be protected? Of what nature are the gods?
By what are the hosts of earth and stars [sustained], and how do the moon and sun [function]? (Lank_2.34)
What constitutes a field of knowledge? What is liberation? How many kinds of yogis are there?
How many kinds of disciples are there, and how does one become a teacher?
How many kinds of Buddhas are there, and of what nature are the Jātaka tales?
How many kinds of Māras are there, and how many kinds of heretics?

O best of speakers, tell me: how many kinds of intrinsic nature (svabhāva) are there? How many kinds of mind (citta) might there be? And how is it that [all things] are merely designations (prajñaptimātra)?
By what means do dense clouds arise in the sky, and how does the wind come to be?
How and by what means do trees and creepers come into existence? Tell me, O Lord of the Three Worlds. (Lankavatara Sutra 2.38)
By what means do horses, elephants, and deer—those who are foolish—come to be captured? And by what means are men carried away? Tell me, O charioteer of the mind! (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 2.39)

By what means and how is the grasping of the six seasons [of rebirth] explained? How does one become an icchantika? And tell me, how is the birth of females, males, and neuters brought about? Lank_2.40.
How is one turned away from yoga? How does yoga proceed?
And how should men such as these be established in yoga? Tell me this.
What is the mark and what is the characteristic of beings who come and go? O Lord of Wealth, how and by what means do they do so? Tell me, you who are like the sky. (Lankavatara Sutra 2.42)
How and by whom did the Śākya lineage arise? How did it originate from Ikṣvāku? By what means did the sage Dīrghatapas come to be, and how was [the lineage] established by him?
Why is it that you alone are seen everywhere in all fields,
surrounded by sons of the Victorious One who possess various names and forms?
How indeed is meat unfit to be eaten, and how is meat forbidden?
By what means do those born of the lineage of flesh-eaters eat meat?
How is it that the lands have the appearance of the moon and the sun, or resemble Mount Meru and a lotus?
Tell me, by what cause do the fields have the forms of the Śrīvatsa and the lion?
How is it that they are inverted and upside down, resembling Indra’s net?
How and by what means are all the realms composed of every kind of jewel? Tell me this.
They have the shape of lutes and drums and resemble various flowers and fruits;
they are stainless like the sun and moon—tell me, how and by what means do they come to be? Lank_2.48.
By what means are there emanation Buddhas, and by what means are there Buddhas born of maturation?
How indeed are there Buddhas of suchness and of gnosis? Tell me this.
Tell me, how and why is one not awakened in the desire realm? For what purpose do you awaken in Akaniṣṭha among those who are already free from passion?
Once the Sugata has entered nirvāṇa, who will uphold the teaching?
How long will the Teacher remain, and for how long will the method (naya) endure?
How many kinds of established tenets do you have, and of what nature is your view?
Tell me: what is discipline, and what is the state of being a monk; by what means and how does it come about?
By what means does the transformation of the basis occur, and how is the state free from appearances attained?
Tell me this regarding the Pratyekabuddhas, the Jinas' sons, and the Śrāvakas. (Lankavatara 2.53)
By what means do the worldly supernormal powers arise, and how do those that are supramundane?
Tell me, how is it that the mind constitutes the seven stages, and by what means? Lank_2.54.
How many kinds of Saṃgha might there be for you, and how does the schism of the Saṃgha occur?
Tell me, by what means and in what manner is the medical science for sentient beings taught?
Kāśyapa, Krakucchanda, Konākamuni, and I myself—you speak thus to the sons of the Jinas; tell us why, O Great Sage? (Lank_2.56)
Why do you speak of a non-existent self, and how can there be talk of eternalism or nihilism? Why do you not declare that reality is everywhere "mind-only"? (Lank_2.57)
By what means did the grove of men and women become a grove of *harītakī* and *āmalaka* trees?
And how did Kailāsa and Cakravāla become possessed of adamantine structure?
In that interval, what are those immovable mountains adorned with various jewels, crowded with sages and gandharvas? Tell me, by what means and how did they come to be?
Having heard this, the Great Hero, the Buddha, the best among those who know the world,
[taught] the mind consisting of the Mahāyāna, which is the heart and the power of the Buddhas.
Excellent, excellent, O Mahāmati of great wisdom! You have understood;
I shall explain in due order that which you have asked.
Arising and non-arising, nirvāṇa as having the characteristic of emptiness,
transmigration, and the absence of intrinsic nature— these are the Buddhas, the sons of the Perfection.
The Śrāvakas and the sons of the Victors, as well as the non-Buddhists who dwell in the formless realms;
Mount Meru, the oceans, the mountains, the continents, the fields, and the earth.
The constellations, the sun, the moon, the followers of other teachers, the gods, and likewise the asuras;
the liberations, the masteries, the superknowledges, the powers, the meditations, and the concentrations.
Cessation, the bases of psychic power, the factors of enlightenment, and the path itself;
the meditative absorptions, the immeasurables, the aggregates, and the comings and goings.
Meditative attainments, cessations, emergence, and the teaching on the mind;
mind, intellect, and consciousness; selflessness, and the five dharmas.
How can there be intrinsic nature, conceptualization, the object of conceptualization, the visible, and the two views?
How can there be the vehicles, the forms, and the lineages born of gold, jewels, and pearls?
The icchantikas, the great elements, the bees, and the state of being a single Buddha;
knowledge, the object of knowledge, the path, attainment, and the existence and non-existence of sentient beings.

Tell me, by what means are horses, elephants, and deer captured? How is it so? Furthermore, how is the teaching established as a definitive conclusion (siddhānta) through the application of analogies and logical reasons? || 2.69 ||
By what means are effect and cause distinguished? Such is the error of dualism;
according to this principle, there is only mind, no object of perception exists, and indeed there is no sequence of stages.
By what means do you speak to me of the hundredfold transformation into the signless,
as well as the science of medicine, the arts, and the traditional systems of crafts and sciences?
Tell me, how is the measure of the immovable mountains and of Meru, as well as that of the earth? And how is the measure of the oceans, the moon, and the sun? Tell me this. (Lank_2.72)
How many particles of dust are there in the body of a being—whether inferior, superior, or middling?
How many particles of dust are there in each field, and how many bows' lengths are there in each bow's length?
In the hand, the bow, the *krama*, the *krośa*, and the *yojana*, as well as half a *yojana*—how many rabbit-hairs, window-dusts, nit-eggs, sheep-wool fibers, and barley grains are there? Lank_2.74.
Indeed, how many barley grains would there be in a *prastha*, and how many in half a *prastha*?
Likewise, how many hundreds of thousands (*lakṣas*), millions (*koṭis*), or billions (*vibharas*) would there be in a *droṇa* or a *khārī*?
How many atoms are there in a mustard seed? How many mustard seeds are there in a *rakṣikā*?
How many *rakṣikās* would constitute a *māṣa*, and how many *māṣakas* are there in a *dharaṇa*?
"How many *dharaṇas* are there in a *karṣa*, and how many *karṣas* are there in a *pala*? By this measure of mass, how many *palas* would Mount Meru be?
Ask me thus, my son; why else do you ask? (Lankavatara Sutra 2.77)
Indeed, how many atoms would constitute the body of the Pratyekabuddhas, the Śrāvakas, and the Buddhas, the sons of the Conquerors? Why do you not ask such a thing?
How many atoms are there in the flame of fire? How many atoms are there in the wind?
How many are in each sense organ, in the pores of the skin, and how many are there in the two eyebrows?
By what means do men become lords of wealth, and by what means do they become universal monarchs?
How is their kingdom to be protected, and how may liberation be attained by them?
How do you speak of prose and verse? How is sexual union renowned in the world? How is there the variety of food and drink, and how are there forests of men and women? (Lankavatara Sutra 2.81)
Why are they possessed of adamantine joints? Tell me, how are they immovable?
Why are they like illusions and dreams? How are they comparable to a mirage?
Where does the origin of clouds arise, and from what do the seasons come into being?
From what does the "savoriness" of flavors derive, and from what do female, male, and neuter genders arise?
"O son, ask me about the splendors and the sons of the Jinas; for how is it that the divine, immovable [lands] are adorned by ṛṣis and gandharvas? (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 2.84)
Where does the liberated one go? Who is bound, and by whom is one liberated?
What is that object of meditation for those who practice dhyāna? And what are the emanations and the heterodox teachers?
By what means and how does the activity of the non-existent and the existent cease?
How is reasoning purified, and by what does reasoning proceed? (Lank_2.86)
By what does activity proceed? Tell me, how does going occur?
By what is the cutting off of perception effected, and by what is meditative concentration said to arise?
Having pierced through the three realms of existence, who is he? What is his station? What would be his body?
By what means is there discourse on a non-existent self, and how is the teaching given through conventional truth?
Why do you ask about characteristics? Why do you ask how selflessness is [attained]?
O sons of the Victor, why do you ask me about the *garbha* and the Naiyāyikas?
By what means is the mind cultivated regarding the views of eternalism and nihilism?
[Likewise, by what are] verbal expression, knowledge, ethical conduct, lineage, and the sons of the Victor [established]?
The logical exposition of teacher and disciple, the diversity of sentient beings,
food and drink, the sky, clouds, and the Māras— all these are mere designations.
"O son of the Jina, why and how do you ask me about trees and creepers? Why [do you ask] about the variety of fields, and likewise about the sage Dīrghatapas?"
“O son of the Jina, what is your lineage? Who is your teacher? Why do you question me?
These men are merely impostors; you do not understand the yoga in the realm of desire. (Lankavatara Sutra 2.93)
The established doctrine indeed resides among the Akaniṣṭha gods; how then do you ask me about reasoning?
By what means is worldly supernormal knowledge attained, and how is the state of a monkhood itself achieved?
How do you ask me about the transformation Buddhas and those established in the state of maturation?
And how indeed do the Buddhas of suchness-knowledge and the Saṅgha come to be?
The lands that have the luster of lutes, drums, and flowers are devoid of worldly beings;
for the seven stages are indeed the mind. O son of the Jina, you ask me about these, and you ask me many other such questions, my son.
Each [teaching] is endowed with its own characteristics and is free from the defects of dogmatic views;
I shall now suddenly proclaim the established conclusion and the instruction—listen to me!
I shall set forth an exposition of the terms; listen to me, my son, regarding the one hundred and eight terms as they were described by the Buddhas.
Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, what is the one hundred and eightfold set of terms?
The Blessed One replied: "The term 'arising' and the term 'non-arising';
the term 'permanent' and the term 'impermanent'..."
The term "characteristic" is the term "non-characteristic"; the term "alteration of duration" is the term "non-alteration of duration"; the term "momentary" is the term "non-momentary."
The term "intrinsic nature" is the term "absence of intrinsic nature"; the term "emptiness" is the term "non-emptiness"; the term "annihilation" is the term "non-annihilation."
The state of mind and the state of no-mind;
the middle state and the non-middle state; the eternal state and the non-eternal state.
The word for condition is the word for non-condition; the word for cause is the word for non-cause;
the word for affliction is the word for non-affliction.
The locus of craving and the locus of non-craving;
the locus of skillful means and the locus of non-means;
the locus of skillfulness and the locus of unskillfulness.
The term for purity and the term for impurity;
the term for logic and the term for illogic; the term for illustration and the term for non-illustration.
The state of being a disciple is the state of not being a disciple; the state of being a teacher is the state of not being a teacher; the state of lineage is the state of no lineage.
The state of the three vehicles is the state of no-three-vehicles; the state of non-appearance is the state of non-non-appearance;
the state of aspiration is the state of non-aspiration.
The term "threefold circle" and the term "non-threefold circle," the term "sign" and the term "signless."
The position of existence and non-existence; the position of non-existence and non-non-existence; the position of both; the position of neither;
the position of noble self-realized wisdom; and the position of non-noble self-realized wisdom.
The state of happiness in the present life and the state of happiness in lives yet to come;
the state of a field and the state of a non-field;
the state of the minute and the state of the non-minute.
The word "water" is the word "non-water"; the word "desert" is the word "non-desert";
the word "being" is the word "non-being."
The category of numerical calculation and the category of non-numerical calculation;
the category of supernormal knowledge and the category of non-supernormal knowledge;
the category of weariness and the category of non-weariness.
The term "dense" is a term for non-density; the term "arts, crafts, and sciences" is a term for non-arts, non-crafts, and non-sciences; the term "wind" is a term for non-wind.
The stage of the ground is the non-stage of the ground; the stage of the conceivable is the inconceivable stage;
the stage of designation is the non-designation stage.
The term "intrinsic nature" is the term "absence of intrinsic nature"; the term "aggregates" is the term "non-aggregates";
the term "sentient being" is the term "non-sentient being."
The state of intellect and the state beyond intellect; the state of nirvana and the state beyond nirvana; the state of the knowable and the state beyond the knowable.
The term of the heterodox, the term of the non-heterodox; the term of turmoil, the term of the absence of turmoil; the term of illusion, the term of the absence of illusion.
The state of dream is the state beyond dream;
the state of a mirage is the state beyond a mirage;
the state of a reflection is the state beyond a reflection.
The station of the wheel is the non-station of the wheel;
the station of the gandharva is the non-station of the gandharva; the station of the god is the non-station of the god.
The locus of food and drink is the non-locus of food and drink; the locus of sexual intercourse is the non-locus of sexual intercourse;
the locus of the seen is the non-locus of the seen.
The term "perfection" is the term "non-perfection"; the term "ethical discipline" is the term "non-ethical discipline";
the term "moon, sun, and constellations" is the term "no moon, no sun, and no constellations."
The word "truth" and the word "untruth," the word "fruit" and the word "no fruit," the word "cessation" and the word "non-cessation."
The phrase of emergence from cessation and the phrase of non-emergence from cessation; the phrase of treatment and the phrase of non-treatment;
the phrase of characteristics and the phrase of non-characteristics.
The limb-word and the non-limb-word; the word of arts and sciences and the word of non-arts and sciences; the word of meditation and the word of non-meditation.
The state of delusion is the state of non-delusion;
the state of the visible is the state of the invisible;
the state of what is to be guarded is the state of what is not to be guarded.
The station of lineage and the station of no-lineage;
the station of sages and the station of non-sages;
the station of sovereignty and the station of non-sovereignty.
The term "grasping" is the term "non-grasping"; the term "jewel" is the term "non-jewel";
the term "prediction" is the term "non-prediction."
The term "icchantika" is the term "non-icchantika";
the term "female, male, or neuter" is the term "neither female, male, nor neuter";
the term "taste" is the term "no taste."
The word for action and the word for non-action;
the word for body and the word for bodilessness;
the word for logic and the word for non-logic.
the state of movement and the state of non-movement,
the state of the faculties and the state of the non-faculties,
the state of the conditioned and the state of the unconditioned.
the term cause-and-effect, the term no-cause-and-effect;
the term Akaniṣṭha, the term non-Akaniṣṭha;
the term season, the term non-season.

The state of trees, shrubs, and the spreading of creepers is the state of no-trees, no-shrubs, and no-spreading of creepers; the state of manifoldness is the state of non-manifoldness; the state of entering into teaching is the state of not entering into teaching.
A point of discipline and a point not of discipline; a point concerning a monk and a point not concerning a monk;
a point of formal authorization and a point not of formal authorization.
The syllable-word and the non-syllable-word—
this, Mahāmati, is that one hundred and eight words described by the Buddhas of the past.

(Vaidya 18) Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Blessed One in this way: "Blessed One, how many kinds of arising, abiding, and cessation of the consciousnesses are there?
The Blessed One said: "Mahāmati, the arising, abiding, and cessation of the consciousnesses are of two kinds."
Furthermore, the logicians do not understand that there is both the cessation of continuity and the cessation of characteristics;
likewise, there are two kinds of arising for consciousnesses:
the arising of continuity and the arising of characteristics.
Abiding is twofold: abiding as continuity and abiding as characteristic.
Consciousness is threefold: characterized by activity, characterized by action, and characterized by birth.
Mahāmati, consciousness is twofold in brief, as described by eight characteristics: the consciousness of manifestation and the consciousness of the discrimination of objects.
Mahāmati, just as a mirror reflects forms,

so will the manifesting consciousness (khyātivijñāna) be explained. And, Mahāmati, the manifesting consciousness is the same as the consciousness that discriminates objects (vastuprativikalpavijñāna).
Both of these have non-different characteristics and are mutual causes for one another.
In this regard, Mahāmati, the consciousness of manifestation has as its cause the transformation of inconceivable habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

And the consciousness that discriminates objects, Mahāmati, has as its cause the discrimination of sense-objects and the habitual tendencies of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) from beginningless time.
In this regard, Mahāmati, the cessation of all sensory consciousnesses is the cessation of the manifold habitual tendencies of unreal imagination within the *ālayavijñāna*.
This, Mahāmati, is indeed the cessation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇanirodha*).
Furthermore, Mahāmati, as for the cessation of continuity (*prabandhanirodha*), it is that from which [the consciousnesses] arise.
"Because," Mahāmati, [it arises] by means of that which is its basis (*āśraya*) and that which is its object (*ālambana*).

Therein, the basis is the habit-energy (*vāsanā*) of the turbulence of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) from beginningless time; the object consists of the discriminations regarding the objects of consciousness that are the manifestations of one's own mind.
Just as, Mahāmati, a lump of clay [arises] from the atoms of clay, so it is here.
It is neither different nor non-different, just as gold is [neither different nor non-different] from its ornaments.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, if a lump of clay were something other than the atoms of clay, [it would not be produced from them].
It would not have been commenced by them;
yet it was commenced by those clay atoms,
therefore it is not something other than them.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, if they were non-different, there would be no distinction between the lump of clay and its atoms;
in the same way, the evolving consciousnesses would not be different from the characteristic of the genus of the storehouse-consciousness.
They would either have the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) as their cause, or they would be non-different from it.
In that case, upon the cessation of the active consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), there would be the cessation of the storehouse consciousness;
however, such a cessation does not occur, for there is no cessation of the characteristic of its own kind.

Therefore, Mahāmati, there is no cessation of the consciousnesses' own-characteristic of birth; rather, it is the cessation of their characteristic of karma. If, however, the own-characteristic of birth were to cease, there would be a cessation of the *ālayavijñāna*.
If the *ālayavijñāna* were to cease, this doctrine would be indistinguishable from the nihilism of the non-Buddhist teachers (*tīrthakara*).
Mahāmati, this is the doctrine of the Tīrthakaras: namely, that from the cessation of the grasping of objects, there is the cessation of the continuity of consciousness;
and from the cessation of the continuity of consciousness, there would be the severance of the continuity that has existed since beginningless time.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Tīrthakaras describe the activity of this continuity as arising from a cause.
They do not describe the arising of visual consciousness as resulting from the assembly of form and light, but rather from a cause;
moreover, Mahāmati, that which they call the "cause" consists of the doctrines of primordial matter (pradhāna), the person (puruṣa), the Lord (īśvara), time (kāla), and atoms (aṇu).

Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are seven kinds of intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of entities: namely, the intrinsic nature of origination, the intrinsic nature of existence, the intrinsic nature of characteristics, the intrinsic nature of the great elements, the intrinsic nature of cause, the intrinsic nature of condition, and the seventh is the intrinsic nature of accomplishment.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is sevenfold: namely, the range of the mind (*citta*), the range of knowledge (*jñāna*), the range of wisdom (*prajñā*), the range of the two views, the range that transcends the two views, the range of traversing the stages of the sons [of the Buddha], and the range of the Tathāgata’s personal realization.

Mahāmati, this is the heart of the ultimate reality of the intrinsic nature of phenomena belonging to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future, and present; endowed with which, the Tathāgatas establish, by means of their noble eye of wisdom, the mundane and supramundane dharmas as they fall within their specific and general characteristics.

And they establish things in such a way that they do not become common with the false views of the doctrines of the non-Buddhist teachers (tīrthakara). And how, Mahāmati, would they become common with the false views of the doctrines of the non-Buddhist teachers?
Namely, through the failure to realize that the views regarding objects are the conceptual constructions of one's own mind, [which is the nature] of the consciousnesses.

Mahāmati, because they do not enter into the realization that [the world] is merely the manifestation of one's own mind, foolish common people become proponents of the two views regarding existence and non-existence, as well as intrinsic nature and ultimate reality.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, I shall speak of the turning back of the suffering of the three realms of existence through conceptualization, the cessation of the conditions of ignorance, craving, and karma, and the observation that the objects of the world are like a magical illusion manifested by one's own mind. Mahāmati, there are certain ascetics or brahmins who maintain that things come into being from what previously did not exist, asserting the manifestation of cause and effect, the substantiality of things, their persistence over time, and the arising, abiding, and passing away of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields within various conditions.
Mahāmati, they become proponents of the non-existence of continuity, activity, arising, destruction, existence, nirvāṇa, the path, karma, its fruit, and the truths; and of annihilationism.
Why is that?
Because there is no perception of the present, due to the absence of seeing the beginning.
For example, Mahāmati, just as the absence of a jar’s shards does not perform the function of a jar,
nor does a burnt seed perform the function of a sprout;
even so, Mahāmati, those states of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases that have ceased, are ceasing, or will cease—
Because the vision of conceptual constructions, which are the manifestations of one's own mind, is without cause, there is no continuous occurrence.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, if the arising of faith and the consciousnesses through the application of the causal activity of the threefold conjunction occurred after having previously not existed,
then, Mahāmati, even non-existent things such as tortoise hair would arise,
or oil from sand.

Mahāmati, for one who asserts both existence and non-existence, there follows the loss of one's thesis and the contradiction of established rules, as well as the futility of action, object, and instrument.

Nevertheless, Mahāmati, even for them, there exists an instruction based on the application of the causal activity of the threefold conjunction, by way of the specific characteristics of cause and fruit.

Abiding on the level of speculation, those who rely on reasoning and scripture will, due to the habitual tendencies of their own views and faults, declare that there is an existence characterized by the non-existence or existence of the past, future, and present.
In this very way, Mahāmati, foolish commoners bitten by false views and possessed of uneven minds will say that what is composed by the ignorant is the work of the truly enlightened.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, those other ascetics or brahmins who—by seeing that external objects are devoid of intrinsic nature, like a dense mass of clouds, a whirling firebrand, a city of the Gandharvas, non-arising, an illusion, a mirage, the moon reflected in water, or a dream; and that they are the manifestations of one’s own mind and the conceptual constructions of what is seen—lack the cessation of the conditions of their own mental conceptualizations; and who are free from imagined designations, the characterized, the characteristics, and the designated;

and who [realize] that which is dissociated from the body, enjoyments, and the locus, as well as from the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), its objects, the grasped, and the grasper; and which is a sphere free from appearances, devoid of arising, abiding, and ceasing—[they do not perceive the truth].

They will cultivate the realization that follows the arising of their own minds; and before long, Mahāmati, those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas will attain the equality of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa through a practice that proceeds effortlessly by means of great compassion and skillful means, and through the equality of all beings with illusions and reflections.
By way of the non-arising of conditions, by being liberated from internal and external objects, and by not perceiving anything external to the mind, they follow the basis of the signless;

through the successive progression into the spheres of meditative concentration according to the stages of the levels, and by means of resolute conviction that the triple world is one's own mind, they discern this and attain the illusion-like samādhi.

By entering into the mere absence of appearances within one’s own mind, they attain the dwelling of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā-vihāra*), which is devoid of the conjunction of arising and activity;

it resembles the vajra-image of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), conforms to the body of the Tathāgata, and conforms to the emanations of suchness (*tathatā*); it is adorned with the powers (*bala*), superknowledges (*abhijñā*), masteries (*vaśitā*), compassion (*kṛpā*), pity (*karuṇā*), and skillful means (*upāya*);

it extends to all Buddha-fields and the abodes of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*); and, being free from mind, mentation, and mental consciousness, it follows the sequence of the transformation of the basis (*parāvṛtti*).
Mahāmati, those bodhisattvas will attain the body of the Tathāgata;
therefore, Mahāmati, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should, by following after the body of the Tathāgata, become its attainers.

Those who follow the principle of mind-only should become free from the conceptual proliferation of discrimination regarding the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, the mind, causes, conditions, activity, conjunction, arising, abiding, and cessation.

Seeing that the three realms of existence have as their cause the habitual tendencies of conceptualization and the depravity of beginningless proliferation, he—having reached the state of the noble dharma through personal realization by means of recollecting the non-arising of the non-manifest Buddha-stage; having attained mastery over his own mind; having entered the path of effortless conduct; resembling a jewel that manifests all forms;

and by means of subtle transformation bodies that enter the minds of sentient beings—establishes others in the successive progression of the stages through the determination that [all things] are mind-only.
Therefore, Mahāmati, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should become skilled in his own established doctrine.

Again Mahāmati said: "May the Blessed One teach me the Dharma-discourse on the Flower of the Mind, Manas, Manovijñāna, the Five Dharmas, and the Three Natures, which is followed by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; which severs the connection with the sphere of what is seen as one's own mind; which shatters the characteristics of the reality of all verbal arguments and reasonings; which is the heart of all the Buddha’s teachings; and which concerns the Bodhisattvas dwelling on Mount Malaya in Laṅkāpuri—the realm of the ocean waves and the Ālayavijñāna."
Proclaim the Dharmakāya, which has been praised by the Tathāgatas.

Then, indeed, the Blessed One spoke again to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati: "Mahāmati, eye-consciousness proceeds by means of four causes. What are these four? Namely: (1) from the failure to realize that what is grasped is the manifestation of one's own mind; (2) from the attachment to the habitual tendencies of forms arising from the depravity of beginningless conceptual proliferation; (3) from the intrinsic nature of the consciousnesses themselves; and (4) from the curiosity regarding the various characteristics of forms."
Mahāmati, by these four causes, the waves of the evolving consciousness arise from the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which is like the water within a river.

Mahāmati, just as it is with visual consciousness, so it is with all the sense organs, atoms, and pores of the skin; they arise simultaneously or in succession according to their objects, like the appearance of reflections in a mirror.

O Mahāmati, like waves on the ocean stirred by the wind, the waves of the ocean of the mind, which are the objects of the senses, arise as the five groups of consciousness; they are characterized by uninterrupted causal activity, are mutually distinct, and—being firmly bound by the characteristics of karma and birth—fail to discern the intrinsic nature of forms. Thus, O Mahāmati, do the five groups of consciousness proceed.

Mahāmati, together with those very five groups of consciousness, the mental consciousness—which is characterized by the determination of causes, objects, and distinctions—arises as a body born from those [five] as its cause.
Yet, neither they nor it have the thought: "We are here mutually caused, proceeding through the attachment to the conceptualization of what is seen of one's own mind."
Moreover, they proceed together with mutually non-different characteristics in the discernment of the objects of representation;
and as they proceed in this way, even for a yogin who has attained meditative absorption, their subtle movement and latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) do not become apparent.
And it occurs to the yogins: "Having ceased our consciousnesses, we shall enter into absorption."

And they enter [into meditative absorption] with consciousnesses that are indeed unceased; they are "unceased" because the seeds of latent impressions have not ceased, yet they are "ceased" because of the deficiency in grasping as it functions toward objects.
Thus subtle, Mahāmati, is the movement and course of the *ālayavijñāna*, such that—setting aside the Tathāgatas and those Bodhisattvas established on the stages—it cannot be perceived by others.

It is not easy for others—whether Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or practitioners of the paths of non-Buddhist ascetics—to attain this, nor even to discern it through the application of the powers of meditative concentration and wisdom.

Except for those, Mahāmati, who dwell in forest thickets and mountain caves, who possess skill in the characteristics of the stages, in wisdom, in knowledge, and in the definitive analysis of the distinctions among words; who have accumulated the infinite roots of merit of the Victors; and who are free from the conceptual proliferation of the false imaginings that are the manifestations of one's own mind—it is impossible for such practitioners of inferior, superior, or middling yoga to perceive the stream of what is seen as the false imagination of one’s own mind, nor to attain the empowerments of the Victors in infinite fields, the masteries, the powers, the superknowledges, and the meditative concentrations.

Mahāmati, it is possible for those who are supported by spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and the Victors (*jina*) to cross the ocean of cyclic existence (*saṃsārabhava*), which consists of the mind, intellect, and consciousness (*cittamanovijñāna*), and whose domain is the conceptualization of the nature of what is seen as one's own mind; this ocean has karma, craving, and ignorance as its cause.
For this reason, Mahāmati, a practitioner (*yogin*) should apply himself to the yoga of spiritual friends and the Victors.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"Just as the waves of the great ocean, driven by the condition of the wind,
arise dancing and continue without interruption, so too [is the nature of consciousness]."
In the same way, the stream of the *ālaya* is constantly stirred by the winds of sense objects;
it proceeds dancing with the various waves of the consciousnesses.
In blue, red, salt, conch, milk, and sugar-cane, as well as in decoctions, fruits, flowers, and so forth, rays appear just as they do in the sun. (Lankavatara Sutra 2.101)
The waves are considered neither different nor non-different from the ocean;
likewise, the seven consciousnesses are conjoined with the mind.
Just as the diversity of waves is a transformation of the ocean,
so too does the manifold storehouse-consciousness (ālayavijñāna), known as "cognition," proceed.
Mind, intellect, and consciousness are conceptualized for the sake of defining characteristics;
however, these eight are indeed non-distinct in their characteristic—they are neither the characterized nor the characteristic.
Just as there is no distinction between the ocean and its waves,
so too no transformation of the consciousnesses apart from the mind can be found.
Karma is accumulated by the mind (citta) and gathered by the intellect (manas);
one discerns through consciousness (vijñāna), and with the five [sensory cognitions], one conceptualizes the visible world.
Consciousness indeed appears to people in the form of blue, red, and other such varieties;
O Mahāmati, tell me why there is this similarity between the waves and the mind.
