so does the Buddha, who is honored by the world, yet the Buddha feels no pride. ||| Lank_2.175 ||| Just as a great sage is reviled by the world, yet the sage feels no anger; so does the Buddha, who is reviled by the world, yet the Buddha feels no anger. ||| Lank_2.176 ||| Just as a great sage is praised by the world, yet the sage feels no joy; so does the Buddha, who is praised by the world, yet the Buddha feels no joy. ||| Lank_2.177 ||| Just as a great sage is indifferent to the world, yet the sage does not become weary; so does the Buddha, who is indifferent to the world, yet the Buddha never becomes weary. ||| Lank_2.178 ||| Just as a great sage is free from attachment, yet the sage does not seek liberation; so does the Buddha, who is free from attachment, yet the Buddha does not seek liberation. ||| Lank_2.179 ||| Just as a great sage is free from desire, yet the sage does not dwell in cessation; so does the Buddha, who is free from desire, yet the Buddha does not dwell in cessation. ||| Lank_2.180 ||| Just as a great sage is free from views, yet the sage does not dwell in emptiness; so does the Buddha, who is free from views, yet the Buddha does not dwell in emptiness. ||| Lank_2.181 ||| Just as a great sage is free from marks, yet the sage does not dwell in signlessness; so does the Buddha, who is free from marks, yet the Buddha does not dwell in signlessness. ||| Lank_2.182 ||| Just as a great sage is free from wishes, yet the sage does not dwell in wishlessness; so
In the same way, by means of the various characteristics that are reflections of phenomena,
I declare the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), which is to be personally realized, to my sons.

Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati spoke again to the Blessed One: "May the Blessed One teach me that which is free from existence and non-existence, oneness and otherness, bothness and not-bothness, neither-existence-nor-non-existence, permanence and impermanence; that which is beyond the range of all the movements of the various non-Buddhist schools; that which is to be realized through the noble, internal, personal gnosis; and that which is turned away from the imagined nature of specific and general characteristics."

[Explain] the entry into the reality of ultimate truth; the characteristic of progressive purification through the successive connection of the stages; the characteristic of entering the stage of the Tathāgata; the manifestation of infinite objects resembling a wish-fulfilling jewel that spontaneously fulfills previous vows;
and the characteristic of the differentiation of the movement within the range of what is seen as one’s own mind regarding all phenomena.
[Explain] how I and other Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas [should understand] such things as the imagined nature and the specific and general characteristics.

With our views turned away from the [notion of] characteristics, may we swiftly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and may we bring to fulfillment all the perfections of every quality for all sentient beings.
The Blessed One said: "Excellent, excellent, Mahāmati! It is indeed excellent of you, Mahāmati, that you consider it necessary to inquire about this matter."

"Mahāmati, you have set out for the benefit of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, and for the sake, benefit, and happiness of the great multitude of beings, both gods and humans.
Therefore, Mahāmati, listen; pay close and careful attention."
"I shall explain it to you.
"Very well, Blessed One," Mahāmati, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, replied to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One said this to him: "Mahāmati, because they do not understand that [the world] is merely the manifestation of their own minds, foolish common people conceptualize through an attachment to external, diverse entities; and through an attachment to the conceptualizations and habitual tendencies regarding existence and non-existence, oneness and otherness, bothness and neither-existence-nor-non-existence, permanence and impermanence, and intrinsic nature.
Mahāmati, it is just as deer, scorched by the summer heat, conceptualize the water of a mirage as being real water and run toward it with the desire to drink."

Because they do not understand the delusion of the perceptions of their own minds, they do not realize that there is no water here; in the same way, Mahāmati, foolish common people— whose intellects have been perfumed by the various conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) and discriminations (*vikalpa*) of beginningless time, whose minds are scorched by the fires of passion, hatred, and delusion, who long for objects of various forms, whose inclinations are fixed on views of arising, ceasing, and abiding, and who are unskilled regarding the existence and non-existence of internal and external phenomena [do not realize the truth].
They fall into the grasping for oneness and otherness, and for non-existence and existence.
For example, Mahāmati, just as those who are ignorant perceive a city in a city of the Gandharvas where no city exists,
and that appearance of a city manifests due to their attachment to the habitual tendencies of the seeds of a city from beginningless time.
And that city is neither a non-city nor a city.

In the same way, Mahāmati, those who are obsessed with the habitual tendencies of the conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) of the non-Buddhist teachers (*tīrthika*) from beginningless time become attached to doctrines of oneness and otherness, existence and non-existence; their intellects fail to discern that [the world] is nothing but the manifestation of their own minds.

Mahāmati, it is just as if some man, while sleeping, were to see in a dream a place adorned with women, men, elephants, horses, chariots, infantry, villages, cities, towns, cattle, buffaloes, forests, gardens, and various mountains, rivers, and ponds.
Having entered the countryside and the inner palace, he would wake up;
having woken up, he would then recollect that very same countryside and inner palace.
What do you think, Mahāmati—would that man be considered wise?
"Who would recollect that unreal variety of dreams?
He replied, "Certainly not, Blessed One.

The Blessed One said, "In the same way, Mahāmati, foolish common people, bitten by false views and possessing the intellects of non-Buddhists, do not correctly understand that the states appearing as their own mind are like a dream."

They rely upon views of oneness and otherness, and of non-existence and existence. For example, Mahāmati, just as regions painted by an artist, though being neither depressed nor elevated, are imagined as depressed and elevated by the foolish;
even so, Mahāmati, in the future time there will be those nourished by the conceptual discrimination of the latent tendencies of the views of non-Buddhists.

Attached to doctrines of identity, difference, both, or neither, they are themselves ruined and will also declare others—who are free from the positions of existence and non-existence and who advocate non-arising—to be nihilists.
These proponents of the denial of cause and effect have uprooted the virtuous and white side of causes by their false views;
they will be declared by those seeking the highest good to be persons who must be avoided from afar.

And they, with their mental dispositions fallen into views of self, other, and both; with their mental dispositions fallen into the evil views of superimposition and denial through the conceptualization of non-existence and existence, will have hell as their ultimate destination.
Mahāmati, it is just as when those afflicted by ophthalmia see a mass of hair and say to one another, "This is wonderful! This is wonderful! Look, O sirs!
Yet that mass of hair, because it is unarisen in either [subject or object], is neither an entity nor a non-entity, depending on whether it is seen or not seen.

In the same way, Mahāmati, those who are attached to the conceptual dispositions of the false views of the heterodox, and who are fixated on doctrines of existence and non-existence, identity and difference, bothness and neitherness, will disparage the true Dharma and cause both themselves and others to fall into ruin.
Mahāmati, it is just as a firebrand-circle, which is not a wheel, is imagined to be a wheel by the foolish, but not by the wise.

In the same way, Mahāmati, those who have fallen into the inclinations of false views and heretics will conceptualize identity, difference, both, or neither in regard to the arising of all entities. Just as, Mahāmati, when it rains from the sky, water bubbles appear resembling crystal gems, and therein the foolish, having become attached to them as being crystal gems, run after them.
And those water bubbles, Mahāmati, are neither jewels nor non-jewels, depending on whether they are grasped or not grasped.

In the same way, Mahāmati, those whose mental dispositions are perfumed by the conceptualizations and views of the non-Buddhists will describe the arising of what does not exist through conditions, and the destruction of what exists.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, having established the three means of valid cognition and the five members of a syllogism, they will conceptualize that an entity— which is to be personally realized through noble wisdom and is free from the two natures— exists by way of its own intrinsic nature.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, for those yogins who have undergone the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) of the mind, the intellect, and the mental consciousness; who have abandoned the conceptualization of subject and object regarding what is seen as one's own mind; and who have attained the noble, personal realization-knowledge of the stage of the Tathāgata—the notions of existence and non-existence do not arise.
If, however, Mahāmati, such notions of existence and non-existence were to arise even for yogins whose sphere of activity is this very state, [they would not be yogins].

This very thing would be for them a grasping at a self, a grasping at a soul, a grasping at a person, and a grasping at a pudgala. Furthermore, Mahāmati, this teaching on the specific and general characteristics of the intrinsic nature of phenomena is, Mahāmati, the teaching of an emanation-body Buddha (nairmāṇika-buddha), not the teaching of a dharma-nature Buddha (dharmatā-buddha).

Furthermore, Mahāmati, teaching proceeds from the views residing in the mental dispositions of the ignorant; it does not manifest the dwelling in the bliss of samādhi, which is the internal realization of the noble knowledge of the nature of reality as it is established in its own being.
Mahāmati, it is just as the shadow of a tree appears within water.
And that [reflection] is neither shadow nor non-shadow, because it has the configuration of a tree or lacks configuration;

in the very same way, Mahāmati, those whose conceptualizations are perfumed by the latent impressions of the views of the heterodox teachers will conceptualize oneness, otherness, both, neither, non-existence, and existence, their minds failing to discern that these are merely what is seen of their own mind.
Just as, Mahāmati, all reflected images of forms appear within a mirror according to conditions and through one's own conceptualization, so it is with this.
Those images are neither images nor non-images, because they are seen as both images and non-images.
Nevertheless, Mahāmati, these conceptual constructions appearing as the objects of one's own mind manifest to the foolish in the form of images.
In the same way, Mahāmati, the reflections of one's own mind manifest through the modes of views concerning identity, difference, both, or neither.
For example, Mahāmati, just as an echo arises from the conjunction of a person, a river, and the wind, and is heard accordingly;

yet it is neither an entity nor a non-entity, because of the hearing of sound and the absence of sound— exactly so, Mahāmati, the conceptualizations of the latent impressions of one's own mind appear as views of existence and non-existence, oneness and otherness, both and neither.
For example, Mahāmati, on a ground devoid of grass, shrubs, creepers, and forests, mirages flow like waves through contact with the sun;
yet they are neither existent nor non-existent, depending on whether one is greedy or not.

In the same way, Mahāmati, the discriminative consciousness of the ignorant—perfumed by the habitual tendencies of the wickedness of beginningless conceptual proliferation—operates by way of the objects of noble personal realization regarding arising, abiding, and destruction; identity and difference; both and neither; and existence and non-existence.
It wavers like a mirage.
For example, Mahāmati, just as a Vetāla and a mechanical man— though devoid of a sentient being— perform the action of moving through the application of a Piśāca or a mechanism,
so too do fools become attached to that unreal conceptualization by means of coming and going.

In the same way, Mahāmati, foolish commoners, fallen into the inclinations of those with wrong views and heretical doctrines, adhere to theories of identity and difference. That is a superimposition of what does not exist.

Therefore, Mahāmati, you should be free from the conceptualization that perceives the noble, internal realization of reality—free from [notions of] arising, abiding, and ceasing; identity and difference; both and neither; and existence and non-existence.
In this regard, it is said:
The aggregates, with consciousness as the fifth, are like the shadow of a tree reflected in water;
they resemble illusions and dreams.
Do not conceptualize by means of representation.
When one discerns that these three worlds are like a mass of hair [seen by the visually impaired], a delusion like water in a mirage, and are termed a dream or an illusion, one is liberated.
Just as in the summer heat a mirage flickers, deluding the mind, and deer perceive it as water while no such substance exists therein; (Lank_2.149)
In the same way, the seed of consciousness vibrates within the range of vision;
fools grasp it as something being born, just as those with cataracts perceive a visual distortion.
In the beginningless cycle of existence, the fool is embraced by the grasping at phenomena;
just as one might extract a wedge by means of another wedge, he should turn away from it.

One who perceives the world as always resembling an illusion, a corpse animated by magic, or a mechanical device; as like a dream, lightning, or a cloud; and as severed from the three continuities, is liberated. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 2.152)
For there is no representation here at all, just as with mirages in the sky;
thus, those who understand phenomena do not assert anything whatsoever.
This representation is merely a name; it does not exist by way of its own characteristic.
The aggregates have the appearance of a hair-net where this [representation] is conceptualized.
The mind appears to men as a hair-net, an illusion, a dream, a city of Gandharvas, a whirling firebrand, and a mirage— all these indeed manifest though they do not exist.
The eternal and the non-eternal, as well as unity, both, and neither— fools, deluded by their connection to beginningless defects, conceptualize these.
For a reflection is seen in a mirror, in water, in the eye, in vessels, and in gems; yet that reflection does not exist anywhere at all.
Likewise, the mind appears as existing entities, just as a mirage appears in the sky;
it is seen in various forms, like the son of a barren woman in a dream.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Dharma teaching of the Tathāgatas is free from the fourfold [extremes];
that is to say, it is devoid of the positions of oneness, otherness, both, or neither; it is liberated from the superimposition of existence and the denial of non-existence.
Mahāmati, the Dharma teaching of the Tathāgatas is preceded by the non-reality of dependent origination, cessation, the path, liberation, and worldly activity.
Mahāmati, the Dharma teaching of the Tathāgatas is not bound by [the doctrines of] primordial nature, a creator god, causality, chance, atoms, time, or inherent self-nature.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, for the sake of purifying the two obstructions— those of afflictions and those of the knowable— the Tathāgatas, like a caravan leader, gradually establish [beings] in the one hundred and eight states of non-appearance and in the characteristics of the well-differentiated divisions of the vehicles, the stages, and the limbs of enlightenment.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of dhyāna.
What are the four? They are as follows: the dhyāna of the practice of the ignorant (bālopacārika-dhyāna),...
The meditation on the discernment of phenomena,
the meditation having suchness as its object, and the fourth, the Tathāgata meditation.
In this regard, Mahāmati, what is the meditation practiced by the ignorant (*bālopacārika-dhyāna*)?

It is that which belongs to the practitioners of the yoga of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, preceded by an attachment to the characteristics of the non-existence of a person (*pudgala-nairātmya*), as well as to individual and general characteristics, to the collection of elements (*saṃkalā*), and to impermanence, suffering, and impurity— thinking,
"These are the characteristics, and not otherwise."
For one who perceives [the stages] from the preceding to the subsequent, up to the cessation of perception (*saṃjñānirodha*), there is the meditation practiced by the ignorant (*bālopacārika*).
In that regard, Mahāmati, what is the meditation for the discernment of meaning (*arthapravicayadhyāna*)? It is as follows:

having established the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and the absence of external characteristics—whether particular or universal—as well as the non-existence of outsiders, self, other, or both, the meditation for the discernment of meaning proceeds through a gradual discernment for the sake of the characteristics and meaning of the stages of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).
It is so. In that regard, Mahāmati, what is meditation having suchness as its object?
It is this: because conceptualization no longer proceeds due to the abiding in the reality of the two kinds of imagined selflessness, I say that suchness is the object.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, what is the Tathāgata-dhyāna?

It is that which enters the mode of the Tathāgata-stage, and by virtue of abiding in the bliss of the three characteristics of the noble wisdom realized within oneself and performing inconceivable deeds for the sake of sentient beings, I call it the Tathāgata-dhyāna.
In this regard, it is said:

The meditation that investigates objects, the meditation practiced by the ignorant, the meditation that takes suchness as its object, and the auspicious meditation of the Tathāgatas. *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* 2.159.

The yogi, while practicing yoga, perceives forms resembling the moon and the sun, resembling the lotus and the underworld (pātāla), and resembling the variegated sky or fire. (Lankavatara Sutra 2.160)
And those various signs lead them along the path of the heterodox teachers; they cause them to fall into the state of a Śrāvaka or within the domain of a Pratyekabuddha.
When, having shaken off all these, one becomes free from appearances,
then the Buddhas, like suns, assemble from all realms and stroke the head of that person as a sign of their conformity with suchness.
Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati spoke again to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, it is said, 'Nirvāṇa, Nirvāṇa.
Of what, Blessed One, is this the designation, namely, 'Nirvāṇa'?

The Blessed One said: "The revolution (*parāvṛtti*) of the habit-energies (*vāsanā*) of the nature of all consciousnesses—the storehouse-consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*), the manas, and the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*)—along with the habit-energies of [wrong] views, is called 'Nirvāṇa' by all the Buddhas and by me. It is the sphere of reality whose nature is emptiness and which has as its objective domain the state of Nirvāṇa."

Furthermore, Mahāmati, nirvāṇa is the domain of the personal realization of noble wisdom; it is free from the conceptual constructions of permanence and annihilation, and of existence and non-existence.
How is it not permanent?
Because it is devoid of the conceptual constructions of specific and general characteristics.
Therefore, it is not eternal.
In this regard, non-annihilation means that all objects—past, future, and present—also proceed within each individual;
therefore, there is no annihilation.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, great parinirvāṇa is neither destruction nor death.
If, Mahāmati, great parinirvāṇa were death, there would again be a continuity of birth.
If it were subject to destruction,
it would fall under the characteristics of the conditioned;
for this reason, Mahāmati, Great Parinirvāṇa is neither destruction nor death.
Yogins attain a death that is free from transmigration.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, great parinirvāṇa is called "nirvāṇa" because it is neither abandoned nor attained, neither annihilated nor eternal, and neither a single entity nor multiple entities.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, the nirvāṇa of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas arises from the awakening to specific and general characteristics and from non-association;
because they perceive objects without error, conceptual construction does not arise.
Consequently, the thought of nirvana arises in them there.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, the characteristic of the two kinds of intrinsic nature is twofold.
What are the two kinds?
Namely, attachment to the intrinsic nature of verbal expression and attachment to the intrinsic nature of things.
In this regard, Mahāmati, attachment to the intrinsic nature of verbal expression proceeds from attachment to the habitual tendencies of beginningless conceptual proliferation of speech.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, attachment to the intrinsic nature of things proceeds from the failure to realize that [the world] is nothing but the manifestation of one's own mind.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, bodhisattvas, empowered by two kinds of empowerment, prostrate at the feet of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas and ask questions. By which two empowerments are they empowered?
Namely, by the empowerment of meditative absorption and attainment, and by the empowerment of the consecration upon the entire body, face, and hands.
In that regard, Mahāmati, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas on the first stage, sustained by the empowerment of the Buddhas, enter the Bodhisattva-samādhi called "Radiance of the Mahāyāna.
As soon as those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have entered the Bodhisattva-samādhi of the Radiance of the Mahāyāna,
the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas residing in the world-systems of the ten directions manifest their faces and bestow their empowerment by revealing their entire bodies, faces, and voices.
Mahāmati, just as it was for the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajragarbha and for other Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas endowed with such characteristics and qualities,
so too, Mahāmati, do Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas on the first stage obtain the empowerment of meditative concentration and attainment.
Through roots of merit accumulated over hundreds of thousands of eons, they gradually reach the realization of the characteristics of the factors conducive to the stages and their opposites.

On the Bodhisattva stage called Dharmameghā, for the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva seated upon a throne in a great lotus palace, surrounded by Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas of corresponding rank, his crown adorned with ornaments of every kind of jewel—
the hands of the Jinas arriving from the world-systems of the ten directions are like the rays of yellow orpiment, gold, campaka flowers, moonbeams, and lotuses.

As the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva sits upon a lotus throne in a celestial palace, they consecrate him on the crown of his head with a consecration of the entire body, face, and hands, like a sovereign Wheel-turning King or a Lord of the Vaśavartin gods.
That Bodhisattva and those other Bodhisattvas are said to be "empowered by the empowerment of the hand-consecration.
Mahāmati, this is the twofold empowerment of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas.
Empowered by these two empowerments, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas behold the faces of all Buddhas;
otherwise, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are not to be beheld.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, whatever flashes forth for the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, in the form of meditative absorptions, supernatural powers, or teachings,
all of that belongs to those who are sustained by the twofold empowerment of the Buddhas.

If, however, Mahāmati, the inspired eloquence of the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, were to flash forth without such empowerment, [it would be as if they were speaking from their own independent intellect].
Even the inspired eloquence of foolish commoners, Mahāmati, would manifest;
for what reason?
Because it is not sustained by the power of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

Mahāmati, even grasses, shrubs, trees, and mountains, as well as various musical instruments, cities, palaces, houses, celestial mansions, seats, and dwellings, resound through the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Tathāgata’s entrance.
How much more so, Mahāmati, those with consciousness—indeed, even the mute, the blind, and the deaf—are liberated from their own defects, Mahāmati.
Such, Mahāmati, is the excellence of the great qualities of the Tathāgata’s empowerment.

Furthermore, Mahāmati said: "Blessed One, do the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas bestow the empowerment of consecration (*abhiṣekādhiṣṭhāna*) upon the Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas, at the time of their entering into the meditative attainments (*samādhisamāpatti*), and upon the stage of distinction (*viśeṣabhūmi*)?

The Blessed One replied: "It is for the purpose of separating them from the deeds of Māra and the afflictions (*kleśa*), so that they do not fall back into the stages of the Śrāvaka's dhyānas, and so that they may personally realize the stage of a Tathāgata; it is for the sake of increasing the realization of the Dharma already attained."
And for this reason, Mahāmati, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas empower the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, with their empowerments.

For, Mahāmati, if Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, were not so empowered, they would fall into the inclinations of false teachers, Śrāvakas, and Māras, and would not awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Therefore, for that reason, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are favored by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
Regarding this, it is said:
The empowerment of the lords of men is purified by their vows;
beginning with the consecration and meditative absorption, it extends from the first to the tenth stage.

Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāmati spoke again to the Blessed One: "Furthermore, Blessed One, when you teach dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), you have merely provided an explanation of causes; you have not spoken of the abiding nature of our own system.

Blessed One, even the non-Buddhist teachers (*tīrthakara*) describe the arising of things from a cause, namely that the production of entities proceeds from such conditions as Primordial Matter (*pradhāna*), the Lord (*īśvara*), the Person (*puruṣa*), Time (*kāla*), and atoms (*aṇu*)."
However, the Blessed One describes the arising of entities by means of another synonym for conditions,
yet there is no difference in the specific tenet.
For, O Blessed One, even the non-Buddhist teachers describe the arising of both the existent and the non-existent.
And since the destruction of entities occurs through conditions,
that which was stated by the Blessed One— "conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces, up to old age and death"—
is described by the Blessed One as a teaching concerning the absence of a [permanent] cause.
That is not a discourse on causality,
Blessed One; for this principle— "when this exists, that comes to be"— applies to things existing simultaneously,
not to things existing in dependence upon a sequential process.
However, Blessed One, it is the designation of the *tīrthakaras* alone that is distinguished, not yours.
Why is that?
Because, Blessed One, for the *tīrthakaras*, a cause that is not dependently originated brings about an effect.
But for you, O Blessed One, the cause depends upon the effect, and the effect depends upon the cause;

thus, there is a confusion of causes and conditions, and a mutual infinite regress follows. Furthermore, O Blessed One, for one who asserts "this being, that arises," the world would be without a cause.

The Blessed One said: "Mahāmati, for me, who asserts that 'this being present, that arises,' there follows neither a doctrine of causelessness nor a confusion of causes and conditions, because of the absence of the grasped and the grasper, and because of the realization that [all things] are merely the manifestation of one's own mind."

But those, Mahāmati, who are attached to the grasped and the grasper and do not realize that it is merely the manifestation of their own minds— failing to understand the existence and non-existence of external objects as their own domains— for them, Mahāmati, this fault follows; but not for me, who employ the designation of dependent causation.
Furthermore, Mahāmati said: "Is it not the case, Blessed One, that all things exist because of the existence of verbal expression?
For if, Blessed One, things did not exist, verbal expression would not arise."
And it proceeds.
Therefore, Blessed One, because of the existence of verbal expression, all things exist.
The Blessed One said: "Mahāmati, verbal expression is also made for things that do not exist."

That is to say, in the world, there is seen the verbal expression of things such as a rabbit’s horn, a tortoise’s hair, or the son of a barren woman; yet, Mahāmati, these are neither existent entities nor non-existent entities,
and yet they are expressed in words.
Regarding what you said, Mahāmati— that all things exist because of the existence of verbal expression— that argument has been refuted.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, verbal expression is not established in all Buddha-fields.
Mahāmati, verbal expression is something created. In some Buddha-fields, Mahāmati, the Dharma is taught by means of a steady, unblinking gaze; in others, by means of gestures.
In some places by a movement of the eyebrows, in some places by a shifting of the eyes, and in some places by the mouth;
In some places by yawning, in some places by the sound of coughing,
and in some places by the recollection of the field.
In some cases, it is by means of a movement;

as, for example, Mahāmati, in the world-system Animiṣā and Gandhasugandhā, which is the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Samantabhadra, those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas gaze with unblinking eyes.
They attain the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) and other distinguished meditative absorptions (samādhi).
For this very reason, Mahāmati, all things do not exist by virtue of the existence of verbal expression;
and this, Mahāmati, is directly perceived.
In this world, specific types of beings such as worms and flies perform their own respective functions even without verbal expression.
Regarding this, it is said:
"Space, a hare's horn, and even the son of a barren woman—though non-existent, they are spoken of; so too is conceptual construction regarding entities. (Lankavatara 2.164)
Fools, ignorant of this principle, imagine the arising of things from the assemblage of causes and conditions; thus they wander in the abode of the three realms of existence.
Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati spoke again to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, where has the word 'eternal' been spoken?
The Blessed One said: "In delusion, Mahāmati;
because this delusion appears even to the Noble Ones through error."

For example, Mahāmati, just as in the world the mirage, the fire-brand circle, the hair-net, the city of the Gandharvas, illusion, a dream, a reflection, and a mechanical man are misapprehended by the ignorant, but not by the wise; yet, they are not,
however, non-manifest.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, that delusion appears in many forms; yet it does not render the delusion itself impermanent. Why is that?
That is to say, because it is devoid of existence and non-existence.
But how, Mahāmati, is delusion devoid of existence and non-existence?
It is because it is the diverse sphere of experience for all fools, like the waves of the ocean or the water of the Gaṅgā, appearing or not appearing to hungry ghosts.
Therefore, Mahāmati, for this reason, the nature of delusion does not exist; yet,
because that water appears to others,
it is for this reason that it is not non-existent.
Thus, the delusion of the noble ones is devoid of both perversion and non-perversion.
For this reason, Mahāmati, delusion is eternal; that is to say, because there is no distinction between the cause and its characteristics.
Indeed, Mahāmati, delusion does not undergo differentiation even when it is conceptualized through the conceptualization of various and manifold signs.
Therefore, for this reason, Mahāmati, error is eternal.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, how does delusion become reality?
It is because, Mahāmati, regarding this delusion, the cognition of perversion does not arise for the noble ones,
nor does the cognition of non-perversion.
Mahāmati, it is not otherwise; in this delusion, the noble ones do not have any notion of "something," nor do they have a notion of the reality of noble gnosis.
Mahāmati, that which is called "something" is the prattle of fools, not the prattle of the noble ones.
Furthermore, that delusion, when conceptualized through either inversion or non-inversion, brings about two lineages: namely, the lineage of the noble ones or the lineage of foolish ordinary beings.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, the noble lineage (āryagotra) proceeds in three ways, namely, through the distinctions of the Śrāvaka, the Pratyekabuddha, and the Buddha.
In this regard, Mahāmati, how is it that delusion, when conceptualized by the ignorant, gives rise to the lineage of the Śrāvaka vehicle?
That is to say, Mahāmati, by becoming attached through attachment to specific and general characteristics (svasāmānyalakṣaṇa), it leads to the lineage of the Śrāvaka vehicle.
Thus, Mahāmati, that delusion brings about the lineage of the Śrāvakayāna.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, how does that very same delusion, when being conceptualized, bring about the lineage of the Pratyekabuddhayāna?
It is because, Mahāmati, through the non-association with attachment to the specific and general characteristics of that very delusion, it brings about the lineage of the Pratyekabuddhayāna.

In that regard, Mahāmati, how is it that the very same delusion, when conceptualized by the wise, becomes the carrier of the lineage of the Buddha-vehicle? That is to say, Mahāmati, through the realization that [the world] is merely the manifestation of one's own mind, and by ceasing the conceptualization of external existence and non-existence, when it is thus conceptualized, it becomes the carrier of the lineage of the Buddha-vehicle.
Therefore, Mahāmati, this is the lineage;
this is the meaning of lineage.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, when the cultivation of diverse objects is conceptualized as a delusion by the ignorant, it brings about the lineage for the vehicle of saṃsāra.
"It is thus, and not otherwise.
For this reason, Mahāmati, delusion is conceptualized by the foolish as having the nature of diverse entities;
yet it is neither an entity nor a non-entity.

Mahāmati, that very delusion, when it is no longer conceptualized by the Noble Ones due to the transformation (*parāvṛtti*) of the nature of the habitual tendencies of the corruption of mind, intellect, and mental consciousness, is called "Suchness" (*tathatā*) for the Noble Ones.
Therefore, Mahāmati, this is what is meant: "Even Suchness is liberated from the mind.
To illuminate the meaning of this very point, Mahāmati, I have said: "It is devoid of conceptual constructions" and "it is free from all conceptual constructions"—this is what is being expressed.
Mahāmati said: "Does delusion exist, Blessed One, or does it not?
The Blessed One replied: "Mahāmati, delusion does not exist as an adherence to characteristics, like a magical illusion.
However, Mahāmati, if delusion were to exist through adherence to characteristics,"
"Mahāmati, attachment to entities would remain unceasing.
Mahāmati, this would be like dependent origination, yet it would be like the production from a cause as taught by the non-Buddhist teachers.
Mahāmati said: "Blessed One, if delusion is like an illusion,"
"Therefore, it will become the cause of another delusion.
The Blessed One said: "No, Mahāmati, illusion is not the cause of delusion.
Because it does not bring about the fault of *dauṣṭhulya* (inner corruption), for indeed, Mahāmati, illusion does not bring about the fault of *dauṣṭhulya*."
Furthermore, Mahāmati, when illusion is not being conceptualized, it proceeds from the empowerment of another person's knowledge,
and not from the empowerment of the habitual tendencies of one's own conceptualization and corruption;
thus, it does not bring about any fault.
Mahāmati, this is merely the delusion of the mind's vision for the foolish, arising from their attachment to whatever [objects] there may be; it is not so for the noble ones.
Regarding this, it is said:
The noble one perceives neither delusion nor reality in between them;
for that which is reality is precisely the delusion, since reality exists within it. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 2.166)
If, having indeed shaken off all delusion, a sign were to arise,
that itself would be his delusion, like an impure cataract.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, it is not that illusion does not exist;
rather, because of the observation of their common characteristics, all phenomena are like an illusion.
Mahāmati said: "But, Blessed One, is it by virtue of the characteristic of attachment to various illusions that all phenomena are like an illusion?"
Now, [is it] by way of the characteristic of adherence to what is unreal?
If, Blessed One, all phenomena possess the nature of being like an illusion by way of the characteristic of adherence to various illusions,
then, alas, Blessed One, entities are not like illusions.
For what reason? Because one perceives that form has no cause for its diverse characteristics.
Indeed, Blessed One, there is no cause whatsoever by which form appears with diverse characteristics and forms, like an illusion.
Therefore, Blessed One, for this reason, things are not like an illusion because of a similarity consisting in the adherence to the characteristics of diverse illusions.
The Blessed One said: "Mahāmati, it is not because of a similarity in the attachment to the characteristics of various illusions that all dharmas are like an illusion.
Rather, Mahāmati, it is by virtue of a similarity to something false and as fleeting as lightning that all dharmas are like an illusion.
For example, Mahāmati..."
Just as a flash of lightning appears to children as something seen and then vanished in an instant,

even so, Mahāmati, all things— which possess the general characteristics of one's own conceptual construction— do not appear [as real] due to the absence of analytical investigation, because of the attachment to the characteristics of form.
Regarding this, it is said:
It is not that illusion does not exist; rather, the existence of phenomena is spoken of because of their similarity to it.
Since they are false, fleeting, and like lightning, they are therefore remembered as being comparable to an illusion.
Furthermore, Mahāmati said: "As for that which was stated by the Blessed One— that all phenomena are unproduced and like an illusion—
does not a fault of contradiction between earlier and later statements accrue to you, O Blessed One, who thus describe the non-arising of phenomena by means of their being like an illusion?"
The Blessed One said: "Mahāmati, for me who describes the non-arising of all things as being like an illusion, there is no fault of contradiction between preceding and succeeding statements.
Why is that?

Because, Mahāmati, through the awakening to the fact that arising and non-arising are merely what is seen of one's own mind, and because of the vision that external entities—whether existent or non-existent—do not arise, the fault of contradiction between preceding and succeeding statements does not apply."
However, Mahāmati, this is said for the purpose of setting aside the notion of the production of causes held by the non-Buddhist teachers: "All things are unproduced, like an illusion.

For, Mahāmati, the groups of deluded non-Buddhists desire the production of things from existence and non-existence, rather than [understanding it] as arising from the conditions of their own various attachments to conceptual construction.
But for me, Mahāmati, no fear arises.
Therefore, Mahāmati, for this reason, it is precisely the term "non-arising" that is expressed.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, the teaching of "existence" is for the purpose of upholding cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) and for the purpose of preventing the nihilistic view that "nothing exists. By employing the word "existence," my disciples uphold cyclic existence so as to maintain the various bases of rebirth resulting from diverse karmic actions.

Mahāmati, by means of this teaching on the characteristic of the nature of illusion, I teach that all phenomena have the nature of illusion and dreams, for the purpose of turning back the notion of the intrinsic nature of things among foolish commoners— those whose inclinations have fallen into the characteristics of false views, who do not discern that [the world] is merely what is seen of their own minds, and who are attached to the characteristics of the arising of activity through causes and conditions.
These foolish common people, characterized by wrong views and attached to their own dispositions, will deceive both themselves and others because they do not see all phenomena as they truly abide.
In this regard, Mahāmati, the seeing of all phenomena as they truly abide is the entry into the realization that they are merely the manifestation of one's own mind.
Regarding this, it is said:
"In non-arising there is an absence of causes; in existence, there is the inclusion within saṃsāra.
One should view things as being like illusions and the like, and not conceptualize their characteristics. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 2.169)

Furthermore, Mahāmati, we shall explain the characteristics of the collections of names, phrases, and phonemes, by means of which well-defined collections of names, phrases, and phonemes, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas following the meaning, phrases, and phonemes will quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and in that very same way,
cause all sentient beings to awaken.
In this regard, Mahāmati, "body" (kāya) refers to that thing which, depending upon a substance, a name is applied;
that body is the substance itself.
"Body" and "physical form" (śarīra) are not different in meaning.
This, Mahāmati, is the collection of names (*nāmakāya*).

Furthermore, Mahāmati, the collection of phrases (*padakāya*) refers to the determination of the actual existence of the meaning of a phrase; "finality," "attainment," and "perception" are synonymous terms.

This, Mahāmati, is the instruction on the collection of words (padakāya) that has been given. Furthermore, Mahāmati, the collection of phonemes (vyañjanakāya) is that by which the manifestation of names and words occurs.
Phoneme, mark, characteristic, apprehension, and designation—these are synonymous terms.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, the body of phrases (*padakāya*) refers to the culmination of the function of phrases.
Moreover, Mahāmati, "name" (*nāman*) refers to the distinction between the intrinsic nature of syllables and names, from the letter *a* up to the letter *ha*.

In this regard, Mahāmati, "phoneme" (vyañjana) refers to short, long, and protracted phonemes. Furthermore, Mahāmati, "phrase-body" (padakāya) refers to those that follow the path of phrases and receive the designation of "phrase-body," such as elephants, horses, humans, deer, cattle, buffaloes, goats, sheep, and so forth.
Moreover, Mahāmati, "name" (nāma) and "phoneme" (vyañjana) refer to the four formless aggregates (skandhas).
It is called "name" (*nāman*) because it is expressed by means of a name;
it is called "syllable" (*vyañjana*) because it is manifested by its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Mahāmati, this is the definition of the expression of names and phrases within the collections of names, phrases, and syllables.
In this regard, you should cultivate familiarity.
Regarding this, it is said:
"In respect of phonemes, the collection of phrases, and especially the names, the foolish and the dull-witted become attached, like elephants in a great mire. (Lankavatara 2.170)

Furthermore, Mahāmati, due to a deficiency in reasoning, logic, and intelligence, those who are false dialecticians with corrupted intellects will, in the future age, when questioned by the wise—who inquire about the method that is free from the two extremes and characterized by being beyond the views of oneness, otherness, both, or neither—say this: "This is not a valid question; this is not a fundamental inquiry."
Namely: whether impermanence is different or not different from form and so forth;

likewise, whether nirvāṇa is different from conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) from what is characterized (*lakṣya*), a possessor of qualities (*guṇin*) from qualities (*guṇa*), a derivative element (*bhautika*) from the primary elements (*bhūta*), vision (*darśana*) from the visible (*dṛśya*), atoms (*aṇu*) from dust, or a yogi from knowledge—when questioned regarding such matters by means of this method of successive sequential characteristics, they will say that the Blessed One has declared them "unexpounded" (*avyākṛta*) as something to be set aside (*sthāpanīya*).

But those deluded persons will not understand that, due to the deficiency in the intelligence of listeners, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas do not provide explanations on the indeterminate (avyākṛta) points in order to avoid causing fear among sentient beings.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Tathāgatas do not teach them for the purpose of refuting the views and doctrines of the non-Buddhist teachers (tīrthakara).
For, Mahāmati, the non-Buddhist teachers maintain such doctrines as: "The soul (jīva) is identical to the body."
"The soul is one thing and the body another"—such statements constitute the doctrine of the undeclared (*avyākṛtavāda*).
For the non-Buddhist teachers (*tīrthakara*), Mahāmati, who are deluded regarding causes, there is the undeclared; but such is not the case in my teaching.
But in my teaching, Mahāmati, which is free from the grasped and the grasper, conceptual construction does not arise. How, then, could there be anything to be set aside for them?

However, Mahāmati, for those who are attached to the grasped and the grasper and whose minds have not realized that [the world] is merely what is seen of one's own mind—for them, there is something to be set aside.
Mahāmati, through the fourfold method of answering questions, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas teach the Dharma to sentient beings.
Mahāmati, that which is to be set aside is a teaching by me intended for another time, for those whose faculties are not yet mature;
it is not something to be set aside for those whose faculties are mature.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, all phenomena do not arise because they are devoid of action and agent, since there is no agent;
therefore it is said that all phenomena are unarisen. Moreover, Mahāmati, for what reason are all entities without intrinsic nature?

Because, Mahāmati, when things are investigated by one's own intelligence, their specific and general characteristics cannot be determined as existing; therefore, it is said that "all dharmas are without intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, for what reason are all dharmas neither brought forth nor cast out?

Because, Mahāmati, when the specific and general characteristics are being brought forward, they are not brought forward; when they are being cast out, they are not cast out— for this reason, Mahāmati, all dharmas are free from bringing forward and casting out.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, for what reason are all phenomena unceasing?
That is to say, because the characteristics of the intrinsic nature of entities do not exist, all phenomena are not apprehended;
therefore, it is said that "all phenomena are unceasing."
In this regard, Mahāmati, for what reason are all dharmas said to be impermanent?
Namely, because their arising as characterized phenomena is impermanent in nature.
Therefore, it is said that all phenomena are impermanent.

In this regard, Mahāmati, for what reason are all phenomena permanent? That is to say, because they are neither produced nor unproduced in terms of their characteristics, they are permanent by virtue of their impermanence.
Therefore, Mahāmati, it is said that all dharmas are eternal.
In this regard, it is said:

There are four kinds of categorical responses: the direct answer, the answer by inquiry, the answer by analysis, and the answer by setting aside; [the last] serves to ward off the doctrines of the non-Buddhists.
For the non-arising of both the existent and the non-existent is taught by the Sāṃkhyas and Vaiśeṣikas;
indeed, all [theories] regarding the indeterminate have been proclaimed by them alone.
When analyzed by the intellect, their intrinsic nature cannot be apprehended;
therefore, they are taught to be inexpressible and devoid of intrinsic nature.

Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Blessed One in this way: "May the Blessed One teach me the characteristics of the method for distinguishing the states of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) for those who have entered the stream;

by means of which characteristics of the method for distinguishing the states of stream-entry, I and other Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas may become skilled in the characteristics of the method for distinguishing the states of stream-entry, and likewise come to know the rules and characteristics of the successive stages of the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), the non-returner (*anāgāmin*), and arhatship."
May they teach the Dharma to sentient beings so that,

having thoroughly purified the two characteristics of selflessness and the two obscurations, they may reach the state of transcending the characteristics of each stage; and having attained the sphere of activity of the inconceivable course of the Tathāgatas,
may they become like a *viśvarūpa* jewel, reaching the state of being the source of sustenance for all sentient beings.
May they become objects of enjoyment and sustenance for the bodies that reach the domain of all phenomena.
The Blessed One said: "In that case, Mahāmati, listen and attend well and thoroughly;
I shall speak to you."
"Excellent, Blessed One," the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this to him: "Mahāmati, there are these three distinctions among the fruits of stream-entry for those who have entered the stream. What are the three?"
That is to say, they are inferior, middling, and superior. In this regard, Mahāmati, the inferior [bodhisattva] has at most seven more births;
the middling, Mahāmati, attains parinirvāṇa after three or five births;
and the superior, Mahāmati, attains parinirvāṇa in that very life.
However, Mahāmati, for these three [types of persons], there are three fetters that are indeed weak, middling, and intense.
In this regard, Mahāmati, what are the three fetters?
Namely: the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), doubt (vicikitsā), and the adherence to rules and rituals (śīlavrataparāmarśa).
Mahāmati, these three fetters lead, through successive stages of distinction, to the state of an Arhat and the fruit of Arhatship.

In this regard, Mahāmati, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is of two kinds: namely, the innate (*sahajā*) and the imagined (*parikalpitā*), corresponding respectively to the dependent nature (*paratantrasvabhāva*) and the imagined nature (*parikalpitasvabhāva*).
For example, Mahāmati, based upon the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), there occurs an attachment to the various imagined natures (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
And that [attachment] is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent therein, because it has the characteristic of unreal imagination (*abhūta-parikalpa*).
Nevertheless, it is conceptualized by the ignorant through an attachment to the characteristics of diverse intrinsic natures, just as a mirage is [imagined] by deer.
Mahāmati, this imagined view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) of a stream-enterer is accumulated through ignorance and long-standing attachment;
and that is abandoned for him because of the absence of grasping at a personal self (*pudgala-nairātmya*).

Furthermore, Mahāmati, the innate view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) of a stream-enterer (*srotaāpanna*) is [abandoned] through the equality of one's own body and the bodies of others. This is because form consists of the characteristics of the four aggregates; because form arises from the primary elements (*bhūta*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*); and because the primary elements possess the characteristic of being mutually causal.
Since form does not truly arise, the stream-enterer—by seeing the view of the positions of existence and non-existence—has abandoned the view of a self-identity.
For this very reason, passion does not arise in one who has abandoned the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Mahāmati, this is the characteristic of the view of a self-identity.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, as for the characteristic of doubt (*vicikitsā*): because one possesses the well-observed characteristic of the realization of the Dharma that has been attained, and because one has previously abandoned the dualistic conceptualization of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), there is no doubt regarding the teachings;
nor does one hold any other view of a teacher based on notions of purity or impurity.
Mahāmati, this is the characteristic of doubt in one who has entered the stream.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, how is it that a stream-enterer does not cling to moral precepts (*śīla*)? It is because he clearly perceives the characteristics of the bases for the arising of suffering; therefore, he does not cling. Moreover, Mahāmati, "clinging" refers to when foolish commoners, desiring the pleasures of enjoyment, pray for rebirth in existence by means of moral precepts, vows, austerities, and observances.
And they do not grasp at them;
rather, they dedicate [their merit] toward attaining the excellence of their own internal realization.
They apply themselves to the factors of ethical discipline (*śīlāṅga*) by way of the aspect of the characteristics of non-conceptual, untainted phenomena (*anāsravadharma*).
Mahāmati, this is the characteristic of the attachment to rules and rituals of a stream-enterer;
however, Mahāmati, for a stream-enterer who has abandoned the three fetters, lust, hatred, and delusion do not arise.
Mahāmati said: "The Blessed One has taught that passion (*rāga*) is of many kinds. Which among these is the passion that is abandoned here?

The Blessed One replied: "It is the passion for union with women, characterized by the desire for sense objects and the senses, which provides pleasure in the present but is the cause for the arising of suffering in the future—[a passion manifested] through scratching, slapping, embracing, kissing, hugging, smelling, and glancing with sidelong looks."
In that regard, Mahāmati, passion does not arise for him.
Why is that? Because he has attained the dwelling in the bliss of samādhi.
Therefore, this [attachment] is abandoned,
but not the attachment to the attainment of nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, what is the characteristic of the fruit of the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*)?
It is this: conceptualization regarding the appearance of the characteristics of form arises only once.

Because of the absence of the characteristics of signs, views, and the characterized object, and because the characteristics of the stages of meditation have been clearly seen, one will return to this world only once more and attain parinirvāṇa for the sake of making an end to suffering.
Therefore, he is called a "once-returner.
In that regard, Mahāmati, how does one become a "non-returner"?

It is because of the non-arising of views, faults, latent tendencies, and conceptualizations regarding the existence and non-existence of the characteristics of form in the past, future, and present; and because of the non-returning and the abandonment of the forms of the fetters, one is called a "non-returner."

Furthermore, Mahāmati, one is called an Arhat because of the absence of conceptual constructions regarding meditation, the object of meditation, meditative absorptions, liberations, powers, superknowledges, afflictions, and suffering.
Mahāmati said: "Furthermore, three kinds of Arhats have been spoken of by the Blessed One.
To which of these, Blessed One, is this term 'Arhat' applied?
Is it, Blessed One, for one who has attained the path of the single vehicle of tranquility?"
"Is it for one who is deluded regarding the roots of merit cultivated through the vow for enlightenment,
or for one who is a created emanation?
The Blessed One said, "Mahāmati, it is for the Śrāvaka who has attained the path that leads exclusively to tranquility."
But it is not so for others.

However, Mahāmati, there are those who have practiced the conduct of a bodhisattva and those who are emanations created by Buddhas; because they are preceded by skillful means, roots of merit, and vows, they manifest birth within the circles of assemblies for the purpose of adorning the circles of the Buddha's assemblies.

Mahāmati, this teaching of various distinctions in the movement and configuration of conceptualization is as follows: because of the seclusion of the attainment of the fruit, the meditation, the meditator, and the object of meditation, and because of the realization that these are but the manifestations of one's own mind, the characteristic of attaining the fruit is taught.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, if it had occurred to a stream-enterer: "These are the fetters," [he would not have been so].
If one thinks, "I am not conjoined with these," that would entail a duality, whereby one would have fallen into the view of a self and remain with fetters unabandoned.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, in order to transcend the realms of the meditative absorptions (dhyāna), the immeasurables (apramāṇa), and the formless (ārūpya), one must effect the turning away from the characteristics of what is seen as one's own mind.

Moreover, Mahāmati, it is not tenable for one to enter the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (saṃjñāveditanirodhasamāpatti) by merely transcending the movement of what is seen as one's own mind, because [all things] are nothing but mind (cittamātra).
Regarding this, it is said:
The meditations, the immeasurables, the formless attainments, and the cessation of perception—none of these exist in Mind-only. (Lankavatara 2.174)
The fruit of stream-entry, as well as that of the once-returner,
the fruit of non-returning, and arhatship— these are but the delusions of the mind.
The meditator, the meditation, and the object of meditation; abandonment and the vision of the truths—all this is merely conceptual construction. He who understands this is liberated.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are two kinds of intellect (*buddhi*): the analytical intellect (*pravicaya-buddhi*) and that which establishes the grasping and adherence to the characteristics of conceptual construction (*vikalpa-lakṣaṇa-grāha-abhiniveśa-pratiṣṭhāpikā*).

In this regard, Mahāmati, what is called the analytical intellect is that by which, when the characteristics of the intrinsic nature of phenomena (*bhāva-svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*) are analyzed, they are not perceived as being devoid of the four extremes (*catuṣkoṭi-rahita*);
that is the analytical intellect.

In this regard, Mahāmati, the "fourfold alternative" (catuṣkoṭikā) refers to that which is free from unity, difference, both, neither, existence, non-existence, permanence, and impermanence; this is what I call the fourfold alternative.
Mahāmati, all phenomena are said to be devoid of this fourfold alternative.
This fourfold alternative, Mahāmati, should be applied when examining all phenomena.
In this regard, Mahāmati, what is the intellect that establishes the grasping and adherence to the characteristics of conceptual construction?

It is that by which, Mahāmati, through the grasping and adherence to the characteristics of the mind’s conceptual construction, one superimposes— by means of false attribution— the great elements, whose characteristics are heat, fluidity, motion, and solidity, based on an adherence to propositions, reasons, characteristics, and examples.
That is the intellect which establishes the grasping and adherence to the characteristics of conceptual construction.

Mahāmati, this is the characteristic of these two types of intellect; endowed with this characteristic of the two types of intellect, Bodhisattvas attain the realization of the selflessness of phenomena and persons, and become skilled in the stages of practice that investigate the non-manifesting intellect.
They attain the first stage and enter into a hundred samādhis;
through the attainment of these distinguished samādhis, they behold a hundred Buddhas and bodhisattvas.
They penetrate a hundred eons from the past and the future,
and they illuminate a hundred buddha-fields.
Having illuminated a hundred buddha-fields, being experts in the methods and characteristics of the progressively higher stages, they sport through the excellence of their vows.

Having been consecrated by the empowerment of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghābhiṣeka*) and having attained the stage of the Tathāgata’s personal realization (*pratyātma-bhūmi*), those whose dharmas are firmly bound to the ten points of ultimate perfection shine forth with various rays of emanation for the sake of maturing sentient beings, while remaining composed in the bliss of their own internal realization.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should become skilled in the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derived matter (*bhautika*).
And how, Mahāmati, does a bodhisattva become skilled in the primary elements and their derived matter?

In this regard, Mahāmati, a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains himself thus: "That is the truth wherein there is no arising of the primary elements," and he perceives that these elements, Mahāmati, are unarisen.

Observing in this way, one realizes that "name" is merely conceptual construction and nothing more than what is seen of one's own mind; because external entities do not exist, one perceives that this so-called triple world is merely a conceptual construction of what is seen by the mind, devoid of the great elements and their derivatives.

One perceives it as purified according to the method of the four alternatives, free from self and what belongs to a self, established in the state of its own characteristic as it truly is, and perfected in the characteristic of non-arising.
In that regard, Mahāmati, how does the derivative element arise from the primary elements?

That is to say, Mahāmati, the primary element of the discrimination of moisture produces the water-element, both internal and external. The primary element of the discrimination of energy produces the fire-element, both internal and external.
Mahāmati, the great element of the conceptualization of movement produces the internal and external wind-element.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, the great element of the conceptualization of the differentiation of form generates the internal and external earth-element together with space.
Through adherence to false truths, the collection of the five aggregates—the primary elements and their derivatives—proceeds.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, consciousness proceeds toward the transition to another state of existence because it is caused by the attachment to and desire for various words and objects; thus consciousness functions.
Mahāmati, there is a cause for the primary elements and their derivatives—the great elements—but there is no cause for the great elements themselves.
For what reason?

Because, Mahāmati, the arising of the conjunction of activity occurs for those who possess the grasping of the characteristics of signs and forms, as well as the application of action; it does not occur for those who lack such signs.
Therefore, Mahāmati, this characteristic of the great elements and their derivatives is conceptualized by the non-Buddhist teachers, but not by me.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, we shall explain the characteristic of the intrinsic nature of the aggregates.
In this regard, Mahāmati, there are five aggregates.
Which are they? Namely: form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
In this regard, Mahāmati, there are four formless aggregates: feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Form, Mahāmati, consists of the four great elements, and these elements are mutually distinct in their characteristics.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, for those things that are formless, there is no numerical designation of four, just as in the case of space.
For example, Mahāmati, space transcends the characteristics of number; nevertheless, it is conceptually constructed as "space."

In the same way, Mahāmati, the aggregates (*skandha*) transcend number, characteristics, and calculation; they are devoid of existence and non-existence and free from the four alternatives (*cātuṣkoṭika*). They are described by means of numerical enumeration and calculation only for the sake of fools, not for the noble ones (*ārya*). Furthermore, Mahāmati, like the various forms and shapes of an illusion, they are designated as being free from identity and difference, like a dream or a reflected image. Because their basis is not different [from consciousness], and because of the delusion regarding the movement of noble wisdom, Mahāmati, the conceptualization of the aggregates appears.
Mahāmati, this is the characteristic of the intrinsic nature of the aggregates of the aggregates;
and that conceptual construction must be turned away by you, and having turned it away, you must provide instruction on the dharmas that are secluded from conceptual proliferation.

Mahāmati, when the teaching of the secluded Dharma is given in all the assembly circles of the Buddhas to ward off the views of the non-Buddhists, the vision of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) is purified,
and there is entry into the *Dūraṅgamā* (Far-Reaching) stage.
Having entered that great stage of *Dūraṅgamā*, one becomes a master of many meditative concentrations (*samādhi*).
And by attaining the mind-made body, one attains a concentration that is like an illusion.
Having reached mastery over the powers and superknowledges, one becomes a source of sustenance for all sentient beings, just like the earth.
Mahāmati, just as the great earth is a source of sustenance for all sentient beings, so too does this person become a support for all beings.
In the same way, Mahāmati, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva becomes the sustainer of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of nirvāṇa.
What are the four? They are:

(1) the nirvāṇa that is the non-existence of the intrinsic nature of things; (2) the nirvāṇa that is the non-existence of the variety of characteristics and things; (3) the nirvāṇa that is the realization of the non-existence of specific characteristics and things; and (4) the nirvāṇa that is the severance of the continuity and succession of the specific and general characteristics of the aggregates.
Mahāmati, these four kinds of nirvāṇa belong to the non-Buddhist teachers, but not to my teaching.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, in my teaching, the cessation of the discriminating mental consciousness is called nirvāṇa.
Mahāmati said: "Has it not been established by the Blessed One that there are eight consciousnesses?
The Blessed One replied: "They have been established, Mahāmati.
Mahāmati said: "If, Blessed One, they have indeed been established..."
"In that case, how is it that only the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) ceases, and not the seven [other] consciousnesses?
The Blessed One said: "Mahāmati, because they have that as their cause and object, the seven consciousnesses come into operation."

Furthermore, Mahāmati, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), functioning through attachment to the discernment of objects, nourishes the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) by means of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
The mind (*manas*), together with it, functions in the form of conceit (*manyana*) through its attachment to the grasping of "self" and "mine.

Having a characteristic inseparable from the body of the storehouse-consciousness, and taking that storehouse-consciousness as its cause and object, the collection of minds (*cittakalāpa*) proceeds, mutually causal, due to attachment to objects that are but the manifestations of one's own mind.
O Mahāmati, like the waves of the ocean, they arise and cease, driven by the winds of the objects perceived as one's own mind.
Therefore, O Mahāmati, when that mental consciousness (manovijñāna) ceases, the cessation of the seven consciousnesses occurs.
Regarding this, it is said:
"I do not enter nirvana through existence, activity, or characteristics;
for when the consciousness that is the cause of conceptual construction has ceased, I am indeed extinguished. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 2.177)
Having that as its cause and taking that as its object, it relies upon the movement of the mind;
it provides the cause for the mind, and consciousness is dependent upon it.
Just as when a great flood has subsided there is no arising of waves,
so too, when the variety of consciousnesses has ceased, it does not proceed.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, we shall teach the characteristics of the method for distinguishing the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), so that by means of this well-distinguished method for distinguishing the imagined nature, you and other Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, being free from the conceptualizations of discrimination, with minds that clearly perceive the internal noble self-realization and the methods of the non-Buddhist paths, and having abandoned the discrimination of grasped object and grasping subject, [will understand] the various and manifold characteristics of the dependent nature (*paratantra*).
They will not conceptualize the forms of the imagined nature (*parikalpitasvabhāva*).
In this regard, Mahāmati, what is the characteristic of the method for distinguishing the imagined nature? It is as follows:

the conceptualization of verbal expression, the conceptualization of non-compliance, the conceptualization of characteristics, the conceptualization of objects, and the conceptualization of intrinsic nature.

Discrimination of causes, discrimination of views, discrimination of reasoning, discrimination of arising, discrimination of non-arising, discrimination of connection, and discrimination of bondage and non-bondage— Mahāmati, these are the characteristics of the method for distinguishing the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
In this regard, Mahāmati, what is the conceptualization of verbal expression?
It is the attachment to the sweetness of various tones and songs.
This, Mahāmati, is the conceptualization of verbal expression.

In this regard, Mahāmati, what is the conceptualization of the signified (abhidheya-vikalpa)? It is the conceptualization that there exists some signified entity possessing an intrinsic nature (svabhāva) accessible through the range of noble wisdom (āryajñāna), depending upon which verbal expression proceeds. In this regard, what is the conceptualization of characteristics (lakṣaṇa-vikalpa)?

That is to say, regarding that very object of expression called a "mirage," one adheres through an adherence to the diversity of characteristics; namely, one conceptualizes all things based on the characteristics of heat, fluidity, mobility, and solidity.
In that regard, what is the conceptualization of objects (*arthavikalpa*)? It is the verbal expression directed toward objects such as gold, silver, and various kinds of jewels.
In that regard, what is the conceptualization of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvavikalpa*)?

It is as follows: the determination of the intrinsic nature of entities, thinking "this is thus and not otherwise," which they conceptualize through the views of the conceptualizations of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
In that regard, what is the conceptualization of cause (*hetuvikalpa*)?

That is to say: when existence and non-existence are differentiated by whatever cause and condition through the arising of the characteristics of a cause, that is the conceptualization of causes (*hetu-vikalpa*).
In that regard, what is the conceptualization of views (*dṛṣṭi-vikalpa*)?
It is the dogmatic adherence to the false views of non-existence, existence, identity, difference, both, or neither, as well as the conceptualizations of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
In that regard, what is the conceptualization of reasoning (*yuktivikalpa*)?
It is the instruction on the logical analysis of the characteristics of "self" and "what belongs to the self.
In that regard, what is the conceptualization of arising (*utpādavikalpa*)?
That is to say, it is the adherence to the arising of an entity that is either existent or non-existent by means of conditions.
In that regard, what is the conceptualization of non-arising?
It is the notion that all entities, having never arisen before, come into being through conditions after not having existed, possessing no causal body.
In that regard, what is the conceptual construction of connection?
It is as follows: it is connected simultaneously, like a golden thread.
In that regard, what is the conceptual construction of binding and non-binding?
That is to say, it is like the adherence to the cause of bondage and that which is bound.
Just as a person is made into a knot by the conjunction with a cord and is released from it,
so too, Mahāmati, is the characteristic of the method for distinguishing the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

Mahāmati, in this characteristic of the method for distinguishing the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), all foolish commoners (*bāla-pṛthagjana*) become attached. Clinging to the dependent nature (*paratantra*) as being either existent or non-existent, they become attached to the manifold variety of the imagined nature.
Just as one sees the various forms based on an illusion, fools conceptualize them through the cognition of seeing another illusion.
Moreover, Mahāmati, illusion is neither different from its variety nor non-different from it;
for if it were different, the variety would not have illusion as its cause.
If, on the other hand, it were non-different [from illusion], there would be no distinction between the variety of illusion and the variety [of the world];
yet that distinction is observed.
Therefore, it is neither different nor non-different.
For this reason, Mahāmati, you and other Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should not adhere to the view that illusion exists or does not exist.
Regarding this, it is said:
Mind functions in connection with objects; cognition proceeds toward reasoning;
but wisdom indeed operates within the non-manifest and the particular.
The imagined nature does not exist within the dependent nature;
the imagined is grasped through delusion, but the dependent is not imagined.
Just as a magical illusion is not established through the production of various limbs,
so too the manifold sign is not established when it is being conceptualized.
The sign, consisting of inner corruption, is a bond arising from the mind;
for one who does not understand that it is imagined, it is conceptualized through the dependent nature.
That which is the imagined nature is indeed the dependent nature itself;
for it is the imagined nature, appearing in various forms, that is conceptualized within the dependent nature.
There are the conventional and the ultimate; there is no third cause.
The imagined is said to be the conventional, and by cutting that off, one reaches the sphere of the noble ones.
Just as for yogins a single object appears as manifold, yet there is no actual multiplicity therein; so too is the nature of the imagined.
Just as those with cataracts perceive a variegated vision of forms,
so do the ignorant perceive the dependent nature— which is neither form nor non-form— as being like the cataract itself.
Just as gold may be pure and water free from turbidity,
and just as the sky is pure due to the absence of clouds, so too is the [mind] conceived as pure.
The imagined nature does not exist, yet the dependent nature is found;
for by conceptualizing through superimposition and denial, one is destroyed. (Lankavatara Sutra 2.189)
If the imagined nature were non-existent by virtue of the dependent nature,
then existence would indeed exist without non-existence, and existence would be born from non-existence.
Based upon the imagined (parikalpita), the dependent (paratantra) is perceived; through the connection between signs and names, the imagined arises. (Lankavatara 2.191)
When the imagined nature is seen to be absolutely unestablished and not arising from another,
then the pure ultimate intrinsic nature is realized.
The imagined is of ten kinds, and the dependent is of six kinds;
the suchness known within oneself is therefore without distinction.
The five dharmas are reality, and likewise the three intrinsic natures;
the yogi who contemplates these does not transcend suchness.
The sign is indeed the dependent nature, while that which is called "name" is the imagined;
however, the imagined sign proceeds from the dependent nature.
When analyzed by the intellect, however, there is neither the dependent nor the imagined;
since the perfected nature does not exist as a real entity, how can it be conceptualized by the intellect?
The perfected nature exists as a reality that is devoid of both existence and non-existence;
being free from both existence and non-existence, how indeed could those two natures [the imagined and the dependent] exist?
Within the imagined nature (parikalpitasvabhāva), the other two natures are established:
the imagined is seen as manifold, while the pure is the domain of the noble ones (ārya).
For that which is imagined, appearing in manifold ways, is conceptualized by means of the dependent nature;
indeed, if it were conceptualized otherwise, one would resort to the doctrines of the non-Buddhists.
It is said that "imagination" (kalpanā) is "imagined" (kalpita) because it arises from causes through perception;
indeed, that very same [reality] is the perfected (niṣpanna), being free from the two-fold conceptual construction (vikalpa).
Again, Mahāmati said: "May the Blessed One teach me the characteristic of the realization of noble self-knowledge and the Single Vehicle (ekayāna).
