By means of this characteristic of the realization of noble self-knowledge and the Single Vehicle, O Blessed One, I and other Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas shall become skilled in noble self-knowledge and the Single Vehicle, and thus not be led by others regarding the Buddha-dharmas."
The Blessed One said: "In that case, Mahāmati, listen and attend well and thoroughly;
I shall speak to you."

"Excellent, Blessed One! Mahāmati, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this to him: "Mahāmati, because of the absence of conceptualization regarding the teachings of authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and reliable authorities (*āpta*), the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, alone and retired to a secluded place, investigates by means of his own internal realization; he is not led by others and is free from the conceptualization of views."
One exerts effort by way of entering the successive stages of the Tathāgata.
Mahāmati, this is the characteristic of the realization of noble wisdom within one's own self.
In that regard, what is the characteristic of the realization of the Single Vehicle?
That is to say, because of the realization and awakening to the path of the single vehicle, I speak of it as the "single vehicle.
What is the realization and awakening to the path of the single vehicle? It is this:

through the non-occurrence of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) due to abiding in the reality of the absence of the duality of grasped and grasper, the awakening to the single vehicle is accomplished.
This realization of the Single Vehicle, Mahāmati, has never before been attained by any outsiders, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, Brahmās, or others, except by me;
for this reason, Mahāmati, it is called the "Single Vehicle."
Mahāmati said: "For what reason, Blessed One, have three vehicles been taught by you, while a single vehicle is not taught?
The Blessed One replied: "Mahāmati, because all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not possess the nature of attaining parinirvāṇa by themselves, I do not speak of a single vehicle."
Because, Mahāmati, all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are liberated through the instruction on the discipline, seclusion, and yoga of the Tathāgata, and not by themselves.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, because all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas have not yet abandoned the karmic latencies of the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), there is not a single vehicle for them.

Also, because they have not realized the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) and have not attained the inconceivable transformation-death (*acintyapariṇāmacyuti*), I teach three vehicles to the Śrāvakas. However, Mahāmati, when all their faulty latencies have been abandoned through the realization of the selflessness of phenomena, [then the single vehicle is established].
Then, due to the absence of the intoxication of meditative absorption caused by the defects of their latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), they awaken within the untainted realm (*anāsravadhātu*).
Furthermore, having again fulfilled the provisions included within the supramundane untainted realm, they will attain mastery over the inconceivable Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

Regarding this, it is said: "The vehicle of the gods, the vehicle of Brahmā, likewise that of the Śrāvakas, and that of the Tathāgatas and Pratyekabuddhas—these vehicles I proclaim. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 2.201)
There is indeed no finality of vehicles as long as the mind continues to function;
but when the mind has undergone revolution, there is neither vehicle nor those who ride it.

There is no actual establishment of vehicles; I speak of the distinction between vehicles only for the sake of leading on the foolish. I speak of the distinction between vehicles for the purpose of guiding the ignorant.
Likewise, there are three kinds of liberation and the selflessness of phenomena;
those [Buddhas] are distinguished by their liberation through the knowledge of equality regarding the afflictions.
Just as a piece of wood is carried away by the waves in the ocean,
so indeed is the deluded disciple carried away by the marks.
Bound by the afflictions of latent tendencies yet dissociated from the outbursts [of passion],
they remain in the untainted realm, intoxicated by the pride of meditative concentration.
There is no final attainment for him, nor does he ever return;
having attained the body of meditative concentration, he does not awaken until the end of the eon.
Just as a drunken man awakens from his intoxication when the liquor has worn off,
so shall they attain my body, which is called the Buddha-dharma.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Compendium of All Dharmas," in the *Laṅkāvatāra* consisting of thirty-six thousand [verses].
START Chapter 3 (Vaidya 56):
The Third Chapter, titled "Impermanence."

Then the Blessed One spoke again to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati: "Mahāmati, I shall teach you the characteristics of the method for distinguishing the various modes of the mind-made body (*manomayakāya*). Listen to this, and attend to it well and thoroughly;
I shall speak to you."
"Excellent, Blessed One," the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this to him: "Mahāmati, the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*) is of three kinds. What are the three kinds?"

Namely: the mind-made body consisting of the attainment of the bliss of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the mind-made body consisting of the realization of the intrinsic nature of phenomena (*dharma-svabhāva*), and the mind-made body consisting of the activity of formative forces innate to the [spiritual] class.
Yogins attain these through the thorough knowledge of the characteristics of the successive higher stages.
In this regard, Mahāmati, what is the mind-made body consisting of the attainment of the bliss of meditative concentration?

That is to say, on the third, fourth, and fifth stages, through dwelling in the various forms of solitude of one's own mind, there is the non-activity of the mind that experiences the blissful attainment characterized by the consciousness-waves arising from the ocean of the mind;
because of the thorough knowledge of the non-existence and existence of objects as manifestations of one's own mind, it is called the "mind-made body" (*manomaya-kāya*) of the mind.
In that regard, what is the "mind-made body of the realization of the intrinsic nature of phenomena" (*dharmasvabhāvāvabodha-manomaya-kāya*)?

That is to say, on the eighth stage, through the awakening that discerns the non-appearance of phenomena such as illusion and so forth, one undergoes the revolution of the basis of the mind; by attaining the illusion-like samādhi and other gateways of samādhi, there arises [an appearance] that is blossomed with the various characteristics of mastery and supernormal powers,
resembling the speed of thought, appearing like an illusion, a dream, or a reflection, non-material yet resembling material elements, and endowed with all the diverse and variegated limbs of form.

The body that follows the circles of assemblies in all Buddha-fields is called "mind-made" (*manomaya*) because it has reached the realization of the intrinsic nature of phenomena (*dharma-svabhāva*).
In this context, what is the mind-made body consisting of the activities of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) co-nascent with the [Buddha-]class?

It is called the mind-made body consisting of the activities of the formative forces co-nascent with the class because of its awakening to the characteristic of bliss in the personal realization of all Buddha-dharmas.
In this regard, Mahāmati, you should apply yourself to the practice of investigating and realizing the characteristics of the three bodies.
Regarding this, it is said:
"My vehicle is not the Mahāyāna; it is neither sound nor syllables.
It is indeed neither truths nor liberations, nor is it the sphere of the non-manifest. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 3.1)
But what is the Mahāyāna? It is mastery over meditative concentrations;
it is the manifold mind-made body adorned with the flowers of sovereign powers.
Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Blessed One as follows: "The five acts of immediate retribution have been taught by the Blessed One.
What, O Blessed One, are those five acts of immediate retribution, by committing which a son of good family or a daughter of good family becomes one who belongs to the Avīci hell?
The Blessed One said: "In that case, Mahāmati, listen."
"Pay close and careful attention;
I shall speak to you.
"Very well, Blessed One," the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati replied to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One said this: "In that regard, Mahāmati, what are the five acts of immediate retribution? They are: the killing of one's mother, the killing of one's father, the killing of an Arhat, causing a schism in the Saṅgha, and with a malicious mind, drawing blood from the body of a Tathāgata."
In this regard, Mahāmati, who is the mother of sentient beings?
It is craving, which leads to renewed existence and is accompanied by delight and passion; she stands as the mother.
Ignorance stands as the father for the arising of the village of the sense-bases.
Because of the absolute and fundamental eradication of both these parents, there is the "killing of mother and father.

In that context, because of the total uprooting of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), which resemble enemies and possess the nature of being provoked like the venom of a rat, there is the "killing of an Arhat.
In that regard, what is the "breaking of the Saṃgha"?

That is to say, Mahāmati, because of the total destruction of the very root of the aggregate of the skandhas— which have mutually distinct characteristics— it is called "schism in the Saṅgha. Furthermore, for those who understand that the eight bodies of consciousness, which are external to both specific and general characteristics, are merely the manifestation of one's own mind, to utterly destroy them through the defiled conceptualization of the three liberations and the outflows— this is called "shedding the blood of a Buddha with a malicious mind" and being a perpetrator of an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*).

Mahāmati, these are the five internal immediate transgressions; by committing these, a son of good family or a daughter of good family becomes an immediate offender who has nonetheless realized the Dharma.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, I shall teach you the external acts of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*), by the teaching of which you and other bodhisattvas will not fall into delusion in the future age.
What, then, are they?
That is to say, regarding those immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*) described in the recitations of the teachings—
having committed which one does not realize any of the three liberations (*vimukti*), except for the realization through the empowerment of a manifestation (*nirmitādhiṣṭhāna*)—
for a disciple empowered by a manifestation, Mahāmati, [realization occurs] either through the empowerment of a Bodhisattva or through the empowerment of a Tathāgata.

For the sake of turning back the remorse and the view of remorse of anyone else who has committed an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*), and for the sake of ensuring that one who has laid down the burden is free from the view of remorse;
thinking, "I shall once again provide encouragement," I demonstrate the realization through the empowerment of emanations.

Mahāmati, there is no realization at all for one who has committed an immediate transgression, except when—through the awakening to the fact that it is merely the cultivation of what is seen of one's own mind—one perceives the separation from the conceptualizations of body, enjoyment, and abode, as well as from the grasping at self and what belongs to a self. At such a time, [realization occurs].
Having at some time or other encountered a spiritual friend, one is liberated from the faults of one's own conceptual constructions at the junction of another realm of existence.
Regarding this, it is said:
"Craving is indeed called the mother, and ignorance likewise the father;
consciousness, through the awakening to objects, is taught as the Buddha. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 3.3)
The five latent tendencies are indeed the Arhats; the Saṃgha is the collection of the aggregates (skandhas).
Because of the uninterrupted cutting off of the interval, there would be the "immediate" (ānantarya) nature of karma.
Again Mahāmati said: "May the Blessed One teach me how, Blessed One, the Buddhahood of the Blessed Buddhas comes about.

The Blessed One replied: "Mahāmati, the Buddhahood of the Blessed Buddhas comes about through the realization of the selflessness of phenomena and persons, through the thorough knowledge and realization of the two obstructions, through the attainment of the cessation of the two types of death, and through the abandonment of the two types of afflictions, Mahāmati."
Mahāmati, it is through the realization of these very dharmas that the states of śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, and sambuddha come to be.
For this reason, Mahāmati, I teach the Single Vehicle (ekayāna).
In this regard, it is said:
"The two kinds of selflessness, the afflictions, and likewise the two obstructions—by attaining the inconceivable transformational death, one becomes a Tathāgata. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 3.5)

Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati spoke thus again to the Blessed One: "With what intention did the Blessed One, having entered the midst of the assembly, utter these words: 'I myself am all the Buddhas of the past, and the various manifestations of my births in previous lives;
and I myself, at that time and on that occasion, was King Māndhātṛ'?"
"Did the Blessed One teach hundreds of thousands of *jātaka* tales, such as those of Gaja, Śuka, Indra, Vyāsa, and Sunetra?
The Blessed One replied, "Mahāmati, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have taught these with reference to four kinds of equality."
Standing in the midst of the assembly, they utter these words: "At that time, on that occasion, I myself was Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, and Kāśyapa.
With reference to what fourfold equality do they speak thus?
That is to say: the equality of syllables, the equality of speech, the equality of dharmas, and the equality of the body.
Mahāmati, it is with reference to these four kinds of equality that the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas utter words when they have entered the midst of the assembly.
In this regard, Mahāmati, what is the equality of syllables?

That is to say, Mahāmati, those very syllables by which my name is "Buddha" are the same syllables for those Blessed Buddhas; these syllables are without distinction as far as the nature of syllables is concerned. This, Mahāmati, is the equality of syllables.
In this regard, Mahāmati, what is the equality of speech of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas? It is this:

just as my own sixty-fourfold conceptualization of speech proceeds with the resonance and sound of the Brahma-voice, even so, Mahāmati, the sixty-fourfold resonance and sound of the Brahma-voice of those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas proceeds in exactly the same way.
Verbal conceptualization proceeds neither deficient nor excessive, being indistinguishable from the nature of the melodic sound and resonance of the kalaviṅka bird and the voice of Brahmā.
In that regard, what is the equality of the body?

It is this: namely, that I and those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are equal and indistinguishable in terms of the Dharma-body and the body of physical marks and secondary characteristics, except for the sake of those to be trained.
In various instances, according to the specific dispositions of sentient beings, the Tathāgatas manifest a diversity of forms.
In that regard, Mahāmati, what is the equality of phenomena (*dharmasamatā*)? It is this:
namely, that both they and I are attainers of the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣyā dharmāḥ*).
Mahāmati, it is with reference to these four kinds of equality that the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones utter these words when they have entered the midst of the assembly.
Regarding this, it is said: "Kāśyapa, Krakucchanda, Konākamuni, and I myself—
having arisen in equanimity, I speak for the sons of the Jinas."

Again, Mahāmati said: "Regarding that which was spoken by the Blessed One: 'From the night the Tathāgata attained perfect enlightenment until the night he shall pass into final nirvana, in this interval not even a single syllable has been uttered by the Tathāgata, nor will he ever speak one.'"
"Non-speaking is the Buddha’s speech.
With what intention, Mahāmati, did the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, say that "non-speaking is the Buddha’s speech"?
The Blessed One replied: "Mahāmati, it was with reference to two things that I said this."
What are these two dharmas?
Namely, the dharma-nature realized within oneself and the dharma-nature of primordial stability. Mahāmati, it was with reference to these two dharmas that this was spoken by me.
In that regard, what is the continuity with the reality of one's own inner realization (*svapratyātmadharmatā*)?

That which has been realized by those Tathāgatas has also been realized by me—neither deficient nor redundant—the domain of the range of one's own inner realization, free from the conceptualization of speech, and liberated from the two modes of syllables.
In that regard, what is the primordial abiding nature of phenomena (*paurāṇasthitidharmatā*)?

That is to say, Mahāmati, this is the ancient nature of things (dharmatā) which is my own; like a mine of gold, silver, or pearls, Mahāmati, is the stability of the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu-sthititā).

Whether Tathāgatas arise or whether Tathāgatas do not arise, this nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the stability of phenomena (dharmasthititā), and the fixed order of phenomena (dharmaniyāmatā) remains ever established for these phenomena.
It is like the path to an ancient city, O Mahāmati. For example, Mahāmati, suppose a certain man wandering in a wilderness were to see an ancient city with its entrance and paths intact;
he would then enter that city.
Having entered there and settled down, he would experience the pleasure of the city's activities.
What do you think, Mahāmati? Was that path created by that man by which he entered the city and experienced its various wonders?
He replied, "No, Blessed One.

The Blessed One said: "In this very way, Mahāmati, that which has been realized by me and by those Tathāgatas—this nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the stability of phenomena (*dharma-sthititā*), the fixed order of phenomena (*dharma-niyāmatā*), suchness (*tathatā*), reality (*bhūtatā*), and truth (*satyatā*)—remains ever-abiding.
For this reason, Mahāmati, I have said: 'From the night the Tathāgata attained perfect enlightenment until the night he will pass into final nirvāṇa...'"
In this interval, not even a single syllable has been uttered by the Tathāgata, nor will he ever utter one.
Regarding this, it is said:
"Between the night of my attainment [of enlightenment] and the night of my final nirvana,
nothing at all has been revealed by me."
It was spoken by me with reference to the abiding nature of phenomena as realized within each individual;
there is not the slightest distinction between those Buddhas and myself.

Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati again entreated the Blessed One: "May the Blessed One teach me the characteristic of neither-existence-nor-non-existence of all dharmas, so that I and other Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, being free from existence and non-existence, may quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
The Blessed One said: "In that case, Mahāmati, listen; attend well and thoroughly to what I shall say to you."
"Excellent, Blessed One," the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this: "Mahāmati, this world relies upon duality—namely, reliance on existence and reliance on non-existence.
It has fallen into views characterized by desire for being and non-being, and perceives a way of escape where there is no escape."
In this regard, Mahāmati, how is it that the world relies on existence?
That is to say: the world arises from existing causes and conditions, not from non-existing ones;
and that which is already existing arises as it arises, not that which is non-existing.
Speaking thus, Mahāmati, one becomes a proponent of the existence of causes and conditions for the existence of entities and of the world.
In that regard, Mahāmati, how does one rely on non-existence?
That is to say, having accepted the existence of passion, hatred, and delusion, one again conceptualizes the presence or absence of those states of passion, hatred, and delusion.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, regarding one who does not accept the existence of entities because they are devoid of the characteristics of entities,

and who does not accept that the Buddhas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas possess passion, hatred, and delusion because they are liberated from the characteristics of entities, saying "they do not exist"— which of these two, Mahāmati, is the nihilist?
Mahāmati said: "Blessed One, regarding this one who, having admitted passion, hatred, and delusion, does not admit them again.
The Blessed One said: "Excellent, excellent, Mahāmati! Indeed, it is excellent of you, Mahāmati!"
Since you have spoken thus, Mahāmati, it is not only because of the existence or non-existence of passion, hatred, and delusion that one becomes a nihilist;
one also becomes a nihilist with respect to the Buddhas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas.
For what reason?
Because, Mahāmati, afflictions are non-apprehendable both internally and externally;
for indeed, attachment, aversion, and delusion are not apprehended internally or externally, because they are bodiless.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, because he does not admit the existence of the absence of passion, hatred, and delusion, one becomes a nihilist regarding the Buddhas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas.
Those Buddhas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas are liberated by nature, owing to the absence of both bondage and the cause of bondage.
For when there is bondage, Mahāmati, there is both the bound and the cause of bondage.
Speaking thus, Mahāmati, one becomes a nihilist.
This, Mahāmati, is the characteristic of non-existence and existence. And it was with this in mind, Mahāmati, that I said: "It would indeed be better [to hold a view] as large as Mount Sumeru..."
But for one who is conceited regarding non-existence and existence, there is no view of emptiness;
rather, Mahāmati, such a person is a nihilist who is conceited regarding non-existence and existence.
Their inclination has fallen into the views of specific and general characteristics, and they do not realize that what appears is merely the manifestation of their own mind.

Because he does not accept [a self], because of his view that external objects exist, and because of his view that things are eternal, the Vaināśika— conceptualizing the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases as being devoid of conceptual constructs and words, yet distinct through a succession of moments and repeatedly ceasing and arising in a continuous stream— once again becomes a nihilist.
In this regard, it is said:
"As long as the mind has 'existence' and 'non-existence' as its two extremes within its range, when that range is ceased, the mind itself is rightly ceased. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 3.9)
Because there is no grasping of objects, cessation is neither non-existent nor existent;
the reality of suchness exists as it is the sphere of experience for the noble ones.
Those for whom there is arising after non-existence, or destruction after having existed,
and who maintain that things are both existent and non-existent through conditions— they do not abide in my teaching.
Existence is not established by conditions through the heterodox teachers, nor by the Buddhas, nor by me, nor by anyone else; how then could it be non-existent?
By whom has the existence of that which lacks inherent existence through conditions been established?
Through the evil view of the doctrine of arising, one conceptualizes "it exists" and "it does not exist."
For one for whom nothing arises and nothing ceases,
the notions of "existence" and "non-existence" do not occur, as they behold the world as solitary.
Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati again entreated the Blessed One: "May the Blessed One teach me;
may the Sugata teach me;
may the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, the most excellent among speakers, teach me the characteristics of the method of the established tenet."

"By means of this well-distinguished characteristic of the method of the established doctrine (*siddhāntanayalakṣaṇa*), may I and other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain mastery over the course of the method of the established doctrine, and quickly become unsurpassed and no longer led by others among all logicians and non-Buddhist teachers.
The Blessed One said: "In that case, Mahāmati, listen."
"Pay close and careful attention;
I shall speak to you.
"Very well, Blessed One," the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati replied to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One said this to him: "Mahāmati, there are two kinds of characteristics for the method of established tenets (*siddhāntanaya*) for all Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas; namely, the method of established tenets (*siddhāntanaya*) and the method of teaching (*deśanānaya*).

In this regard, Mahāmati, the method of established tenets refers to the specific characteristic of internal realization (*pratyātmādhigama*), which is devoid of speech, conceptual construction, and syllables; it leads to the attainment of the state of the untainted realm (*anāsravadhātu*); it possesses the self-characteristic of the stages of internal realization and the stages of attainment; and it is free from all logic, heterodox views, and Māras."
Having struck down those Māras of the heterodox teachers, the state of personal realization shines forth.
Mahāmati, this is the characteristic of the method of established tenets (*siddhāntanaya*).
In that regard, what is the method of teaching (*deśanānaya*)?

That is to say, it is the diverse instruction of the ninefold teaching, free from the positions of identity, difference, existence, or non-existence, preceded by the methods of skillful means, and an introduction to the vision for sentient beings.
Whatever a person has faith in, that one should teach to them.
This, Mahāmati, is the characteristic of the method of teaching.
In this regard, Mahāmati, you and other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should apply yourselves with diligent practice.
In this regard, it is said:
Those who understand the distinctions between the established tenets, the methods of reasoning, and the instruction for personal realization do not fall under the sway of speculative logic.
No entity exists in reality as it is conceptualized by the ignorant;
yet why do the logicians not accept liberation through the absence of such entities? (Lankavatara 3.16)
For one who perceives the conditioned as bound by arising and ceasing, the two views flourish; they do not see [reality] because of their perversion.
Nirvāṇa alone would be the truth, devoid of mind;
one should view the world, which is imagined, as resembling the trunk of a plantain tree or a magical illusion. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 3.18)
Passion does not exist, nor does hatred or delusion, nor even a person;
for it is from craving that the aggregates arise, appearing like a dream.
Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati again entreated the Blessed One: "May the Blessed One teach me; may the Sugata teach me the characteristic of unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*).
How, what, by what, and for whom, O Blessed One, does unreal imagination proceed when it proceeds?"
“O Blessed One, it is said that ‘unreal imagination’ is ‘unreal imagination.
O Blessed One, of what dharma is this a designation, namely, ‘unreal imagination’? Or, by imagining what does one become unreal imagination?”
The Blessed One said: "Excellent, excellent, Mahāmati!
It is indeed well of you, Mahāmati, that you consider it necessary to inquire about this matter."

"Mahāmati, you have set out for the benefit of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the sake, welfare, and happiness of the great multitude of beings, both gods and humans.
Therefore, Mahāmati, listen; pay close and careful attention."
"I shall speak to you.
"Excellent, Blessed One," Mahāmati, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this to him: "Mahāmati, discrimination proceeds as it does due to the attachment to the unreal imagination of the various diversities of objects."

Furthermore, Mahāmati, for those people who are obsessed with the attachment to the grasped and the grasper, whose minds have not realized that [the world] is merely the manifestation of their own minds,
who have fallen into the positions of views regarding existence and non-existence, and who are nourished by the habitual tendencies of the conceptual discrimination of the views of the *tīrthakas*—
for them, the collection of mind and mental factors, termed "conceptual discrimination," proceeds due to the attachment to the perception of external, diverse objects.
It proceeds from the attachment to a self and what belongs to a self.

Mahāmati said: "If, Blessed One, the conceptualization of people proceeds by way of attachment to the unreal imagination of the various diversities of objects—proceeding for those who have fallen into the positions of the views of existence and non-existence, and who are nourished by the counter-conceptualizations of the views of the non-Buddhist teachers regarding the grasped and the grasper—"

Due to the persistent attachment to the perception of various external objects, the collection of mind and mental factors— designated as "conceptualization"— proceeds by functioning through an attachment to diverse states, whether real or unreal, arising from a failure to realize that these are merely the manifestations of one's own mind. Blessed One, it is just as if those various characteristics of external objects were characterized by falling into the positions of existence or non-existence, yet were actually devoid of both being and non-being, and free from the characteristics of [wrong] views.

In the same way, Blessed One, [reality] is free from the characteristics of ultimate truth, means of valid cognition, sense faculties, members of a syllogism, examples, and logical reasons. Therefore, Blessed One, how is it that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) proceeds by conceptually constructing an attachment to various unreal objects within a single [reality],
yet conceptual construction does not proceed by conceptually constructing an attachment to the characteristics of ultimate truth?
"O Blessed One, does it not follow that you advocate a doctrine of inconsistent causes,
by asserting that [the result] arises in one case and not in another? Furthermore,

for you who speak of the activity of views based on unreal conceptualization, there is an adherence to the positions of existence and non-existence— just as one might conceptually construct a single, perfected form from the variety of figures produced by various magical illusions."

Through conceptual construction, there is the existence and non-existence of the diversity of characteristics; yet, because of the cessation of conceptual construction, one falls into the views and inclinations of the Lokāyatikas.
The Blessed One said: "Indeed, Mahāmati, conceptual construction neither proceeds nor ceases. For what reason?"

That is to say, Mahāmati, because the conceptual construction of existence and non-existence does not arise, and because of the absence of external objects of perception, and through the realization that [all] is merely the manifestation of one's own mind, conceptual construction neither arises nor ceases.
However, Mahāmati, it is due to the conceptualization of the diversity of one's own mind by the ignorant that [it appears].
I declare that conceptual construction, preceded by the engagement in activity, arises from attachment to the characteristics of diverse entities.

How indeed, Mahāmati, can foolish common people— by awakening to the fact that [all things] are merely their own mind’s conceptualization, by turning away from views concerning self and what belongs to self, by ceasing the faults of causes, effects, and conditions, and by transforming the basis of their minds through the awakening to mind-only— become perfected in knowledge across all stages and attain the sphere of the Tathāgata’s personal realization, which is the cessation of the conceptualization of views regarding the five dharmas, the three natures, and the reality of things?

Therefore, for this reason, Mahāmati, it is said by me: "Discrimination proceeds from attachment to the variety of unreal objects; one is liberated through the thorough knowledge of the variety of objects of one's own discrimination as they truly are."
Regarding this, it is said:
Those for whom the world proceeds by means of causes and conditions, and who are occupied with the fourfold logical alternatives (cātuṣkoṭika), do not understand my system. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 3.20)
The world is not born from the non-existent, nor from the existent, nor from both existent and non-existent at any time;
it is merely conceptualized by the foolish through conditions and causes.
When one perceives the world as neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent,
then the mind turns back and one realizes selflessness.
All phenomena are unarisen because they arise from conditions;
for all conditions are effects, and existence is not born from an effect.
An effect is not produced from an effect; otherwise, duality would result within the effect.
Furthermore, no entity is perceived as arising from an effect through the consequence of such duality.
When one perceives that conditioned phenomena are devoid of both the object and the subject, then,
having ascertained that it is indeed mind-only, I declare it to be mind-only.
The measure (mātrā) is established as intrinsic nature, devoid of entities produced by conditions;
it is the ultimate state of non-existence, the Supreme Brahman—this is the measure that I proclaim.
For the self exists as a conventional truth (prajñaptisatya), but it does not exist as a substantial reality (dravyasat);
likewise, the "aggregateness" of the aggregates exists through convention, but not as a substantial reality.

Indeed, there are four kinds of equality: the equality of characteristics, that which arises from the state of causality, the equality of selflessness, and for yogins, the fourth is the equality of yoga.
The turning away from all views, free from the imagined and the imagining,
non-apprehension, and non-arising— this I call "mind-only."
Neither existence nor non-existence, free from both existence and non-existence,
suchness that is liberated from the mind— this I call "mind-only. (Lankavatara Sutra 3.30)
Suchness, the limit of emptiness, nirvāṇa, and the realm of phenomena—
the manifold body made of mind— I declare to be mind-only.
Bound by the latencies of conceptual construction, the manifold world arises from the mind; indeed, what appears as external to people is merely the mundane mind itself.
No external object of perception exists; it is indeed the mind that appears as manifold.
Body, enjoyment, and habitat—these I declare to be mind-only.

Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati said this to the Blessed One: "Regarding that which was said by the Blessed One— that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, as well as others, should not grasp the meaning according to the literal expression—
how is it, Blessed One, that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not become one who grasps the meaning according to the literal expression?"
Furthermore, what is "utterance" (ruta), and what is its meaning?
The Blessed One said: "In that case, Mahāmati, listen."
"Listen well and pay close attention;
I shall speak to you.
"So be it, Blessed One," the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati replied to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One said this to him: "In that regard, Mahāmati, what is 'sound' (ruta)? It is the conceptualization of the conjunction of speech and syllables; it is the mutual discourse issued from the teeth, jaws, palate, tongue, and lips, having the habitual tendencies of conceptualization as its cause—this is called 'sound. Furthermore, Mahāmati, what is the 'meaning' (artha)?"

That is to say, by means of the wisdom consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having gone alone to a secluded place, becomes skilled in the meaning as he investigates— by his own intellect, preceded by the revolution of the basis of latent tendencies— the specific characteristics and the progression through the stages and levels that constitute the domain of one's own internal realization, which is the path leading to the city of Nirvana.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, a bodhisattva mahāsattva skilled in words and their meanings perceives that words are neither different from meanings nor non-different from them, and likewise meanings are not different from words. Moreover, Mahāmati, if meaning were different from words, [it would follow that]...
It would have as its cause the manifestation of meaning through speech, and that meaning is entered into by means of speech, just as wealth is revealed by a lamp.
For example, Mahāmati, it is like a certain man who, having taken a lamp, might look at his wealth and think: "This is my wealth; it is of such a kind, and it is in this place."

In the same way, Mahāmati, by means of the lamp of the sounds of verbal conceptualization, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas—being themselves free from verbal conceptualization—enter into the noble state of personal realization.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, regarding those things that are unceasing, unarisen, and by nature in a state of parinirvāṇa— the three vehicles and the one vehicle— within the context of the five consciousnesses, the self-nature, and so forth, one falls into the views of superimposition and denial by adhering to the literal meaning of words.
By conceptualizing them as otherwise than they actually exist, it is like the conceptualization of the various manifestations of an illusion.
For example, Mahāmati, the variety of illusions is seen in one way, yet it is conceptualized in another way by the foolish, but not so by the noble ones.
In this regard, it is said:
Having conceptualized according to the literal sound [of the teachings], they superimpose [their own views] upon the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
And because of that superimposition, they indeed fall into the abode of hell. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 3.34)
For the self does not exist in the aggregates, nor do the aggregates exist in the self;
they are not as they are conceptualized, yet it is not that they do not exist at all. (Lankavatara Sutra 3.35)
If the existence of all things were as it is conceptualized by the foolish,
then everyone would be seers of reality, for they see them exactly as they appear.
Because all phenomena are non-existent, there is no affliction from the perspective of purity;
they are not as they are perceived, yet it is not that they do not exist at all.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, I shall teach you the characteristics of gnosis (*jñāna*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*), so that by means of this well-discriminated knowledge of the characteristics of gnosis and consciousness, you and other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, having mastered the course of the characteristics of gnosis and consciousness, will swiftly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
In this regard, Mahāmati, gnosis is of three kinds: mundane, supramundane, and supremely supramundane.

In this regard, Mahāmati, consciousness perishes once it has arisen, whereas gnosis does not perish until it has arisen. Furthermore, Mahāmati, consciousness falls into the categories of the characterized and the uncharacterized, and is caused by the various marks of existence and non-existence.
Knowledge has the characteristic of transcending both signs and signlessness.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, consciousness has the characteristic of accumulation,
while knowledge has the characteristic of diminution.
In this regard, knowledge is threefold: that which determines specific and general characteristics, that which determines arising and ceasing, and that which determines non-arising and non-ceasing.

Among these, mundane knowledge belongs to all heterodox teachers and ordinary worldlings who are attached to the positions of existence and non-existence. Supramundane knowledge belongs to all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas whose inclinations are fixed upon falling into [the notions of] specific and general characteristics.

In this regard, Mahāmati, the most transcendent supramundane gnosis of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas proceeds from the discernment of phenomena as being without appearance, from the vision of non-cessation and non-arising, and from the realization of selflessness on the stage of the Tathāgata, thereby being free from the positions of existence and non-existence.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, gnosis has the characteristic of non-attachment,
whereas consciousness has the characteristic of attachment to the diversity of objects.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, consciousness (*vijñāna*) is characterized by the conjunction of the threefold attachment and the arising [of phenomena], whereas gnosis (*jñāna*) is characterized by the nature of non-attachment.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, gnosis is characterized by non-attainment; it is the domain of the realization of noble self-reflexive gnosis, because, like the moon in water, it is neither entering nor emerging.
In this regard, it is said:
By the mind, karma is accumulated; by knowledge, it is determined;
and by wisdom, one attains the non-manifest and its sovereign power. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 3.38)
The mind is bound to sense objects, while cognition proceeds through reasoning;
it is indeed wisdom that functions toward the non-manifest and the specific.
Mind, intellect, and consciousness are devoid of conceptualization and discrimination;
yet the Śrāvakas, having attained the nature of conceptualized phenomena, are not the sons of the Jina.
When the distinguished state of patience has become tranquil, the auspicious Tathāgata-knowledge arises for the sake of the distinguished meaning, free from all active mental engagement.
For my wisdom is threefold, by which the noble ones are distinguished:
that by which characteristics are conceptualized, that by which [objects] are imagined, and that which covers over all entities.
Wisdom indeed is free from the two vehicles and devoid of non-existence;
it proceeds for the Śrāvakas through their attachment to the existence of real entities.
By entering into mind-only, the wisdom of the Tathāgatas is attained.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are nine kinds of views regarding transformation held by the non-Buddhist teachers who advocate transformation (*pariṇāmavādin*):

namely, transformation of shape, transformation of characteristics, transformation of cause, transformation of reasoning, transformation of views, transformation of arising, transformation of existence, transformation of the manifestation of conditions, and transformation of the manifestation of activity.

Mahāmati, these are the nine views of transformation; relying upon these, all the heterodox teachers become proponents of the theory of transformation as the arising of the positions of existence and non-existence.
In this regard, Mahāmati, transformation of shape (*saṃsthāna-pariṇāma*) refers to the observation of a change in shape, just as one observes the various transformations of ornaments made from gold.
For example, Mahāmati, gold, when being transformed through the production of bracelets, earrings, svastikas, and so forth, is seen to be transformed into a variety of shapes.
Gold does not undergo transformation in its essential nature.
In the same way, Mahāmati, the transformation of all things is conceptualized by some non-Buddhist teachers as being due to change, while others conceive it as arising from a cause;
yet they are not so.
And it is not otherwise, except by relying on conceptual construction (*parikalpa*).
Thus, all the various types of transformation (*pariṇāma*) are to be viewed as being like the transformation of curd, milk, wine, and the ripening of fruit.

For example, Mahāmati, just as the transformation of each individual thing—such as curd, milk, wine, and fruit—is conceptually constructed as a transformation of conceptualization by the non-Buddhist teachers (*tīrthakara*), so too is it with all things.
And herein nothing at all undergoes transformation, because of the non-existence of external entities—whether existent or non-existent—which are but the manifestations of one's own mind.
In this very way, Mahāmati, the activity of the cultivation of the conceptual constructions of one's own mind by foolish common people is to be viewed.
Herein, Mahāmati, no dharma whatsoever proceeds or ceases.
It is like the perception of forms proceeding from illusion or a dream.
For example, Mahāmati, just as arising and ceasing are perceived in a dream, they are like the birth or death of the son of a barren woman.
Regarding this, it is said:

Those who conceptualize transformation, the configuration of time, and [the nature of] the elements, phenomena, and the sense faculties as being comprised within the intermediate state— they are not wise.
The Victors do not conceptualize the world as dependently originated;
rather, this world is merely a condition, resembling a city of Gandharvas.
Then indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati again entreated the Blessed One for the sake of liberation regarding the meaning of the junctions of all dharmas: "May the Blessed One teach me;

may the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, teach me the characteristic of the junctions and non-junctions of all dharmas, so that by means of this well-discriminated penetration into the characteristic of junctions and non-junctions, I and other Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas may become skilled in all the methods of junctions and non-junctions regarding the attachment to the meaning according to the literal expression."
They would not fall away.
Through skill in the junctions and non-junctions of all phenomena, having destroyed the conceptualization of speech and syllables by means of their intellect,

they roam through the assemblies of all Buddha-fields, well-sealed with the seals of the powers, masteries, superknowledges, and dhāraṇīs, [proceeding] toward the ten stages of culmination by means of various rays of emanations.

With well-established intellects, they are equal to the effortless activity of the moon, the sun, jewels, and the great elements; having turned away from views characterized by their own conceptual constructions across all stages (*bhūmi*), and because they perceive all phenomena as being like dreams and illusions, they have entered the foundation of the stage of Buddhahood. Having drawn in the entire realm of sentient beings through the teaching of the Dharma according to their spiritual capacity, they should establish them in that which is free from the positions of existence and non-existence regarding all phenomena—such as dreams and illusions—and devoid of the conceptualization of destruction and arising, by means of relying on the functioning of various linguistic expressions and synonyms.
The Blessed One said: "Excellent, excellent, Mahāmati! Therefore, Mahāmati, listen and pay close and careful attention."
"I shall speak to you.
"Excellent, Blessed One," Mahāmati, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this to him: "Mahāmati, the connection [consisting in] the adherence to the meaning of all phenomena according to their literal expression is immeasurable."
The junction of adherence to characteristics, the junction of adherence to conditions,
and the junction of adherence to existence and non-existence.
The seam of conceptual attachment to the discrimination between arising and non-arising; the seam of conceptualization and attachment to cessation and non-cessation;
the seam of conceptualization and attachment to vehicles and non-vehicles.
The junction of attachment to the conceptual differentiation between the conditioned and the unconditioned;
the junction of attachment to the conceptual differentiation regarding the specific characteristics of the stages and non-stages;
and the junction of the conceptualization of the realization of one's own conceptualization.
The junction of conceptualizing based on the positions of existence and non-existence held by various sectarians,
and the junction of conceptualizing the realization of the three vehicles as being one vehicle—
these and others, Mahāmati, are the junctions of the own-conceptualizations of foolish common people.

Relying upon which junction, foolish ordinary people, while engaging in conceptual discrimination, wrap themselves and others in the thread of the junction of their own views of conceptualization— like silkworms— with a delight in that very thread of their own views of conceptualization, being attached to the characteristics of the junction of existence and non-existence.
But here, Mahāmati, there is no junction whatsoever, nor any characteristic of a junction, because of the vision of the solitude of all dharmas.
Mahāmati, because conceptual construction does not arise, the bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells seeing all phenomena as secluded.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, because of the awakening to the characteristic of external existence and non-existence as being the manifestation of one’s own mind, and because of following the state of mind-only which is free from appearances, one sees that all conceptual constructions regarding the continuity of existence and non-existence are secluded. Thus, for all dharmas, there is neither the characteristic of continuity nor the characteristic of non-continuity. Herein, Mahāmati, no one is bound and no one is liberated.
Elsewhere, bondage and liberation are perceived only through a cognition fallen into falsehood.
Why is that?
Because, namely, the junction between existence and non-existence is not to be found in all phenomena.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are three connections for foolish ordinary people, namely: passion, hatred, and delusion;
and craving which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and passion—it is with reference to this that the connections of the realms of rebirth arise.

In that regard, Mahāmati, the connection and the act of connecting of sentient beings within the five realms of rebirth ceases when the connection is severed; thus, neither "connection" nor the "characteristic of non-connection" is perceived.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, the connection of existence arises from attachment to the conjunction of the activity of the threefold causal conditions and from the continuous engagement of the consciousnesses. Through the cessation of the threefold causal conditions and by observing the three liberations, all connections of existence no longer proceed.
In this regard, it is said:
Unreal imagination is indeed called the characteristic of the connection;
through the thorough knowledge of its reality, the web of connections is cleared away.

Just as silkworms are bound by their own cocoons, so too are the ignorant and the unwise bound by their own conceptual constructions through their grasping at the sounds of the knowledge of phenomena. (Lankavatara 3.47)

Again, Mahāmati said: "Furthermore, as for that which was said by the Blessed One: 'By whichever conceptualization whatever entities are conceptualized, their intrinsic nature does not exist; that is merely imagined (parikalpita).'"
In that case, Blessed One, if this is merely imagined and not a determination of the characteristic of the intrinsic nature of things,
then, Blessed One, for you who speak thus, it follows that affliction and purification do not exist, because all phenomena are permeated by an imagined intrinsic nature.
The Blessed One said: "It is so, Mahāmati, just as you say.
Mahāmati, the intrinsic nature of things does not exist in the manner that it is conceptualized by foolish common people."
Mahāmati, this is merely a mental construction; it is not a definitive determination of the characteristic of the intrinsic nature of things.

Rather, Mahāmati, the intrinsic nature of things exists in the way that it is determined by the noble ones through noble knowledge, noble vision, and the noble eye of wisdom. In that manner, the intrinsic nature of things comes to be.

Mahāmati said: "If, Blessed One, the intrinsic nature of things is as it is determined by the Noble Ones through noble knowledge, noble vision, and the noble eye of wisdom— not by the divine or fleshly eye— and if it is not as the intrinsic nature of things is conceptualized by foolish common people,"
Therefore, Blessed One, how will the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of foolish commoners be averted, given their failure to realize the reality of the noble state?
And yet, Blessed One, they are neither perverted nor non-perverted.
Why is that?
That is to say, it is because of the failure to realize the intrinsic nature of noble objects, and because of observing the occurrence of the characteristics of existence and non-existence.

Blessed One, even by the Noble Ones, things are conceptualized according to their appearance, yet they do not exist in that way, because they are beyond the range of the domain of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).

O Blessed One, even for them, that which has the characteristic of the intrinsic nature of entities appears as nothing but the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), because of the designation of cause and non-cause.
That is to say, because they have fallen into the view of the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of entities, it becomes the domain of others [the Buddhas] in a way that it does not for them.
Thus, O Blessed One, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would result from the failure to understand the characteristic of the intrinsic nature of entities.
Moreover, Blessed One, the characteristic of the intrinsic nature of entities does not have the imagined nature as its cause.
How could that [intrinsic nature], when being conceptually discriminated by imagination, not exist in the way it is imagined?
Blessed One, the characteristic of conceptual discrimination is indeed something else entirely.
The characteristic of intrinsic nature is indeed something else entirely.
Blessed One, the characteristic of the intrinsic nature of conceptual construction has dissimilar causes;
yet when these two are mutually imagined by foolish common people, they will not exist in that manner.
However, this is stated for the purpose of turning back the conceptual constructions of sentient beings;
they do not exist in the manner that they are conceptually constructed by those very constructions.

“Blessed One, why is it that, having warded off the views of existence and non-existence for sentient beings, you now cause them to fall back into the view of non-existence by means of an attachment to the intrinsic nature of things, and by causing them to cling to the objects and spheres of noble gnosis?
Furthermore, why is the teaching of the dharma of solitude being abandoned through the instruction on the reality of the intrinsic nature of noble gnosis?
The Blessed One replied, “Mahāmati, I do not abandon the teaching of the dharma of solitude.”

Nor is the view of existence (astitva-dṛṣṭi) cast down by means of an exposition on the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of the noble reality; rather, Mahāmati, for the sake of removing the ground for fear in beings who have been attached to the characteristics of the intrinsic nature of phenomena since beginningless time, I provide this instruction on the dharma of solitude through the perspective of the characteristic of attachment to the intrinsic nature of the reality of noble gnosis.
Mahāmati, I do not provide an instruction on the intrinsic nature of entities;
rather, Mahāmati, they shall themselves abide in the dharmas that are secluded and realized as they truly are.

By seeing through delusion as being without signs, they enter into the realization that what is seen is merely their own mind; with their views turned away from the existence or non-existence of external objects, they shall abide in the dharmas that are secluded and realized as they truly are, having attained the three liberations.

They will become free from views based on the signs of delusion, being well-sealed by the seal of reality as it truly is, attained through the three liberations; dwelling in direct perception with an intellect that has realized within themselves the intrinsic nature of all phenomena,
they will be devoid of views regarding the existence or non-existence of things.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not make the proposition that "all dharmas are unarisen.
Why is that?
Because a proposition is itself characterized by the nature of all things, and because it possesses the characteristic of proceeding from causes.
Mahāmati, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva makes a proposition and then speaks while asserting that all dharmas are unarisen, he falls away from his own proposition—
that is, the proposition that "all dharmas are unarisen."
His proposition is undermined,
because that proposition arises in dependence upon those [unproduced phenomena].
Alternatively, if that proposition is also unproduced— because, being included among all phenomena, the proposition possesses the characteristic of non-arising— then [the opponent's position fails].

The assertion that "all phenomena are unarisen" is abandoned by means of the very components of that proposition itself; for the non-arising of existence and non-existence constitutes the proposition. Indeed, Mahāmati, that proposition is internal to all things, because it is characterized by the non-arising of both existence and non-existence.
If, Mahāmati, they make the proposition that "all things are unarisen" by means of that very unarisen proposition,
even so, the fallacy of abandoning the proposition follows;
for since the characteristic of a proposition consists in the non-arising of both existence and non-existence, no proposition should be made at all.
For, Mahāmati, their proposition has the characteristic of being unarisen by nature;
therefore, Mahāmati, no proposition should be made.

Because the members [of the syllogism] are corrupted by many faults, and because the members are produced as mutually distinct causes, no proposition should be made—namely, that "all phenomena are unarisen."

Thus, Mahāmati, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should not make the proposition that "all dharmas are empty and without intrinsic nature. Rather, Mahāmati, because all things have the characteristic of being visible and invisible, and because all dharmas delude the intellect through [wrong] views, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should teach that all existents are like an illusion or a dream. This is done except for the purpose of avoiding a state of terror in the foolish.
"O Mahāmati, for these foolish ordinary people have fallen into the views of non-existence and existence; lest they should become terrified,
O Mahāmati, if they are made to feel terror, they will distance themselves from the Mahāyāna."
In this regard, it is said:
There is no intrinsic nature, no representation, no objective entity, and no storehouse-consciousness;
these are indeed conceptualized by fools, those bad logicians who are like corpses.
All phenomena are unarisen for the sake of establishing [the truth] for all non-Buddhist outsiders;
indeed, no entities whatsoever have arisen, being dependent upon conditions.
All phenomena are unarisen; one should not conceptualize them through wisdom.
Because they possess that as their cause and are established thereby, the [false] intellect regarding them is abandoned. (Lankavatara 3.50)
Just as a mass of hair is falsely perceived by people with cataracts,
so too is this conceptualization of entities falsely imagined by the foolish.
The three realms of existence are mere designation; they do not exist by way of an intrinsic nature of things.
Yet, through the conceptualization of designations as real entities, the dialecticians will continue to imagine them.
Having transcended signs, objects, representations, and the movement of the mind, my sons move about free from conceptual construction.
Just as there is the perception of water in what is not water, like a mirage in the sky,
so too is the visible world for the foolish, and especially for the noble ones.
The vision of the noble ones is pure, arising from the three liberations;
it is free from arising and ceasing, belonging to those who move within the non-manifest.
For yogins, there is indeed no appearance when things are non-existent;
through the equality of existence and non-existence, the fruit is born for the noble ones.
For how can the non-existence of things bring about their equality? How [can this be]? (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 3.56)
When the mind no longer perceives the fluctuating external and internal,
it then brings about the destruction [of duality] through the vision of the mind as equality.

Again, Mahāmati said: "Furthermore, as for that which was stated by the Blessed One: 'When cognition no longer perceives an object to be apprehended, then there is the establishment of representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*). Because of the absence of an object to be grasped (*grāhya*) for the representation, there is also the non-apprehension of the grasper (*grāhaka*). Due to that non-apprehension, the cognition designated as conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) does not proceed.'"

In that case, Blessed One, is it because of a failure to perceive the distinct variety of the specific and general characteristics (*svasāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena that knowledge does not apprehend them? Or is it because knowledge does not apprehend them due to the obscuration of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of phenomena by their specific and general characteristics? Or is it that knowledge does not apprehend the object of knowledge because it is obstructed by walls, mats, mounds, ramparts, earth, water, wind, or fire, or because it is too distant or too near?
Now, due to the association with the immature, the blind, and the elderly, cognition does not perceive the objects of knowledge through the sense faculties.

If, Blessed One, cognition does not perceive because of the failure to understand the variety of specific and general characteristics as non-different from one another, then, Blessed One, it should not be called "cognition."
“O Blessed One, this is ignorance: that which does not perceive an object that exists.

Furthermore, O Blessed One, if knowledge does not perceive [an object] because it is overwhelmed by the intrinsic nature of entities—the diversity of their specific and general characteristics—that is indeed ignorance, not knowledge.”
"Blessed One, when there is an object of knowledge (*jñeya*), cognition (*jñāna*) proceeds; it does not arise from non-existence.

And because of its connection with that object of knowledge, it is called 'cognition. Furthermore, one does not perceive [an object] due to obstructions such as walls, mats, mounds, ramparts, earth, water, wind, or fire, or due to excessive distance or proximity. Nor does cognition fail to perceive due to defects of the sense faculties, as in the cases of children, the elderly, the blind, or those practicing yoga."
Therefore, O Blessed One, that which does not perceive in this way is not knowledge;
it is simply non-knowledge, because of a deficiency in intelligence regarding an existing object.
The Blessed One said: "Indeed, Mahāmati, it is not that there is such ignorance;

rather, Mahāmati, that is knowledge itself, not ignorance. And it was with this in mind that I said: 'When cognition no longer perceives an object to be apprehended, then the establishment of representation-only occurs.'"

However, through the realization that what is seen is merely one's own mind, and because of the absence of external existence or non-existence—whether real or unreal—knowledge no longer perceives an object.
Due to that non-perception, there is the non-occurrence of both knowledge and the known.
Through the following of the three liberations, even knowledge itself is not apprehended.
Furthermore, those logicians, whose minds have been perfumed by the conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) of existence and non-existence since beginningless time, do not understand it in this way.

Not understanding it, they—having established the existence or non-existence of external objects characterized by shape and form—will teach "mind-only" as the non-occurrence of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

Clinging to the grasping of the characteristics of "self" and "mine," and failing to realize that [the world] is merely the manifestation of their own minds, they conceptually differentiate between knowledge (*jñāna*) and the object of knowledge (*jñeya*).

And through the conceptualization of knowledge and the object of knowledge, because they do not perceive the investigation into the existence or non-existence of external entities, they resort to the view of nihilism.
Regarding this, it is said:
"If cognition does not perceive an existing object of apprehension, that is indeed non-cognition and not cognition; such is the system of the logicians. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 3.58)
If cognition does not perceive [an object] because of the absence of any characteristic other than itself,
yet perceives it as obstructed, distant, or near, that is called false cognition.
If knowledge does not arise due to the association with children, the elderly, or the blind,
then that object of knowledge, though existing, is called false knowledge. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 3.60)

Furthermore, Mahāmati, foolish common people— dancing in a drama due to their own conceptualizations of the depravity of beginningless discursive proliferation, unskilled in the teaching of the method of their own established tenets, and clinging to the characteristics of external objects as manifestations of their own minds— cling to the mere recitation of the teachings on skillful means.
They do not discern their own established tenet-system, which is purified by the method of the four alternatives (*cātuṣkoṭika*).
Mahāmati said: "It is so, Blessed One; it is just as you say.
May the Blessed One teach me the characteristics of the method of the established tenets of the teaching, by means of which I and other bodhisattvas [may understand them]."

"Mahāsattvas, in the future age, being skilled in the methods of the teachings and the established tenets, shall not be deceived by false dialecticians belonging to the vehicles of the non-Buddhists, Śrāvakas, or Pratyekabuddhas.
The Blessed One said: "Therefore, Mahāmati, listen; attend well and thoroughly to it."
"I shall speak to you.
"Excellent, Blessed One," Mahāmati, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, replied to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One said this to him: "Mahāmati, the system of the Dharma of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future, and present is of two kinds, namely: the system of teaching and..."
And there is the method of establishing the definitive conclusion (*siddhāntapratyavasthānanaya*).
Among these, Mahāmati, the method of teaching and recitation refers to the instruction on various collections of sūtras;
they teach to sentient beings according to their mental dispositions and inclinations.
In that regard, Mahāmati, what is the method of the established tenet (*siddhāntanaya*)?

It is that by which practitioners turn away from the conceptual constructions of what is seen as their own mind—that is, by not falling into the positions of oneness, otherness, both, or neither; it transcends mind, mentation, and mental consciousness; it is the domain of the noble realization attained within oneself; it is free from the characteristics of causes, logic, and views; and it is untouched by all false dialecticians, including those of the paths of the outsiders, the Śrāvakas, and the Pratyekabuddhas, who have fallen into the two extremes of non-existence and existence.
I call that the established tenet (*siddhānta*).
Mahāmati, this is the characteristic of the teaching of the method of the established tenet, in which you and other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should apply yourselves.
Regarding this, it is said:
"My method is indeed twofold: the established tenet (*siddhānta*) and the teaching (*deśanā*).
That which I teach to the ignorant is the teaching; I [teach] the established tenet to the practitioners of yoga. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 3.61)

Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati spoke thus again to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, it was said by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, at one time, on one occasion: 'A Lokāyatika, possessed of various spells and eloquence, should not be served, nor honored, nor attended upon.'"
And as for the fact that by serving such a person there is an accumulation of worldly material things but no accumulation of the Dharma—
what is the reason, then, that the Blessed One has said this regarding the Lokāyatika, who possesses diverse spells and eloquence,
and that by serving him there is an accumulation of worldly material things but no accumulation of the Dharma?

The Blessed One said: "Mahāmati, the Lokāyatika, possessing the eloquence of various mantras, deludes the foolish with various words, phrases, and syllables; [his teaching] is neither logically consistent nor endowed with meaningful purpose. Rather, he teaches nothing but whatever is mere idle chatter of the foolish. For this reason, Mahāmati, the Lokāyatika is called one who possesses the eloquence of various mantras."
She attracts children through the beauty of her varied syllables,
but she does not enter by means of entering the method of reality.
Because she herself has not realized all dharmas, she deludes children with a view that has fallen into the two extremes.
And he destroys his own self.

Because he is not liberated from the transition between states of existence, because he does not understand that which is merely the manifestation of his own mind, and because of his attachment to the intrinsic nature of external entities, his conceptual construction does not cease.
For this reason, Mahāmati, one is a Lokāyatika.

Possessing the eloquence of various mantras, yet not being truly liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair, he deludes the foolish with various words and phrases, through the application of reasons, examples, and conclusions.
Even Indra, O Mahāmati, whose intellect was refined by his mastery of many treatises and who was the author of his own grammatical system,

had a disciple who assumed the form of a serpent and made a vow in the assembly of the gods in heaven: "Either your thousand-spoked chariot shall be shattered, or the hoods of each and every one of my serpent-forms shall be cut off."

And having defeated Indra, the lord of the gods, by means of a follower of the Lokāyata who assumed the guise of a Nāga and employed right reasoning, he shattered his thousand-spoked chariot and returned once more to this world.

Thus, Mahāmati, this system of the Lokāyatas is bound together with various causes and illustrations; by it, even animals, having studied it, delude the worlds of gods and asuras with its diverse words and expressions.
Through its insistence on the views of arising and passing away, it causes others to adhere to them—how much more so, then, human beings?
Therefore, Mahāmati, for this reason, the Lokāyatika must be avoided, because he brings about the causes for the arising of suffering;
he should not be served, nor associated with, nor attended upon.
For, Mahāmati, the Lokāyatas teach—by means of various words and phrases—that there is merely the perception of the body, the intellect, and their objects.

Mahāmati, the Lokāyata consists of a hundred thousand [verses]. However, in the future world, during the final five-hundred-year period, it will become fragmented because it is composed of fallacious reasoning, logic, and views.
It will become fragmented because it is not upheld by true disciples.

Mahāmati, this Lokāyata is indeed fragmented and composed of various causes; it is taught by the non-Buddhist teachers who are attached to their own specific causal theories, and not as my own system.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, no non-Buddhist teacher possesses a system of his own within his own treatises.
Except for the Lokāyata itself, they teach it through many forms and hundreds of thousands of methods of reasoning;
yet they do not recognize their own system, and out of delusion and ignorance, they think, "This is the Lokāyata."

Mahāmati said: "If, Blessed One, all the non-Buddhist teachers teach nothing but the Lokāyata through various words, phrases, illustrations, and conclusions— being attached to their own systems and their own causal theories—
then why does the Blessed One also teach nothing but the Lokāyata with various words and phrases to the gods, asuras, and humans who come from various lands and assemble here?"
"Is it not your own doctrine because it is included within the teachings of all the heterodox teachers?
The Blessed One said: "Mahāmati, I do not teach Lokāyata, nor do I teach arising and passing away;
rather, Mahāmati, I teach that which is neither arising nor passing away."
In this regard, Mahāmati, "arising" (āya) refers to a mass of production that arises from the coming together of a collection [of causes].
In this regard, Mahāmati, "passing away" (vyaya) refers to destruction.
"Neither arising nor passing away" is a designation for non-arising.
Mahāmati, I do not teach that which is within the conceptual constructions of all the non-Buddhist teachers.
Why is that?

Because there is no external existence or non-existence, because there is no attachment, because one abides in what is merely the manifestation of one's own mind, and because conceptual construction does not arise due to the cessation of its dualistic movement.

Because there is an absence of the objective sphere of signs and because of the realization that [all] is merely the manifestation of one's own mind, the conceptual construction of what is seen as one's own mind does not arise.
Due to the non-arising of conceptual construction, one enters the three liberations—signlessness, emptiness, and wishlessness—and is therefore said to be "liberated."

I remember, Mahāmati, that once while I was staying in a certain region of the earth, a Lokāyatika Brahmin approached me. Having approached, even before being granted permission, he said this to me: "O Gautama, everything is created."
To him, Mahāmati, I said: "O Brāhmaṇa, if everything is created, this is the first Lokāyata doctrine.
He replied: "O Gautama, everything is uncreated."
If, O Brāhmaṇa, everything were unconditioned, this would be a second Lokāyata [materialist doctrine]:
namely, that everything is impermanent, everything is permanent, everything is produced, and everything is unproduced.

“O Brahmin, this is the sixth Lokāyata doctrine. Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Lokāyatika Brahmin spoke to me thus: “O Gautama, everything is a unity; everything is a diversity; everything is both; everything is neither; and everything is dependent upon causes, because we observe the arising of various effects from various causes.”
"O Brahmin, this too is the eleventh Lokāyata doctrine.
Furthermore, O Gautama, you say that everything is undeclared, or that everything is declared;
that there is a self, or that there is no self."
"This world exists; this world does not exist;
there is a future world; there is no future world;
and there both is and is not a future world."
"Is there liberation? Is there no liberation?
Is everything momentary? Is everything non-momentary?
O Gautama, are space, analytical cessation, and nirvana created, or are they uncreated?"

"Whether there is an intermediate state (*antarābhava*) or whether there is no intermediate state—regarding this, Mahāmati, it was said: 'O Brāhmaṇa, if it is thus, then this too, O Brāhmaṇa, is merely Lokāyata; it is not my teaching.'"
"This Lokāyata system, O Brahmin, is yours.
However, O Brahmin, I describe the three realms of existence as having their cause in the depravity of the habitual tendencies of conceptual proliferation and discrimination from beginningless time.
O Brahmin, discrimination arises because of the failure to realize that which is merely the manifestation of one's own mind; it does not arise from the perception of external entities."
Just as for the Tīrthakaras there is [the notion of a self] from the conjunction of the three—self, sense-faculty, and object—it is not so for me.

O Brahmin, I am neither a proponent of causality nor a proponent of non-causality; rather, having designated conceptual construction alone as the state of grasped and grasper, I teach dependent origination.
Yet others like you do not understand it, because their mental continuum has fallen into the grasp of a self.
Mahāmati, even the reality of nirvāṇa, space, and cessation cannot be apprehended in terms of enumeration; how much less, then, can there be any quality of being produced?
Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Lokāyatika Brahmin spoke thus: "O Gautama, is this triple existence caused by ignorance, craving, and karma, or is it causeless?
"Brahmin, both of these views belong to the Lokāyata."
"O Gautama, all phenomena fall within the scope of specific and general characteristics.
This too, Brahmin, is merely Lokāyata.
As long as there is mental agitation, O Brahmin, consisting of the conceptualization that clings to external objects, so long is it Lokāyata."
Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Lokāyatika brahmin said this to me: "Venerable Gautama, is there anything that is not Lokāyata?
Venerable Gautama, everything that is renowned among all the tīrthakaras is taught by you using various words and phrases, with reasons, illustrations, and conclusions.
"O Brahmin, there is indeed something that is not yours, yet it is not unrenowned; it is taught, and it is not without various words and phrases, nor is it devoid of meaningful content."
"What is that which is non-materialistic (alokāyata), which is not well-known yet is taught?

O Brahmin, there indeed exists a non-materialistic [teaching] wherein the intellects of all the founders of other schools and yours do not penetrate—those who are attached to the proliferation of unreal conceptualizations arising from external entities.

That is to say: the non-occurrence of conceptualization; because of the realization that what is seen is merely one's own mind, conceptualization does not arise with respect to existence or non-existence."
Because there is no grasping of external objects, conceptual construction remains in its own place; this is what is observed.
Therefore, this [view] of mine is not Lokāyata, nor is it yours.
