"Remains in its own place" means that it does not proceed [toward external objects].
The non-occurrence of the conceptualization of non-arising is what is called [the state of] non-proceeding.
Thus it is, O Brahmin, that this is not Lokāyata.
In brief, O Brahmin, wherever there is no coming or going of consciousness, no death or rebirth, and no longing, attachment, or clinging—[that is this state].
Seeing, views, standing [in them], grasping, adherence to various characteristics, association with beings, and adherence to the causes of craving—
this, O Brahmin, is your Lokāyata, not mine.
In this way, Mahāmati, having been questioned by the Lokāyatika brāhmaṇa who came to me,
he was dismissed by me in this manner and departed in silence.

Then, indeed, the Naga king Kṛṣṇapakṣika, having approached in the guise of a brahmin, said this to the Blessed One: "In that case, Gautama, the world beyond does not exist at all. [The Blessed One replied: "In that case, young man, from where have you come?"
"O Gautama, I have come here from Śvetadvīpa;
that indeed is the supreme world of Brahmā.
Then the young brahmin, rendered speechless and defeated, vanished without even having asked me about the discourse on the establishment of one's own method.

Reflecting thus, the son of the Śākyas—a wretched man who stands outside my teaching and propounds a doctrine of non-arising as the characteristic of causes—describes the non-occurrence of conceptualization through the awakening to the characteristics of the objects perceived by one's own conceptualization.

Now, Mahāmati, you ask me: "For what reason does the service of a Lokāyatika, with his various spells and eloquence, result in the gathering of worldly gain (*āmiṣa*) and not the gathering of the Dharma?
Mahāmati said: "Then, Blessed One, what is the meaning of the term *dharma* and *āmiṣa*?"
The Blessed One said: "Excellent, excellent, Mahāmati! This investigation regarding these two matters has been undertaken out of regard for future generations. Therefore, Mahāmati, listen."
"Pay close and careful attention;
I shall speak to you.
"Very well, Blessed One," the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati replied to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One said this to him: "In that regard, Mahāmati, what is material food (*āmiṣa*)? It is as follows: touching, grasping, rubbing, handling, tasting, attachment to external objects, and entering into the two extremes.

Furthermore, through false views, there is the manifestation of the aggregates (*skandha*), and the arising of birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, dejection, and despair, beginning with the craving for rebirth."
"This is called 'material gain' by me and by other Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
Mahāmati, this is the gathering of material gain and not the gathering of the Dharma, which one obtains by serving a Lokāyatika and thereby acquires the Lokāyata."
In this regard, Mahāmati, what is the compendium of the Dharma?

It is as follows: through the awakening to the non-duality of the selflessness of phenomena within one's own mind, and through the vision of the characteristics of the selflessness of persons and phenomena, there is the non-arising of conceptual construction;
and through the thorough knowledge that transcends the stages, there is the turning back of the mind, the mentation, and the mental consciousness.

The attainment of the consecration of all Buddha-knowledge, the non-acceptance of a state of being supported, and the sovereign mastery over all phenomena without effort— this is called "Dharma," because it does not fall into the two extremes of existence and non-existence, nor into the conceptual proliferation of views and mental constructions. For generally, Mahāmati, the doctrine of the non-Buddhist teachers causes the ignorant to fall into the two extremes, but not the wise.
Namely, regarding both annihilationism and eternalism:
from the adoption of the doctrine of causelessness, the view of eternalism arises; and from the non-existence of a cause for the destruction of a causal factor, the view of annihilationism arises.
However, Mahāmati, because I perceive arising, abiding, and ceasing, I speak of "dharmas. This, Mahāmati, is the definitive determination regarding the gift of Dharma,
in which you and other Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should train.
In this regard, it is said:

One should discipline sentient beings through the means of integration (saṃgraha), bring them under control through ethical conduct (śīla), destroy false views through wisdom (prajñā), and cause them to increase in liberation (vimokṣa). (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 3.62)
All this which is falsely taught by the heterodox teachers is merely Lokāyata;
because of their adherence to the view that cause and effect are real, they possess no established doctrine of their own.
I alone teach my own doctrine, which is devoid of cause and effect, to the assembly of disciples, and which is free from the Lokāyata.
There is only mind; no object of perception exists, for the mind appears in two ways:
as the grasped and the grasper, free from the extremes of eternalism and nihilism.
As long as the mind continues to function, so long will it be worldly materialism;
when the activity of conceptual construction ceases, one sees the world as one's own mind.
Inflow is the accomplishment of the purpose of an action; outflow is the perception of that action.
Through the thorough knowledge of inflow and outflow, conceptual construction does not arise.
"Permanent," "impermanent," "produced," "unproduced," "superior," "inferior"—all such [categories] constitute the Lokāyata system. (Lankavatara 3.68)
Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati spoke again to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, it is said, 'Nirvāṇa, Nirvāṇa.
Of what is this a designation—that which is called 'Nirvāṇa' and which is conceptualized by all the non-Buddhist teachers?
The Blessed One said: "In that case, Mahāmati, listen."
Pay close and careful attention;
I shall speak to you concerning how the heterodox teachers conceptualize nirvāṇa.
"And yet, for them, there is no nirvāṇa corresponding to their conceptual constructions.
"Excellent, Blessed One," Mahāmati the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva replied to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One said this to him: "In that regard, Mahāmati, some non-Buddhist teachers [assert] that due to the cessation of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases; due to detachment from sense-objects; and due to seeing the lack of commonality [with suffering], the collection of mind and mental factors..."
It does not proceed.

They explain that because one no longer recollects objects of the past, future, and present, and because the appropriation [of the seeds] has ceased—like a lamp, a seed, or a flame—the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) ceases to function;
therefore, they conceive of that state as *nirvāṇa*.
Moreover, Mahāmati, one does not attain nirvāṇa through the view of annihilation.
Others, moreover, describe liberation as the departure to another realm, like the wind ceasing when the conceptualization of sense objects has subsided.
Still other teachers describe liberation as the destruction of the intellect (*buddhi*), the object of cognition (*boddhavya*), and the act of seeing (*darśana*).
Others postulate liberation through the non-occurrence of conceptualization by means of perceiving the eternal and the non-eternal.
Others, however, who are unskilled in the fact that what appears is merely their own mind, describe the conceptualization of various signs as that which brings about suffering and rebirth.
Terrified by signs, they perceive Nirvana in the very sign of their longing for happiness.

Still others [assert it] because of the awakening to the specific and general characteristics of all internal and external phenomena, and because of the non-destruction of the existence of past, future, and present states.
They conceptualize nirvāṇa.
Others, moreover, conceptualize nirvāṇa from the non-destruction of the self, sentient being, life-principle, nourisher, person, individual, and all phenomena.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, other non-Buddhist teachers of corrupted intellects conceptualize nirvāṇa from the perception of the distinction between primordial nature and the spirit, and from the agency of the transformation of the qualities.
Some [attain] it through the exhaustion of merit and demerit; others through the destruction of the afflictions by means of knowledge;
and others imagine the nirvāṇa of the world through the vision of a sovereign, independent creator.
Others [claim] that this arising of the world proceeds from mutual dependence and not from a cause;
yet that is merely an adherence to the notion of a cause,
and they do not understand it due to delusion.
Due to their failure to understand that, others imagine it to be nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, other non-Buddhist teachers imagine nirvāṇa through the realization of the path of truth.

Others conceive the notion of nirvāṇa from the view of the identity, difference, bothness, or neitherness of the qualities and the possessor of qualities, because they perceive them as being bound together.

Others, having observed the intrinsic nature of things—by way of their inherent existence—like the variegation of a peacock’s plumage, the diversity of a mine of jewels, or the sharpness of a thorn, conceptualize that as nirvāṇa. Furthermore, Mahāmati, others [conceptualize it] from the realization of the twenty-five principles; others [conceptualize it] from receiving the instruction on the sixfold policy by a protector of subjects.

Some imagine that because they perceive time as the creator, the activity of the world depends upon time, and they imagine that nirvāṇa consists in the realization of that [time]. Furthermore, Mahāmati, others [imagine it] through becoming.
Some conceive of nirvāṇa through non-existence; others through the thorough knowledge of existence and non-existence; and others through the vision of no distinction between existence and nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, others who roar the lion’s roar of omniscience describe it thus: through the realization that [the world] is merely the manifestation of one's own mind, through non-attachment to the existence or non-existence of external objects, through seeing things as they truly abide—free from the four extremes—and through not falling into the two extremes of the conceptualization of what is seen by one's own mind; because the apprehended and the apprehender are not perceived, and because one sees the non-occurrence of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is no grasping of reality, since reality itself would otherwise cause delusion.

By the elimination of that [duality], through the realization of the noble dharma within one's own self, through the awakening to the two kinds of selflessness, through the cessation of the two kinds of afflictions, and through the purification of the two kinds of obscurations; and by the turning back of the earths in their successive order up to the Tathāgata-bhūmi, as well as the mind, the mental faculty, and the mental consciousness—consisting of the various illusions and meditative absorptions—they conceptualize this as nirvāṇa.
In this same way, whatever other [theories] have been propounded by logicians and false teachers are devoid of reason and are avoided by the wise.
Mahāmati, all these [thinkers] imagine nirvāṇa through a mental continuity that has fallen into the two extremes.
Mahāmati, by means of such conceptual constructions as these, nirvāṇa is imagined by all the non-Buddhist teachers;
yet herein, nothing whatsoever proceeds or ceases.
Mahāmati, when the nirvāṇa of each individual non-Buddhist teacher is examined through the intelligence of their own scriptures, it proves inconsistent;
it does not abide in the manner that they conceptualize it.
Because of the movement and fluctuation of the mind’s coming and going, there is no nirvāṇa for anyone.
Having trained in this, Mahāmati, you and other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas must turn back the view of nirvāṇa held by all the non-Buddhist teachers.
Regarding this, it is said:
The non-Buddhists hold various views concerning nirvāṇa and conceptualize them individually;
for them, there exists no means to liberation other than mere conceptualization.
Freed from the bondage of what is to be bound, yet devoid of skillful means,
the non-Buddhists conceptualize liberation, yet no liberation exists.
For the system of the non-Buddhists is seen to be divided into many different sects;
therefore, there is no liberation for them—why is it imagined by the deluded?
All the heterodox teachers are utterly deluded by their faulty views regarding cause and effect;
therefore, there is no liberation for them, as they advocate the positions of existence and non-existence.
For the foolish delight in the proliferation of verbal discourse and do not apply their vast intelligence to reality;
for verbal discourse is the source of suffering in the three realms, while reality is the cause for the destruction of suffering.
Just as a form is seen in a mirror yet does not exist there,
so too the mind is seen in two ways within the mirror of latent impressions by the foolish.
Due to the lack of thorough understanding that what is seen is but the mind, dualistic conceptualization arises;
through the thorough understanding that what is seen is but the mind, conceptualization does not proceed.
The mind itself appears as manifold, devoid of both the characterized and the characteristics;
there is no visible object existing in the form of what is seen, as it is imagined by the foolish. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 3.76)
The three realms of existence are mere conceptual construction; no external object exists.
Diverse conceptual constructions are perceived, yet they are not discerned by the foolish.
In every sūtra, conceptual construction is described by means of various designations and names;
apart from the expression, no expressed object is perceived.

Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati said this to the Blessed One: "May the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, teach me the state of Buddhahood of a Buddha himself, so that I and other Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas may become skilled in the Tathāgata’s own nature and awaken both ourselves and others.
The Blessed One said: "In that case, Mahāmati, you yourself ask [what you wish]."
"I shall answer according to what is appropriate for you.

Mahāmati said: "Furthermore, Blessed One, is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, uncreated or created? Is he effect or cause, the characterized or the characteristic, the designation or the designated, the intellect or the object of intellect?"
"By means of such etymological definitions of terms as these, is the Blessed One other [than them] or not other?

The Blessed One said: "Mahāmati, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is not, by means of such etymological definitions of terms as these, uncreated, nor created, nor an effect, nor a cause. Why is that?"
That is to say, because it would entail the consequence of both faults.
For if, Mahāmati, the Tathāgata were something produced, he would be subject to impermanence.
For if [the Tathāgata] were [produced], then because of impermanence, everything would be a Tathāgata;
and this is undesirable both to me and to other Tathāgatas.
Now, suppose he were unconditioned (*akṛtaka*).
Because it would lack an inherent nature, the accumulation of the provisions for enlightenment would be rendered futile;
furthermore, because it would be unconditioned, it would be like a rabbit's horn or the son of a barren woman.
And that which, Mahāmati, is neither effect nor cause, is neither existent nor non-existent.
And that which is neither existent nor non-existent is outside the fourfold alternative;
and the fourfold alternative, Mahāmati, is worldly convention.
And that which is outside the fourfold alternative (cātuṣkoṭika) results in being mere words, like the son of a barren woman.
For the son of a barren woman, Mahāmati, is mere words and does not fall within the fourfold alternative;
because it does not fall [into any category], it is not an object of valid cognition for the wise.
In this way, the meanings of all the Tathāgatas' words should be understood by the wise.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, you must also comprehend the meaning of what I have said: "All phenomena are selfless."

Mahāmati, selflessness (*nairātmya*) is the absence of intrinsic nature (*nirātmabhāva*). All phenomena exist by way of their own nature (*svātmanā*), not by way of another's nature (*parātmanā*), just like a cow and a horse.
For example, Mahāmati, the nature of a cow does not consist of the nature of a horse, nor does the nature of a horse consist of the nature of a cow.
They are neither existent nor non-existent, yet they do not fail to exist by way of their own specific characteristics; indeed, those two do exist by way of their own specific characteristics.
In the same way, Mahāmati, all dharmas do not exist by way of their own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*),
yet they do indeed exist.
And it is on the basis of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that foolish common people fail to understand the meaning of selflessness (*nirātmatā*).
But it is not non-conceptual.
In this way, the emptiness, non-arising, and lack of intrinsic nature of all phenomena are to be understood.
Likewise, the Tathāgata is neither different from nor non-different from the aggregates.
If it were not different from the aggregates,
it would be impermanent because the aggregates are produced.
Or, if it were different [from them],...
If duality exists, it becomes otherwise, like a cow's horn.

In that regard, Mahāmati, the non-difference of all things arises from the perception of similarity, while their difference arises from the perception of shortness and length. For, Mahāmati, the right cow-horn is different from the left,
and the left is likewise different from the right.
In this way, shortness and length are mutually [dependent];
likewise, so too are the various colors.
Therefore, they are not other than one another.
Nor is the Tathāgata other than the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
Likewise, the Tathāgata is neither other than liberation nor not other;
the Tathāgata himself is designated by the word "liberation."
If the Tathāgata were other than liberation, he would possess the characteristics of form;
because of possessing the characteristics of form, he would be impermanent.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, if they were non-different, there would be no distinction characterized by attainment for yogins;
yet such a distinction is indeed observed by yogins.
Therefore, it is neither different nor non-different.
In this way, knowledge is neither different nor non-different from the object of knowledge.
For that which, Mahāmati, is neither eternal nor impermanent, neither effect nor cause, neither conditioned nor unconditioned—

There is no intellect and no object of cognition; there is no characteristic and no that which is characterized; there are no aggregates, nor anything other than the aggregates; there is nothing denotable and no denotation;
it is not connected with identity, difference, both, or neither;
thus, it is beyond all means of valid cognition.
That which is devoid of all means of valid cognition becomes mere words;
that which is mere words is unarisen;
that which is unarisen is unceasing.
That which is unceasing is equal to space.
And space, Mahāmati, is neither an effect nor a cause. That which is neither an effect nor a cause is without a basis for apprehension.
That which is without objective support transcends all conceptual proliferation;
that which transcends all conceptual proliferation is the Tathāgata.
For this, Mahāmati, is true and perfect buddhahood.
This is that very state of Buddhahood, which transcends all means of valid cognition and all sensory faculties.
Regarding this, it is said:

Free from the means of valid cognition and the sense faculties, it is neither effect nor cause; devoid of intellect and the object of intellect, and abandoned by the characterized and the characteristic. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 3.79)
A perfectly awakened one dependent upon the aggregates has never been seen by anyone, anywhere.
How can there be a conceptualization of that which has never been seen by anyone, anywhere?
It is neither created nor uncreated, neither an effect nor a cause;
it is neither the aggregates nor non-aggregates, nor is it anything other than their combination.
For that which, when conceptualized as having a certain nature, is not perceived, should not be concluded as being non-existent; such is the very nature of phenomena.
Non-existence is preceded by existence; existence is preceded by non-existence.
Therefore, one should not proceed toward non-existence, nor should one conceptualize existence.
Deluded regarding self and selflessness, clinging solely to faults, those fools are submerged in the two extremes; being ruined themselves, they ruin others.
When they see my system as completely free from all defects, then they see correctly; they do not revile the Leaders.

Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati spoke thus again to the Blessed One: "May the Blessed One teach me; may the Sugata teach me: why has the Blessed One, in the recitation of his teachings, employed the terms 'non-cessation' and 'non-arising'?"
And you have said that "non-cessation and non-arising" is a designation for the Tathāgata.
Therefore, Blessed One, is this non-cessation and non-arising a state of non-existence, or is it another synonym for the Tathāgata?
As the Blessed One has said: "The Blessed One teaches that all phenomena are unceased and unarisen, because neither the position of existence nor the position of non-existence is perceived.
If, O Blessed One, all phenomena are unarisen, then the apprehension of phenomena would not be possible.
Because all phenomena are unarisen.
If this is another synonym for some phenomenon,
then let it be explained, O Blessed One.
The Blessed One said: "In that case, Mahāmati, listen and attend well and thoroughly;
I shall speak to you."
"Excellent, Blessed One! Mahāmati, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this to him: "Mahāmati, it is not that a Tathāgata is non-existent, nor is it a grasping at the non-arising and non-ceasing of all phenomena.
A causal condition is not to be expected [as the basis for such a statement], yet the grasping at non-arising is not made by me in vain."

However, Mahāmati, this is a designation for the Tathāgata’s mind-made dharma-body, which is beyond the range of all non-Buddhist teachers, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas established on the seven stages;
that non-arising is the state of the Tathāgata.
This, Mahāmati, is a synonymous expression.
For example, Mahāmati, Indra, Śakra, and Purandara; the laugh, the hand, and the palm; the body, the form, and the physical frame.
"Earth," "ground," and "bearer of wealth" (vasuṃdharā);
"space," "sky," and "vault of heaven"— for such entities as these, there are many conceptualized words that serve as synonyms for each individual entity.
Nor is a multiplicity of entities imagined based on the multiplicity of their names;
yet it is not that they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
In the same way, Mahāmati, I too appear within the reach of the hearing of the ignorant in this Sahā world-system under three hundred thousand incalculable names.
And they speak of me by those names, yet they do not realize that these are synonyms for the Tathāgata.
In this regard, Mahāmati, some recognize me as the "Tathāgata."

Some recognize him as the Self-Existent (Svayambhū); others recognize him as the Leader (Nāyaka), the Guide (Vināyaka), the Conductor (Pariṇāyaka), the Buddha, the Sage (Ṛṣi), the Bull (Vṛṣabha), Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Īśvara, Pradhāna, Kapila, Bhūtānta, Ariṣṭanemi, Soma, Bhāskara, Rāma, Vyāsa, Śuka, Indra, Bali, or Varuṇa. Thus do some understand him.

Others perceive non-cessation and non-arising, emptiness, suchness, reality, truth, actuality, the limit of reality, the realm of phenomena, nirvana, the eternal, equanimity, non-duality, the unceasing, the signless, the causal condition, the teaching on the causes of Buddhahood, liberation, the truths of the path, the omniscient one, the Victor, and the mind-made body.

Mahāmati, by such means as these—through three hundred thousand complete and innumerable names, neither deficient nor redundant—people here and in other world-systems perceive me, like the moon in water, which has neither entered nor emerged.
Yet the foolish do not understand this because their mental continuity has fallen into the two extremes;
nevertheless, being unskilled in the etymological analysis of things and possessing undifferentiated perceptions, they honor, revere, respect, and worship me.
Attached to the sounds and recitations of the teachings, they do not understand the internal method (*svanaya*);

they will conceptualize non-cessation, non-arising, and non-existence, yet they do not recognize that the various synonyms for the name of the Tathāgata—such as Indra, Śakra, and Purandara—are merely different expressions.
Because they follow the literal meaning of the recited texts, they do not have faith in the reading that establishes the internal method regarding all phenomena.
And thus, Mahāmati, those deluded persons will say: "The meaning is exactly according to the literal expression; the meaning is not other than the expression.
For what reason?
That is to say, because the meaning is bodiless (*aśarīra*), the meaning does not exist apart from the expression;

rather, the expression itself is the meaning. However, due to their failure to fully understand the nature of expression, those of unrefined intellect do not realize it in this way, Mahāmati: that expression arises and perishes.
The meaning, Mahāmati, is neither arisen nor destroyed; speech, however, falls into the realm of syllables,
whereas the meaning does not fall into the realm of syllables.
Because it is devoid of existence and non-existence, it is unborn and bodiless.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Tathāgatas do not teach a Dharma that has fallen into the realm of letters,
because letters are not perceived as either existent or non-existent.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, one whose intention has fallen into letters, who teaches a Dharma that has fallen into letters, merely prattles; for the Dharma is beyond letters.

For this reason, Mahāmati, it has been stated by me and by other Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in the scriptural teachings that the Tathāgatas neither utter nor reproduce even a single syllable. Why is that? It is because all phenomena are beyond syllables.
And they do not utter that which is devoid of meaningful purpose;
rather, they do indeed utter it by taking recourse to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Mahāmati, if there were no such recourse, there would be the destruction of the teaching of all dharmas.
Furthermore, due to the disappearance of the teachings, there would be an absence of Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, and Bodhisattvas. In their absence, what would be taught, and to whom?
For this reason, Mahāmati, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should not be attached to the sounds of the recitation of the teachings.
Mahāmati, that scriptural teaching is subject to deviation;

for the sake of beings who possess various inclinations, the teaching of the Dharma is performed by me and by other Tathāgatas, Arhats, out of conformity with the dispositions of sentient beings, in order to turn back the mind, the manas, and the mental consciousness.

This is because of the non-contradiction of the realization of noble, personal, self-realized gnosis; because of the awakening to the fact that all phenomena are without appearance and are merely the manifestation of one's own mind; and because of the turning away from the two-fold conceptual construction.
Mahāmati, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should rely on the meaning and not rely on the letter.
Mahāmati, a son of good family or a daughter of good family who follows the letter ruins themselves.
Furthermore, he does not cause others to understand the meaning for their benefit;

rather, with a mental continuum fallen into wrong views, he is led astray from his own position by those of false doctrines who are unskilled in the specific characteristics of the stages and all phenomena, and who lack knowledge of the etymological definitions of terms.

Then, they become skilled in the specific characteristics of all stages of phenomena (*sarvadharma-bhūmi-svalakṣaṇa*), having mastered the understanding of words, synonyms, and etymologies, and being proficient in the reasoning of the meaning of entities.
Thereupon, they satisfy themselves with the bliss of the correct signless (*animitta*) and firmly establish others in the Mahāyāna.
And, Mahāmati, when the Mahāyāna is correctly embraced, there is the embracing of the Buddhas, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas.
Through the embracing of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas, there is the embracing of all sentient beings.
Through the embracing of all sentient beings, there is the embracing of the True Dharma.
And because they uphold the true Dharma, Mahāmati, the lineage of the Buddhas is rendered unbroken.
Due to the non-interruption of the Buddha-lineage, the attainment of distinguished sense-bases (*āyatana*) becomes manifest.
Therefore, having taken rebirth in those distinguished sense-bases, the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas [abide] in the Mahāyāna.

By means of establishing [themselves in this way], having assumed various forms and attire through the ten masteries, they teach the Dharma for the sake of suchness, having become those who have entered into the dispositions, latent tendencies, characteristics, and destinies of sentient beings.
In this context, reality (*tattva*) is suchness (*tathātva*), non-alteration (*ananyathātva*).
Reality is said to have the characteristic of being without mental exertion or withdrawal, and to be the cessation of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Therefore, Mahāmati, a son of good family or a daughter of good family should not be one who is skilled in adhering to the meaning according to the literal expression.
Because reality is devoid of syllables,
one must not be like one who gazes at a fingertip.
For example, Mahāmati, it is as if someone were to point something out to another with their finger.
And he would look only at the tip of the finger;

even so, Mahāmati, those of a foolish nature— the classes of ignorant worldlings— will pass away while remaining attached to the literal meaning of the "tip of the finger," and they will not arrive at the ultimate truth by setting aside the literal meaning of the "tip of the finger."
For example, Mahāmati, it is like food that is to be eaten by children;
if someone were to consume it without having prepared it, they would be considered insane because of their failure to understand the gradual preparation of the food.
In the same way, Mahāmati, non-arising and non-ceasing do not shine forth without being intentionally constructed.
There must necessarily be intentional construction here;
yet it is not like the case of pointing out an object by grasping the tip of a finger.
Therefore, for this reason, Mahāmati, one should apply oneself to the meaning.
Mahāmati, the meaning is secluded and is the cause of Nirvāṇa;
words are bound up with conceptual construction and lead to saṃsāra.
Moreover, Mahāmati, the meaning is obtained from those who are well-versed in the scriptures;
and what is called being well-versed in the scriptures, Mahāmati, is skill in the meaning, not skill in the words.
In this regard, skill in meaning (*arthakauśalya*) is that vision which is unmixed with the doctrines of all the non-Buddhist teachers (*tīrthakara*),
such that one does not fall oneself nor cause others to fall.
It is in this way, Mahāmati, that there is great learning regarding the true meaning.
Therefore, those who desire the true goal should serve them; conversely, those who are the opposite—those who are fixated on the literal meaning of the words—should be avoided by one seeking reality.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, spoke thus: "The Blessed One, through the vision of non-cessation and non-arising, does not distinguish himself from anything.
Why is that?
Because, Blessed One, even for all the non-Buddhist teachers, causes are likewise unarisen and unceasing."
O Blessed One, for you as well, space, analytical cessation, and the realm of nirvana are unceasing and unarisen.
O Blessed One, even the non-Buddhist teachers describe the arising of the world as being caused by causal conditions;
yet the Blessed One also describes the arising of the world as resulting from the conditions of ignorance, craving, karma, and conceptual construction.
Having generated a specific distinction in the designation for that very same cause, they are called "conditions.
Thus, external conditions [act] upon external things;
both those and you [are conditions] for the arising of phenomena.
Therefore, Blessed One, this teaching is no different from the doctrines of the non-Buddhist teachers (*tīrthakara*).
Atoms, *pradhāna*, Īśvara, Prajāpati, and so forth—along with the nine substances—are unceased and unarisen.
For you too, Blessed One, all phenomena (*bhāva*) are unarisen and unceased, because neither existence nor non-existence is perceived.
Because the primary elements are indestructible, their own-characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) neither arises nor ceases;
having gone to whatever state they may go, the primary element does not abandon its nature as a primary element.

"Bhagavat, this transformation of the conceptualization of real entities is conceptualized by all the non-Buddhist teachers as well as by you. For this reason, this doctrine is not distinguished [from theirs]. Therefore, a distinction must be stated here by which the Tathāgata’s doctrine is distinguished."
This is not the doctrine of any of the non-Buddhist teachers (tīrthakara).

Blessed One, if your own teaching were no different [from theirs], it would follow that even the non-Buddhist teachers are Buddhas, because they too teach non-cessation, non-arising, and the absence of a cause.
Furthermore, the Blessed One has stated that it is impossible and out of the question for many Tathāgatas to arise simultaneously in a single world-system.
And thus, this plurality of Tathāgatas follows as a consequence for one's own doctrine, which is no different from the [Sāṃkhya] position that accepts an effect as both existent and non-existent.

The Blessed One said: "Mahāmati, my teaching of non-cessation and non-arising is not the same as the non-arising and non-cessation doctrine of the non-Buddhists (tīrthakara), nor is it the same as their doctrine of arising and impermanence.
Why is that?
Because, Mahāmati, for the non-Buddhists, the intrinsic nature of things (bhāvasvabhāva) truly exists, having attained the characteristics of being unarisen and immutable."

But for me, Mahāmati, it does not fall into the positions of existence or non-existence. Rather, for me, it is free from the positions of existence and non-existence, devoid of arising and ceasing; it is neither an entity nor a non-entity, yet it is not a non-entity because it is like the perception of the various forms of an illusion.
How is it that there is no existence?
It is because of the absence of grasping at the characteristics of the intrinsic nature of form, due to its being visible or invisible, and its being grasped or ungrasped.
For this reason, all things are neither existents nor non-existents.

However, Mahāmati, through the realization that [the world] is merely the manifestation of one's own mind, conceptual construction ceases to function; thus, the world remains in its natural state, free from activity.
It is the foolish who imagine it to possess activity, but not the noble ones.
This delusion regarding objects arising from the conceptual construction of unreal things, Mahāmati, is like a city of the Gandharvas or a magical man.
For example, Mahāmati, suppose some person of childish nature were to imagine a diverse multitude of illusory beings and creatures entering or exiting a city of the Gandharvas, thinking,
"These have entered; these have exited," even though no one at all had actually entered or exited there.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, to the extent that this state consists of the delusion of conceptual construction, such is the delusion regarding arising and non-arising for the foolish;
yet herein there is nothing conditioned or unconditioned, just like the manifestation of an illusory person.
Furthermore, an illusory person neither arises nor ceases, because existence and non-existence are incapable of producing anything.
In the very same way, all phenomena are devoid of destruction and arising;
it is only through a perception fallen into falsehood that the foolish conceptualize arising and cessation, but not so the noble ones.
In this regard, Mahāmati, "unreal" means that it is not as the intrinsic nature of things is conceptualized,
nor is it otherwise;
for if it were conceptualized otherwise, there would be nothing but attachment to the intrinsic nature of all things.
If there were no vision of the secluded [nature] due to the absence of vision of the secluded, there would be no cessation of conceptual construction at all.
For this reason, Mahāmati, the vision of the signless (*animitta*) alone is superior, not the vision of signs (*nimitta*).
Furthermore, because a sign is the cause of birth, it is not superior.
"Mahāmati, 'signlessness' (animitta) means the non-occurrence and non-arising of conceptual construction; this, I say, is nirvāṇa.
In that regard, Mahāmati, 'nirvāṇa' refers to the vision of the abiding state of reality as it truly is, preceded by the revolution of the complex of conceptual mind and mental factors.
I declare that the attainment of the noble, self-realized wisdom of a Tathāgata is nirvāṇa."
In this regard, it is said:
"For the purpose of ceasing [the notion of] arising, I teach the doctrine of causelessness which establishes non-arising; yet it is not understood by the foolish. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 3.86)
All this is unarisen, yet it is not the case that entities do not exist;
entities known as Gandharva-cities, dreams, and illusions exist without a cause.
Tell me, by what means are things empty, having an unarisen nature?
When separated from causal aggregation, no entity is apprehended by the intellect;
therefore, I declare that which is empty, unarisen, and without intrinsic nature.
Likewise, inherence does not exist, because each individual [element] is not perceived;
inherence does not exist because it is not the dissolution [proposed] by the views of the non-Buddhists.
Just as dreams, hair-nets, illusions, city-of-the-gandharvas,
and mirages are seen without a cause, so too are the diversities of the world perceived.
Having refuted the doctrine of causelessness, one should establish non-arising;
when non-arising is established, my guiding principle does not perish.
When the doctrine of causelessness is taught, fear arises among the heretics.
How, by what means, from where, and where could there be an uncaused arising?
When one perceives that the conditioned is neither without cause nor produced from causes,
then the view that asserts destruction and arising is overturned.
Is non-arising indeed non-existence, or is it the observation of conditions? Or is this a name for existence, or is it meaningless? Tell me.
Non-arising is neither non-existence nor the observation of conditions;
it is neither the name of an entity nor is it a meaningless name.
That which is beyond the range of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and non-Buddhist outsiders,
as well as those who have reached the seven stages— that is the characteristic of non-arising.
The cessation of causes and conditions, the stopping of the [efficient] cause,
and the establishment of mind-only— this I call non-arising.
I teach non-arising as the causeless occurrence of phenomena, devoid of the imagined and the imagination, and free from the positions of existence and non-existence. (Lankavatara Sutra 3.97)
I declare that non-arising is the revolution of the basis (āśrayaparāvṛtti), wherein the mind is liberated from the visible and devoid of the two natures.
There is no external existence, nor non-existence, nor even the grasping of the mind;
it is like a dream, a mass of hair [seen by the ophthalmic], an illusion, a city of Gandharvas, and a mirage.
The abandonment of all views is the characteristic of that non-arising.
In this way, one should contemplate all such terms as "empty" and "without intrinsic nature";
it is never empty by means of an emptiness that is itself empty, but rather by means of the emptiness of non-arising.
The collection of conditions arises and ceases;
that which is separate from the collection is neither born nor extinguished.
No other entity exists apart from the collection;
it is nowhere found as either identical to or different from it, just as it is conceptualized by the non-Buddhists.
An entity is never born from that which is non-existent, nor from that which is both existent and non-existent;
rather, it is only this collection [of causes] that proceeds and ceases.
This is merely a conventional designation, a mutual interdependence;
there is no other object whatsoever existing apart from the construction of conceptual cognition.
Because there is no produced thing, I teach non-arising, which is free from the faults of the heterodox; it is merely a mental construction, yet it is not perceived by the foolish.

He who holds that there exists some entity produced from the causal chain (saṃkalā) as something separate from it should be known as a proponent of causelessness (ahetuvādin) and a destroyer of the causal chain.
A lamp is the manifester of various kinds of substances; there might be a "chain" [of causes], if some entity were to exist anywhere apart from that chain.

For those phenomena which are imagined by the ignorant to be distinct from the causal chain (saṃkalā) are indeed without intrinsic nature, unarisen, and by their very nature like space. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 3.108)
The non-arising of one thing after another is the dharma-nature attained by the Noble Ones;
for that which has no birth, there is the patient acceptance of non-arising (*anutpādakṣānti*).
When one perceives this entire world as nothing but a mental construction, and sees that this is merely a construction, then the mind becomes concentrated in samādhi.
Ignorance, craving, karma, and so forth constitute the internal causal chain;
the sky, clay, pots, wheels, and so forth, as well as seeds and the elements, constitute the external.

For one who maintains that an entity arises from another through conditions at some point, this world is not merely a causal chain; such persons do not abide by either logic or scripture. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 3.112)
If no produced entity exists, of what could cognition arise through conditions?
For these [factors] are mutually productive; therefore, they are known as "conditions" (pratyaya).
Heat, fluidity, mobility, and solidity—these phenomena are conceptualized by the ignorant;
this is merely a collection, no phenomenon exists here, and for this very reason there is a lack of intrinsic nature.

Just as physicians perform various treatments according to the condition of the patient, yet there is no division in the medical science itself, so too [the teachings] differ only due to the difference in afflictions.

In the same way, having understood the strength of the faculties of living beings, I teach the method to them, seeing that the continuum of sentient beings is thoroughly defiled by the faults of the afflictions.
My teaching is not divided according to the differences in afflictions or faculties;
there is but a single vehicle, the auspicious Eightfold Path.
Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati spoke again to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, 'impermanence, impermanence' is conceptualized by all the non-Buddhist teachers (*tīrthakara*).
Yet, in the recitation of all your teachings, you teach: 'Alas, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent; they have the nature of arising and passing away.
Therefore, Blessed One, is this [impermanence] real or is it false?"
“Blessed One, how many kinds of impermanence are there?
The Blessed One replied, “Mahāmati, eight kinds of impermanence are conceptualized by all the non-Buddhist teachers, but not by me. What are these eight kinds?”
In this regard, Mahāmati, some say that impermanence is the cessation of commencement;
"commencement," Mahāmati, means arising, and non-arising is impermanence.
Others describe impermanence as the cessation of configuration.
Some [hold] that form itself is impermanent;
others [hold] that impermanence is a transformation of form.

Through a continuous succession, the breaking apart by way of its own inherent nature occurs in all phenomena; like the transformation of milk into curd, this change proceeds in all entities as something unseen and vanished, and not as permanence.
Furthermore, some conceive of existence as impermanence; others conceive of the non-existence of existence as impermanence;
and others conceive of non-arising as impermanence, because all phenomena are included within that [non-arising].

In this regard, Mahāmati, what is called the impermanence of existence and non-existence is as follows: it is the non-perception of the destruction of the specific characteristics of the primary elements and their derivatives, and the non-occurrence of the intrinsic nature of the elements.

Therein, what is called the impermanence of non-arising is as follows: it is that which is eternally impermanent; it is the non-occurrence of both existence and non-existence regarding all phenomena; it is the non-perception [of phenomena] due to the analysis down to the level of atoms.
This is a designation for non-arising, not for arising.

For this, Mahāmati, is the characteristic of the impermanence of non-arising; through the lack of understanding of which all the heterodox teachers fall into the doctrine of the impermanence of arising.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, for one who holds that an entity is eternal, that eternity is merely an entity through the conceptual construction of their own intellect; it is not [truly] impermanent.
Why is that?
That is to say, because impermanence itself is not subject to destruction.
Here, Mahāmati, the non-existence of all things is the effect of impermanence;
and without impermanence, the non-existence of all things is not perceived, just as [the distinction between] the striker and the struck cannot be found in the case of a staff, a stone, or a mallet.
The observation of no distinction between them is seen;
therefore, impermanence is the cause and the non-existence of all things is the effect.
Furthermore, there is no distinction between cause and effect such that one could say, "this is impermanence" and "this is the effect."
Because there is no distinction between cause and effect, all entities are eternal, since an entity lacks a cause;
for indeed, Mahāmati, the non-existence of all entities is causeless,
yet foolish common people do not understand this.
Furthermore, a cause does not produce an effect that is dissimilar to itself.
If it were to produce such an effect, then the impermanence of all things would result in effects that are dissimilar [to their causes].
There would be no distinction between cause and effect;
yet, a distinction between cause and effect is observed among them.
Alternatively, if impermanence were non-existence, [the same consequence would follow].
Furthermore, it would either fall within the characteristics of being an agent or a cause,
or it would be fully contained within all entities as a single entity.
And because it would fall within the characteristics of being an agent or a cause, impermanence itself would be permanent.
All things, such as impermanence and so forth, would be eternal; they would indeed be permanent.
Now, if impermanence were included within all entities,
it would consequently fall within the three times. In that case, whatever form is past would have perished along with it.
That which is future has likewise not arisen;
by virtue of the non-arising of form, it possesses a characteristic non-different from present form.
And form is a specific arrangement of the primary elements (*bhūta*).

The elemental nature of the primary elements (*bhūta*) does not perish, because it is free from being either identical to or different [from them]. Since none of the non-Buddhist teachers (*tīrthakara*) accept the destruction of any primary element, the entire triple world consists of primary elements and their derivatives (*bhautika*), wherein the arising, abiding, and transformation of all things are designated.
Apart from these primary elements and their derivatives, what else could there be that is impermanent, for which the non-Buddhist teachers would postulate impermanence?
And the elements neither proceed nor cease because of their adherence to the characteristic of intrinsic nature.

In this regard, the cessation of undertaking is called impermanence: the primary elements do not again initiate another primary element, nor is a specific quality initiated from their own-characteristics which are mutually distinct.

Because there is no such distinction, because they do not undertake [further] again, and because of the impossibility of a twofold [process], there arise the cognitions of impermanence regarding non-undertaking.
In this regard, what is called the cessation of configuration is impermanence; that is to say, the primary elements and their derivatives do not perish until the final dissolution (*pralaya*).

Mahāmati, "dissolution" refers to the destruction of the configuration of the primary elements and their derivatives through analytical investigation down to the level of atoms, wherein one no longer perceives length or shortness due to seeing the configuration as having changed into something else.
It is not because of the destruction of the atoms themselves, but because of seeing the cessation of the configuration of the elements, that they do not fall into the doctrine of the Sāṃkhyas.

In this regard, what is called the impermanence of shape (*saṃsthāna*) is as follows: namely, for that whose form (*rūpa*) alone is impermanent, it is the impermanence of the shape and not of the primary elements (*bhūta*).
If there were impermanence of the primary elements themselves, there would be an absence of worldly convention (*lokasaṃvyavahāra*).
Because of the absence of worldly convention, one would fall into the view of the Lokāyatas, since all things would be mere words;
it is not, however, because of the perception of the arising of specific characteristics.

In this context, what is called "impermanence through transformation" refers to the perception of matter (*rūpa*) as having changed its state, rather than a change in the primary elements (*bhūta*). It is like seeing the transformation of gold into a particular shape and ornament; the gold does not perish because of its existence, but rather the shape and configuration of the ornament perish.
And other such views concerning impermanence are conceptualized by the non-Buddhist teachers (tīrthakara) through these and other modes, all of which fall into the category of transformation.
For when the primary elements (bhūta) are burned by fire, they are not actually consumed because of their own intrinsic nature (svalakṣaṇa).
Due to the mutual loss of their own specific characteristics, there would be the annihilation of the state of the primary elements and their derivatives.
But for me, Mahāmati, it is neither eternal nor non-eternal.
Why is that?

Because, namely, since external entities are not admitted and because of the teaching that the three realms of existence are mind-only, and because there is no teaching of various characteristics, the specific arrangement of the great elements neither proceeds nor ceases.

Because conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is neither an element (*bhūta*) nor a derivative of elements (*bhautika*), it proceeds in two ways, characterized by the nature of the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*).

Through the thorough knowledge of these two modes of the activity of conceptual construction, through the disappearance of the view of the existence and non-existence of external objects, and through the realization that there is only one's own mind (*svacittamātra*), conceptual construction proceeds by means of the formative activity (*abhisaṃskāra*) of conceptualization; it does not proceed for one who is without such formative activity.
This is because of the disappearance of the existence and non-existence of the conceptualization of the mind, [and thus] of all phenomena—whether mundane, supramundane, or supreme.
There is neither permanence nor impermanence.

Due to a lack of understanding that [the world] is merely the manifestation of one's own mind, and because their mental continuity has fallen into the two extremes of false views, all the non-Buddhist teachers—who are like mere storytellers and have not previously established [any truth]—conceive of impermanence through their own unawakened conceptualizations.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, the characteristics of all phenomena—whether mundane, supramundane, or supreme supramundane—as conceived by all the non-Buddhist teachers, are merely issues emerging from the conceptualization of speech.
And yet, foolish ordinary people do not understand this.
Regarding this, it is said:
Deluded, the heterodox teachers conceptualize the cessation of activity, the alteration of configuration, existence, impermanence, and form as being [the nature of] *anityatā*. (Lank_3.118)
There is indeed no destruction of entities, for they exist as beings with the nature of being;
yet those outsiders, submerged in various views, conceptualize them as eternal.
For no heterodox teacher [admits] either destruction or origination;
since the elements are eternal by their very nature as elements, for whom could one imagine impermanence?
All this is mind-only; the mind evolves in two ways through the state of the grasped and the grasper. Self and what belongs to self do not exist.
I declare that everything from the realm of Brahmā down to the lowest station is mind-only;
apart from mind-only, Brahmā and the others are not to be found.
Thus ends the third chapter, "On Impermanence," in the Laṅkāvatāra Mahāyāna Sūtra.
START Chapter 4 (Vaidya 86):
The Fourth Chapter, titled "The Clear Realization" (Abhisamaya).

Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati spoke again to the Blessed One: "May the Blessed One teach me skill in the characteristics of the sequential transition of the cessation of all Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas;

by means of this skill in the characteristics of the sequential transition, may I and other Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas not be deluded by the gateway of the meditative attainment of the bliss of cessation."
"And may we not fall into the delusions of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and non-Buddhist teachers.
The Blessed One said: "Therefore, Mahāmati, listen; attend well and thoroughly to it."
"I shall speak to you.
"Excellent, Blessed One," the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this to him: "Mahāmati, beginning from the sixth stage, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as well as all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas enter into cessation.

However, on the seventh stage, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas enter into it at every moment of thought through the elimination of the characteristics of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, whereas the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not."

For the cessation-attainment (*nirodha-samāpatti*) of those Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas is produced through volitional effort (*ābhisaṃskārikī*) and falls within the characteristics of the grasped and the grasper (*grāhya-grāhaka-lakṣaṇa*).
Therefore, on the seventh stage, they enter it moment by moment (*citta-kṣaṇe citta-kṣaṇe*), lest there be the attainment of the non-distinctive characteristic (*aviśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena,
and lest there be the absence of diverse characteristics (*vicitra-lakṣaṇa*).
Because they do not understand the characteristics of the nature of wholesome and unwholesome states regarding all phenomena, there is no attainment [of mastery].
Therefore, on the seventh stage, there is no skill in attainment moment by moment in each thought-instant, by which they might enter into meditative absorption.

On the eighth stage, Mahāmati, there occurs for the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, as well as for the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, the turning away from the conceptualizations and perceptions of mind, mentation, and mental consciousness. On the first and sixth stages, they perceive the triple world as being nothing but mind, mentation, and mental consciousness— devoid of self and what belongs to a self, arising from the conceptualization of one’s own mind— and they do not fall into the perception of the diversity of external entities, seeing instead that it is nothing other than their own mind.

Having transformed their own cognition into the dual mode of grasped object and grasping subject, fools do not realize it, being permeated by the habitual tendencies of the proliferation of conceptual constructions and the dysfunctions of beginningless time.
Mahāmati, on the eighth stage, there is the nirvāṇa of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas,

and bodhisattvas. However, the bodhisattvas are sustained by the Buddhas of Samādhi within that bliss of samādhi, so that they do not pass into final nirvāṇa because the stage of a Tathāgata is not yet fully perfected.
Furthermore, all activities would come to a standstill if one were not to maintain [the lineage], and there would be the severance of the family line of the Tathāgata clan.
Those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, teach the inconceivable majesty of a Buddha;
therefore, they do not enter final nirvana.
The Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, however, are carried away by the bliss of meditative concentration.
Therefore, they conceive the thought that they have attained final nirvana there.

Mahāmati, on the seven stages I shall make a distinction among the factors conducive to enlightenment—consisting of skill in familiarizing oneself with the characteristics of mind, mentation, and mental consciousness; skill in [understanding] self and what belongs to self, the grasped and the grasper, and the non-self of phenomena and persons; the arising and ceasing of things; the familiarization with specific and general characteristics; mastery in the determination of the four analytical knowledges; and the blissful taste of the stages through their gradual entry.

This is done so that Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas, through lack of understanding regarding specific and general characteristics and lack of skill in the transition between the stages, do not fall into the path of the evil views of the non-Buddhist outsiders.
For this reason, the systematic arrangement of the stages is established.

However, Mahāmati, herein no one proceeds or recedes; rather, this—namely, the transition through the sequence of stages and the various conventional designations of the triple world—is merely the manifestation of one's own mind.
And yet, the ignorant do not realize this.

Due to the lack of understanding on the part of the ignorant, the designation of the sequence of stages, the various conventional expressions regarding the three realms, and the foundation of the Buddha-dharmas are established.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, intoxicated by the pride of the bliss of the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) on the eighth Bodhisattva stage, being unskilled in the fact that [all things] are merely the manifestation of their own minds, fall into views that grasp at the selflessness of persons and phenomena, which are themselves the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the obstructions regarding specific and general characteristics.
There are those whose minds and intellects conceive of nirvāṇa as a conceptual construction, and not those whose minds and intellects perceive the nature of phenomena as being secluded.

However, Mahāmati, Bodhisattvas— having beheld the gateway to the bliss of the samādhi of cessation, yet being endowed with their former vows and compassion, and possessing the knowledge that discerns the distinctions between the ultimate state and the realms of existence— do not enter final parinirvāṇa.
And they have entered final nirvana because conceptual construction no longer functions.
Their conceptual construction of grasped object and grasping subject has ceased.
Through the realization that all phenomena are merely the manifestation of one's own mind, conceptual construction does not arise.
One conceptualizes the attachment to the characteristics of the intrinsic nature of external objects, [which are merely] mind, mentation, and mental consciousness.
Because of that, the cause for the qualities of a Buddha does not proceed;
rather, it proceeds preceded by knowledge through the attainment of the Tathāgata’s own stage of self-realization, like crossing a flood of people in a dream.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, it is as if someone, while asleep, were in a dream to cross a great flood with great effort and exertion;
yet, before having crossed it, he would wake up.
Having woken up, he would reflect thus: "Was this real, or was it false?"

He should contemplate thus: "This is neither true nor false; rather, it is that which has fallen into the conceptualizations of beginningless time—consisting of various forms and configurations born from the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of what has been seen, heard, thought, known, and experienced—and is perceived by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) as in a dream, yet is devoid of the conceptualizations of the views of existence and non-existence.
In this very way, Mahāmati, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas [realize] the non-arising of conceptualization on the eighth Bodhisattva stage.

Having seen that, through the transition from the first to the seventh stage and the clear realization of all dharmas, the proliferation of conceptualizations of mind and mental factors has ceased—due to the equality of all dharmas such as illusion—and having seen that all conceptualizations of eagerness for dharmas and of subject and object have subsided, they apply themselves to the qualities of a Buddha.

This application, Mahāmati, is for the sake of attaining what has not yet been attained; it is the *nirvāṇa* of Bodhisattvas, not annihilation. And because of the departure from the notions of the conceptualizations of mind, intellect, mentation, and consciousness, there is the attainment of the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
It exists.
And herein, Mahāmati, in the ultimate truth, there is neither sequence nor connection of sequences, because of the teaching of dharmas that are secluded from appearances and conceptual construction.
In this regard, it is said:
"The dwellings and the stage of Buddhahood exist within mind-only, which is free from appearances.
This indeed has been spoken by the Buddhas; they speak it and cause it to be spoken. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 4.1)
For the seven stages are the mind; the eighth here is the signless.
Two stages are indeed a dwelling here, while the remaining stage is of my own nature.
This stage, to be personally realized and pure, is my own nature;
it is the supreme abode of Maheśvara, shining as the Akaniṣṭha realm.
For just as rays issue forth from a fire,
those variegated, captivating, and gentle [rays] of his construct the triple world.
Having emanated a portion of the triple world and another portion previously emanated, I teach the vehicles therein; this is my own ground.
The tenth would become the first, and the first would become the eighth;
the ninth would also become the seventh, and the seventh would become the eighth.
The second would be the third, and the fourth would become the fifth;
the third would become the sixth—wherein there is no appearance, how could there be a sequence?
Thus ends the fourth chapter, "The Chapter on Realization," in the Laṅkāvatāra [Sūtra].
START Parivarta 5 (Vaidya 88):
The Fifth Chapter, titled "The Discussion on the Permanence and Impermanence of the Tathāgata."
Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Blessed One in this way: "Blessed One, is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, permanent or is he impermanent?
The Blessed One said: "Mahāmati, the Tathāgata is neither permanent nor impermanent. For what reason?"
That is to say, because it would entail the fallacy of both faults.
For in either case, Mahāmati, there would be the entailment of faults:
if [the cause] were eternal, it would entail the fallacy of [an eternal] cause.
For, Mahāmati, the causal principles of all the non-Buddhist teachers are indeed eternal and uncreated.
Therefore, the Tathāgata is not eternal, because [if he were], he would be an uncreated eternity.
If he were impermanent, the consequence would be that he is something created.
Because of the absence of the aggregates, the object, and the characteristic, and because of the destruction of the aggregates, there would be annihilation;
yet the Tathāgata is not subject to annihilation.
For everything that is produced, Mahāmati, is impermanent—such as jars, cloths, grass, wood, bricks, and so forth.

Because it would follow that everything is impermanent, the accumulation of the requisites for the knowledge of an omniscient one would be rendered useless, since [everything] would be created. For everything that is created would be the Tathāgata, as there would be no cause for distinction.
Therefore, Mahāmati, for this reason, the Tathāgata is neither permanent nor impermanent.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Tathāgata is not eternal. Why? Because it would follow that the accumulation of provisions [for enlightenment] would be as futile as empty space.

Just as, Mahāmati, empty space is neither eternal nor non-eternal—it is inexpressible due to the faults of being eternal, non-eternal, both, or neither, and due to the categories of oneness, otherness, both, or neither—so too is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, [if it were eternal], the Tathāgata would be like the horns of a rabbit, a horse, a donkey, a camel, a frog, a snake, a fly, or a fish, because of the eternity of non-arising.
Therefore, due to the consequence of being eternally unarisen, the Tathāgata is not eternal.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there is another way in which the Tathāgata is eternal.
Why is that?
It is because the Tathāgata is eternal due to the eternity of the knowledge resulting from the realization of direct intuition (*abhisamaya-adhigama-jñāna*).
Mahāmati, the wisdom of the realization of direct insight belongs eternally to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.

Whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise, this *dharmatā*, this *dharmaniyāmatā*, and this *dharmasthititā* remain constant throughout the realizations of all Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and non-Buddhist teachers.
However, such a stability of phenomena does not exist in empty space.
Furthermore, O Mahāmati, foolish common people do not understand this. The realized knowledge of the Tathāgatas is manifested through the wisdom of insight (prajñā-jñāna).

O Mahāmati, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are not manifested by the mind, the intellect, the mental consciousness, the aggregates, the elements, the sense-bases, or the latencies of ignorance.
For indeed, Mahāmati, the entire triple world arises from the false discrimination of the unreal;
yet the Tathāgatas do not arise from the false discrimination of the unreal.
For when there is duality, Mahāmati, there exist both permanence and impermanence, but not from non-duality.
For duality, Mahāmati, is devoid of the characteristics of non-duality and non-arising of all dharmas.
For this reason, Mahāmati, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are neither eternal nor non-eternal.
As long as verbal conceptualization proceeds, Mahāmati, [so long does this dualistic appearance persist].
Until then, the fault of permanence and impermanence persists;

however, Mahāmati, through the cessation of conceptualizing thought, the grasping at permanence and impermanence is averted for the ignorant, but not through the cessation of a mind that perceives things as being in their true isolation.
In this regard, it is said:

Those who always perceive the Buddhas as being free from permanence and impermanence, yet manifested through permanence and impermanence, have not fallen under the sway of dogmatic views. *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* 5.1.
The futility of realization follows if [things] were both eternal and non-eternal;
because of the deficiency of conceptualizing intellect, "eternal" and "non-eternal" are both refuted. (Lankavatara Sutra 5.2)
As long as a thesis is maintained, everything is mixed with confusion;
seeing that all is merely one's own mind, one should not engage in dispute.
Thus ends the fifth chapter of the Laṅkāvatāra [Sūtra], titled "The Examination of the Permanence and Impermanence of the Tathāgata."
START Chapter 6 (Vaidya 90):
The sixth chapter, named "The Momentary."

Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati again entreated the Blessed One: "May the Blessed One teach me; may the Sugata teach me the arising and ceasing of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
If there is no self, whose is the arising or whose is the ceasing?"
And fools, relying on engagement and withdrawal, do not understand the cessation of suffering and thus do not know nirvāṇa.
The Blessed One said: "Therefore, Mahāmati, listen; attend well and thoroughly."
"I shall speak to you.
"Very well, Blessed One," the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati replied to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One said this to him: "Mahāmati, the *tathāgatagarbha*, which is the cause of both the wholesome and the unwholesome, proceeds as the creator of all births and destinies; it functions like an actor within the narrow straits of the various realms of existence, devoid of self and what belongs to a self.

Due to the lack of understanding of that [garbha], the conjunction of the activity of the threefold causal conditions proceeds. Yet the heterodox teachers do not understand this, being obsessed with their attachment to [the notion of] a cause."

Perfumed by the habitual tendencies of the manifold conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) and dysfunctions (*dauṣṭhulya*) from beginningless time, that which is designated as the *ālayavijñāna* proceeds with its body eternally uninterrupted— like waves upon the great ocean— together with the seven consciousnesses born from the ground of the habitual tendencies of ignorance; it is free from the fault of impermanence,
devoid of the doctrine of a self (*ātman*), and absolutely pure by nature.
The other consciousnesses that arise and perish—beginning with the mind and mental consciousness—are momentary.

All seven depend upon a collection of specific shapes and forms produced by the cause of unreal imagination; they are attached to names and signs, fail to realize that the characteristics of form are but the manifestations of one's own mind, do not experience pleasure or pain, and are causes for non-liberation. They take as their objects the very causes that produce and are produced by the outbursts of passion based on names and signs.

And when those appropriated things called the sense-faculties are exhausted and cease, because others do not arise immediately thereafter— being those who do not experience pleasure and pain through their own mental conceptualizations,
who have entered the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, and who are yogins skilled in the four dhyānas, the truths, and the liberations—
there arises in them the notion of liberation due to the non-occurrence [of further existence].

And as long as the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), which is designated by the term *tathāgatagarbha*, has not undergone transformation, there is no cessation of the seven evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
Why is that?
Because the consciousnesses arise with that [storehouse consciousness] as their cause and object.

Furthermore, because it is not an object for all Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or practitioners of non-Buddhist yoga, the Tathāgatagarbha proceeds by virtue of their awakening to the selflessness of their own person and their grasping at the specific and general characteristics of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases. It ceases through the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) via the sequential transition of the stages, upon seeing the five dharmas, the intrinsic nature, and the selflessness of phenomena.
It cannot be investigated by the views of the paths of other non-Buddhist teachers.
Therefore, established upon the immovable stage (*acalā bhūmi*), which is a stage of a bodhisattva, one attains the ten gateways to the bliss of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Sustained by the Buddhas through their meditative concentrations, and by virtue of the contemplation of one’s own vows regarding the inconceivable qualities of a Buddha, one [abides] in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) which is the bliss of meditative concentration.

Having turned away from [the mundane] by means of the paths of yoga— which are accessible through the noble realization of each individual and are not shared with any śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or non-Buddhist teachers— one attains the path of the ten noble lineages,
as well as a body made of mind consisting of gnosis, which is free from the formative activity of meditative concentration.
Therefore, Mahāmati, the *tathāgatagarbha*, designated as the *ālayavijñāna*, must be purified by bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas who seek excellence.

For if, Mahāmati, the *tathāgatagarbha* designated as the *ālayavijñāna* were not present here, then, Mahāmati, in the absence of the *tathāgatagarbha* designated as the *ālayavijñāna*, there would be neither arising nor cessation. Yet, Mahāmati, there is indeed arising and cessation for both the foolish and the noble ones.

And by means of the dwelling in the bliss of the Dharma seen through the noble realization within their own individual self-awareness, yogins dwell without laying down their burden, being difficult to penetrate.

Mahāmati, this sphere of the *tathāgatagarbha* and the *ālayavijñāna*—though naturally pure—is, for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the speculative views of outsiders, as if impure due to being defiled by adventitious afflictions; yet it does not appear so to the Tathāgatas.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, for the Tathāgatas, this becomes an object of direct perception, like an amalaka fruit in the palm of the hand.

It was precisely with reference to this, Mahāmati, that I spoke in the scriptural discourse concerning Queen Śrīmālā, and by empowering other Bodhisattvas of subtle, skillful, and pure intelligence, [taught] the *tathāgatagarbha* designated as the *ālayavijñāna* along with the seven consciousnesses.

In order to demonstrate the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) to those Śrāvakas who are attached to [the notion of] active engagement, the Tathāgata, having empowered the goddess Śrīmālā, taught this domain of the Tathāgata.

It is not the domain of the reasoning of Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or other non-Buddhist teachers; rather, Mahāmati, the Tathāgatagarbha is the domain of the Tathāgatas and the domain of the *ālayavijñāna*, accessible only to those like you whose intellects possess subtle, skillful, and discerning wisdom.
This applies to the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, who rely on the meaning and not on those who are attached to the literal reading of the teachings,
as is the case with all other outsiders, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas.

Therefore, Mahāmati, you and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas should apply yourselves to the thorough understanding of the Tathāgatagarbha and the Ālayavijñāna within this domain of all the Tathāgatas.
One should not be satisfied with mere learning.
Regarding this, it is said:
"The embryo of the Tathāgatas, indeed endowed with the seven consciousnesses, proceeds through non-dual grasping; through thorough knowledge, it ceases. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 6.1)
The mind, conditioned by beginningless conceptualization, appears like a reflection;
yet for one who perceives reality as it truly is, there is no object existing in the form of an external thing.
Just as a child does not grasp the moon by its fingertip, so too one who is attached to syllables does not know my reality. *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* 6.3.
The mind dances like an actor; the intellect is like a jester;
and consciousness, together with the five [sensory cognitions], constructs the object of perception like a stage.
Then indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati again entreated the Blessed One: "May the Blessed One teach me;

may the Sugata teach me the characteristics of the penetration into the distinctions of the five dharmas, the self-natures, the consciousnesses, and the two kinds of selflessness, by means of which penetration into the distinctions of the two kinds of selflessness, I and other Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas may clearly discern these dharmas throughout the successive transitions of all the stages."

"In such a way that through those dharmas there may be an entry into all the Buddha-dharmas, and from that entry into all the Buddha-dharmas, there may be an entry into the stage of the Tathāgata’s own self-realization.
The Blessed One said: "In that case, Mahāmati, listen."
"Pay close and careful attention;
I shall speak to you.
"Very well, Blessed One," the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati replied to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One said this to him: "Mahāmati, I shall teach you the characteristics of the penetration into the distinctions of the five dharmas, the self-nature, the cognitions, and the two kinds of selflessness. That is to say: name, appearance, conceptualization, right knowledge, and suchness. Through these, there occurs for yogins the entry into the noble state of the Tathāgata’s personal realization—a dwelling in the bliss of meditative attainment and the happiness of the present dharma, free from the views of eternalism, nihilism, existence, and non-existence."

In this regard, Mahāmati, discrimination arises for the foolish—due to their failure to understand that the five dharmas, the [three] natures, the [eight] consciousnesses, the two kinds of selflessness, and external existence and non-existence are but the manifestations of one's own mind—but it does not arise for the noble ones.
Mahāmati said: "But how, Blessed One, does the conceptual construction of the ignorant arise, while it does not arise for the noble ones?"

The Blessed One said: "Mahāmati, through attachment to names, designations, and conventions, the foolish follow after the mind. Following it, they fall into the views of 'self' and 'mine' by means of the application of various characteristics; they become attached to the abundance of colors. And being attached, they are impassioned, shrouded by ignorance."
