Being thoroughly impassioned, they perform karma born of passion, hatred, and delusion.

Having performed it, like silkworms, their minds are enveloped by their own conceptual constructions; fallen into the ocean-wilderness of the realms of existence, they revolve incessantly like a waterwheel.

Out of delusion, they do not understand that all phenomena—which arise from unreal conceptualization, are devoid of self and what belongs to a self, and are free from both the characterized and the characteristics—are by nature like an illusion, a mirage, or the moon reflected in water.

Mahāmati, those who have turned away from [the notions of] destruction, arising, stability, and movement— [which arise] from the conceptualization of what is seen as one's own mind, and not from Īśvara, time, atoms, or primal matter— the foolish follow after signs by following along with names and signs.
In this regard, Mahāmati, the "sign" (*nimitta*) is that which appears to visual consciousness under the designation of "form.

Likewise, for auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental consciousnesses, that which appears under the designations of sound, odor, taste, tangible object, and mental phenomena—this, I say, is the sign.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, "discrimination" (*vikalpa*) is that by which one utters names.

This is the indicator of signs—that "this is thus and not otherwise"—whereby conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) proceed regarding things designated as elephants, horses, chariots, infantry, women, men, and so forth.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) is that by which name and sign are not apprehended.

Because they are mutually adventitious, consciousness does not proceed; because it is neither annihilated nor eternal, and because it does not cause one to fall into the stages of any heterodox teachers, Śrāvakas, or Pratyekabuddhas, it is called right knowledge.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, by means of that right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not turn the name into an entity,
nor does he turn the sign (*nimitta*) into a non-entity.

It is a consciousness that does not function with respect to name, sign, or object, and is free from the two extremes of false attribution (*samāropa*) and denial (*apavāda*), as well as from evil views.

In this way, Mahāmati, I speak of this suchness; and a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in suchness, because he has attained the sphere of the non-manifest, attains the Bodhisattva stage called the Joyful (Pramuditā).

Having attained the Bodhisattva stage of Pramuditā, he turns away from all the destinies of the heterodox and the miserable states, and becomes fully integrated into the supramundane course of reality. Through familiarity with the [Buddha-]marks, he discerns the course of all phenomena as being preceded by illusion and the like;

his curiosity regarding the characteristics of the noble dharmas of personal realization having ceased through the turning away from speculative views, he proceeds gradually up to the Dharmameghā stage.
Immediately after the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*), he attains the stage of a Tathāgata, which is blossomed with the powers of meditative concentration, masteries, and superknowledges.
Having attained it, he shines forth with various rays of emanations for the sake of maturing sentient beings, like the moon reflected in water.
With the Dharma firmly established upon the eightfold path, he teaches the Dharma to sentient beings according to their diverse inclinations.
The body is devoid of mental representation;
it is this, Mahāmati, that Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas attain through entry into suchness.
Again Mahāmati said: "Furthermore, Blessed One, are the three natures included within the five dharmas, or are they established by their own specific characteristics?
The Blessed One replied: "In this very context, Mahāmati, the three natures are included."
There are also the eight consciousnesses and the two kinds of selflessness.
In this context, both the name and the sign should be understood as the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

Furthermore, Mahāmati, that discrimination which proceeds based on that [dependent nature], designated as mind and mental factors, arising simultaneously like the sun together with its rays, possessing a nature of diverse characteristics and serving as the support for discrimination—
that, Mahāmati, is called the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Perfect knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) and suchness (*tathatā*), Mahāmati, should be understood as the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), because they are indestructible.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, when one becomes attached to what is seen as one's own mind, discrimination is divided into eight kinds.
Because signs are imagined through unreal characteristics, and because the twofold grasping of self and what belongs to the self is stilled, the two kinds of selflessness arise.
Mahāmati, within these five dharmas are included all the qualities of a Buddha,
as well as the sequential distinctions of the stages for Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas,
and the entry into the noble, individual self-realized gnosis of the Tathāgatas.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are five dharmas: appearance (*nimitta*), name (*nāman*), conceptualization (*vikalpa*), suchness (*tathatā*), and right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).

In this regard, Mahāmati, that which is seen as having the characteristics of form, color, and so forth, with specific shapes, configurations, and particular aspects—that is "appearance. That which is a mental designation applied to that appearance, such as "this is a jar" or "it is thus and not otherwise"—that is "name."
That by which one utters that name— whether it be called the "manifestor of signs" (*nimittābhivyañjaka*) or "the same as phenomena" (*samadharmā*)—

is, Mahāmati, the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) designated as mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*). That which is the absolute non-apprehension of both name and sign, due to the dissolution of the intellect and because these phenomena are neither mutually experienced nor imagined— that is suchness (*tathatā*).

Reality (*tattva*) is that which is real, certain, ultimate, fundamental nature, intrinsic being, and non-apprehensibility; such is its characteristic. Having realized it, I and other Tathāgatas have taught, established, disclosed, and clarified it exactly as it is—that by realizing which, through correct awakening, there is the non-occurrence of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) due to neither annihilation nor permanence, which is conducive to the noble self-realized knowledge (*svapratyātmāryajñāna*), and which is characterized by not entering the positions of the heterodox teachers, nor those of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
That is right knowledge. And these, Mahāmati, are the five dharmas;
within these very [five] are the three natures.
The eight consciousnesses, the two kinds of selflessness,
and all the qualities of a Buddha are included therein.
In this regard, Mahāmati, you should exercise skill with your own intellect,
and you should cause others to do so as well;
you must not be led by others.
In this regard, it is said: "The five dharmas, the [three] intrinsic natures, and the eight consciousnesses,
along with the two kinds of selflessness— this constitutes the entirety of the Mahāyāna."
Name, sign, and conceptualization are the characteristics of the two natures;
correct knowledge and suchness are the characteristic of the perfected nature.

Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati spoke again to the Blessed One: "Regarding that which was said by the Blessed One in the recitation of the teachings—that the Tathāgatas of the past, future, and present are equal in number to the sands of the river Gaṅgā—how is this to be understood, O Blessed One? Is it to be taken according to the literal meaning?"
"Or is there some other distinct meaning?
Let it be told, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said: "Mahāmati, one must not grasp the meaning according to the literal expression."
Moreover, Mahāmati, the measure of the Buddhas of the three times does not depend on the measure of the sands of the Ganges River.
Why is that?
Because, Mahāmati, since they transcend all worldly excellence, an analogy is not truly an analogy due to the disparity between the likeness and the unlikeness.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas do not manifest examples that are either similar or dissimilar, nor those that transcend the world.
Rather, Mahāmati, this which has been set forth by me and by those Tathāgatas is merely a metaphor.

It is for the purpose of causing alarm in foolish commoners— who are obsessed with the dogmatic adherence to permanence and impermanence, who possess the evil views of the sectarian teachers' inclinations, and who follow the wheel of existence in saṃsāra— so that, once alarmed by the narrow straits of the wheel of existence and destinies, these seekers of distinction may apply themselves to distinction; and it is for the purpose of demonstrating that Buddhahood is easily attained, [by saying] that the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā.
Thinking that "the appearance of Tathāgatas is as rare as the *udumbara* flower," they will apply themselves with vigor;
however, in my teaching, out of consideration for those to be trained, I have taught that the manifestation of Tathāgatas is as extremely difficult to encounter as the *udumbara* flower.
Moreover, Mahāmati, the udumbara flower has never been seen by anyone before, nor will it ever be seen;
yet, Mahāmati, Tathāgatas have appeared in the world, and they are seen even now.

This statement—that "the appearance of Tathāgatas is as extremely rare as the blooming of the Udumbara flower"—is not made with reference to discourse concerning the establishment of one's own method (*svanaya*).

Mahāmati, when discourse concerning the establishment of one's own method is being taught, examples that transcend the world and its conventions are employed because [otherwise] they would be unbelievable;
for such things would be unbelievable to ordinary, foolish people.
In the domain of the noble wisdom of one's own self-realization, no analogies apply;
and the Tathāgatas are that very reality.
Therefore, no analogies are adduced for them.

However, Mahāmati, this which has been stated is merely a metaphorical illustration: that the Tathāgatas are equal to the sands of the river Gaṅgā—equal and not unequal—by virtue of being free from conceptualization and discursive thought (*avikalpana*).

Just as, Mahāmati, the sands in the river Gaṅgā, though being agitated by fish, tortoises, porpoises, crocodiles, buffaloes, lions, elephants, and other creatures, do not conceptualize or discriminate, thinking, "We are being agitated" or "we are not," they remain free from discursive thought (*nirvikalpa*).
They are clear and free from impurity.

In the same way, Mahāmati, the great river Gaṅgā of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas—the sands of which consist of the powers, superknowledges, and masteries of their own noble, personal, and direct gnosis—is not disturbed by all the fish-like heterodox teachers and other disputants; it neither conceptualizes nor discriminates.
Because of the Tathāgatas’ former vows and because they have fulfilled all meditative attainments of happiness for the sake of sentient beings, they do not conceptualize and do not discriminate.
Therefore, those Tathāgatas, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, are without distinction, being free from both attachment and aversion.
For example, Mahāmati, the sands of the river Gaṅgā are earth because their intrinsic nature possesses the characteristic of earth;
even when burned during the conflagration at the end of an eon, they do not abandon their own nature as earth.

Yet, Mahāmati, the earth is not actually burned because it is dependent upon the element of fire; it is only that foolish common people, through a continuity fallen into falsity, imagine it to be burning.
And it is not burned because it is the cause of fire.

In the same way, Mahāmati, the *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgatas is like the sands of the river Gaṅgā and is indestructible. Just as, Mahāmati, the sands in the river Gaṅgā are immeasurable, so too is the *dharmakāya*.

In the same way, Mahāmati, the light from the rays of the Tathāgatas is immeasurable; for the sake of rousing and maturing sentient beings, it is radiated by the Tathāgatas throughout all the circles of the assemblies of the Buddhas.
Just as, Mahāmati, the sands in the river Gaṅgā do not initiate any other nature apart from that of sand—the sands remain simply in the state of being sand.
In the same way, Mahāmati, for the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, there is neither proceeding nor ceasing in saṃsāra,
because the cause for the proceeding of existence has been severed.
Just as, Mahāmati, the sands of the river Gaṅgā cannot be perceived even when they are removed, [so it is with the Buddhas].
Even when they are cast in, Mahāmati, they are not perceived; in the same way, the wisdom of the Tathāgatas neither decreases nor increases through the process of maturing sentient beings,
because the Dharma is bodiless.
For, Mahāmati, destruction occurs for those who possess a body, but not for those who are bodiless;
and the Dharma is bodiless.
Just as, Mahāmati, the sands of the river Gaṅgā, when pressed by those seeking ghee or oil, are devoid of ghee, oil, and the like; [so too is the Dharma].

In the same way, Mahāmati, although the Tathāgatas are oppressed by the sufferings of sentient beings, they do not abandon the bliss of the vow for mastery over the *dharmadhātu*, Mahāmati, because they are endowed with great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*); [this continues] until all sentient beings have been led to *nirvāṇa* by the Tathāgatas.
Just as, Mahāmati, the sands in the river Gaṅgā flow along with the current and not against the water;
In the same way, Mahāmati, the teaching of all the Buddha-dharmas by the Tathāgatas flows in accordance with the stream of Nirvāṇa;
therefore, they are said to be as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā.
Mahāmati, this meaning of "going" does not apply to the Tathāgatas.
Mahāmati, "destruction" has the sense of "going.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, the prior limit of saṃsāra is not known.
Being unperceivable, how can it be explained by means of the sense of "going"?
Mahāmati, the sense of "going" is annihilation;
yet foolish common people do not understand this.

Mahāmati said: "If, Blessed One, the prior limit of beings wandering in saṃsāra is not known, then how is liberation known for living beings? The Blessed One said: "Mahāmati, it is the cessation of the cause—the habit-energy of conceptualization and the depravity of beginningless discursive proliferation—that constitutes liberation. Mahāmati, it is the revolution of the basis of conceptualization through the thorough knowledge that external objects are but the manifestations of one's own mind."
Liberation is not annihilation;
therefore, O Mahāmati, talk of "infinity" is of no avail.
O Mahāmati, "the limit of infinity" is merely a synonym for conceptual construction itself.
And herein, when examined by the intellect internally or externally, there exists no other entity whatsoever apart from conceptual construction.
For, Mahāmati, all phenomena are devoid of both the knower and the known.
Elsewhere, conceptual construction proceeds due to the lack of full understanding of the conceptualization of one's own mind; through the realization of that, it ceases.
Regarding this, it is said:
Those who perceive the Vināyakas as being equal in number to the sands of the Gaṅgā,
they indeed perceive the Tathāgatas as having reached the ultimate end of the state beyond destruction.
Just as the sands of the Ganges are free from all defects,
flow favorably with the current, and are eternal, so too is the Buddhahood of the Buddha.
Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati spoke thus again to the Blessed One: "May the Blessed One teach;
may the Sugata, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, teach me the momentary destruction of all dharmas and their characteristic of differentiation.
How is it, Blessed One, that all dharmas are momentary?"
The Blessed One said: "In that case, Mahāmati, listen and pay close and careful attention;
I shall speak to you."

"Excellent, Blessed One! the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this to him: "Mahāmati, 'all dharmas, all dharmas' refers to those that are wholesome and unwholesome, conditioned and unconditioned, mundane and supramundane, faulty and faultless, with outflows and without outflows, and appropriated and unappropriated."

In brief, Mahāmati, the five aggregates of grasping have the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of mind, intellect, and mental consciousness as their cause; they are conceptualized as wholesome or unwholesome by foolish commoners who are nourished by those very latent impressions of mind, intellect, and mental consciousness.
Mahāmati, the attainments of the bliss of meditative concentration are called "wholesome and untainted" for the Noble Ones because they constitute a dwelling in happiness in the present life.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, the wholesome and unwholesome refer to the eight consciousnesses.
What are these eight?
Namely, the *tathāgatagarbha*—which is designated as the *ālayavijñāna*—the *manas*, the *manovijñāna*, and the five bodies of consciousness (*pañca-vijñānakāya*) as described by the non-Buddhists.

In this regard, Mahāmati, the five bodies of consciousness, together with the *manovijñāna*, proceed as they arise, distinguished by a continuous succession of wholesome and unwholesome characteristics, their individual bodies appearing undivided due to the uninterrupted continuity of the stream.
Having arisen, they perish.
Due to the failure to realize that what is seen is one's own mind, as soon as one ceases, another consciousness arises.

The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), which grasps the distinctions of shape and form, arises in conjunction with the five groups of sensory consciousnesses, persisting for no more than a single moment.

I say that it is momentary. Furthermore, Mahāmati, the ālayavijñāna—which is designated as the *tathāgatagarbha*—together with the *manas*, is momentary by virtue of the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), yet it is non-momentary by virtue of the untainted latencies (*anāsravavāsanā*).
However, foolish common people, being attached to the doctrine of momentariness, do not understand this momentariness and non-momentariness of all phenomena.
Due to a lack of understanding of that, they will destroy even the unconditioned dharmas through the view of nihilism.
Mahāmati, the five bodies of consciousness do not transmigrate; they have not experienced pleasure and pain, and they are not causes for nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, the *tathāgatagarbha* is accompanied by the causes for the experience of pleasure and pain.
It proceeds and ceases, being thoroughly deluded by the four habitual tendencies;
yet the ignorant do not realize this, their minds being perfumed by the conceptualization of the view of momentariness.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, things that endure for an eon— such as gold, vajras, and the attainment of the relics of the Victors— are characterized by their excellence and are indestructible.
If, Mahāmati, the attainment of realization were momentary, then the Noble Ones would be non-noble.
And non-nobility does not belong to the noble ones.
Mahāmati, gold and diamond remain constant even for an eon; when weighed, they neither decrease nor increase.
How then can the ignorant—who are unskilled in the intentional language regarding all internal and external phenomena—conceptualize them as being momentary?

Again, Mahāmati said: "Furthermore, as for that which was stated by the Blessed One— that Buddhahood is attained by fulfilling the six perfections— what are those six perfections, and how do they reach fulfillment?"
The Blessed One said: "Mahāmati, there are these three distinctions of the perfections (pāramitā).
What are the three? Namely: the mundane, the supramundane, and the most supramundane."
In this regard, Mahāmati, the worldly perfections (*laukika-pāramitā*) are characterized by an adherence to and attachment to the notions of "self" and "mine.
Grasping at the two extremes and desiring the objects of form and so forth for the sake of various bases for rebirth within existence, fools fulfill the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*).
In the same way, Mahāmati, they fulfill the perfections of morality, patience, vigor, meditation, and wisdom.
And they bring forth the superknowledges (*abhijñā*) for the sake of attaining the state of Brahmā.

In that regard, through the supramundane perfections (*pāramitā*), Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas—who possess intentions fallen into the grasping of Nirvāṇa—apply themselves to giving and the other virtues, just as fools do who desire their own happiness and Nirvāṇa.

However, Mahāmati, those who are most supramundane [the Bodhisattvas], because they grasp that which is merely the conceptualization of what is seen of one's own mind, and because they awaken to the duality of their own mind, there is no further arising of conceptualization.

Due to the absence of grasping at acquisitions and due to non-attachment to the characteristics of the forms of their own minds, the perfection of giving arises for the sake of the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings among the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, who are practitioners of supreme yoga.
This occurs because they cultivate the non-arising of conceptual construction regarding that very object of focus.
That morality is also a perfection;
that capacity for enduring the non-occurrence of that very conceptualization through the thorough knowledge of the grasped and the grasper is the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*).
That vigor by which one exerts oneself during the first and last watches of the night, through the turning away of conceptual construction due to seeing what is conducive to yoga,
is the perfection of vigor.
That non-falling into the grasp of the nirvāṇa of the non-Buddhists resulting from the cessation of conceptual construction is the perfection of meditation.

In that regard, the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is that which, through the discernment of the intellect, does not fall into the two extremes because of the absence of conceptual constructions of one's own mind; and, by means of the transformation of the basis (āśrayaparāvṛtti) and the destruction of prior karma,
it applies itself toward the attainment of the noble state of personal realization—
that is the perfection of wisdom.
These, Mahāmati, are the perfections; this is the meaning of the perfections. Regarding this, it is said:
Fools conceptualize the conditioned as empty, impermanent, and momentary;
the meaning of momentariness is illustrated by the analogies of a river, a lamp, and a seed.
I declare that the meaning of momentariness is that phenomena are devoid of activity, instantaneous, solitary, free from destruction, and non-arising.
I do not indeed teach the destruction of things immediately after their arising to the foolish;
rather, it is through the uninterrupted succession of entities that conceptual construction vibrates within the course of existence. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 6.11)
That knowledge is the cause that brings those thoughts into activity;
in the interval before form arises, what state does it abide in? (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 6.12)
Immediately upon its destruction, another mind arises;
form does not remain for even a moment—upon what, then, will it arise?
Since the mind, having false causes,
functions toward that which is not established, how can its momentary destruction be determined?
For the meditative attainments of yogins, gold, the relics of the Victors, and the celestial palaces of the Ābhāsvara heaven are indestructible by worldly causes. (Lankavatara Sutra 6.15)

How indeed can the states of stability, the qualities of attainment, the perfections of the Buddhas' wisdom, the state of a monk, and the attainment of the vows be seen as momentary? (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 6.16)
Are not forms such as a city of Gandharvas or an illusion indeed momentary? Some things are non-existent, some are existent, and some existents have come into being through the hand of a creator.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, "On Momentariness," in the Laṅkāvatāra [Sūtra].
START Chapter 7 (Vaidya 98):
The seventh chapter, named "The Emanated Body."

Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati spoke thus again to the Blessed One: "Furthermore, the Blessed One has prophesied that Arhats shall attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; and he has declared that sentient beings whose nature is not to enter final nirvana shall likewise attain the state of a Tathāgata.
From the night the Tathāgata fully awakened to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment until the night he entered final nirvana—"
In the meantime, not even a single syllable was uttered or spoken by the Blessed One;
for Tathāgatas are always in a state of meditative equipoise, neither engaging in discursive thought nor investigation.
Rather, having manifested emanations, they perform the work of a Tathāgata through them.
And for what reason is the characteristic of the distinction between the succession of moments of consciousnesses taught?
Furthermore, Vajrapāṇi is constantly and perpetually attached [to him],
and the prior limit is not discerned.
And nirvāṇa is designated;

likewise, Māras, the deeds of Māra, and the snares of karma— such as Cañcā the young woman, Sundarī, and the female ascetic, as well as the bowl-washing and other such acts, O Blessed One— are seen as karmic obstructions.
"In that case, how was omniscience (sarvākārajñatā) attained by the Blessed One without having abandoned the defects?
The Blessed One said: "Therefore, Mahāmati, listen; pay close and careful attention."
"I shall speak to you.
"Excellent, Blessed One," Mahāmati, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, replied to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One said this to him: "It is with reference to the realm of nirvana without remainder (nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu) and for the purpose of encouraging those who have practiced the conduct of a bodhisattva."

Indeed, Mahāmati, there are bodhisattvas practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva here and in other buddha-fields who desire the nirvāṇa of the Śrāvaka vehicle; for the sake of turning them away from their attachment to the Śrāvaka vehicle and for the sake of encouraging them toward the attainment of the Mahāyāna, the Buddhas manifest emanation bodies as created śrāvakas and grant them prophecies,
but not by means of the Buddhas of the true nature of reality (dharmatā).
It was with this in mind, Mahāmati, that the prophecy for the Śrāvakas was taught.
For, Mahāmati, there is no distinction in the abandonment of the afflictive obscurations for Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, due to the single flavor of liberation;
however, in this case, there is no abandonment of the cognitive obscurations.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is purified through the excellence of the vision of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*);

however, the afflictive obscuration (*kleśāvaraṇa*) is abandoned by means of the prior cultivation of the vision of the selflessness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*), through the cessation of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Furthermore, liberation from the obscuration of phenomena is purified through the cessation of the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

With reference to the primordial abiding nature of phenomena (*pūrvadharmasthititā*), and because there is neither prior nor subsequent [in that state], the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma without applied thought (*vitarka*) or sustained thought (*vicāra*), by means of the very same syllables previously abandoned,
due to his state of acting with full awareness and his possession of unforgetting mindfulness.

One neither applies initial mental application nor sustained mental application, because of having abandoned the four levels of latent tendencies (*vāsanā*), because of being free from the two types of death, and because of having eliminated the two obstructions: those of afflictions (*kleśa*) and the knowable (*jñeya*).

Mahāmati, the seven—the mind, the mental consciousness, and the visual consciousnesses and so forth—are momentary; because they have habitual tendencies as their cause, they are devoid of the side of the wholesome and the untainted, and thus they do not transmigrate.
However, Mahāmati, the *tathāgatagarbha* transmigrates, being the cause of both the happiness and suffering of *nirvāṇa*.
Yet, foolish common people, whose minds are distracted by emptiness, do not understand this.
Mahāmati, Vajrapāṇi attends upon the Tathāgatas who are emanations of emanations, but not upon the fundamental Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
For, Mahāmati, the fundamental Tathāgata transcends all means of valid cognition and all sense faculties of all children, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and non-Buddhist teachers.
Those who dwell in the bliss of the present life approach him through the patient acceptance of the knowledge of the Dharma of realization.
Therefore, Vajrapāṇi does not follow after them;
for all emanation-buddhas do not arise from karma.
The Tathāgata is not in them, nor is the Tathāgata elsewhere than in them.
Like a potter using clay and other materials as his basis for practice, he performs the tasks of sentient beings and teaches endowed with the [thirty-two] marks;
yet he does not speak of the discourse on the re-establishment of his own method, which is the domain of the noble realization within his own personal experience.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, upon the cessation of the six groups of consciousness, foolish ordinary people resort to the view of annihilation;
because they do not understand the *ālayavijñāna*, they fall into the view of eternalism.
Mahāmati, the prior limit of one’s own mental conceptualization is not known;
liberation is known as the cessation of that very mental conceptualization.
Through the abandonment of the four habitual tendencies, there is the abandonment of all defects.
Regarding this, it is said:
"The three vehicles and the non-vehicle—there is no final cessation for the Buddhas;
all have been prophesied for Buddhahood and taught as being free from faults. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 7.1)
The knowledge at the conclusion of realization, the state of the Nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa,
and the encouragement of those who are despondent— this has been taught for the sake of the Saṅgha.
The wisdom produced by the Buddhas is the path taught by them alone;
they proceed by that very path and not by any other, and therefore there is no final cessation for them.
The fourfold latent impressions of existence, desire, form,
and views arise from the mental consciousness and reside in the storehouse-consciousness and the mind.
For those with extreme views, there is the annihilation of mental consciousness, the eye, and so forth, through impermanence;
and there is the view of eternalism regarding a beginningless nirvāṇa.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, "On the Emanated Body," in the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra.
START Parivarta 8 (Vaidya 100):
The eighth chapter, titled "On the Consumption of Meat."

Then indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati, having questioned the Blessed One with verses, again made this request: "May the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, teach me the virtues and faults regarding the eating of meat,

so that I and other Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, in the future and present times, may bring about the abandonment of the thirst for flavors among those beings who are perfumed by the habitual tendencies of the destiny of carnivorous beings and who are greedy for the consumption of meat."

We shall teach the Dharma so that those beings who feed on flesh, having become dispassionate toward the thirst for flavors, may desire the nourishment of the flavor of the Dharma; and, endowed with love for all beings as if they were their only child, may they attain great mutual loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*).
Having attained it, becoming proficient in all the stages of a bodhisattva, may they swiftly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi*).
Or, having rested upon the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, they might eventually approach the unsurpassed stage of the Tathāgatas.

Blessed One, even those of other sects who have poorly expounded the Dharma— those who are obsessed with the Lokāyata view and who advocate for the extremes of nihilism and eternalism regarding existence and non-existence— refrain from eating meat for at least a month and do not eat it themselves.
How much more so in the case of the Perfectly Awakened One, the Sugata, the Protector of the World, whose sole essence is compassion—
yet in your teaching, meat is consumed by oneself,
and its consumption is not prohibited.

"Therefore, it would be well if the Blessed One, who has compassion for all the world, who regards all beings as his own children with an equal eye, and who is possessed of great compassion, would out of pity teach me the virtues and faults regarding the eating of meat, so that I and other bodhisattvas may teach the Dharma to sentient beings according to reality.
The Blessed One said: "In that case, Mahāmati, listen."
"Pay close and careful attention;
I shall speak to you.
"Very well, Blessed One," the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati replied to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One said this to him: "Mahāmati, for immeasurable reasons, meat is entirely unfit to be eaten by a Bodhisattva whose nature is compassion. However, I shall provide you with a mere summary of those reasons.

Here, Mahāmati, as sentient beings wander through this long course of saṃsāra, there is no such creature easily found who has not been one's own mother, father, brother, sister, son, daughter, or relative."
He who has not been one's mother, father, brother, sister, son, daughter, or any other relative, kinsman, or friend— such a person,
whose physical basis has changed through the cycle of other births, having entered among the wombs of beasts, cattle, or birds, remains nonetheless a kinsman and a friend.

Or how could meat produced from all living beings, creatures, and sentient beings be fit to be eaten by a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who desires to realize that he is identical with the self-nature of all beings, and who desires the Buddha-dharma? Even Rākṣasas, Mahāmati, having heard this true nature of the Dharma of the Tathāgatas, abandon their demonic state, become compassionate, and desist from eating meat.
How much more so for those who desire the Dharma?

Thus, Mahāmati, throughout various cycles of birth, because all sentient beings have been one's own kin and relatives, and for the purpose of cultivating the perception that all sentient beings are like an only son, meat is not to be eaten by a compassionate Bodhisattva; meat is unfit to be consumed.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, because of its inconsistency, all meat is unfit to be eaten by a Bodhisattva who maintains proper conduct.
For, Mahāmati, meats such as those of dogs, donkeys, camels, horses, oxen, and humans are not fit to be eaten by the world;
yet, Mahāmati, butchers sell these very things in the streets for the sake of profit, claiming they are edible. Therefore, [all meat is unfit].
Therefore, Mahāmati, meat is also unfit to be eaten by a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, because it originates from semen and blood, and out of a desire for purity, meat is unfit to be eaten by a bodhisattva.
Moreover, Mahāmati, because it causes terror among living beings, all meat is unfit to be eaten by a bodhisattva who is a practitioner seeking loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Mahāmati, it is just as when dogs, upon seeing from afar those flesh-eating beings such as *ḍombas*, *caṇḍālas*, and fishermen, bark out of fear.
And some become subject to death [thinking], "They will kill us too.

In the very same way, Mahāmati, there are other minute creatures dwelling in the sky, on earth, or in water who eat flesh; upon merely seeing them, or smelling their scent from afar with their keen sense of smell—like a human smelling the odor of a *rākṣasa*—some become subject to the uncertainty of death.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, because it causes agitation, meat is unfit to be eaten by a Bodhisattva who dwells in great loving-kindness; it is practiced by ignoble people and is foul-smelling.
Moreover, Mahāmati, because it brings ill repute and because it is shunned by noble people, meat is unfit to be eaten by a Bodhisattva.
For, Mahāmati, noble people have the food of the sages as their sustenance, not the food of flesh and blood.
For this reason as well, the flesh of a bodhisattva is unfit to be eaten.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, for the sake of protecting the minds of many people and desiring to avoid slander against the teaching, meat is not to be eaten by a compassionate Bodhisattva.
For instance, Mahāmati, there are those in the world who speak in disparagement of the teaching, saying: "What asceticism (*śrāmaṇya*) do they possess?"
Or whence comes their status as Brahmins, when—

having abandoned the foods of the ancient seers— they wander everywhere throughout this world like carnivorous beasts, their bellies full from a diet of meat, terrifying and utterly alarming the minute creatures dwelling in the air, on the earth, and in the water?
Their state of being a śramaṇa is destroyed; their state of being a brāhmaṇa is ruined;
for them there is neither Dharma nor Vinaya.
Thus, with their minds obstructed in these various ways, they disparage the very teaching.
Therefore, Mahāmati, even for the sake of protecting the minds of many people and desiring to avoid such disparagement, all meat is non-edible for a compassionate Bodhisattva of the teaching.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, meat is unfit to be eaten by a bodhisattva because it shares the common quality of being repulsive due to the foul odor of a dead corpse.
For indeed, Mahāmati, when the flesh of a dead human being is being burned, as well as the flesh of any other living creature, there is no difference whatsoever in their odor.
When both types of flesh are being burned, they produce an identical foul odor.
For this reason as well, Mahāmati, all meat is unfit to be eaten by a Bodhisattva, the yogin who desires purity.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, for those forest-dwellers—yogins and practitioners of yoga who reside in remote lodgings in wildernesses, forests, and mountain retreats frequented by non-humans; for those dwelling in loving-kindness, and for the holders of spells (*vidyādharas*) desiring to accomplish their mantras—the dwellings in cemeteries create obstacles to the accomplishment of spells and liberation.
Therefore, Mahāmati, you should also perceive that these places create obstacles to all yogic accomplishments for sons and daughters of good family who have set out in the Mahāyāna.

For a bodhisattva who desires the welfare of himself and others, all meat is unfit for consumption. Because it produces a relish based on consciousness that takes form as its object, all meat is unfit for consumption for a bodhisattva whose self is compassion and who has become the very self of all beings. Furthermore, Mahāmati, because even the deities avoid him, all meat is unfit for consumption for a bodhisattva whose self is compassion.
Moreover, Mahāmati, even in this very life, his mouth becomes extremely foul-smelling; for these reasons, a compassionate Bodhisattva must not eat any meat whatsoever.
He sleeps in suffering.
One awakens in suffering and sees evil, hair-raising dreams; moreover,
while dwelling alone in a secluded place within an empty house, non-human beings steal one's vital energy.
They are even startled, sometimes they are even terrified, and they suddenly fall into a state of panic.
Furthermore, he does not know the proper measure in food, nor does he attain the correct digestion, nourishment, and so forth of what has been eaten, drunk, chewed, or tasted;
his digestive tract becomes a breeding ground for numerous worms and creatures, a primary cause of leprosy, and he is beset by many diseases,
yet he does not perceive it as something disagreeable.

Mahāmati, while teaching that food is like medicine made of one's own son’s flesh, how could I ever permit my disciples to consume a diet of meat and blood— a practice resorted to by ignoble people and shunned by noble ones, one which is fraught with many faults and devoid of many virtues, not prescribed by the sages, and considered unfit? On the contrary, Mahāmati, I have permitted a diet that is practiced by all noble beings and avoided by the ignoble, which brings forth many virtues, is free from many faults, and was prescribed by all the ancient seers.

That is to say, it is because food consisting of rice, barley, wheat, mung beans, black gram, lentils, and so forth, along with ghee, oil, honey, molasses, sugar-candy, jaggery, rock-sugar, and the like, is considered suitable when available. However, Mahāmati, in the future age, this exquisite food will not be spoken of to certain deluded men who propound various false interpretations of discipline, who are steeped in the habits of carnivorous families, and who are obsessed with a thirst for flavors.

But, Mahāmati, it is not for those sons of good family or daughters of good family born into the Śākya clan— who have performed services under previous Victors, who have planted roots of merit, who are faithful and free from conceptual construction, who are numerous, who are unattached to body, life, or enjoyments, who are not greedy for flavors, who are not covetous, who are compassionate, who desire to attain the state of being the self-nature of all beings, and who regard all sentient beings as dear as an only son.
I speak thus of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas.
In the past, Mahāmati, in a time long gone, there was a king named Siṃhasaudāsa.

Through excessive addiction to the consumption of meat, and due to his extreme attachment to the craving for its flavor, he even ate human flesh. On account of that, he was abandoned even by his circle of friends, ministers, kinsmen, and relatives.
How much more so by the people of the city and the countryside;
for the sake of meat, he even incurred a great calamity through the abandonment of his own kingdom and territory.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, even Indra, having attained sovereignty over the gods, was once in a previous life—
due to the fault of latent tendencies from eating meat— assumed the form of a hawk and attacked Viśvakarman, who was wearing the guise of a pigeon;
he even placed himself upon the scale.
Because King Śibi, who was compassionate toward innocent beings, was himself brought to great suffering;
thus, O Mahāmati, even for Śakra, when he had become the Lord of the Devas, that which was practiced through many lifetimes resulted in bringing faults upon both himself and others,
let alone for anyone else.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, there were others who, having been kings but then carried off by horses and wandering in the wilderness, engaged in sexual union with lionesses; out of fear for their lives, they fathered offspring, and due to the lineage of living among lions, princes such as Kalmāṣapāda and others became meat-eaters even though they had become lords of men, because of the latent tendencies toward the fault of eating meat from previous births.

Moreover, Mahāmati, even in this very life, those who excessively indulge in meat out of a craving for abundant flesh—even in a small village of seven huts—become fierce *ḍākas* or *ḍākinīs* who eat human flesh.

And upon the transition of birth, Mahāmati, because of their persistent attachment to the taste of meat, they are cast into the wombs of lions, tigers, leopards, wolves, hyenas, cats, jackals, owls, and other such creatures that consume abundant flesh; they are further cast down into the most terrible wombs of *rākṣasas* and the like.

Mahāmati, for those who have fallen into such states, even rebirth in a human form is difficult to attain through suffering, let alone liberation; such are the faults of meat-eaters that arise even before they have begun to consume it.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are many more virtues [in the former case], whereas through the opposite [the latter], there are many faults; yet foolish ordinary people do not comprehend these and other such virtues and faults.
"Mahāmati, because of seeing such qualities and faults as these, I declare that all meat is unfit to be eaten by a Bodhisattva whose nature is compassion."
Furthermore, Mahāmati, if no one were to eat meat under any circumstances, they would not be killed on that account.
For, Mahāmati, it is generally for the sake of profit that innocent living beings are slaughtered, and only rarely for any other reason.
It is a tragedy, Mahāmati, that for those who excessively indulge in the thirst for flavor, even human flesh is eaten by humans,

let alone the flesh produced from other beasts, birds, and living creatures. Generally, Mahāmati, this mechanism of the net has been set in motion in such and such ways by deluded men who are afflicted by the thirst for the taste of flesh.
Fowlers, shepherds, fishermen, and others slaughter innocent creatures that move through the air, on the earth, or in the water in many ways for the sake of profit.
Yet, Mahāmati, in those who have made their minds cruel like Rākṣasas and are devoid of compassion—those who, perceiving them as living beings, kill and eat living beings—compassion never arises.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there is no such thing as "unmade," "uncaused," or "unintended" meat that could be deemed permissible; how then could I authorize its consumption by my disciples?

Furthermore, Mahāmati, in the future age there will arise within my very teaching certain deluded men who, having gone forth and professing to be sons of the Śākya, carry the banner of the saffron robe; yet their minds are struck by false discursive thoughts, they propound various conceptualizations regarding the Vinaya, they are possessed by the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), and they are obsessed with the thirst for flavors. They will compose various treatises presenting fallacious reasons for the eating of meat.
They will think that a false accusation should be leveled against me;
having fabricated various origins and causes for those matters, they will say: "In this context, based on this cause, the Blessed One permitted the eating of meat and declared it to be allowable."
And regarding exquisite foods,
it is said that they were indeed consumed by the Tathāgata himself; yet, Mahāmati, nowhere in any sūtra has it been authorized that they should be partaken of.
Or it is taught that among refined foods, that which is permissible is allowable.
But if, Mahāmati, I were desirous of permitting it, or if it were permissible for me to allow my disciples to consume it,

I would not [have forbidden it] for those sons of noble family who abide in loving-kindness, who are practitioners of yoga, who follow the conduct of yoga, who dwell in cemeteries, and who have set out upon the Mahāyāna.
And for the sake of cultivating the perception of all sentient beings as one's only son among noble daughters, I shall— and indeed have— prohibited the eating of all meat.
Mahāmati, this [prohibition] is for the sake of those sons of good family and daughters of good family who desire the Dharma and have set out upon any of the vehicles.

For the sake of accomplishing all yogas for those who dwell in cemeteries, who abide in loving-kindness, who live in the forest, and who are practitioners of yoga— namely, the yogācāras— for the purpose of cultivating the perception of all sentient beings as one's only son,
there is a prohibition against all meat.

In various recitations of the teachings, the sequence of the training rules (*śikṣāpada*) was established by arranging them like the rungs of a ladder; having thus bound them into three categories, those [meats] prepared specifically for [the practitioner] were prohibited.
Subsequently, even the ten kinds of meat that are naturally dead were prohibited.
However, in this sutra, everything—absolutely everything, in every way and entirely—is prohibited without exception.
Therefore, Mahāmati, I have not permitted the eating of meat for anyone,
I do not permit it, and I shall not permit it.

"Mahāmati, I declare that the consumption of meat is unfit for those who have gone forth into homelessness. Furthermore, Mahāmati, as for those who will think to bring false accusations against me, saying, 'The Tathāgata himself has consumed it,' that will lead to the long-term misfortune and harm of other deluded men who are shrouded by the obscurations of their own karmic faults."
For indeed, Mahāmati, the noble Śrāvakas do not partake of the food of ordinary humans; how much less would they partake of the unallowable food of flesh and blood?
For, Mahāmati, my Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas subsist on the food of the Dharma, not on the food of material things.

How much more so, Mahāmati, are the Tathāgatas? For the Tathāgatas are the Dharma-body; they subsist on the food of the Dharma, not on a body of flesh, nor do they subsist on any food of worldly things.

They have vomited out all cravings, desires, and latent impressions regarding the requisites for existence; they are free from the latent impressions of all afflictions and faults; and their minds and wisdom are perfectly liberated.
They are omniscient, all-seeing, possessors of great compassion who regard all sentient beings as equal to an only son.
Therefore, Mahāmati, being one who perceives all sentient beings as an only son, how could I ever permit my disciples to consume the flesh of their own son, much less consume it myself?
"Mahāmati, it is impossible that I have permitted my disciples to eat [meat] or that I have eaten it myself."
In this regard, it is said: "O Great Sage, I shall not consume intoxicants, meat, or onions,
as taught by the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, the preeminent among the Victors."
O Great Sage, tell me that meat is unfit for consumption—it is enjoyed by the ignoble, it is foul-smelling, it brings ill repute, and it is the food of flesh-eaters. Lank_8.2.
O Mahāmati, understand those faults that arise from eating [forbidden food] and those virtues that arise from abstaining; learn also of the faults inherent in the consumption of meat. Lank_8.3.
Due to its kinship, its susceptibility to error, and its origin from semen and blood, the yogi should avoid meat, which causes revulsion among living beings. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 8.4)
A yogin should always avoid meats, onions, various kinds of liquor, leeks, and garlic. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 8.5)
One should avoid applying oil as an ointment and should not sleep in places pierced by thorns;
one should avoid the various vulnerable points of sentient beings and any place that is a source of great danger.
From food arises pride; volition is born from pride; and passion is produced by volition; therefore, one should not consume it. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 8.7)
From conceptual construction arises passion; the mind is deluded by passion.
For the deluded one there is attachment, and thus he is born and is not liberated.
A sentient being is killed for the sake of profit, and wealth is given for the sake of meat;
both of those who perform such evil deeds are cooked in the Raurava and other hells.
That evil-minded person who, though initiated into the teaching of the Śākyas, disregards the word of the Sage and eats meat, acts for the sake of destroying both worlds.
Those evildoers go to the most terrible hell;
the eaters of flesh are cooked in the fierce hells, such as Raurava and others.
Meat that is pure in three respects—unimagined, unasked for, and unsolicited—does not exist at all; therefore, one should not eat meat. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 8.12)
A yogi should not eat meat, which is censured by me and by the Buddhas;
beings who devour one another are born into the families of carnivorous creatures.
One is born foul-smelling, contemptible, and even insane, again and again among the Caṇḍālas, Pukkāsas, and Ḍombas. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 8.14)
That lowest of men is born into the wombs of ḍākinīs and those who eat flesh; he is born from the wombs of rākṣasīs and cats. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 8.15)
In the *Hastikakṣya*, the *Mahāmegha*, the *Nirvāṇa*, the *Aṅgulimālīka*,
and the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, meat has been forbidden by me.
If one eats [forbidden food] out of shamelessness, it is censured by the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Śrāvakas; such a person becomes perpetually insane. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 8.17)
By abstaining from meat and such things, one will be born among brahmins or in the family of yogins, endowed with wisdom and wealth. (Lankavatara Sutra 8.18)
One should avoid all meat out of apprehension regarding what has been seen or heard;
logicians, born into the lineage of flesh-eaters, do not understand this.
Just as passion becomes an obstacle to liberation,
so too do meat, liquor, and the like become obstacles.
In a future time, meat-eaters who speak out of delusion will say:
"Meat that is permissible and blameless has been praised by the Buddhas. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 8.21)
Furthermore, the yogi should partake of alms-food with moderation, regarding it as medicine or meat, and even as the flesh of his own son, perceiving it as something repulsive. Lank_8.22.

I have always and in every way censured those who dwell in loving-kindness [yet act otherwise]; they might even come to live together in one place with lions, tigers, wolves, and the like. *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* 8.23.
Therefore, one should not eat meat, for it causes revulsion among men;
because it is contrary to the dharma of liberation, this is indeed the banner of the Noble Ones.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, on the Consumption of Meat, from the *Laṅkāvatāra*, the heart of all the Buddha’s teachings.

Namely:

Whether it be an asura or an asurī, a garuḍa or a garuḍī, a kinnara or a kinnarī, a mahoraga or a mahoragī,
a gandharva or a gandharvī, a bhūta or a bhūtī, a kumbhāṇḍa or a kumbhāṇḍī, a piśāca or a piśācī, an ostāraka or an austārakī, an apasmāra or an apasmārī, or a rākṣasa or a rākṣasī.

Even if there should be an affliction by a malevolent spirit (*viṣamagraha*), [it shall not prevail].
Thus, by means of this [mantra] empowered with one hundred and eight recitations, he will weep and wail, and seeing which direction, where will he go?

Mahāmati, whatever son of good family or daughter of good family shall take up, retain, recite, and master these mantra-words,
no one— whether a god or goddess, a nāga or nāgī, a yakṣa or yakṣī, an asura or asurī, a garuḍa or garuḍī, a kinnara or kinnarī, or a mahoraga or mahoragī— shall find an opportunity to harm them.
or a gandharva or a gandharvī, or a bhūta or a bhūtī, or a kumbhāṇḍa or a kumbhāṇḍī, or a piśāca or a piśācī, or an ostāraka or an ostārakī, or an apasmāra or an apasmārī;
Whether it be a male rākṣasa or a female rākṣasī, a ḍāka or a ḍākinī, or an ojahara or an ojaharī;
Whether it be a kaṭapūtana or a kaṭapūtanī,
a human or a human woman—

Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati said this to the Blessed One:
"The world is devoid of arising and destruction; it is like a flower in the sky.
This [world] is perceived as neither existent nor non-existent by you through wisdom and compassion. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.1)
The world, which is always devoid of eternalism and nihilism, is like a dream;
it is neither existent nor non-existent, as you have perceived through your wisdom and compassion.
All phenomena are like illusions, devoid of mind and consciousness;
through both wisdom and compassion, you do not perceive them as either existent or non-existent.
The selflessness of phenomena and persons, as well as the afflictions and the objects of knowledge,
are always purified for you through signless wisdom and compassion.
You do not enter nirvāṇa, nor are you in nirvāṇa, nor does nirvāṇa abide within you;
you are devoid of intellect and the object of cognition, and free from the positions of existence and non-existence.
Those who see the Sage as thus peaceful and devoid of arising become free from grasping, stainless both in this world and the next.
Just as in the summer heat a mirage flickers, deluding the mind, and deer perceive it as water though that substance does not exist; so too is this world.
Thus this seed of consciousness vibrates within the range of perception;
fools grasp at it as it arises, just as those with cataracts perceive a visual distortion.
The meditator, the meditation, and the object of meditation; abandonment and the vision of the truths—all this is merely conceptual construction. He who understands this is liberated.
These phenomena are without essence, having arisen from conceptualization;
even that conceptualization by which one thinks "they are empty" is itself empty.
The five aggregates, with consciousness as the fifth, are like the shadow of a tree reflected in water;
the visible world is like an illusion or a dream—one should not conceptualize it through mere representation.

Seeing the world as always resembling an illusion, a corpse animated by magic, a mechanical device, a dream, lightning, or a cloud, and as utterly severed from the three continuities, one is liberated. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.12)
Through improper conceptualization,
consciousness proceeds in eightfold and ninefold variety, like the waves upon the great ocean.
Constantly nourished by latent impressions (*vāsanā*), with the intellect as its root and a stable basis,
the mind wanders within the field of sensory objects, just as iron moves toward a magnet. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.14)
Abiding in all beings, the lineage-ground (gotrabhū) is free from conceptual reasoning;
released from activity, it turns back, being devoid of both knowledge and the object of knowledge.
Behold the king of the mind, which is like an illusion, transcends the ten stages, and is devoid of perception and consciousness.
When the mind has undergone revolution, it then abides eternally in a celestial palace resembling a lotus, which arises from the sphere of illusory activity.
Established in that, having attained effortless conduct,
he performs the works of sentient beings like a jewel of manifold forms.
There is neither the conditioned nor the unconditioned, for it exists nowhere except as a mental construction;
yet fools, wretched and deluded, grasp at it like barren women grasping at a son in a dream.

The absence of intrinsic nature, non-arising, the person, the continuity of the aggregates, the conditions, the elements, emptiness, and existence and non-existence are to be known [as such]. (Lankavatara 10.20)
My teaching of skillful means is not that I teach characteristics;
it is the foolish who grasp at characteristics and the characterized as having substantial existence.
The Knower of All is not the Knower of Everything; amidst all things, nothing exists as a whole.
Fools conceptualize this, and so does the world of the wise; yet I neither awaken nor cause others to awaken.
This is merely a conceptual designation; it does not exist by way of its own characteristic.
Therein, the aggregates appear like a mass of hair, yet they are conceptualized as such by the foolish.
Nothing whatsoever arises that did not previously exist, nor does anything perish through conditions.
When one perceives conditioned phenomena as being like the son of a barren woman or a flower in the sky,
then, having seen the error, both the grasper and the grasped cease.

I do not enter nirvāṇa by way of essence, activity, or characteristic; for I am indeed extinguished through the cessation of the consciousness that is the cause of conceptual construction. (The characteristic which is imagined by the foolish does not perish therein. // Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.25 //
Just as when a great flood has subsided there is no arising of waves,
so too, when the diversity of consciousnesses has ceased, it does not proceed.
Empty and devoid of intrinsic nature, like illusions and unarisen; these entities, whether existent or non-existent, are not found; they are like dreams. (Lankavatara 10.27)
I teach the single intrinsic nature, which is free from ratiocination and representation;
it is the divine sphere of the noble ones, devoid of the two-fold intrinsic nature.
Just as the various [colored] lights of a firefly do not exist for one who is intoxicated, yet appear so;
likewise, the world appears by its own nature through the agitation of the elements.
Just as an illusion appears within grass, wood, and rubble,
yet that illusion does not exist [in reality], so too are all phenomena by their very nature.
There is no grasper and no grasped, no bound and no binding;
it is like a magical illusion or a mirage, like what is called a dream, or like an optical aberration. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.31)
When one who seeks the ultimate reality perceives it—free from conceptual construction and stainless—then, having attained yoga, he will behold me; of this there is no doubt.
For here there is no representation whatsoever, just as rays in the sky;
thus, those who understand phenomena do not assert anything at all.
There is no arising of phenomena within conditions, whether they be existent or non-existent,
because the mind, deluded within the triple world, appears in manifold ways.

Dreams and the world are of an identical nature; for there too, diverse forms are seen, as well as enjoyments, tactile sensations, the body, its end, the Teacher of the World, and activity—all of which are equal. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.35)
For the mind is the womb of the three realms; this deluded mind is seen here and there.
One should not conceptualize the world as non-existent once one has understood such a course of the world. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.36)
Fools, out of delusion, perceive both arising and passing away;
one endowed with wisdom perceives neither arising nor passing away.
In the divine abode of Akaniṣṭha, which is free from all evil,
they are always free from conceptual construction, ever disciplined, and devoid of mind and mental factors.
Having attained mastery over the powers and superknowledges, and having reached the realization of that samādhi,
the perfectly awakened ones awaken there, while it is the emanation that awakens here.
Indeed, infinite millions of emanations of Buddhas go forth; everywhere the foolish hear the Dharma from them as if it were an echo. (Lankavatara 10.40)
Free from beginning, middle, and end, devoid of existence and non-existence,
all-pervading, immovable, pure, without variety, yet the source of all variety.
Concealed by the lineage of representation (vijñapti-gotra), it is latent in all embodied beings;
illusion exists because of error, yet illusion is not the cause of error.

Due to the delusion of the mind, there exists whatever little may be found—bound by the two natures, fashioned by the ālayavijñāna: the world, mere representation, the flood of views, and the phenomena and the person. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.43)
When one has thus contemplated the world and undergone transformation,
then one becomes my son, who sets in motion the perfected Dharma.
The qualities of heat, fluidity, motion, and solidity are conceptualized by the ignorant;
this is a false superimposition, for there is neither the characterized object nor the characteristic.
This physical form, consisting of eight substances, is the sense-faculty; indeed, the deluded fools within the cage of saṃsāra conceptualize it as "form. (Laṅkāvatāra 10.46)
Through the assembly of causes and conditions, the foolish imagine an arising;
not understanding this principle, they wander in the abode of the three realms of existence.
All phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature, and even the speech of men is so; emanations arise from conceptual construction, and existence is like a dream.
One should examine this [thus], neither transmigrating nor attaining nirvana.

The mind, variegated and called the "seed," appears as the objective field of the mind; when it appears, fools who delight in the two types of conceptualization imagine its arising. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.49)
Ignorance, craving, and karma, as well as the mind and mental factors, do not create the Māra;
for it is from these that [the world] proceeds, and thus it is considered to be dependent on others.
And they conceptualize whatever object is a delusion within the range of the mind;
it is unestablished through conceptualization and falsely imagined through erroneous delusion. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.51)
The mind of embodied beings proceeds bound to conditions;
I declare that I do not see it as liberated from conditions.
When that which is free from conditions and devoid of specific characteristics no longer abides in the body, it is therefore beyond my range of perception.
Just as a king or a merchant entices his sons with various deer-like objects and plays with them at home, [the Buddha] brings about an encounter with the deer in the forest. (Lankāvatāra Sūtra 10.54)
In the same way, O Son, I speak of the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi), which is to be personally realized within, by means of the various characteristics that are like reflections of phenomena.
Just as waves of the ocean, stirred by the condition of the wind, arise dancing and proceed without any interruption being found; ||| Lank_10.56 |||
In the same way, the flood of the ālaya, constantly stirred by the winds of sense objects, proceeds dancing with the various waves of consciousness. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.57)
The mind of embodied beings inclines toward the state of grasped object and grasping subject;
yet the characteristic of the visible world does not exist in the manner it is conceptualized by the foolish.
The supreme ālayavijñāna is again the representation that is the storehouse;
because of the departure from grasped object and grasping subject, I teach it as suchness.
Within the aggregates there is no self, no sentient being, and no person;
yet consciousness arises and consciousness ceases.
Just as depressions and elevations are seen in a painting but do not exist,
so too the substantiality of phenomena is seen but does not exist.
Just as a city of Gandharvas and as a mirage, so does the visible world constantly appear; yet it is not found by means of wisdom.
That which is produced by the means of valid cognition and the sense faculties is neither an effect nor a cause;
it is devoid of intellect and the object of intellect, and is free from both the characterized and the characteristic.
Dependent upon the aggregates, the Perfectly Awakened One has never been seen by anyone, anywhere.
Since he has not been seen by anyone anywhere, how can there be a conceptualization of him?

By means of conditions, reasons, and examples, as well as by the thesis and its cause, [the nature of things is explained] through dreams, gandharva-cities, wheels, mirages, the moon, and the sun. *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* 10.65.
I teach that the world is unperceivable, like the examples of a lineage [of ancestors] and so forth;
it is an imagined void, known as a dream, a delusion, and an illusion. (Lankavatara 10.66)
Not dependent upon the three worlds, whether internally or externally,
and seeing existence as unarisen, the patience of non-arising is born.
Furthermore, there is the illusion-like samādhi and the mind-made body;
his supernormal powers, masteries, and strengths are the manifold manifestations of the mind.
For those for whom phenomena are indeed unarisen, empty, and devoid of intrinsic nature,
delusion arises and is ceased by conditions.
For it is the mind that appears; it appears as external forms.
There exists no other visible object such as it is imagined by the ignorant. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.70)
The chain, the image of the Buddha, and the rending of the elements—
those well-trained in designation indeed preside over the manifold world through such designations.
The body, the locus, and experience—these three are the representations of the grasped;
the mind, the apprehension, and the conceptualization—these three are the graspers. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.72)
As long as there is conceptual construction and that which is conceptually constructed, and as long as one remains within the sphere of syllables,
so long do the dialecticians not perceive reality, due to the delusion of their reasoning.
When yogis realize through wisdom that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, they then find rest, established in the signless.
Just as a foolish person might seize a cock smeared with poison,
so too do the ignorant and childish grasp at the three vehicles.
For here there are no śrāvakas at all, nor are there any followers of the pratyekabuddha vehicle.
And as for this form that is seen— belonging to both śrāvakas and jinas—
it is these bodhisattvas, whose nature is compassion, who manifest these emanations and teach them.
The three realms of existence are representation-only, imagined through the two natures;
but when there is the revolution [of the basis], it is suchness, due to the cessation of the movement of phenomena and persons.
Just as the moon, the sun, the flame of a lamp, the elements,
and likewise jewels function without conceptual construction, so too does the Buddhahood of a Buddha proceed.
Just as a mass of hair is falsely perceived by people suffering from ophthalmia,
so too is this conceptualization of existence falsely imagined by the foolish.

Entities designated as defilement and purification are devoid of stability, destruction, and arising; they are free from both permanence and impermanence, and are like the optical illusion of a hair-net.
Just as someone might perceive a world of golden hue in a statue, yet there is no gold there at all—it is merely the earth that appears as gold. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.81)
Thus indeed are the foolish corrupted by beginningless mental states and mental factors;
they grasp at things arising from illusion and mirages as being real.
Behold this manifold mind: as the single seed, as the seedless, as the one ocean-seed, and as the seed of all.

When the single seed is purified and becomes seedless through transformation, it is indeed equal due to its non-conceptual nature; yet, through the intensity [of past impressions], there is a confusion of births. It brings forth a manifold seed, and thus it is called "the possessor of all seeds. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.84)
For herein nothing at all is produced by conditions, nor does anything cease;
it is only the conceptualized conditions themselves that are produced and cease. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.85)
The three realms of existence are mere designation; no entity exists by way of its own-being.
Yet, through the notion that designations are real entities, the dialecticians will continue to conceptualize.
The desire to know the intrinsic nature of phenomena is not itself an error that needs to be removed;
rather, one is liberated by seeing that the intrinsic nature of phenomena is non-arising.
The existence of things is not said to be due to their similarity to non-existent illusions;
rather, because they are false and as fleeting as lightning, they are remembered as being like illusions.
Neither that which is to arise nor those already arisen exist, nor do any conditions whatsoever exist anywhere; nevertheless, conventional discourse is spoken by means of them.
The defilement of the arising and ceasing of conditions is not being denied;
rather, that which the foolish conceptualize by means of conditions is what is being refuted.
There is no intrinsic nature, no representation, no objective entity, and no storehouse-consciousness;
these are indeed conceptualized by fools and by bad logicians who have fallen under the power of delusion.
When the sons of the Conquerors perceive the world as mind-only,
they then attain the body of nirvāṇa, which is free from activity and conditioned formations,
and is endowed with the powers, superknowledges, and masteries.
When the mind arises manifesting as all forms, there is neither mind nor forms therein; it is the beginningless mind that is deluded.
Then the yogi indeed perceives the world as non-manifest through wisdom;
having transcended signs, the representation of things, and whatever is the movement of the mind, my sons move about free from conceptual construction.
A city of Gandharvas, an illusion, a hair-net, and a mirage—though unreal, they appear as real; so too does the conceptualization of entities appear among all things.
All phenomena are unarisen, for only delusion is perceived;
yet fools, delighting in the two-fold conceptualization, imagine that delusion has arisen.
The mind, which arises from various latent impressions and constitutes the factors of rebirth, proceeds like a surging flood of waves; when those [impressions] are severed, it no longer proceeds.
Just as a variegated object with diverse appearances arises within the mind,
why does it not likewise arise in space or on a wall?
If the mind proceeds by apprehending some sign,
then the mind produced by conditions cannot be "mind-only."
Mind is grasped by mind; there is nothing whatsoever that possesses a cause.
The nature of mind is pure; in the sky, there is no habitual tendency (*vāsanā*). (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.100)
Through attachment to one's own mind, the mind indeed proceeds;
there is truly nothing to be seen externally, therefore it is mind-only.
Mind is the storehouse-consciousness (ālayavijñāna), and that which consists of mentation is the manas;
that by which one grasps objects is indeed called consciousness (vijñāna).
The mind (*citta*) is always indeterminate, while the intellect (*manas*) moves between both;
for consciousness (*vijñāna*) in its present state is indeed either wholesome or unwholesome.
For the gateway to ultimate reality is devoid of the two types of representation;
since one abides in the non-manifest, how can there be the establishment of the three vehicles?
Mind-only is without appearance; this is the dwelling and the stage of the Buddhas.
This indeed has been spoken by the Buddhas, they speak it, and they cause it to be spoken.
For the seven stages are the mind, while the eighth is without appearance;
two stages are the dwelling, and the remaining stage is my own nature.
The stage that is personally realized and pure is my own nature;
the supreme abode of Maheśvara shines forth in Akaniṣṭha.
Just as rays issue forth from a fire, so did his rays—
variegated, enchanting, and gentle— which fashion the triple world.
Having emanated some portion of the triple world and some portion previously emanated, they teach the vehicles therein; this is my own ground.
For there is no fixed time for the realization of the stages or for the transition to the state of a Kṣatriya;
having transcended mind-only, the fruit consists in abiding in the non-manifest.
Non-existence and existence are seen, as well as manifold diversity;
the foolish are perverted by grasping, for this diversity is indeed perversion.
If cognition were non-conceptual, it would not be logical for an object to exist;
because the mind does not take on forms, it is therefore non-conceptual. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.112)
The sense faculties are called illusion, and the objects are like dreams;
the agent, the action, and the instrument do not exist in any way whatsoever. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.113)
The meditative absorptions, the immeasurables, the formless attainments,
and the cessation of perception— all these do not exist in Mind-only.
The fruit of stream-entry, as well as the fruit of once-returning,
the fruit of non-returning, and even arhatship— these are but the delusions of the mind. (Lankavatara Sutra 10.115)
Fools conceptualize the conditioned as empty, impermanent, and momentary;
the meaning of momentariness is illustrated by such examples as a river or a lamp.
I declare that the meaning of momentariness is that phenomena are devoid of activity, instantaneous, isolated, free from action, and non-arising.
For the non-arising of both the existent and the non-existent is taught by the Sāṃkhyas and Vaiśeṣikas;
indeed, it is they themselves who have proclaimed that all things are indeterminate.

The fourfold explanation consists of: that which is to be answered categorically, that which is to be answered by inquiry, that which is to be answered by analysis, and that which is to be set aside; this serves to ward off the doctrines of the non-Buddhists.
Everything exists conventionally; in the ultimate sense, it does not exist.
The absence of intrinsic nature in all phenomena is seen even in the ultimate sense.
Because perception lacks intrinsic nature, it is therefore called "conventional."
If an entity whose nature is caused by verbal expression were to exist,
then an entity arising from verbal expression would not exist, and thus it is not found.
For an expression devoid of a referent does not exist even conventionally;
and because error has no reality, its apprehension does not exist.
If error exists, then the absence of intrinsic nature does not exist;
for if that which is perceived were a real entity because of its erroneous nature,
it would indeed be devoid of intrinsic nature, yet it would not exist in any way whatsoever.
This manifold variety that is perceived is the mind perfumed by latent dysfunctions;
the grasping of appearances as forms is an external delusion of the mind.
For conceptual construction is abandoned by means of conceptual construction and non-conceptualization;
through conceptual construction and non-conceptualization, there is the vision of the reality of emptiness.
Just as a magical elephant, a painting, or gold leaves [seen in a dream], so does the visible world appear to people whose minds are perfumed by ignorance. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.126)
The noble one perceives neither delusion nor reality in between them;
for that which is reality within that interval would itself be delusion. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.127)
But if, having shaken off all delusion, a sign should nevertheless arise,
that itself would be his delusion, like an impure visual disorder.
Just as one with cataracts perceives a mass of hair due to delusion, so too does the grasping of fools proceed toward sense objects. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.129)

Perceiving this triple world as resembling a mass of hair [seen by the ophthalmic], as the delusion of water in a mirage, and as appearing like a dream or an illusion, one is liberated. (Lankavatara Sutra 10.130)
Conceptualization, the object of conceptualization, and the process by which conceptualization proceeds—bondage, the object of bondage, and the bound: these six are the causes of liberation.
There are no stages, no truths, no fields, and no emanations;
even the Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas are merely conceptual constructs.
The person, the continuum, the aggregates, as well as conditions and atoms,
the primal matter, the Lord, and the creator— these are all conceptualized within mind-only.
For the mind indeed exists everywhere and in all bodies;
it is perceived as manifold by the ignorant, yet mind-only is without defining characteristics.
