For the self does not exist in the aggregates, nor do the aggregates exist in the self;
they are not as they are conceptualized, yet it is not that they do not exist at all.
If the existence of all things were as it is conceptualized by the foolish,
then everyone would be seers of reality, exactly as they perceive those things.
Because all phenomena are non-existent, there is neither affliction nor purity;
they are not as they are perceived, yet it is not that they do not exist at all.
Error, the causal sign, and conceptualization are the characteristics of the dependent nature;
the name that is applied to that causal sign is the characteristic of the imagined nature.
When for him no conceptualization of names and signs arises,
that which is the conventional designation of conditions and things is the perfected nature.
Those Buddhas who are the result of maturation and those who are emanations,
as well as sentient beings, bodhisattvas, and the fields in every direction— Lank_10.140.
The Jinas who are of the nature of natural outflow, of the Dharma, and of transformation—
all of them have indeed emerged from Amitābha’s Sukhāvatī.
Understand the intentional meaning (saṃdhi) of that which is spoken by the emanated [buddhas] and that which is spoken by those born of maturation— the method of the extensive sūtras.
Whatever has been spoken by the sons of the Jina, and whatever is spoken by the Leaders,
and that which is spoken by the Nirmāṇakāya Buddhas, but not by the Jinas who are the result of maturation (vaipākika).
For these phenomena are indeed unarisen, yet they are not non-existent;
they are like a city of Gandharvas, a dream, an illusion, and a magical creation.
The mind functions; the mind alone is liberated.
For it is the mind that is born, and the mind alone that ceases; nothing else. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.145)
The mind of humans appears as objects; indeed, it is the imagined mind that manifests.
There is no object; this is mind-only. One who is free from conceptual construction is liberated.
For the bad habituation of conceptual proliferation from beginningless time has been accumulated;
discrimination, having been cultivated by that, proceeds as a false appearance.
When consciousness appears as an object, knowledge that has its range in suchness becomes revolutionized;
for this [knowledge] is without appearance in the range of the noble ones.
The meditation of the investigation of objects, the meditation practiced by the ignorant,
the meditation with suchness as its object, and the auspicious meditation of the Tathāgatas.
All phenomena are unborn by way of their imagined nature;
it is by relying upon the dependent nature that the conceptual construction of human beings revolves.
When the dependent nature is purified and dissociated from conceptual construction, it is indeed the revolution of the basis; suchness is the dwelling free from all mental constructs.
Do not conceptualize through conceptualization; conceptualization does not exist in reality. For one who conceptualizes delusion, there is no [duality of] grasped and grasper;
the perception of external objects is a construction, the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
By whatever conceptualization they conceptualize, the intrinsic nature [of things] arises from conditions;
the perception of external objects is false, for there is no object, but only mind.
For those who perceive through reasoning, the grasper and the grasped cease;
for no external object exists in the way it is conceptualized by the foolish.
The mind, agitated by latent impressions, proceeds as the appearance of objects;
through the cessation of the two types of conceptualization, gnosis has suchness as its domain.
For that which arises is non-manifest and inconceivable, the domain of the noble ones;
name, sign, and conceptualization are the characteristics of the two natures.
Right knowledge and suchness are the characteristic of the perfected nature.

Through the union of mother and father, conjoined with the storehouse-consciousness (ālayavijñāna) and the mind (manas), it grows together with the semen, just like a mouse in a jar of ghee. *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* 10.157.
The fleshy tumor, the mass, and the foul pustule, variegated by karma, come into being like a fruit through the great elements and the winds of karma. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.158)
There are five times five, and five indeed; and there are nine wounds.
Covered with nails, teeth, and hair, it is born quivering. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.159)
Just as a person upon waking perceives a dung-worm immediately after it has been born, so too does one flash upon a form with the eye; it attains growth through conceptual construction.
Through the conjunction of the palate and the lips, it is determined by conceptualization;
speech proceeds for humans like the conceptualization of a parrot. *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* 10.161.
The doctrines of the non-Buddhists are fixed, whereas the Mahāyāna is not fixed; this [Mahāyāna] proceeds based on sentient beings and is no object for those with wrong views.
"My vehicle is to be realized within oneself; it is not the domain of logicians.
After the Protector has passed away in a future time, tell me: who will uphold this?"
After the Sugata has passed into nirvāṇa, when a later time has elapsed, Mahāmati, you must understand who will uphold the guiding principle.
In Vedalī in the southern region, there will be a monk of great renown and glory;
he shall be named Nāga, and he will be the destroyer of the positions of existence and non-existence.
Having revealed in the world my unsurpassed Mahāyāna vehicle and having attained the stage of Joy (Muditā), he shall go to Sukhāvatī.
When things are analyzed by the intellect, no intrinsic nature (svabhāva) can be apprehended;
therefore, they are taught to be inexpressible and devoid of intrinsic nature.
For when an object is produced by conditions, the notions "it exists" or "it does not exist" do not apply.
Those who conceptualize an entity as being within the range of conditions as either existing or non-existing— I consider such heterodox views to be far removed from my teaching.
The designation of all things has been constantly practiced throughout hundreds of previous births,
both by those who have already practiced it and by those currently practicing it through mutual conceptualization.
If it were not explained, the entire world would fall into confusion;
therefore, a name is given for the purpose of dispelling that confusion.
Entities are conceptualized by the ignorant through three kinds of conceptualization:
through the conceptualization of names, and through that which is produced by conditions, which is delusion. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.171)
For those things which are unceasing and unarisen, by nature like the sky,
and whose intrinsic nature is non-existence— they are characterized by conceptual construction.
They arise like reflections, images, illusions, mirages, dreams, firebrands whirled into circles, gandharva cities, and echoes. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.173)

Non-dual suchness, emptiness, the reality-limit, and the true nature of phenomena— these, which possess the characteristic of the perfected, I teach as being free from conceptual construction. (Lankavatara 10.174)
The sphere of speech and mind is false; wisdom is conceptualized as truth.
The mind has fallen into the two extremes; therefore, wisdom is not conceptualized.
"Existence" and "non-existence" are two extremes as long as there is the range of the mind;
when that range is shaken off, the perfectly correct mind ceases.
Due to the absence of grasping at objects and because of cessation, it does not exist;
yet the state of suchness exists, as it is the sphere of experience for the noble ones.
To the ignorant, things do not appear as they appear to the wise;
to the wise, all phenomena appear as being without characteristics.
Just as brass is imagined to be gold by the ignorant— though it is not gold but merely has the appearance of gold— so too are phenomena [imagined] by bad logicians.
Those for whom there is arising after non-existence and destruction after having existed,
and who maintain that things are both existent and non-existent through conditions— they do not abide in my teaching.
Because they lack beginning and end, [all things] abide in the characteristic of reality;
yet logicians in the world do not realize this, due to their attachment to causes and conditions.
Because a past entity exists, a future one exists,
and a present one is perceived, therefore all entities are unborn.
Those who conceptualize the transformation, the duration of time, the configuration, the primary elements, the states of being, the sense faculties,
and the inclusion of the intermediate state— they are not wise.
The Jinas do not indeed describe the world as dependently originated;
rather, this world is merely a causal condition, resembling a Gandharva-city.
This is merely a conventional designation for that; thus it is said:
apart from convention, it is neither born nor does it cease.
For a reflection is seen in a mirror, in water, in the eye, in vessels, and in jewels; yet that reflection does not exist anywhere at all.
Likewise, the mind appears as an object, like a mirage in the sky;
it is seen in various forms, like the son of a barren woman in a dream.
My vehicle is not the Mahāyāna; it is neither sound nor syllables.
It is indeed neither truths nor liberations, for its sphere is free from appearances.
But what is the vehicle? It is the Mahāyāna, the mastery over meditative concentrations, and the manifold mind-made body adorned with the flowers of sovereign powers.
An entity does not exist as either identical or distinct within a causal condition;
birth is said to be merely a combination, and cessation is indeed destruction. (Lankavatara Sutra 10.190)
The emptiness of the unborn and the emptiness of those things already born are each one and the same;
yet the emptiness of the unborn is superior, for the emptiness of the born perishes.
Suchness, emptiness, the limit, nirvana, and the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu)—
these are synonyms for the manifold mind-made body (manomayakāya) taught by me through various enumerations.
Those who imagine purity through the Sūtra, Vinaya,
and Abhidharma by means of the letter and not the meaning have not taken refuge in selflessness.
Its existence has not been established by the non-Buddhists, nor by the Buddhas, nor by me, nor by anyone else through causal conditions; how then could it be non-existent?
By what means can the existence of that which has no existence through conditions be established?
Through the evil view of the doctrine of origination, one would falsely conceptualize "it exists" or "it does not exist."
For one for whom nothing arises and nothing whatsoever ceases,
there is neither existence nor non-existence, as they perceive the world as solitary.
That which is called a hare’s horn is seen, yet conceptual construction exists for men;
those who construct it are deluded, like deer [perceiving] a mirage.
Through attachment to conceptual construction, conceptual construction proceeds;
for if conceptual construction were without a cause, even conceptual construction would not be tenable.
Just as there is the perception of water in what is not water, like a mirage in the sky,
so indeed is an object perceived by the foolish, but not specifically by the noble ones.
The vision of the noble ones is pure, arising from the three liberations;
it is free from arising and ceasing, and functions within the realm of non-appearance.
I teach the sons of the Victors the profound, noble, and vast knowledge, as well as the splendors of the buddha-fields; but for the śrāvakas, I teach impermanence.
The three realms of existence are impermanent, empty, and devoid of self and what belongs to a self;
I teach this as the common characteristic to the śrāvakas.
Non-attachment to all phenomena, solitude, and wandering alone—
this is the fruit of the Pratyekabuddha sons, which I teach as being beyond discursive thought.
Not perceiving the imagined external world, the dependent nature, and the self-delusion of embodied beings, the mind subsequently proceeds from that [delusion].
The tenth stage becomes the first, and the first becomes the eighth;
the ninth also becomes the seventh, and the seventh becomes the eighth. (Lankavatara Sutra 10.205)
The second would be the third, and the fourth would become the fifth;
the third would become the sixth—wherein there is no appearance, how could there be a sequence?
For yogins, there is indeed no non-existence of things that is devoid of appearance;
through the equality of existence and non-existence, the fruit arises for the noble ones.
For how can the non-existence of phenomena bring about their equality?
When the mind does not perceive the flickering external and internal [objects],
then, through the vision of the mind as equality, it brings about cessation.
In beginningless saṃsāra, the grasping at existence has embraced [beings] like a wedge driven by fools against another wedge; once it is enticed away, it is withdrawn.
Having that as its cause and that as its object, it serves as the support for the movement of the mind;
it provides the cause for the mind, and consciousness is dependent upon it.
Because of the manifestation of the destiny and realm [of rebirth] through the empowerment of the maturation [of karma],
one indeed attains the fourfold supernormal powers even within a dream.
Whatever is obtained in a dream and whatever arises through the grace of the Buddha— the various classes, destinies, and lineages— all these are born from the maturation of consciousness.
The mind, permeated by latent impressions, proceeds as the appearance of entities;
when the foolish do not understand this, one should then teach them the doctrine of arising.
As long as speech conceptualizes an entity endowed with characteristics, so long does the mind remain unawakened, for it does not perceive its own delusion.
Why is arising described, and why is the visible not described?
For when the invisible is being seen, what is described for whom, and from where?
The mind is pure by its very nature, while the intellect (manas) is that which causes defilement;
and the intellect, together with the consciousnesses, constantly casts down habitual tendencies (vāsanā).
The *ālaya* releases the body; the mind seeks a destination;
consciousness appears as objects; and having perceived this delusion, one becomes attached.
"My own mind is seen; external objects do not exist.
In this way, one should analyze delusion and likewise recollect suchness.
The object of those in meditative concentration, their activity, and the majesty of the Buddha—these three are inconceivable; the inconceivable is the domain of wisdom.
The future and the past, nirvāṇa, the person, and speech—
I teach these by way of conventional truth; but the ultimate truth is beyond syllables.
The followers of the Ekāyana and the non-Buddhist heretics rely on one-sided views;
deluded regarding mind-only, they imagine external existence.
Pratyekabuddha-enlightenment, Buddhahood, Arhatship, and the vision of the Buddhas—these are the hidden seeds for awakening; indeed, that which is accomplished in a dream [is realized] in awakening.
Tell me: where, for whom, how, from what cause, and for what purpose do you teach the doctrine of existence and non-existence, which is beyond the mind and supremely tranquil? Lank_10.223
For those who are deluded regarding mind-only, there is the teaching that illusion neither exists nor does not exist;
it is associated with arising and ceasing, yet devoid of both the characterized and the characteristics.
The conceptualization called "mind" (manas), together with the five consciousnesses, proceeds from the seed of the mind (citta) like a reflection in water or a mirage. Lank_10.225.
When mind, intellect, and consciousness no longer function,
then one attains the mind-made body and the stage of Buddhahood.

Conditions, elements, and aggregates, as well as the specific characteristics of phenomena, designations, the person, and the mind, are like a dream or a mass of hair seen by one with an eye disease. (Lankavatara 10.227)
Having seen the world as resembling an illusion or a dream, one should take refuge in reality;
for reality is free from defining characteristics and devoid of logical reasoning and causes.
One should always remember the dwelling of the noble ones, which is to be personally realized within;
one should establish the world, which is deluded regarding reasoning and causes, in the true reality.
Due to the cessation of all conceptual proliferation, delusion no longer proceeds;
as long as there is conceptualization through wisdom, for that long does delusion proceed.
The absence of intrinsic nature and existence, as well as emptiness and the permanence or impermanence [of things],
are the views of those who advocate for arising, but not of those who advocate for non-arising.
The world is conceptualized by others through various conditions—such as identity, difference, both, or from Īśvara, chance, time, or primordial matter (pradhāna). Lank_10.232.
Consciousness, the seed of saṃsāra, proceeds as long as there is an object of perception;
just as a painting exists when there is a wall, it ceases through thorough knowledge.
Just as the birth and death of people proceed like a magical illusion,
so too do bondage and liberation proceed for the ignorant due to delusion.
Internal and external phenomena are of two kinds: the dharmas and their conditions.
By contemplating this, the yogi becomes established in the signless.
The mind is not differentiated by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*), nor is the mind together with the latent impressions;
the mind has an undifferentiated characteristic, though it is enveloped by the latent impressions. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.236)
For one whose impure latent tendencies arise from the mental consciousness,
the mind— though like a white cloth— is not made radiant by those tendencies.
Just as space is said by me to be neither existence nor non-existence,
so too the storehouse-consciousness (ālaya) within the body is devoid of both existence and non-existence.
When the mind is turned away from mental consciousness and is free from turbidity,
I declare that mind to be a Buddha through its awakening to all phenomena.
Existence is always like an illusion, severed from the three continuities, devoid of both being and non-being, and free from the four alternatives.
Two would be the intrinsic nature (svabhāva), and seven stages (bhūmi) would arise from the mind;
the remaining stages and the Buddha-stage would be the perfected (niṣpanna).
The realm of form, the formless realm, the desire realm, and nirvana—
all these are said to be within this body, the domain of the mind.
As long as something is perceived, to that extent does delusion proceed;
through the awakening to one's own mind, delusion neither proceeds nor ceases.
In non-arising there is an absence of causes; in existence there is the inclusion within saṃsāra.
Seeing that [all things] are like illusions and the like, one should not conceptualize their characteristics.
I speak of the three vehicles, the single vehicle, and the vehicle-less; [I teach] the state of isolation for the noble ones and the dull-wittedness of the foolish.
My arising is twofold: that which consists of characteristics and that which consists of realization;
the fourfold method of reasoning is the teaching of established tenets.
Having seen the delusion through specific shapes and forms, one conceptualizes it;
yet, because it is devoid of name and shape, its true nature is the domain of the noble ones.
As long as something is conceptualized by discursive thought, so long does it possess the characteristic of the imagined;
through the absence of such conceptualization and imagination, there is the intrinsic nature that is the domain of the noble ones.
The reality that is eternal and constant is the lineage (gotra), the intrinsic nature of things;
it is suchness, free from the mind and devoid of conceptual constructions.
If no entity whatsoever were pure, nor would there be affliction for anyone;
yet since the mind is purified and affliction is also observed,
therefore reality must be an entity that is pure and the domain of the noble ones.
Beholding the world as produced by conditions and devoid of conceptual constructions, and as resembling an illusion or a dream, one is liberated. (Lankāvatāra Sūtra 10.251)
The various latencies of depravity are conjoined with the mind;
they appear as external objects to people, for such is not the true nature of the mind.
The true nature of the mind is pure, and the mind does not arise from delusion;
since delusion consists of depravity, the mind is therefore not perceived.
Reality would be mere delusion; reality is not found elsewhere—neither in conditioned phenomena nor apart from them—but rather in the perception of conditioned phenomena.
When one perceives the conditioned as free from both the characterized and the characteristic,
then for that perceiver of the world as one's own mind, it becomes utterly shaken off.
Having ascended to mind-only, one should not conceptualize external objects;
abiding in the focal point of suchness, one should transcend even mind-only.
Having transcended mind-only, one should transcend the non-manifest;
the yogi established in the non-manifest beholds the Mahāyāna.
The effortless state is peaceful and purified by vows;
it is the supreme, selfless gnosis that does not perceive anything in the absence of appearances.
One should perceive the range of the mind, one should perceive the range of knowledge, and one should perceive the range of wisdom; thus, one is not deluded regarding characteristics.
The truth of suffering and its origin are the domain of knowledge regarding the mind;
these two truths and the stage of a Buddha are where wisdom operates.
The attainment of the fruit is nirvāṇa, as well as the eightfold path;
through the awakening to all dharmas, the wisdom of a Buddha is purified.
The eye, form, light, space, and likewise the mind—
by means of these, the consciousness of humans arises, originating from the ālayavijñāna.
The object of apprehension, the act of apprehending, and the apprehender do not exist, for indeed, that which is name-only is without objective reality.
Those who believe that conceptual construction is without cause are certainly not wise.
For the name is indeed non-existent in the object, and the object likewise in the name;
one should not conceptualize a conceptualization that has arisen from neither cause nor non-cause.
The intrinsic nature of all phenomena does not exist, and likewise, speech itself does not exist; yet the fool, failing to see emptiness or the meaning of emptiness, runs about distractedly.
Having perceived the abiding in truth through conceptualization, there is the teaching of provisional designation;
since oneness is not established in five ways, this truth is abandoned. (Lankavatara 10.266)
One who has begun to transcend conceptual proliferation should transcend "is" and "is not";
through the vision of selflessness, there is no false perception and no desire for existence.
For eternalism and agency are merely set in motion by verbal discourse;
the supreme truth is indeed inexpressible, and it is the vision of the Dharma within cessation.
For it is by relying upon the *ālaya* that the *manas* indeed proceeds;
and by relying upon both the *citta* and the *manas*, the [six] consciousnesses proceed. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.269)
Having set aside all superimpositions, suchness is the true nature of the mind;
by contemplating this, the yogi attains the knowledge of "mind-only."
The mind does not conceive of characteristics or entities as being either eternal or non-eternal;
likewise, in yoga, the yogi does not conceive of arising or non-arising.
They do not conceptualize two objects, for consciousness arises from the ālayavijñāna;
they do not perceive a single object with a dual mind, since that [duality] arises from it.
There is neither speaker nor that which is spoken, yet it is not empty because of the perception of mind;
from the non-perception of one's own mind, the web of views arises.
There is no arrival of conditions; there are no sense faculties whatsoever.
There are no elements, nor aggregates, nor passion, nor anything conditioned.
The fire of karma is indeed neither prior, nor uncreated, nor conditioned;
it has neither limit nor power, neither liberation nor bondage.
There is no indeterminate entity, nor indeed do dharma and adharma exist;
there is neither time nor nirvāṇa, and even the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is not found.
There is neither Buddha, nor the truths, nor the fruit, nor the causes;
there is no perversion, no nirvāṇa, no dissolution, and no origination.
The twelve links do not exist, nor indeed do the finite and the infinite;
for the sake of abandoning all views, I teach "mind-only."
Afflictions, the paths of action, the body, the agents, and the fruits—
these are indeed like a mirage or a dream, comparable to a city of the Gandharvas.
Because of the establishment of mind-only, the characteristic of existence is turned away;
because of abiding in mind-only, the views of eternalism and nihilism are eliminated.
The aggregates do not exist in nirvāṇa, nor does the self, nor its characteristics;
by entering into mind-only, one turns away from the grasping for liberation. (Lankavatara 10.281)
The fault caused by the perception of external objects appears to men as something outside;
however, since the mind is produced from that which is invisible, the mind itself is not seen.
The latent impressions (vāsanā) of humans manifest as the body, objects of enjoyment, and the physical environment;
yet the mind is neither existence nor non-existence, for it does not shine forth as a latent impression.
Impurity is indeed perceived within the pure, yet impurity is not perceived within that which is truly pure;
for just as the sky is not seen when it is overcast by clouds, so too the mind is not seen.
Karma is accumulated by the mind and discerned by knowledge;
through wisdom, one attains the non-manifest and its power.
The mind is bound to sense objects, while cognition operates within conceptual reasoning;
however, cognition indeed proceeds toward the non-manifest and the ultimate distinction.

Mind, intellect, and consciousness—when free from conceptual construction and devoid of perception—they have attained the non-conceptual nature of phenomena; yet these are the disciples, not the sons of the Victorious One.
In each successive stage of patience, indeed, the auspicious Tathāgata-knowledge arises for the sake of excellence, free from all habitual mental activity.
The imagined nature exists, but the dependent nature is not found;
the imagined is grasped through delusion, yet the dependent is not imagined.
For the mind has arisen from what is unreal; nowhere is the mind itself perceived.
It is the latent impressions (vāsanā) of men that manifest as the body, objects of enjoyment, and the environment.
There is no form that consists of the primary elements; there is form that is non-elemental.
For the Gandharva-city, dreams, illusions, and mirages are indeed non-elemental.
For my noble wisdom is threefold, by which the mind is manifested;
since the mind arises as something invisible, therefore the mind is not seen.

The latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of human beings manifest as the body, objects of enjoyment, and the environment; by means of these, characteristics are conceptualized and one’s own nature is veiled. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.293)

Wisdom indeed, which is dissociated from the two vehicles and free from appearances, proceeds for the Śrāvakas through their attachment to the notion of arising; but by entering into Mind-only, the stainless wisdom of the Tathāgatas arises. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.294)
For if both the existent and the non-existent are produced by conditions,
then the views of identity and difference are necessarily resorted to by them.
Just as various courses of existence arise and yet, like an illusion, are not established,
so too the manifold signs, when conceptualized, are not established. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.296)
The bondage arising from the mind, consisting of the depravity of signs, is imagined by those who do not understand it; thus is the dependent nature conceptualized. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.297)
That very imagined entity is indeed the dependent nature;
for the dependent nature, appearing in various forms, is what is conceptualized as the imagined.
There is the conventional and the ultimate; there is no third cause.
The imagined is said to be the conventional; through its cessation, the sphere of the noble ones is attained.
Just as for yogins a single object appears as manifold,
yet there is no actual multiplicity therein, so too is the nature of the imagined.
Just as those with cataracts perceive a variegated vision of forms,
yet the cataract itself is neither form nor non-form, so too is the dependent nature (paratantra) understood by the wise.
Just as gold may be pure, or water free from turbidity, or the sky pure due to the absence of clouds—so too is that which is conceptualized [to be] pure. *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* 10.302.
My disciples are of three kinds: the emanated, those born of vows, and the disciples born of the Dharma who are free from passion and hatred.
The Bodhisattva is also threefold; there is no characteristic of the Buddhas [as separate entities].
Yet, within the mind of every sentient being, the image of the Buddha is clearly perceived.
The imagined nature does not exist, yet the dependent nature is found;
thus, the conceptual construction of superimposition and denial is not destroyed.
If the imagined nature were non-existent by virtue of the dependent nature,
then existence would exist without non-existence, and existence would be the arising of non-existence.
Relying upon the imagined (parikalpita), the dependent (paratantra) is apprehended;
from the connection between signs and names, the imagined arises. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.307)
When that which arises from another is utterly unestablished by means of the imagined nature,
then the pure ultimate intrinsic nature is realized.
The imagined is tenfold, the dependent is sixfold, and suchness is the personal realization; for those who possess this understanding, there is no distinction.
The five dharmas are reality, and likewise the three natures;
by contemplating these, the yogin does not transcend suchness.
The mind of human beings appears like the arrangement of stars and clouds, resembling the moon and the sun; it manifests as a visible object, arising from latent predispositions.
For these elements have no self-nature; they are neither the characterized object nor the characteristic.
If form is indeed composed of the primary elements, then all elements are themselves composed of elements. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.312)
The great elements are unproduced, and there is no derivative matter within the elements;
for the great elements are the cause, while earth, water, and so forth are the effect.
The form of designated substance, likewise that produced by the birth of illusion,
the form of a dream and a gandharva-city, and the fifth, the mirage.
The icchantika is of five kinds, and likewise there are five lineages;
there are five vehicles and the non-vehicle, and nirvāṇa is of six kinds.
There are twenty-four divisions of the aggregates, and form is of eight kinds;
there are twenty-four Buddhas, and the sons of the Victors are of two kinds.
There are one hundred and eight methods, as well as three types of śrāvakas;
indeed, there is but one field for the Buddhas, and likewise, there is but one Buddha.
Likewise, there are three liberations and four kinds of mental streams;
my selflessness is sixfold, and that which is to be known is also fourfold.
Detached from causal conditions and free from the defects of [wrong] views,
it is to be personally realized within, immovable— the unsurpassed Mahāyāna.
Arising and non-arising may be eightfold or ninefold;
there is the single successive sequence and the one and only established tenet.
The formless realm is eightfold, and the distinctions of meditative absorption are sixfold;
for the Pratyekabuddhas and the Sons of the Victorious One, the means of deliverance are sevenfold.
The three times do not exist at all, nor indeed do permanence and impermanence;
action, karma, and its fruit are just like the activities in a dream.
The Buddhas and the Śrāvakas, the sons of the Conqueror, do not admit the existence of extremes and so forth;
their minds are forever dissociated from the visible world and resemble illusory phenomena.
The embryo, the wheel [of Dharma], birth, renunciation, and the abode of Tuṣita are seen even in all fields, yet they are not born from a womb.
Transmigration, the movement of beings, teaching, and likewise liberation, as well as truth, the field, and awakening—these would all be impelled by conditions. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.325)
The world is a forest tree, an island, the practice of the path of selflessness;
it is meditation, the attainment of the vehicle and the abode, whose sphere of activity is inconceivable fruit.
The lineages of the moon and the stars, the lineages of kings, and the abode of the gods;
the lineages of the yakṣas and gandharvas—all these are born of karma and arise from craving.
Death, which consists of an inconceivable transformation and is joined with latent predispositions,
ceases through the absence of severed death; thus the net of afflictions is brought to an end.
Wealth, grain, gold, fields, and property are conceptualized;
likewise, cattle, sheep, slaves, as well as horses, elephants, and so forth.
One should not sleep on a perforated bed, nor should one smear the ground [with lime]. One should not cause vessels to be made of gold, silver, bell-metal, or copper. *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* 10.330.
A yogin should always dye white woolen cloths with indigo, madder, saffron, cow dung, mud, fruits, and leaves. *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* 10.331.
A yogin should possess for the purpose of a vessel one made of stone, clay, metal, conch-shell, or crystal, and it should be filled with Māgadhī wine. Lank_10.332
The surgical instrument should be four finger-breadths long and curved for cutting tissue;
however, a yogin devoted to yoga should not learn the arts and crafts.
A yogin who follows the path of yoga should not engage in buying and selling;
this task should be performed by monastery attendants—this, I declare, is the Dharma.
One whose senses are guarded, who thus understands the meaning of both the Sūtras and the Vinaya,
and who does not associate with householders— him I call a yogin.
In an empty house, a cemetery, at the foot of a tree, or in caves;
upon a bed of straw or in the open air, the yogi should make his dwelling.

Always clothed in three garments, whether in a cremation ground or wherever else one may be, one should provide for clothing; and whatever is offered as a gift should be accepted with a welcoming mind.
One should follow [the path] only as far as the length of a yoke, being devoted solely to the alms-food;
just as bees [take nectar] from flowers, so should one collect alms. Lank_10.338 //
Whatever occurs within a group, in association with a group, or among the bhikṣuṇīs—that is indeed associated with livelihood; it is not fit for yogins.
A yogin devoted to yoga should not teach for the sake of alms to kings, princes, ministers, or guild-leaders.
The food of families where there is death or birth, that which is given out of friendship,
and that which is mixed with the food of monks and nuns— none of these is fit for yogins.
In a monastery where smoke is always produced according to the rules for cooking, even that which is prepared specifically for [the monks] is not suitable for yogins. (Lank_10.342)

The yogi should contemplate the world as being free from arising and destruction, devoid of the positions of existence and non-existence, and characterized by both the object of definition and its defining marks. (Lankāvatāra Sūtra 10.343)
Endowed with the power of meditative concentration, the superknowledges, and the masteries,
the yogi will indeed before long become [perfected], provided he does not conceptualize arising.

A yogin should not conceptualize the world as arising from causes such as atoms, time, or primordial matter (pradhāna); rather, he should understand that the world is produced from causes and conditions. Lank_10.345.

The yogi should always perceive the world as fashioned by one's own imagination, variegated and arisen from latent predispositions—existence as being like an illusion or a dream. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.346)
One's vision should always be free from negation and superimposition;
one should not conceptualize the three realms of existence as appearing as body, objects of enjoyment, and environment.
Having finished the meal and firmly established the body in an upright posture,
one should pay homage again and again to the Buddhas and the Bodhisattvas.
Having condensed the reality [taught] through the Vinaya, the Sūtras, and reasoning, the knower of yoga should contemplate the five dharmas, one's own mind, and selflessness. (Laṅkāvatāra 10.349)
The stages purified by the reality of individual self-realization, as well as the stage of the Buddha—
when a yogi contemplates these, he is consecrated upon the Great Lotus.
Having wandered through all states of existence with a mind weary of worldly becoming,
one sets out upon the various yogas after having entered the auspicious path of Śiva.

The yogin perceives masses [of light] having the appearance of the moon and the sun, radiant with the glow of lotus petals, resembling the variegated colors of the sky and fire. *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* 10.352.
These various signs lead them onto the path of the heterodox teachers;
they cause them to fall into the state of a Śrāvaka or the domain of a Pratyekabuddha.
When one has shaken off all these and becomes free from appearances,
then the Buddhas, like suns with hands, assembled from all realms,
stroke his head, for they follow the nature of suchness.
There is an existence that is without formal characteristics and free from eternalism and nihilism;
those who have abandoned the positions of existence and non-existence will conceive of it as the Middle Way.
In the doctrine of causelessness, they imagine the view of causeless annihilation;
through their failure to understand external existence, they will destroy the Middle Way.
They will not abandon the grasping at existence, lest there be the view of nihilism;
they will teach the Middle Way through the avoidance of superimposition and denial.
Through the realization that there is mind-only, external entities are discarded;
the cessation of conceptual construction is itself the Middle Way. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.358)
One does not perceive mind-only because there is no object to be perceived;
this is the middle way, taught by me and by others.
Arising and non-arising, existence and non-existence, emptiness, and the lack of intrinsic nature in phenomena—one should not conceptualize these as a duality. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.360)
Through the activity of conceptual construction, the foolish do not conceive of existence as liberation;
for as long as there is no awakening to the activity of the mind, the grasping at duality is not abandoned.
Through the awakening to what is seen as one's own mind, the grasping at duality is abandoned;
for this abandonment is thorough knowledge, which does not destroy that which is conceptualized.
Through the thorough understanding that what is seen is but the mind, conceptual construction does not arise.
The non-arising of conceptual construction is suchness, which is devoid of mind.
If activity is observed that is entirely free from the faults of the non-Buddhists, it should be accepted by the wise; likewise, cessation [is to be understood] as being without destruction.
The realization of this has been taught by me and by the Buddhas as the state of Buddhahood;
for if it were conceptualized otherwise, it would result in the doctrines of the non-Buddhist heretics.
The unborn indeed give birth, and the unshakable fall;
like the moon reflected in water, they are seen simultaneously in millions of fields.
Becoming one and then many, they indeed rain down and blaze;
having become mind-made within the mind, they teach that "mind-only" is all.
Within minds, there is mind-only; yet being without mind, they arise from the mind.
Possessing various forms and configurations, they have reached their destination within mind-only.
Through the forms of the Lords of Sages, the Śrāvakas, those resembling Pratyekabuddhas,
and various other forms, they teach that there is mind-only.
For they display formless forms through formless states, and hellish forms to the denizens of hell;
these are shown to sentient beings as the cause of what is merely mind.
They attain the illusion-like samādhi, as well as a mind-made body,
the ten stages, and the masteries, once [the duality] has been overturned.

Fools are bound by their own conceptual constructions and errors, as well as by the fluctuations of mental proliferation, through their perceptions of what is seen, heard, thought, and known. Lank_10.372
The sign is indeed the dependent nature, while that which is named therein is the imagined;
the imagined sign proceeds from the dependent nature. (Lankavatara 10.373)
For when analyzed by the intellect, there is neither the dependent nor the imagined;
since the perfected nature does not exist as a real entity, how can it be conceptualized by the intellect?
The perfected nature exists as a reality free from both existence and non-existence;
how could there be two natures that are liberated from existence and non-existence? (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.375)
And within the imagined nature, two natures are established:
the imagined is seen as manifold, while the pure is the domain of the noble ones.

For that which has the appearance of variety, being imagined, is conceptualized within the dependent nature; for if it were conceptualized otherwise, one would resort to the doctrines of the non-Buddhists.
Conceptualization is said to arise from the cause of perception;
indeed, that very [reality] which is free from the two types of conceptual construction is the perfected nature.
The fields and the Buddhas are emanations; there is one vehicle as well as three.
There is no nirvana for me; all things are empty and devoid of arising.
The thirty-six divisions of Buddhas and the ten distinct divisions—these are the mental continuums of sentient beings; they are the fields, not the vessel.
Just as the vision of a painting appears as an imagined entity,
yet there is no actual variegation therein, so too is the world and the Buddha-dharma.
The Dharma-Buddha is the true Buddha; the others are indeed his emanations.
Sentient beings perceive their own seed-continuum through the visions of the Buddhas.
Due to the connection with the signs of delusion, conceptual construction proceeds;
yet suchness is not other than conceptual construction, nor is conceptualization other than the signs.
The essential body, the enjoyment body, the emanated body, and the fivefold emanated body—
within this assembly of thirty-six Buddhas, the Buddha is the essential one.
Just as rays appear in the sun through blue, red, salt, conch, milk, sugar, decoctions, fruits, flowers, and so forth, [so do they appear in the mind]. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.385)
The seven consciousnesses are neither different nor non-different from the mind, just as waves are related to the ocean. (Lankavatara 10.386)
Just as the diversity of waves is a transformation of the ocean, so too does the manifold storehouse-consciousness (ālayavijñāna), known as "consciousness," proceed. *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* 10.387.
Mind, intellect, and consciousness are conceptualized for the sake of defining characteristics;
yet these eight are non-distinct in their characteristics, being neither the characterized object nor the characteristic itself. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.388)
Just as there is no distinction between the ocean and its waves,
so too, in the mind, no transformation of the various consciousnesses can be found.
Karma is accumulated by the *citta* and gathered by the *manas*;
one discerns through the *vijñāna* and conceptualizes the visible world with the five [sensory consciousnesses]. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.390)
For consciousness appears to people in the form of blue, red, and other such varieties;
O Great Sage, tell me why there is this similarity between the mind and the waves.
Indeed, the modes of blue and red do not exist within the waves;
yet for the sake of defining characteristics, the ignorant describe such functions in the mind.
For him, no mental activity exists, as his own mind is devoid of anything graspable;
for when there is an object to be grasped, the grasper is established along with the waves of consciousness.
For human beings, consciousness manifests as the body, objects of enjoyment, and the environment;
therefore, its activity appears like waves, resembling them in every way. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.394)
Just as the ocean is perceived dancing through the nature of its waves, why is the activity of the *ālayavijñāna* not likewise grasped by the intellect? (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.395)

Because of the deficiency in the intellect of the ignorant, the ālaya is indeed illustrated by the analogy of the ocean, through the similarity of the movement of its waves. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.396)
Just as the sun rises equally upon people who are lowly and those who are superior,
so too do you, O Illuminator of the World, teach the reality to the ignorant.
Having established yourself in the dharmas, why do you not speak of reality?
If you indeed speak of reality, that reality is not found within the mind.
Just as waves arise from the ocean, or as reflections appear in a mirror or a dream,
so does the mind manifest simultaneously within its own sphere; yet,
due to the deficiency of external objects, it proceeds by way of successive activity.
One cognizes by means of consciousness and further reflects with the mind;
the visible world appears to the five [senses], but there is no sequential order in one who is concentrated.
Just as a master painter, or even a pupil of a painter, applies colors for the sake of a painting, so too is my teaching. *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* 10.401.
The painting does not exist in the colors, nor in the wall, nor in the vessel;
yet, for the sake of attracting sentient beings, the painting is conceptualized by means of colors.
Teaching does not deviate from reality, for reality is indeed devoid of syllables;
having established a formal arrangement within the Dharma, I teach reality to the yogins.
I teach the reality that is realized within oneself, free from the imagined and the imagining, to the sons of the Conquerors; for the foolish, the teaching is otherwise.
Just as a manifold illusion is seen yet does not exist,
so too the manifold teaching is seen, though it is non-deviant.
For that which is a teaching for one person is not a teaching for another;
just as a physician administers medicine according to each individual patient, so too do the Buddhas speak of "mind-only" for the sake of sentient beings. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.406)
Conceptual construction proceeds by means of the seeds of external habitual tendencies;
for that by which one grasps the continuum, and that which is grasped, is the imagined nature.
Taking hold of an external object and depending upon the mind, delusion arises in two ways; there is no third cause.
That from which delusion arises and that upon which it depends—
the six, the twelve, and the eighteen— I declare to be nothing but the mind.
Through the connection with one's own seeds as the object of grasping, the grasping at a self is abandoned;
through the entry into the conceptualization of mind, the grasping at phenomena is abandoned.
That which is the storehouse-consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is the consciousness that evolves;
for it becomes the internal sense-field (ādhyātmikam āyatanam), while that which appears as its object is the external one.
Just as the seizing of the hair of a star or the forms in a dream are conceptualized by the ignorant,
so too the conditioned and the unconditioned are eternally imagined, yet they do not exist.
Just as a city of Gandharvas, a magical illusion, or the water of a mirage appear despite being non-existent, so too should the dependent nature (paratantra) be understood.
I teach the metaphorical designation of self and sense-faculties within the three types of mind;
mind, intellect, and consciousness are devoid of their own specific characteristics.
Mind, intellect, and consciousness, as well as the two kinds of selflessness, and the five dharmas and the three natures—this indeed is the domain of the Buddhas. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.415)
By way of their characteristics, there are three [natures], yet they are one, having the latent impressions as their cause;
for just as a single pigment appears as a variegated picture on a wall.
Selflessness, non-duality, mind, mentation, and the fivefold consciousness— these five factors and the [three] intrinsic natures do not exist within my lineage.
Free from the characteristics of the mind, with consciousness not abandoned,
and devoid of the intrinsic nature of phenomena, one attains the Tathāgata-lineage. (Lank_10.418)
Neither by body, speech, nor mind is anything auspicious performed therein;
the pure Tathāgata-gotra is devoid of active conduct.
Pure through the superknowledges and masteries, adorned with the power of meditative concentration,
the mind-made body is the auspicious Tathāgata-gotra.
For that which is to be personally realized, stainless, and devoid of causal characteristics—
the eighth stage and the stage of Buddhahood— is the Tathāgata-gotra.
The Far-Reaching, the Excellent Intelligence, the Cloud of Dharma, and likewise the Tathāgata—this indeed is the lineage of the Buddhas; the others lead to the two vehicles.

The Buddhas, having attained mastery over the mind, teach the seven stages for the sake of the ignorant, according to the distinctions between the mental continuums of sentient beings and for the purpose of defining their characteristics.
The corruption of speech, body, and mind does not arise on the seventh stage;
for on the eighth, its basis is like a dream or a torrent.
On the eighth and fifth stages, the sons of the Victors indeed master the sciences of arts and crafts, and they exercise sovereignty within the abode of existence.
One should not conceptualize arising or non-arising, nor emptiness or non-emptiness;
intrinsic nature and the absence of intrinsic nature do not exist in mind-only.
One might discriminate, "This is real, this is real, and this is false";
such is the teaching for the Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas, not for the sons of the Victor.
For one who is mindful, truth and untruth do not exist at all; indeed, there is no characteristic of momentariness.
Neither that which exists as a designation nor that which exists as a substance is found in "mind-only."
Entities exist conventionally, but in the ultimate sense there are no entities.
That delusion regarding things which lack intrinsic nature is what constitutes conventional truth.
Since all phenomena do not exist, I employ designations;
these expressions and conventional usages are devoid of reality for the sake of the ignorant.
An entity arising from verbal expression exists as the objective domain of meaning;
yet, having seen that an entity arising from verbal expression does not exist, it is truly found to be non-existent.
Just as there can be no painting in the absence of a wall, nor a shadow where a post is missing, so too the pure *ālaya* does not manifest when the waves are absent. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.432)
The mind stands like an actor, and the intellect is like a jester; together with the five consciousnesses, it fashions the perceived world as if on a stage. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.433)
The outflow of the Dharma that is taught and that which is emanated as an outflow—these indeed are the original Buddhas; the rest are manifested forms. (Lankavatara 10.434)
The visible object does not exist; it is the mind that is deluded by the visible. To people, the ālayavijñāna appears as the body, the objects of enjoyment, and the dwelling place.
The Guides proclaim that mind, intellect, and consciousness, as well as intrinsic nature and the five dharmas, are the two kinds of selflessness and purity. Lank_10.436.
That which the Protectors teach is not the domain of logicians, nor indeed of the Śrāvakas; it is the range of the personal realization within oneself.
Long, short, and so forth, arise in mutual dependence;
that which establishes existence is non-existence, and that which establishes non-existence is existence. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.438)
Having analyzed a substance down to its subtle atoms, one should indeed not conceptualize form;
the establishment of "mind-only" is not realized through false views.
Do not conceptualize emptiness, nor again [conceptualize] that which is non-empty;
this is merely the conceptualization of "is" and "is not," for the object to be conceptualized does not exist.
Form is conceptualized by the ignorant as a collection of qualities, atoms, and substances;
yet it does not exist even in each individual atom, and therefore the object does not exist.
One's own mind, appearing as the configuration of the visible world, manifests externally to men; since no external object exists, therefore even the "referent" (artha) does not exist.

A variegated painting, a mass of hair, an illusion, a dream, and a city of Gandharvas, as well as a firebrand’s circle and a mirage—these appear to people though they do not exist. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.443)
The eternal and the non-eternal, as well as unity, both, and neither—
deluded by beginningless defects, the ignorant conceptualize these things.
There is no established distinction of vehicles at all; I teach but a single vehicle.
It is for the sake of leading the ignorant that I speak of the differentiation of vehicles.
Likewise, there are three kinds of liberation and the selflessness of phenomena;
they are devoid of those [liberations] known as the equality-wisdom and the liberation from afflictions.
Just as a piece of wood is carried away by the waves in the ocean,
so too is the deluded disciple carried away by the [perceived] characteristics.
There is no final goal for that [state], nor does one ever return from it;
having attained the body of meditative concentration, one does not awaken until the end of the eon.
Bound by the afflictions of latent tendencies yet dissociated from active outbursts,
they remain in the untainted realm, intoxicated by the pride of meditative concentration.
Just as a person intoxicated by liquor awakens when the liquor has worn off,
so shall they attain my body known as the Buddha-dharma.
Just as an elephant sunk in the mud does not run hither and thither,
so indeed do the śrāvakas remain, immersed in the intoxication of meditative concentration.
The empowerment of the lords of men is purified by their vows;
it consists of the consecration, meditative absorption, and so forth, spanning from the first to the tenth stage.
Space, the horn of a hare, and even the son of a barren woman—though non-existent, they are spoken of; in the same way, conceptual construction operates regarding entities.

Those who see the world as caused by latent impressions (vāsanā)— as neither non-existent, nor existent-and-non-existent, nor existent at any time— and who are skilled in the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya), are liberated.
"In every sutra, I have always taught that the imagined is the self-nature, the dependent is the other-nature, and the perfected is called suchness. (Lankavatara 10.455)
The foolish and dull-witted become attached to phonemes, the collection of words, and especially to names, just as great elephants sink into the mud.
The vehicle of the gods, the vehicle of Brahmā, likewise that of the disciples, and that of the Tathāgatas and the Pratyekabuddhas— these vehicles I proclaim.
There is indeed no finality of vehicles as long as the mind continues to evolve;
but when the mind has undergone revolution, there is neither vehicle nor traveler.
Mind, conceptualization, representation, the intellect, and consciousness,
as well as the storehouse-consciousness, the three realms of existence, and activity— these are synonyms for the mind.
Life-force, warmth, and consciousness, the storehouse-consciousness, the life-faculty, the mind,
and mental consciousness— these are the distinctions of conceptual construction.
The body is sustained by the mind, and the intellect indeed always conceives;
consciousness has the mind as its object and, together with the [five] cognitions, cuts through [objects].
For craving is said to be the mother, and ignorance likewise the father;
consciousness, through its awakening to objects, is taught to be the Buddha.
The latent tendencies (anuśaya) are indeed the Arhats; the aggregates (skandha) are the Saṃgha, consisting of the five aggregates.
Because of the cutting off of the interval without interruption, the action (karman) becomes "immediate" (ānantarya).
The two kinds of selflessness, the afflictions, and likewise the two obstructions; through the attainment of inconceivable transformation-death, one becomes a Tathāgata. (Lankāvatāra Sūtra 10.464)
Those who understand the distinctions between the established doctrine, the method of reasoning, and the teaching for each individual, do not fall under the sway of mere logic.
No entity exists in reality as it is conceptualized by the foolish;
yet why do the logicians not desire liberation through non-existence?
For one who perceives the conditioned as bound by arising and ceasing,
the two views flourish, and they do not understand the conditions.

Nirvana alone would be the single truth, devoid of mental construction; one should view the world, which is imagined, as resembling a plantain tree, a dream, or an illusion. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.468)
Passion does not exist, nor does hatred or delusion, nor even a person.
For it is from craving that the aggregates arise; they exist like a dream.
Between the night of my attainment [of enlightenment] and the night of my final nirvana,
nothing at all has been revealed by me.
Relying upon the abiding nature of phenomena within each individual, I have spoken;
there is not the slightest distinction between those Buddhas and myself.
The self exists as a substantial entity, while the aggregates are devoid of defining characteristics;
the aggregates exist by way of their own being, yet the self is not found within them.
One who discerns right practice is liberated from afflictions and human attachments; seeing the world as one's own mind, one is freed from all sufferings.
Those for whom the world proceeds by means of causes and conditions,
and who are occupied with the fourfold logical alternatives, are not experts in my system.
The world is not born from existence, nor from non-existence, nor ever from both existence and non-existence;
how then can it be conceptualized by the foolish through conditions and causes?
When one perceives the world as neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent,
then the mind turns back and one realizes selflessness.
All phenomena are unarisen because they arise from conditions;
for all conditions are effects, and existence is not born from an effect.
An effect is not produced as an effect; duality would follow in respect to the effect. Yet, through the consequence of duality, the absence of an effect is not perceived.
When one perceives that conditioned phenomena are devoid of both object and subject,
and that the sign is indeed mind-only— then I declare it to be mind-only.

The nature of the measures, established in its own being and devoid of entities produced by conditions— the supreme Brahman which is the ultimate state of non-existence— this is what I call "measure" (*mātrā*). (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.480)
For the self exists as a conceptual truth (prajñaptisatya), yet it does not exist substantially;
likewise, the "skandha-ness" of the aggregates exists through designation, but not substantially.
Indeed, there are four kinds of equality: equality of characteristics, equality of cause, equality of the vessel, and the fourth is the equality of selflessness for the practitioners of yoga.
The turning away from all views, free from the imagined and the imagining,
non-apprehension, and non-arising— this I call "mind-only."
Neither existence nor non-existence, free from both existence and non-existence,
suchness which is liberated from the mind— I call this "mind-only."
Suchness, emptiness, the limit, nirvāṇa, and the realm of phenomena—
the mind-made body and the mind— I declare to be "mind-only."
Bound by the latent impressions of conceptual construction, the manifold world arises from the mind; for what appears externally to people is merely the mundane mind itself.
No external object exists; it is the variegated mind that is perceived as an object.
Appearing as body, enjoyment, and abode, I declare that this is mind-only.
The knowledge of exhaustion belongs to the śrāvakas; that which arises from birth belongs to the Buddhas;
and for the Pratyekabuddhas and the sons of the Jinas, it proceeds from the absence of affliction.
Indeed, external form does not exist; it is one's own mind that appears as the external.
Due to a lack of understanding of their own minds, the foolish conceptualize the conditioned.

Those fools who do not understand that external objects are merely the variegated manifestations of their own minds attempt to refute them by means of arguments employing the fourfold logical alternatives.
There are indeed no causes, no limits, and no illustrative examples or members of a syllogism;
for if the wise understand that it is their own mind that has projected the appearance of objects. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.491)
One should not conceptualize that which is characterized by conceptualization through further conceptualizations;
for it is by relying upon the imagined that conceptualization proceeds.
Because they are related through mutual non-differentiation and have a single latent impression as their cause,
and because those two are adventitious, the mind of humans is not produced.
Conceptual construction consists of the mind and mental factors; they are established within the three realms of existence.
That which proceeds as the appearance of objects is indeed the imagined nature.
Indeed, the twelve sense-bases arise from the conjunction of appearances and seeds;
I shall describe their process as resulting from the union of the support and the object of perception.
Just as a reflection, a hair-net, or a visual aberration appears in a mirror,
so do the foolish perceive the mind as being shrouded by latent predispositions (*vāsanā*). (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.496)
For conceptualization proceeds with respect to an object imagined by one's own conceptualization;
there is no external object as it is conceptualized by the non-Buddhists.
Just as fools, not recognizing a rope, seize it as a snake, so too those who do not understand the objects of their own mind imagine external objects. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.498)
For instance, a rope, in its nature as a rope, is devoid of both oneness and otherness;
rather, this is a defect of one's own mind by which the rope is conceptualized.

For that which, when conceptualized by means of a certain state, is not perceived, should not be understood as being non-existent; this is the true nature (*dharmatā*) of phenomena. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.500)
Non-existence is preceded by existence; existence is preceded by non-existence.
Therefore, one should not proceed toward non-existence, nor should one conceptualize existence.
For that which is imagined and being imagined does not possess a self-nature;
seeing that which is without self-nature, how could conceptual construction arise?
Form does not exist as having the nature of form, nor do jars, cloths, and so forth;
since the object of perception is non-existent, conceptual construction arises because of that.
If this conceptualization is deluded within beginningless conditioned existence, tell me, O Sage: by what have the reality of things been led astray?
The substantiality of phenomena does not exist; there is only mind that is perceived.
Not seeing one's own mind, conceptual construction proceeds.
If that which is imagined does not exist at all in the way the fool imagines it,
then it exists otherwise, yet it is not apprehended by the intellect.
If that [nature] exists for the noble ones, it is not that which is conceptualized by the foolish;
otherwise, if it were false for the noble ones, the noble ones would be equal to the foolish.
For the noble ones there is indeed no delusion, because their minds have been purified;
the foolish, whose mental continuums are impure, conceptualize that which is imagined.
"Just as a mother might bring a fruit from the sky for her son, she would say:
'Do not cry, my son; take this wonderful fruit! (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.509)
In the same way, having enticed all sentient beings with various imagined fruits, I teach the method that is free from the positions of existence and non-existence.

That whose existence arises after having previously been non-existent, and which is not produced by conditions— though it has never been born before, it is born as something that has no inherent self-nature.
For that which has not attained self-nature and is unborn does not exist anywhere without conditions;
likewise, even for you, an entity that has arisen does not exist anywhere without conditions. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.512)
Seeing thus in brief, that which is neither non-existent nor existent, nor both existent and non-existent, arises through conditions; for the wise do not conceptualize it as a real entity.
Foolish followers of false doctrines engage in discourses on identity and difference;
they do not understand that the world is like an illusion or a dream, produced by conditions.
The unsurpassed Mahāyāna is the vehicle whose object is verbal designation;
for I have well-expounded its meaning, yet the foolish do not understand it.
Those [teachings] which have been set forth by the Śrāvakas and the Tīrthikas out of stinginess deviate from the true meaning, because they were taught through mere reasoning.
Characteristic, essence, configuration, and name—these four kinds [of objects] serve as the focal points upon which conceptual construction proceeds. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.517)
Those who, being of one form or many forms, have come under the mastery of the Brahma-body,
and whose states cannot be destroyed by the moon or the sun— they are not [ordinary] sons.
Endowed with noble vision, they have reached the state of things as they truly are;
they are skilled in the reversal of conceptualization and have attained the further shore of consciousness.
For this is the seal of my liberated sons in my teaching,
free from existence and non-existence, and devoid of coming and going.
If karma were to perish once the consciousness of form has ceased,
then neither the eternal nor the non-eternal would be attained, and saṃsāra would not exist.
At the time of cessation, form, having perished, departs from its location;
yet karma, free from the faults of existence and non-existence, remains in the ālayavijñāna.
Form and consciousness perish and fall away within the abode of existence;
yet karma, which is bound to form and consciousness, does not perish.
Then, the karma connected with those [factors] indeed perishes for human beings;
but when the connection to karma has perished, there is neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, if that which has been destroyed by them is born again in saṃsāra along with those [elements],
then form (rūpa) will also exist as connected to it, because of their non-difference.
Mind and form are neither non-different nor indeed different, due to conceptual construction;
there is no destruction of entities, because of the avoidance of the positions of existence and non-existence.

The imagined and the dependent [natures] are not distinct from one another in their characteristics, just as impermanence is in form, and just as things are indeed mutual producers of one another. (Lankavatara Sutra 10.527)
A conceptualized [object], which is neither distinct nor non-distinct, cannot be determined;
how can there be "is" or "is not," as in the case of impermanence in relation to form?
When the imagined is well-seen, the dependent does not arise;
when the dependent is seen, the imagined becomes suchness.
For those who destroy what is imagined, my guide is destroyed;
they commit both superimposition and denial within my teaching.
When such individuals as these exist at any time—those who corrupt the Dharma, all of whom are beyond conversation and destroyers of my guidance. (Lankavatara Sutra 10.531)
They are not to be spoken with by the wise, and one should avoid the business of mendicants;
for therein they destroy what has been constructed through the imputations and denials [of existence and non-existence].

For those who, by seeing neither existence nor non-existence, perceive things as resembling a mass of hair [seen by the visually impaired], an illusion, a dream, a gandharva city, or a mirage; (Lankavatara 10.533)
He who would practice for the sake of gathering them does not train in the teachings of the Buddhas;
for these people have fallen into the two extremes and are destroyers of others as well.
Those yogins who perceive an entity as something imagined and solitary,
being free from both existence and non-existence— for them indeed one should practice inclusion.
For just as in the world there are mines that produce gold, jewels, and pearls— which are diverse, not caused by karma, and provide a livelihood for the ignorant— so it is with these.
For thus, the lineages of sentient beings are indeed diverse and devoid of karma;
since the perceived object does not exist, there is no karma, nor is there any state of existence born of karma.
The substantiality of phenomena does not exist in the way that it is analyzed by the noble ones;
rather, phenomena do indeed exist in the way they are conceptualized by the foolish.
If entities do not exist in the way they are conceptualized by the foolish, then,
since the states of sentient beings are non-existent, there is no affliction for anyone.
Due to the defilement of the diversity of mental states, the embodied beings who have approached the sense-faculties proceed through saṃsāra, bound by ignorance and craving. Lank_10.540
But for those for whom existence does not exist in the way it is conceptualized by the foolish,
there is no functioning of the sense faculties, nor are they practitioners of yoga.
If entities that serve as the causes for the cycle of existence do not exist,
then by that [reasoning], liberation would belong to fools, devoid of action. (Lank_10.542)
How could there be a distinction between the foolish and the noble based on existence and non-existence?
For the noble ones who practice the three liberations, there is indeed no such thing as existence.
The aggregates, persons, and phenomena, as well as specific and general characteristics, conditions, and the sense faculties—these I teach to the Śrāvakas. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.544)
I teach to the sons of the Victorious One that mind-only is without cause, as well as the manifestations, the stages, and the pure suchness realized within oneself.
In future times, there will be those who defile my teaching,
wearing saffron robes while propounding doctrines concerning what exists and what does not exist.
Non-existent entities do not exist through conditions; such is indeed the domain of the noble ones.
An imagined entity does not exist at all, yet the dialecticians will continue to imagine it.
In a future time, there will arise those of the Kaṇabhuj class who are like fools;
through their evil view of the theory that the effect is non-existent [prior to its production], they shall destroy the people.
"The world is produced from atoms, and atoms themselves are without cause;
the nine substances are eternal"—thus will he teach through false views. (Lankavatara 10.549)
Substance is originated by substances, and likewise qualities by qualities;
it will indeed destroy the true existence of the beingness of entities.
If the world were to proceed having previously not existed, it would indeed have a beginning;
yet I declare that there is no prior limit to saṃsāra.
If the three realms of existence, as they are reckoned in their entirety, were to proceed from having previously not existed,
then there would undoubtedly be the production of horns on dogs, camels, and donkeys.
If the eye, form, and consciousness were to come into being without having previously existed,
then mats, crowns, cloth, and so forth would arise from a lump of clay.
Just as there is no mat without cloth, and likewise no cloth without *vīraṇa* grass,
why is it that a single thing does not arise from conditions when they are assembled together?
"That the soul is identical to the body, and that which comes into being having previously not existed—
all these are indeed the doctrines of others that have been set forth by me."
Having articulated the prima facie position, their views are refuted;
having refuted their views, I teach my own position.
For this purpose, I have uttered these discourses on the various philosophical systems (tīrthavāda),
so that my assembly of disciples, being deluded, might not resort to the positions of existence or non-existence.
The evil-minded Kapila also proclaims to his disciples that the world is produced from Pradhāna, as well as the transformation of the Guṇas. (Lankavatara Sutra 10.558)
Neither the real nor the unreal arises from conditions, nor do the conditions themselves exist;
because conditions are non-existent, that which is unreal does not proceed.
Free from the positions of existence and non-existence, devoid of causes and conditions,
lacking arising and destruction, my own position is free from any defining characteristic.
Seeing the world as like an illusion or a dream, devoid of causes and conditions and always without a cause, conceptual construction does not arise.
Seeing existence as always resembling a Gandharva-city, a mirage, or a mass of hair,
free from the positions of being and non-being, and devoid of causes and conditions—
seeing existence as causeless, the stream of consciousness is purified.
Seeing that no objective entity exists, one realizes that "mind-only" does not exist either;
how can there be a mind without an object? Thus, "mind-only" is not tenable.
Since the mind of human beings arises by taking an object as its basis, how could the mind be without cause? It is not tenable that it is "mind-only."
“Suchness and mind-only belong to the system of the noble reality;
those for whom these both exist and do not exist are not skilled in my system. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.565)
If the mind functions by way of the relationship between the grasped and the grasper, this is indeed a worldly mind; it is not tenable that it is "mind-only."
If that which appears as the body, objects of enjoyment, and the environment arises like a dream, then it would follow that there are two minds; yet the mind does not possess two characteristics.
For just as a sword does not cut its own blade, and just as a finger does not touch its own tip, so too the mind does not perceive itself in self-vision. *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* 10.568.
Neither the other-dependent, nor the imagined, nor even the real entity;
the five dharmas and the two minds do not exist at all in the state of non-appearance.
The producer and the produced are the two-fold characteristic of existence;
it is with reference to the producer that I declare the absence of intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, if conceptual construction were to arise regarding various forms and structures,
then there would be the appearance of objects even in space or a rabbit's horn.
The mind appears as an object; that object would be non-conceptualized.
Indeed, no conceptualized object is ever described as being other than the mind.
In beginningless saṃsāra, there is indeed no object anywhere;
for how can an un-nourished mind proceed as an appearance of an object? (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.573)
If nourishment could occur through non-existence, it would also occur in the case of a hare's horn;
yet, a conceptual construction does not arise when it is truly nourished by non-existence.
Just as it does not exist now, so too it did not exist previously; how can the mind function toward what is meaningless as if it were connected to meaning? (Laṅkāvatāra 10.575)
Suchness, emptiness, the limit, nirvāṇa, and the realm of phenomena—
the non-arising of all phenomena is the ultimate intrinsic nature.
Falling into the extremes of existence and non-existence through conceptualizations of causes and conditions,
the foolish do not truly understand that existence is indeed causeless and unarisen.
The mind appears, but no external object exists; this distinction has no beginning.
Even in the beginningless [past], no object exists—by what, then, is this distinction produced?
If growth were to occur through non-existence, then a poor man would become wealthy;
tell me, O Sage, how can the mind arise in the absence of objects?
All this is without cause; it is neither mind nor its objective sphere.
Indeed, the mind is not nourished, for the three realms of existence are devoid of activity.
In order to turn back the notion of arising, I teach the establishment of non-arising; I teach the doctrine of causelessness, which is not understood by the foolish.
All this is unarisen, yet it is not the case that phenomena do not exist.
Entities known as Gandharva-cities, dreams, and illusions exist without a cause;
why do you tell me that things are unarisen, devoid of intrinsic nature, and empty? (Lankavatara 10.582)
When a phenomenon is not perceived as being separate from its inherent aggregation,
then I declare it to be empty, unarisen, and without intrinsic nature.
Just as dreams, hair-nets, illusions, Gandharva cities,
and mirages appear without a [real] cause, so too do the various diversities of the world appear.
Likewise, inherence is a single entity, yet it does not exist because of the non-existence of anything visible;
however, it is not that inherence does not exist due to the views of the heterodox teachers.
One should establish non-arising by means of argumentation that is free from fallacious reasoning;
when established through [the principle of] non-arising, my guiding method does not perish.
When the doctrine of causelessness is taught, fear arises among the heterodox;
for how, by what means, from where, and in what place could there be an arising that is without a cause? (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.587)
When the wise perceive that there is no such thing as causelessness— that is, no state of being without a cause—
then the view that asserts the arising and destruction [of things] is overturned.

Is non-arising indeed non-existence, or does it have the characteristic of the arising of arising? Or is this merely a name for existence? Tell me, or tell me that it is meaningless. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.589)
For non-arising is not an existent thing, nor is it characterized by conditions;
