this is not the name of an existent thing, yet the name is not without meaning.
That which is the range neither of the Śrāvakas and Buddhas nor of the non-Buddhist outsiders,
and which belongs to those who have reached the seven stages, is characterized by non-arising.
The cessation of causes and conditions, the negation of a [substantial] cause,
and the establishment of mind-only— this I call non-arising.
I teach non-arising as the causeless functioning of phenomena, which is free from the imagined and the imagination, and liberated from the positions of existence and non-existence.
Free from what is seen by the mind and devoid of the two natures,
I declare that the revolution of the basis is non-arising.
The non-existence of external entities, the non-appropriation of the mind,
and the abandonment of all views— this is the characteristic of non-arising.
In this way, one should contemplate all phenomena as empty, devoid of intrinsic nature, and so forth;
they are never empty by means of an emptiness that is itself empty, but rather by means of the emptiness of non-arising.
For it is the assemblage of conditions that proceeds and ceases;
that which exists apart from the assemblage is neither born nor extinguished.
For no entity exists anywhere apart from the collection;
it does not exist as either identical to or different from it, as is conceptualized by the heterodox teachers.
An entity is born neither from the existent nor from the non-existent, nor from both the existent and the non-existent at any time;
for it is only this collection [of causes] that proceeds and ceases.
This is merely a conventional designation arising from a mutual interdependence;
there is no produced object whatsoever that exists apart from the assembly of conditions.
For non-arising is indeed the absence of what is produced; it is free from the faults of the heterodox teachers.
I teach it as mere conceptual construction, yet it is not discerned by the foolish.
He who maintains that there exists a produced entity anywhere apart from the causal chain should be known as a proponent of causelessness and a destroyer of the causal chain.
The causal chain would be the manifester of the substances and types of lamps,
if there were some entity that existed anywhere apart from the causal chain.
For that which is without intrinsic nature is unarisen, by its very nature like the sky;
it is a phenomenon distinct from the causal chain, yet imagined by the ignorant. (Lankavatara 10.604)
This other non-arising is the state of dharma attained by the Noble Ones;
that which is its non-arising would be the "receptivity to non-arising" (anutpādakṣānti). // Lank_10.605 //
When one perceives this entire world as nothing but a mental construction, and sees that all this is merely a construction, then the mind becomes concentrated in samādhi.
Ignorance, craving, karma, and so forth constitute the internal causal complex;
the potter’s wheel, clay, staff, and so forth, as well as seeds and the elements, constitute the external.
For one who holds that an entity arises from another through conditions at some point, this [world] is not merely a causal chain; such people do not abide by either logic or scripture.
If there is no produced entity, of what could cognition arise through a condition?
For these [factors] are mutually conditioned; therefore, they are known as "conditions."
Heat, fluidity, mobility, and solidity are conceptualized as phenomena by the ignorant;
this is merely a collection and no phenomenon exists therein, and for this very reason there is the absence of intrinsic nature.

Just as physicians perform different treatments according to the condition of the patient, there is no difference in the medical treatise itself; rather, it is the difference in the [patient's] humors that exists.
In the same way, having understood the strength of the faculties within the mental continua of beings that are severely defiled by the faults of the afflictions, I teach the method to the ignorant.
My teaching is not divided according to the differences in afflictions or faculties;
there is but a single vehicle, the auspicious Eightfold Path.
The non-existence of a rabbit's horn is caused by [the non-existence of] jars, cloths, crowns, and horns;
you must understand that whatever arises from a cause does not exist [independently]. Lank_10.614 //
That which establishes existence does not exist; "non-existence" is not tenable. For existence depends upon non-existence, as they are causes that depend upon one another.

Furthermore, according to the view of one who maintains that something is manifested by depending upon something else, that which depends on a causeless thing cannot itself be causeless. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.616)
If that [appearance] were to appear by depending on something else, and that too by depending on yet another, an infinite regress would result; and nothing at all would ever come into being.
Just as an illusion appears in dependence upon leaves, wood, and so forth,
so too does the manifold variety appear to human beings in dependence upon a real entity.
The net of illusion consists of neither leaves, nor wood, nor gravel;
it is only illusion that is seen by the foolish, along with its basis created by a magician. (Lankavatara 10.619)
Likewise, if something were to perish by depending upon a real entity,
then since both [the entity and its destruction] do not exist at the time of perception, how could anything be conceptualized?
That which is conceptualized by conceptual constructions does not exist, and conceptual construction itself is not found.
When conceptual construction is indeed non-existent, there is neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa.
When conceptual construction no longer exists, conceptual construction does not arise.
If there is non-arising, how can it be appropriate to say that "mind-only" is the mind?
Because the teaching is divided by many conflicting views, it possesses no essence;
due to the absence of essence, there is neither liberation nor the manifold variety of the world.
No external object of perception exists as it is imagined by the foolish;
the mind, driven astray by habitual tendencies, appears like a reflected image.
For all phenomena are indeed unarisen, being impossible as either existent or non-existent;
all this is mind-only, free from conceptual constructions.
Entities are described by the foolish through [the analysis of] conditions, but not by the wise;
the mind of the noble ones is auspicious, liberated from intrinsic nature and mental constructs.
The Sāṃkhyas, Vaiśeṣikas, the naked ones (Jainas), and likewise the Pāśupata Brahmins,
have fallen into the views of non-existence and existence, and are devoid of the meaning of solitude.
For they are without intrinsic nature, unarisen, empty, like illusions, and stainless;
for whom were these taught by the Buddhas, and by you have they been explained?
For yogins of pure mind who are free from views and speculative reasoning,
the Buddhas indeed teach yoga, which has been described by me as well.
If all this is merely mind, upon what is the world established?
By what means is the coming and going of men on the earth perceived?
Just as a bird in the sky, impelled by its own conceptualization, moves across the earth without a fixed point of support or a basis for grasping; so it is with the mind.
For thus all embodied beings, impelled by conceptual construction,
wander within their own minds like birds in the sky.
Tell me, how and by what means does the mind proceed, appearing as the body, objects of enjoyment, and the environment?
How is it that appearance is a mental activity? Explain to me the state of "mind-only."

The appearances of the body, objects of enjoyment, and the physical world, as well as their functioning, arise for those who are undisciplined through latent impressions and conceptual constructions; thus do appearance and functioning come into being. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.634)

The object is a conceptualized entity, and the mind arises from the object; through the thorough knowledge that the visible world is mind, conceptualization no longer proceeds. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.635)
When one perceives that which is imagined as being dissociated from name within name,
and as being devoid of intellect and the object of cognition, then one is liberated from the conditioned.
This is what constitutes awakening: the discernment of the name within the name, which is that which is to be awakened to.
Those who understand it otherwise are neither awakened ones nor teachers of awakening.
The five dharmas, the [three] natures, the eight consciousnesses,
and the two kinds of selflessness— these constitute the entirety of the Mahāyāna.
When the intellect perceives both the object of cognition and the world as distinct and empty,
then conceptual construction no longer arises.
The cessation of the conceptualizations of action and syllables occurs through the vision of the mind;
however, when one's own mind is not seen, conceptualization proceeds.
The four formless aggregates have no numerical designation;
since form is distinct in character from the primary elements, how can there be a multiplicity of forms?
Because of the abandonment of characteristics, there is neither the primary element nor the derivative;
yet, why is form not produced by the aggregates through other characteristics?
When one perceives that the aggregates and the bases of liberation are without characteristics,
then the mind turns back through the vision of the selflessness of phenomena.
Consciousness arises in eight ways through the distinction between objects and sense faculties;
by way of their characteristics there are three, but it ceases in the state of non-appearance.
For the self and what belongs to the self, as well as cognition itself, reside within the mind as the ālayavijñāna;
they proceed from the grasping of duality and cease through thorough understanding.
When one perceives that which is free from being either different or non-different and is without movement,
then one does not conceptualize duality— neither self nor what belongs to the self.
That which has not arisen does not nourish [anything], nor is it a cause for consciousness;
being devoid of cause and effect, that which has ceased does not proceed.
Tell me, by what means do you say that the world is mere conceptual construction and mind-only—
devoid of causal factors and free from both the characterized and the characteristics?
One's own mind appears as a manifold variety, conceptualized in the form of the perceived;
this occurs because one does not fully understand that which is seen by the mind, and because one grasps at objects as being other than the mind.
When one does not perceive with the intellect, the view of non-existence arises; for how could the view of existence not arise from the grasping of the mind? (Lankavatara 10.650)
Conceptual construction is neither existence nor non-existence; therefore, its existence is not produced.
Through the thorough understanding of that which is seen by the mind, conceptual construction does not arise.

When the four positions have been refuted—if phenomena were indeed caused—there would be the non-occurrence of conceptual construction and the revolution [of the basis] that is without support. *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* 10.652.
This is merely a distinction of different names; by whom has it not been established?
For them, there would be an implication based on the object, or it proceeds from a cause.
Through the conjunction of causes and conditions, and by the negation of a [permanent] cause,
the fault of permanence is avoided if conditions are impermanent.
For the foolish, there is neither arising nor passing away because of impermanence;
indeed, nothing that is perishing is ever seen to exist as a cause.
For if the unperceived does not exist, how could existence arise as impermanent?
One should tame sentient beings through the means of attraction and bring them under control through ethical discipline.
One should destroy false views through wisdom and increase [the mind] through the liberations;
all this which is falsely taught by the heterodox teachers is merely Lokāyata.
Through the view that cause and effect are real, one's own established doctrine does not exist;
I alone am the established doctrine, free from cause and effect.

Free from the Lokāyata views, I teach for the sake of my circle of disciples: "There is nothing but mind; there is no visible object. Mind appears in two ways, through the state of the grasped and the grasper, while remaining free from the extremes of eternalism and nihilism. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.659)
As long as the mind continues to function, so long will there be Lokāyata;
for one who perceives the world as one's own mind, there is the non-occurrence of conceptual construction.
Arising is the production of an effect; passing away is the perception of that effect.
Through the thorough knowledge of arising and passing away, conceptual construction does not proceed.
The eternal and the non-eternal, the conditioned and the unconditioned, the higher and the lower—
all such things as these constitute the Lokāyata.
Gods, asuras, humans, animals, hungry ghosts, and the abode of Yama—
these are declared to be the six destinies where embodied beings are born.
One is born among them through inferior, superior, or middling karma;
yet by guarding all wholesome qualities, there is either distinction or even liberation itself.
"Since you teach the monks at every moment regarding death and rebirth, tell me your underlying intention. (Lank_10.665)
Just as the mind, having arisen, breaks apart from one form to another form,
for that reason I teach my disciples the succession of momentary births.
In every form, there arises as well as ceases conceptual construction;
for a living being is indeed conceptual construction, and no other conceptual construction exists.
That which is not joined moment by moment is spoken of as "this-conditioned" (idampratyaya);
it is free from the grasping of form, neither born nor destroyed.
Conditions and those produced from conditions—such as ignorance, suchness, and so forth—proceed by way of a duality of phenomena; yet suchness itself is non-dual.
If phenomena produced from conditions are distinguished as being eternal and so forth, then the effect would be the cause and the cause would be the condition.
Because of the inclusion of cause and effect, your doctrine would be no different from that of the non-Buddhist heretics; therefore, O Great Sage, it is not superior to that of the Buddhas.
Within the body, which is but the measure of a fathom, I teach the world and the arising of the world, as well as the practice leading to its cessation, to the sons of the Conqueror.
By grasping at the three natures, ordinary worldlings perceive views of the grasped and the grasper, and thus they conceptualize mundane and supramundane phenomena.
Therefore, the mention of "intrinsic nature" (svabhāva) is made as a preliminary position;
however, for the purpose of warding off [wrong] views, one should not conceptualize intrinsic nature.
Due to the fault of defects, there is neither restraint nor does the mind proceed;
through the grasping at the two modes of activity, non-dual suchness becomes [dualized].
Ignorance, craving, and karma—consciousness and the other factors are not born from a womb;
existence does not arise without having produced the state of being unestablished and unconditioned.
The destruction of entities is described by the ignorant as being fourfold;
yet for conceptual construction, which functions in two ways, neither existence nor non-existence exists.
It is free from the four alternatives and devoid of the two views.
The conceptualization of dualistic activity does not proceed once [reality] has been seen;
for when all phenomena are unarisen, there is no emergence of the intellect.
Even when entities have arisen, one should not conceptualize them because they are like those [mental constructs];
O Lord, tell me the reasoning for this, so as to ward off the two-fold view.

Just as I and others always avoid the contradiction of "it exists" and "it does not exist," so too [the teachings] are unmixed with the doctrines of the non-Buddhists and are devoid of the views of the Śrāvakas.
And the practice of the realization of the Victors, through the non-perishing of the sons of the Victors.
Liberation has both causes and no cause, and its sole characteristic is non-arising;
these synonyms delude people, and thus they should always be avoided by the wise.

All phenomena indeed arise from one's own conceptual construction; they shine like clouds, mountain peaks, and rainbows, and are comparable to mirages and the optical illusion of floating hairs. Yet the heterodox teachers conceptually construct the world through their own [erroneous] causes.
Non-arising, suchness, the limit of reality, and emptiness—these are synonyms for form; one should not conceptualize them as non-existence.
Just as "hasta" and "kara" are synonyms in the world, and "Indra," "Śakra," and "Puraṃdara" are synonyms,
so too one should not conceptually construct the non-existence of all phenomena.
Emptiness is not other than form, and likewise for non-arising;
one should not conceptualize them as different, for otherwise the fault of [wrong] views would follow. (Lankavatara 10.685)
Both conceptualization (*saṃkalpa*) and discursive thought (*vikalpa*) are included within the characteristics of things;
length, shortness, and so forth, as well as sphericity, are included within the sphere of the imagined (*parikalpa*).
For intention (saṃkalpa) is indeed the mind (citta), and conceptualization (parikalpa) is likewise the intellect (manas);
discursive thought (vikalpa) is the mental consciousness (manovijñāna), which is devoid of both the characterized and the characteristics.

That which is conceptualized as "non-arising" by the heterodox teachers and that which is conceptualized by those who hold views regarding my own system— this fault of speculative view follows as being indistinguishable between them.
Those who know the purpose, non-arising, and the very meaning of non-arising through their knowledge of reasoning— they truly awaken to my teaching.
The purpose is the contraction of views, non-arising, and non-abiding;
because of the thorough knowledge of these two meanings, I speak of non-arising.
O Great Sage, tell me: do phenomena exist as unarisen, or do they not?
To claim that non-arising is causeless is the view of the heterodox teachers regarding the process of worldly existence.
The doctrine of causelessness, non-arising, and the views of heterodox sects regarding inequality— I declare that which is free from existence and non-existence to be Mind-only.
One should avoid both arising and non-arising when they are caused by [wrong] views;
for in the doctrine of causelessness, non-arising implies a reliance on causes within the context of arising.
There is no activity that is effortless; if there were such activity, it would be a confusion of views.
Tell me, therefore, how [activity] arises precisely from views such as skillful means and vows.
Since all phenomena are non-existent, how can a mandala arise?
Due to the dissociation from the grasped and the grasper, there is neither arising nor cessation;
for the mind indeed arises from that very view which perceives one state of being as another.
Tell me how this non-arising of phenomena comes to be; since sentient beings do not realize it, this is being revealed. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.696)
O Great Sage, explain the entire Bhāṣya that is free from internal contradictions,
liberated from the defects of other schools, and devoid of fallacious reasons.
O best of speakers, tell me of non-occurrence and cessation—
that which is free from existence and non-existence, and wherein cause and fruit are not destroyed.
Tell me the sequence of the stages and the characteristic of phenomena;
the world has fallen into the two extremes and is agitated by [wrong] views.
Non-arising is not understood as the cause of peace through [concepts such as] arising and so forth;
for there is no mandala whatsoever for me, nor do I teach any dharma-nature.
For when duality exists, there is indeed fault; duality has been purified by the Buddhas.
All phenomena are empty, momentary, devoid of intrinsic nature, and indeed unborn.
Those obscured by the doctrines of false views do not conceive of things as the Tathāgatas do;
tell me, therefore, of the arising and the cessation of conceptual construction.
Just as an object arises in a certain manner—
its face produced through the combination of abundant colors and assembled by conceptual elaborations (prapañca).
Upon seeing a form externally, conceptual construction indeed arises;
however, through the thorough knowledge of that very [form] and by seeing things as they truly are,
the mind no longer proceeds in a manner concordant with the lineage of the noble ones.
Having rejected the primary elements, the arising of existence is not found;
one should contemplate that the mind, which always has the form of the elements, is unarisen.
Do not conceptualize conceptualization, for the wise are free from conceptualization;
by conceptualizing conceptualization, one remains in duality and there is no nirvāṇa.
For one who maintains the thesis of non-arising, illusion is seen as the method;
that which arises from illusion without a cause is the characteristic of the refutation of established tenets.

The mind, conditioned by beginningless conceptualization, appears like a reflection; it has the form of an object, yet no object exists. One should contemplate this as it truly is. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.708)
Just as a form is seen in a mirror, devoid of being either identical to or different [from it], yet it does not exist [therein], so too is the characteristic of arising.

Just as the Gandharva-city, magical illusions, and the like are characterized by causes and conditions, so indeed is the arising of all phenomena; for there is no such thing as arising without a cause.
Conceptual construction, having the form of a person, proceeds in two modes:
through the metaphorical designations of self and phenomena; yet it is not discerned by the foolish.
For even a Śrāvaka who is an Arhat is dependent upon extensive conditions;
one should lead the fifth type of Śrāvaka to that which is dependent on its own power and dependent on the Jina.
Fools who lack expertise conceptualize four kinds of impermanence: that which perishes after an interval, that which is ultimately destroyed, and that which is mutually exclusive. Lank_10.713

Falling into the two extremes, fools—clinging to the views of existence and non-existence—do not know the means to liberation because they rely on causes such as qualities (guṇa), atoms (aṇu), and primordial nature (prakṛti). Lank_10.714
Just as the foolish and deluded grasp at the moon by means of the tip of a finger,
so too those attached to letters do not perceive my true reality.
The elements are distinct from one another and are the causes for the manifestation of material form;
this configuration of the elements is not a derivative material object produced by those elements.
Form is burned by fire; the water element has the nature of moistening;
form is scattered by wind—how do [these] elements function? (Lankavatara 10.717)
Form and the aggregate of consciousness—these two are not five;
I shall teach the differentiation of the synonyms for the aggregates in a hundred ways.
The mind and its mental factors proceed by functioning through differentiation;
their forms are distinct, and the mind is not material.
White depends upon blue, and blue indeed depends upon white;
having produced cause and effect, emptiness is both existent and non-existent.
The means of proof, the prover, and the object to be proven; cold and heat; the characterized and the characteristic—all such things as these have not been established by the logicians.
Mind, intellect, and the six other consciousnesses, conjoined with a self— devoid of both oneness and difference— this is the ālayavijñāna that proceeds.
The Sāṃkhyas, Vaiśeṣikas, the naked Jains, and the logicians who proclaim a Lord—
all fall into the positions of existence and non-existence, being devoid of the discernment of the true meaning.

There is no specific configuration or form of the primary elements, nor is there anything derived from them; yet the non-Buddhists speak of the birth of both the primary elements and their derivatives. (Lankavatara 10.724)
Since other non-Buddhist teachers imagine [causes] for that which is unarisen through various causal factors,
they do not awaken due to delusion, as they rely upon the positions of existence and non-existence.
Associated with the mind, yet dissociated from the intellect and the other [mental faculties],
the being whose characteristic is purity abides together with primordial wisdom.
Whatever karma there may be, and whatever form exists, have the aggregates and their objects as their causes;
yet beings, being without grasping, do not abide in the formless realm.
If one asserts the existence of a sentient being while maintaining selflessness, it follows that there can be no sentient being due to the absence of a self.
For the proponent of selflessness, there would be annihilationism, and even consciousness would be impossible.
Since he abides in these four [realities] and there is an absence of form, how could [consciousness] arise?
Due to the absence of both internal and external [objects], consciousness does not proceed.
Just as the logicians assert that the aggregates of the intermediate state exist, so too, for one born in the formless realm, why does no formless existence exist? Lank_10.730
Liberation would occur without effort, even in the absence of a sentient being and consciousness;
this is undoubtedly the doctrine of the non-Buddhists, yet the logicians do not realize it. (Lankavatara 10.731)
Form exists there, yet in the formless realm there is no seeing;
the absence of that [seeing] is not the established doctrine, nor the vehicle, nor the traveler.
Consciousness, which arises from latent impressions and is conjoined with the sense faculties,
does not grasp even a single portion of its eightfold nature at any given moment.
When form does not proceed, nor do the sense-faculties with the sense-faculties,
for this reason the Blessed One teaches that the sense-faculties and so forth are momentary.
Without determining form, how can consciousness arise? How can non-arisen cognition produce saṃsāra?
The Leaders do not teach that there is destruction immediately after arising;
for there is no continuity of entities within the movement of conceptual construction.
The sense faculties and their objects belong to the deluded, but not to the wise;
the foolish grasp them by name, whereas the noble ones are indeed experts in the ultimate meaning.
For the sixth [consciousness] is indeed without appropriation; it is not apprehended as having appropriation.
Free from the faults of [reifying] existence, the Noble Ones declare it to be indeterminable.
Frightened by the views of eternalism and nihilism, the logicians who lack true knowledge—
those fools— do not distinguish between the conditioned and the unconditioned self. (Lankāvatāra Sūtra 10.739)
Giving exists in identity, and it also exists in difference;
there is indeed identity with the mind, and difference with the mental factors and so forth.
When giving is determined to be the mind designated as mental factors (*caitta*),
how can it be established as a unity therein through appropriation?
And they will establish the perception accompanied by grasping through actions such as karma and birth,
using human examples both similar and dissimilar, like fire.
Just as fire simultaneously burns both the fuel and the burner,
why is it that the self, together with its appropriation, is not likewise perceived by the logicians?
Whether through arising or non-arising, the mind is indeed always luminous;
why do the logicians who seek to establish a self not provide an illustrative example [for this]? (Laṅkāvatāra 10.744)
Deluded in the thicket of consciousness and devoid of the correct method, the logicians run hither and thither, desiring to establish their own doctrines of the self.
The self, which is characterized by purity, is to be realized through one's own inner realization;
it is the embryo of the Tathāgata, beyond the reach of logicians.
If one knows the characteristic of the division between grasping and the grasper, as well as that of the aggregates, then knowledge according to this method arises.
The *ālaya* is considered by the non-Buddhists to be the locus of the embryo;
it is described as being conjoined with a self, yet the [true] dharmas are not proclaimed to be so.
Through the analytical discernment of these, there is liberation and the vision of the truths;
there shall be the purification of those afflictions that are to be abandoned by seeing the nature of phenomena.
The mind is luminous by nature; it is the auspicious Tathāgata-garbha.
Indeed, it is the appropriation of sentient beings, free from both finitude and infinity.
Just as people perceive the luster of gold, its natural form, and the ore-stone through refinement, so too do they perceive the *sattva* within the abodes of the aggregates (*skandha*).
Neither a person nor the aggregates, but the Buddha is untainted gnosis;
having fully realized perpetual peace, I go for refuge.

The best of speakers teaches that the mind, which is luminous by nature, is conjoined with the self along with the secondary afflictions such as the intellect and so forth. *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* 10.753.
The mind is luminous by nature, while the mental faculty (manas) and so forth are indeed its other [aspect].
Since karmas are accumulated by them, both of these are afflicted.
The self, which is luminous by nature, becomes defiled by adventitious and beginningless afflictions; yet, when endowed with [the path], it is purified like a garment. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.755)
Just as cloth or gold, being free from stains and devoid of defects, remains and does not perish, so too does the self exist without defects. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.756)
Just as one unskilled in music might seek the perfection of sweet melody in a lute, a conch, or a drum, so too does one seek a person (pudgala) within the aggregates (skandhas). Lank_10.757
Just as treasures, jewels, and even water exist within the earth yet are not seen, so too is the person (pudgala) within the aggregates (skandhas).

Just as the unskilled do not perceive the aggregates within the clusters of mind and mental factors, nor their own qualities conjoined with the aggregates, so too they do not perceive a person within the aggregates.
Just as an embryo exists within a pregnant woman but is not seen, so too the self exists within the aggregates; one who does not know the proper reasoning does not perceive it.

Just as those who do not know the proper method do not perceive the essence of medicinal herbs, or fire within its fuel, so too they do not perceive the person (pudgala) within the aggregates (skandhas).
Just as the wise do not perceive impermanence and emptiness in all phenomena,
despite their actual existence, so too they do not perceive a person within the aggregates.

The stages, the masteries, the superknowledges, and the supreme consecration, as well as the specific meditative absorptions—these truly do not exist if a self does not exist. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.763)
When a nihilist approaches and says, "If it exists, let it be shown," that wise person should be told: "Demonstrate your own conceptual construction. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.764)
Those who propound selflessness are not to be spoken with; avoid their monastic activities.
Their views on the positions of existence and non-existence are obstacles to the qualities of a Buddha.
Completely free from the defects of [false] doctrines, this doctrine of self-blazing like the fire at the end of an eon— burning away the forest of selflessness— is now ignited.
In pieces of sugarcane, sugar, honey, and so forth, as well as in curd, sesame, and ghee, the intrinsic essence exists; it is not perceived simply because it has not been tasted.
The self, when grasped in five ways within the accumulation of the aggregates, is not seen by the ignorant; the wise, having seen it, are liberated.
The mind cannot be apprehended through examples such as knowledge and the like,
because a collection [of parts] is not apprehended therein, nor from whence, nor for what purpose.
For phenomena are indeed distinct in character, yet the single mind is not perceived;
thus, for the logicians, the consequence follows that there would be neither cause nor activity.
Furthermore, the yogi who contemplates the mind does not perceive the mind within the mind;
since the seer is produced from the seen, how could the seen have arisen from a cause? (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.771)
I am of the lineage of Kātyāyana, having emerged from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven;
I teach the Dharma to sentient beings that leads to the city of Nirvāṇa.
This is the ancient path; I and those Tathāgatas have taught the Nirvāṇa through three thousand sūtras.
The Buddha does not attain awakening in the desire realm nor in the formless realm;
he awakens in the Akaniṣṭha heaven of the form realm among those who are free from passion.
Objects are not the cause of bondage; rather, the attachment to objects is the cause.
The afflictions are to be destroyed by knowledge, for this is indeed the "sword-edge" vow.
If the self does not exist, how can phenomena such as illusion be said to "exist" or "not exist"?
Why is it that for the foolish, suchness—which is devoid of self—is not perceived? 10.776
Because it is neither produced nor unproduced, there is no causal agent that sets things in motion;
all this is unarisen, yet it is not perceived as such by the foolish.
Causes are unarisen, and conditions are produced;
since both of these are not producers, how can they be conceptualized as causes?
Logicians describe causes as being prior, posterior, or simultaneous;
they explain the birth of entities by means of examples such as light, a jar, or a disciple. *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* 10.779.
Buddhas are not endowed with marks produced through volitional effort;
for these are the qualities of a wheel-turning monarch, not those proclaimed by the Buddhas.
The characteristic of the Buddhas is gnosis, free from the defects of [wrong] views;
it is the domain of personal realization and the destroyer of all faults.
For those who are deaf, blind, one-eyed, or mute; for the elderly; for those whose conduct is hostile;
and especially for children, celibacy does not exist.
Some world-teachers renounce the world because they are manifested with the divine secondary marks and the primary marks of a universal monarch, while others do not.
Vyāsa, Kaṇāda, Ṛṣabha, Kapila, and the Leader of the Śākyas—such as these shall appear after I have entered parinirvāṇa. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.784)
One hundred years after I have passed into nirvāṇa, Vyāsa will indeed appear, as will the Bhārata, the Pāṇḍavas, the Kauravas, and Rāma; thereafter, the Maurya shall come to be.
The Mauryas, the Nandas, and the Guptas, followed by the Mlecchas, the lowest of kings;
at the end of the Mleccha period there will be an upheaval of weapons, and at the end of the age of weapons comes the Kali Yuga.
At the end of the Kali Yuga, the true Dharma will indeed no longer be cultivated by the people.
Thus, with these and other such [teachings], the world revolves like a wheel;
through the conjunction of fire and the sun, the realm of desire is shattered. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.787)
Furthermore, that divine [age] will be established,
and in that world the four castes, the lords of men, the sages, and the Dharma itself will proceed.
The Vedas, sacrifices, and gifts—these abodes of Dharma will flourish once more;
yet through tales, histories, and the like, as well as prose, commentaries, and expositions beginning with "Thus have I heard," the world will indeed fall into delusion. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.789)
Having made it dyed with deep red, one should describe the upper part [as follows]:
one should indeed paint the cloth with blue clay and cow dung;
its limbs variegated with all kinds of colors, yet devoid of the marks of non-Buddhist sectarians.
The yogin should teach the doctrine; this indeed is the banner of the Buddhas.
He should drink water filtered through a cloth and wear a waist-thread.
He should seek alms at the proper time when they are available, avoiding those of low status.
One is born divinely from heaven, and two others are born of human origin;
endowed with the characteristics of jewels, he is a lord of the world born among the gods.
Those who govern by the Dharma enjoy the heavens and the four continents;
yet, after enjoying the continents for a very long time, they perish through craving.
The Kṛta age, the Tretā, the Dvāpara, and likewise the Kali;
I myself appear in the Kṛta age, and the Lion of the Śākyas in the Kali age.
Siddhārtha, the son of the Śākyas, Viṣṇu, Vyāsa, Maheśvara, and others such as these will be the teachers of non-Buddhist sects after my parinirvāṇa. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.795)
"Thus have I heard" and so forth are the teaching of the Lion of the Śākyas;
this shall be the historical narrative of past events belonging to Vyāsa.
Viṣṇu and Maheśvara as well shall teach the nature of emanation;
thus, after I have passed into nirvāṇa, this and other such things will come to pass.
My mother is Vasumatī and my father is the Brahmin Prajāpati;
I belong to the Kātyāyana gotra and am known by the name Viraja Jina.
I was born in Campā, as were my father and grandfather;
he was named Somagupta, born of the Lunar dynasty.
Having fulfilled his vows and gone forth, he taught the system of ten thousand verses;
having prophesied for Mahāmati and consecrated him, I shall enter final nirvāṇa.

Mati will bestow the Dharma upon Mekhala, and Mekhala will bestow it upon his disciple; however, due to weakness, that disciple will cause its destruction at the end of the kalpa. (Lankāvatāra Sūtra 10.801)
Kāśyapa, Krakucchanda, and Kanaka the Guide,
as well as I, the Stainless One— all these others are indeed Victors who have accomplished their task.
Thereafter, in the Kṛta Yuga, there will be a great hero named Mati, a leader who brings about the realization of the five objects of knowledge.
The appearance of the Lords of the World does not occur in the Dvāpara age, nor in the Tretā, nor later in the Kali age; they attain perfect awakening in the Kṛta age.
One should decorate the upper garment with uncut fringes and with moon-like patterns resembling the eye of a peacock feather, which are both irremovable and characterized by their distinct marks.
The space between two moons should be two or three finger-breadths;
otherwise, being painted in a different way, it would surely be a source of temptation for the foolish.
One should constantly extinguish the fire of passion by bathing in the water of knowledge;
at the three junctions of the day, the yogi should diligently take refuge in the Triple Gem.
Arrows, stones, wood, and so forth, when impelled by acts such as throwing, fall one by one; likewise, both the wholesome and the unwholesome [actions] fall one by one.
The one is not manifold, nor is there any distinction anywhere;
all [beings] are like the wind, being perceivers, while the field is the giver.
If the one were indeed manifold, then all things would be uncreated;
that which is created is subject to destruction—this is the doctrine of the logicians.
How could this be like a lamp or a seed through similarity in manifold ways? For the principle of the logicians is that "the one indeed becomes many. (Laṅkāvatāra 10.811)
A mung bean is not born from sesame, nor is rice caused by barley;
how could the various kinds of grain, such as wheat, be one and yet manifold? (Lankavatara Sutra 10.812)
Bṛhaspati will become Akṣapāda, the leader of the school of words [grammar], and Brahmā Garbha will become the founder of the Lokāyata system. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.813)
Kātyāyana the author of the Sūtras, as well as Yājñavalkya, Bhuḍhuka, Jyotiṣa, and others, will appear in the Kali age. (Laṅkāvatāra 10.814)
King Bali shall arise from the world of those who have performed meritorious deeds through the fortune of his subjects;
King Bali, the lord of the earth, will be the protector of all dharmas.
Vālmīki, Masurākṣa, Kauṭilya, Āśvalāyana,
and highly fortunate sages will exist in the future.
Siddhārtha, the son of the Śākyas, Bhūtānta, Pañcacūḍaka,
Vāgbalin, and Medhāvī will appear in a future time.
When one is established in the forest ground, Brahmā and Maheśvara bestow upon them the deerskin, the wooden staff, the girdle, and the water-pot.
There will be a great yogin, the sage named Viraja;
he is the teacher who reveals liberation, the very banner of the sages.
Brahmā, together with hundreds of Brahmās and many other gods, cast down his antelope skin from the sky before me; then, having attained self-mastery, he vanished right there.
Indra, Virūḍhaka, and the other gods together present me with all manner of variegated garments, an alms-bowl, and forest lands in the woodland realm.
One who desires the cause for the doctrine of non-arising may claim that what is unborn is born again;
yet, while he attempts to establish non-arising, it is proclaimed as being merely words.
Ignorance is the cause that sets those thoughts in motion;
what state does it occupy in the interim until one perceives form?
Immediately upon its destruction, another mind arises;
form does not remain for even a moment—upon what, then, will it arise?
Since the mind, having false causes,
operates toward that which is not established, how can its momentary destruction be determined?
For the meditative attainments of yogins, the relics of the Victorious One in gold,
and the celestial palaces of the Ābhāsvara gods are indestructible because they are not produced by worldly causes.

How indeed can the stability of the Buddhas, their attained qualities, their perfections of wisdom, their state of monkhood, and their attainment of the [esoteric] vows be seen as momentary? (Laṅkāvatāra 10.827)
How can forms such as a city of Gandharvas or an illusion be momentary? Since the elements are non-existent, how could beings arise from them, and where could those beings go?
The mind, which has ignorance as its cause and is accumulated through beginningless thought,
is conceptualized by logicians as being bound to arising and ceasing.
The Sāṃkhya doctrine is twofold: that which is transformative from the *pradhāna*, and that the effect exists within the *pradhāna*, established by its own nature. (Laṅkāvatāra 10.830)
The differentiation of the qualities (guṇa) together with their state of being is proclaimed as the primary matter (pradhāna);
in its transformation (pariṇāma), there is no diversity of cause and effect.
Just as pure mercury is not defiled by impurities, so too is the *ālaya* pure, the support for all embodied beings. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.832)
The scent of asafoetida, the onion, the appearance of a fetus in a pregnant woman,
and the salinity produced by salt and other substances— why do these not exist as seeds? (Lankavatara Sutra 10.833)
In otherness and in non-otherness, in both and likewise in neither;
existence is without appropriation, nor is it non-existence, nor is it conditioned.
For the self exists like a horse, devoid of the nature of a cow, characterized by the aggregates;
it is to be described as conditioned or unconditioned, yet its intrinsic nature is inexpressible.

Corrupted by false views and the perspective of logic through both reasoning and scripture, they declare that the self is indeterminable—neither in the appropriation nor elsewhere. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.836)
For it is by determining their defects that the self is analyzed through the aggregates;
yet the logicians do not perceive it as being either identical to them or different from them.
Just as a reflection is seen in a mirror, in water, or in the eye,
so too is the person (pudgala) within the aggregates (skandhas), devoid of both identity and difference.
That which is to be cultivated, the cultivation itself, the meditator, the path, and the vision of the truths—
by cultivating these three, one is indeed liberated from false views.
Just as lightning seen and lost, or like a wheel in a room with holes, one should not, like the foolish, conceptualize the transformation of all phenomena. (Laṅkāvatāra 10.840)
Nirvana as existence or non-existence is a delusion of the minds of the foolish;
for those with the vision of the noble ones, it is seen according to the actual state of things through the realization of true reality.

One should contemplate transformation as being devoid of arising and ceasing, free from existence and non-existence, and liberated from both the characterized and the characteristics. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.842)
One should contemplate transformation as being free from the doctrines of the non-Buddhists, devoid of names and forms, and as the abode of internal views. Lank_10.843.
The realms of the gods and those of hell arise indeed from contact and affliction;
there is no intermediate state, for it is set in motion by consciousness.

One should contemplate how the diverse bodies of sentient beings— born from wombs, eggs, moisture, and so forth, as well as those arising from the intermediate state— come into being through their various movements and transitions.
A wise person should not engage in the prattle of non-Buddhist views, which are devoid of logic and scripture and lead to the destruction of the side of those free from afflictions.
First, the self is determined; one should distinguish it from the appropriated aggregates. To distinguish it without having determined it is like distinguishing the son of a barren woman.
With my divine eye, I behold sentient beings who are devoid of both fleshly and intellectual vision,
liberated from the aggregates of saṃsāra, and existing as the embodied form of all living beings.

One clearly perceives that which pertains to the ugly and the beautiful, distinguished by being liberated or unliberated; it is divine, free from conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), yet abiding within conditioned formations. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.849)
Indeed, at the junction of states of existence, I am possessed of form yet beyond the reach of logicians;
I have transcended the human state, whereas others are but fallacious dialecticians.
There is no self; it is the mind that arises. Why does this proceed?
Why is its emergence not explained as being like a river, a lamp, or a seed? (Laṅkāvatāra 10.851)
And when consciousness has not arisen, ignorance and the rest do not exist;
in their absence, how could consciousness arise through a continuous succession?
The three times, the non-time, and the fifth, the inexpressible—
this is indeed the object of knowledge of the Buddhas, as proclaimed by the logicians.
Cognition, which is caused by the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), is inexpressible in relation to those formative forces;
it perceives what is contained within the formative forces, that which is designated by the term "formative forces. (Laṅkāvatāra 10.854)
"When this exists, that comes to be," yet conditions are also without cause;
they are taught by way of a manifestor, but because of the absence of such a thing, there is no agent.
For wind is indeed the fuel for fire in its act of fanning, but not in its actual production;
since it is by being fanned that the fire is extinguished, how can those [elements] be established as the producers of existence?
The conditioned and the unconditioned are to be described as devoid of grasping;
how indeed can fire be conceptualized by the foolish as something to be accomplished?
Fire indeed arises for humans through the mutual reinforcement of one another;
by what, then, is the *sattva* set in motion, since it is conceived as being like fire?
The selflessness of the collection of aggregates and sense-bases, which indeed has the mind and so forth as its cause, always proceeds together with the mind like a caravan.
These two are eternally luminous and devoid of cause and effect; fire is not the producer of them, yet logicians do not understand this.
Mind, sentient beings, and nirvāṇa are indeed luminous by nature;
though afflicted by beginningless defects, they are undifferentiated and like the sky.
Like the posture of an elephant and so forth, the shadows [of existence] are defiled by the views of the heterodox;
they are concealed by the mental consciousness and purified by fire and other [elements].
Having seen them as they truly are, you have seen through and torn asunder the afflictions;
having abandoned the thicket of metaphors, you have entered the sphere of the noble ones.
Since otherness is conceptualized through the distinction between knowledge and the object of knowledge, those of dull intellect do not understand; thus, it is said to be inexpressible.

Just as a drum made of sandalwood is not treated otherwise by fools, so too is knowledge— resembling sandalwood and agalloch— not treated correctly by those who employ fallacious reasoning. (Lankavatara Sutra 10.865)

Having risen, one who is devoted [to purity] should consume food that is merely contained within the vessel, keeping it free from defects such as facial distortions and the like. (Lankavatara Sutra 10.866)
Whoever, possessing serene faith, is devoted to yoga and free from conceptual construction, infers this method through reasoning;
being non-reliant and intent on the ultimate goal, such a person shall illuminate the golden course of the Dharma.
The conceptualization of delusion regarding the conditions of existence and non-existence is indeed the defiled net of false views;
for him, passion, hatred, and aversion cease, and he, being stainless, is sprinkled by the hands of the Buddhas.

The non-Buddhists are deluded regarding causes; others are overwhelmed by conditions; still others, because of the existence of things without cause, have resorted to the noble doctrine of annihilationism.
The transformation of maturation belongs to both consciousness and the mind;
for the mind is born from the storehouse-consciousness, and consciousness arises from the mind.
All minds proceed from the *ālaya* like waves;
they all have latent impressions (*vāsanā*) as their cause, arising according to conditions.
Bound by a chain of momentary distinctions, they grasp at objects as their own mind;
appearing with the forms and characteristics of shapes, they arise from the mind, the eye, and so forth.
Bound by beginningless defects and arisen from the latent impressions of the non-existence of objects, the mind appears as if external; this is taught to ward off the views of the non-Buddhists.
Another [consciousness] arises having that very thing as its cause and taking it as its object;
when such a view is produced, saṃsāra proceeds. (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 10.874)
All phenomena resemble illusions and dreams, comparable to a city of Gandharvas;
like a mirage or the moon reflected in water, one should discern them as one's own conceptual construction.
However, due to the difference in modes of activity, suchness is right knowledge and its support;
it is also the supreme samādhis, such as Māyā and Śūraṅgama. *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* 10.876.
Upon entering the stages, one attains the superknowledges and the masteries,
as well as the body that is like an illusion and the consecration of the Sugata.
When the mind turns back as one perceives the world as ceased,
one attains the stage of Joy and reaches the stage of a Buddha.
When its basis has ceased, like a jewel of manifold forms,
it performs the activities of sentient beings, just as a reflection appears in water. (Lankavatara 10.879)
Free from the positions of existence and non-existence, neither both nor neither—
having emerged from the individual and the Śrāvaka paths, this would be the seventh [stage].
One should point out the Mahāyāna as that which is purified by the stages of reality (bhūmi) through the dharma realized within oneself, and which is free from external non-Buddhist systems.

The revolution of conceptual construction, which is devoid of falling away or destruction, and which resembles a rabbit’s hair or a jewel— this is the principle that should be taught to those who are liberated.
For just as a textual passage is joined with another passage, so too is reasoning joined with reasoning;
therefore, one should accept reasoning as such, but one should not otherwise imagine it to be reasoning.
The eye, karma, craving, and likewise improper mental attention regarding ignorance;
as well as the mind directed toward the eye and visible forms, and the turbid mind—these are the causes.
Thus ends the noble Mahāyāna sūtra entitled the *Laṅkāvatāra*, together with its verses.
Of those phenomena that arise from causes, the Tathāgata has explained their cause, as well as their cessation; such is the teaching of the Great Śramaṇa.
